AMERICA IN THE MAKING 

This book aims to tell the story of the American people and of the nation which they founded and built in the New World wilderness. 

The making of America is here presented as the magnificent adventure of the rank and file of the American people, inspired by leaders who expressed in their character and in their deeds the basic ideals of America. 

The meaning of America is interpreted in its relation to the progress of the human race. The history of 

America is told in its setting as a part of world history. 

This history of America considers such everyday phases of life as food, clothes, shelter, communication, and transportation, as well as governments, wars, politics, art, science, and religion. 

The story of America's making is not a tale that is told and ended. It is a story which is being lived by men and women to-day. It is a story which growing boys and girls will carry forward in the making of 

America's to-morrow.

It is the hope of the authors that this account of the history and meaning of America will help rising generations to face the tasks and problems of their country with a deep sense of their responsibility as citizens, and with devotion to all that is best in American life and ideals. 

---

STUDYING THIS BOOK 

This book tells a story which you will be called upon to carry forward. It is therefore not enough that you read it for the sheer interest of the plot. It is necessary that you master the facts of American history and realize their meaning in relation to the tasks of citizenship which await you.

Plan of Book. A study of the Table of Contents will serve to make clear the plan of this history and its general outline. 

Style of the Book. The story of America is here told as a dramatic narrative in which each chapter helps to carry the action forward. We have used the dramatic style because we should like to have you feel the continuity of history which flows like life itself along the stream of time. 

Study Helps. At the end of chapters you will find suggestions for study helps. These include questions, problems, and projects which are planned to aid you in your mastery of the story and of its meaning. The study helps provide definite assignments for individual study at home or at the library; for supervised study in school; for socialized recitations in class; for individual or committee reports; and for volunteer exercises in writing, drawing, and other forms of self-expression.

Questions on the Text. The questions on the text of each chapter are designed to help you check your grasp of the facts of history. Without a mastery of the facts there can be no correct historical thinking. 

Charts and Outlines. The study helps include suggestions for charts, chapter outlines, and topical outlines.

These

ví 

STUDYING THIS BOOK 

study helps may be kept in a history notebook, along with other illustrative material. 

Relating History to Geography. Since the earth is the stage on which history is enacted, the study helps include suggestions for globe and map work. By relating the events of history to their geographical setting you can gain a livelier knowledge of geography along with a clearer view of history.

Relating History to Current Events and Civics. The study of history is intended to prepare students for their tasks as citizens in the world of to-day. For this reason current events and civics projects related to the subject matter of each chapter are listed among the study helps. These problems or similar ones may be used as subjects for individual or committee reports, class discussions, or debates. 

Seeing History: The Illustrations in This Book. The illus trations in this book have been so planned that you may see history move by as a pageant in which the past lives again. There are illustrations of picturesque and dramatic episodes, of heroes and heroines, of tools and inventions, of habits and customs. There are illustrations of a cartoon character which are intended to interpret historical ideas. 

The pictures for each chapter serve to practically retell the story of that chapter in a series of visual images which are designed to stimulate your imagination. You will find that a careful study of the pictures, and of the descriptive text which goes with them, will be useful in preparing for reviews and examinations. A study of the table of illustrations will make clear the fact that the illustrations, if studied in series, present a pictorial story of various phases of social life. Many of the illustrations are based upon museum pictures or other material which has come down from the periods treated. 

The Maps. Maps, as well as pictures, serve to illustrate

STUDYING THIS BOOK 

vii history. The maps in this book are of two types: cartoon maps, which help to illustrate historical ideas; and descriptive maps, which show the location of historic places and events. In many cases the descriptive maps used carry an account of the events. By studying these maps and by redrawing them, you will be able to follow the movement of historic events more clearly. 

Collecting Pictures. Although this book has many pictures, students may enjoy collecting others themselves. It is well to plan your picture collection a term ahead by making a list of subjects for which to look, cutting the illustrations out of magazines, newspapers, or other sources, and assembling them in history albums, scrap books, or portfolios ready for use with the chapters which they will best fit.

Museums. The study helps include suggestions for the use of museum material. Museums of art are storehouses filled with the treasure of ages: paintings, statues, rugs, furniture, pottery, coins, models of buildings, and other works which help to illustrate the life and spirit of the past. The class secretary might write to the secretaries of art museums, or other museums, such as Indian museums and historical museums, to learn what aid they are prepared to offer to classes studying American history. If the class is near enough to museums or to historical points of interest, visits can be arranged.

Outside Reading. The reading lists are intended as suggestions for students who undertake to prepare reports on projects or special topics, or who have time for the reading of historical fiction. Librarians will be found ready to suggest other interesting books for outside reading. In preparing reports it would be a good plan for you to practice the use of the dictionary, the encyclopedia, and the statistical almanac, as well as the indexes of books.

viii STUDYING THIS BOOK 

The Index. If you will study the index of this book, you will discover that it has been especially designed to help you in preparing topical outlines of the various social phases of history. For example, under the heading of transportation in the index, you will find page references which will enable you to discover all treatment of this subject in the 

Interpreting History. Among the study helps which are listed, there are suggestions for the writing of poems, plays, and stories, for drawing pictures, for making models, carvings, and cut-outs. These voluntary activities are suggested because you may find it interesting to try to interpret the past through words, pictures, or some other medium. 

Relive the Past; Help Create the Future. And now may we add a final suggestion about the study of this book: that you read this story as the record of the deeds of real men and real women; that you relive the story in your own imagination; that you remember that you are studying the story of your own country so that you may enter with all the more zeal into your part in "America in the Making."

 CHAPTER I The Old World Before Columbus Farmers and Townsmen, Fighting the Old World Wilderness, Help to Bring Forward the Day when Europe will be Ready as well as Eager to Solve the 

Secret of the Atlantic 

The America of To-day. The story of America is the story of the discovery of a New World and of the men and women who helped to build a mighty nation in the New 

World. ⚫ 

To-day this nation, the United States of America, is the home of more than one hundred million people. It is a land of busy farms and towering cities; with mighty steam and electric engines producing and carrying the nation's goods; with a network of electric wires transmitting the nation's messages; with schools, colleges, universities, and churches dedicated to the service of the nation, teaching its ideals and preaching its faith. 1

Bound to the rest of the world by many ties, the United States of America now ranks among the leading nations of the world in wealth, industry, and power. 

The New World Once a Wilderness.-A little over three centuries ago this land now so rich and powerful was a wilderness, the home of a few hundred thousand red men, who paddled their canoes upon the rivers and hunted for food in the wild forests. Less than four and a half centuries ago this wilderness was unknown to the nations of Europe. 

For ages the broad Atlantic, untamed and impassable to men, had guarded its secret. In Europe and in Africa people had heard of the ocean. Many had seen the ocean and not a few had sailed along its shore. But no one knew that beyond the horizon there was a New World. 

Then came the white men from Europe the discoverers, the explorers, the home builders and when they came they brought with them into the New World wilderness something of the tools and industries, the ideas and ideals, of European civilization. It was out of this Old 

World foundation that the America of to-day was to grow. 

To know the story of the growth of America from a wilderness to world power, we must begin with an understanding of the rise and spread of Old World civilization before the New World was discovered.

A Time When the Old World Was All Wilderness. 

There had been a time when the Old World continents, Europe, Asia, and Africa, were all wildernesses without roads, without cleared farms or towns, without wagons or modern means of transportation on land, without a boat upon the rivers or the seas. 

In the wild forests of those days the early hunters had learned to trap animals for meat and furs. 

On the great plains of wild grass there were tribes of herdsmen who had domesticated horses, cattle, and sheep.

These herdsmen lived the lives of nomads, following their grazing herds from pasture to pasture.

Both the hunters and the herdsmen added to their food supply by eating wild grains, wild fruits, and wild berries. 

Farming Helps Make Modern Civilization Possible. 

When men learned that seeds of grain planted in cultivated 

HUNTERS 

"..... Jics.... 

FARMERS HERDSMEN 

ground would yield good harvests, some people settled down as farmers.

The first farmers of whom we have record lived about six thousand years ago in Egypt in the valley of the Nile, and in Mesopotamia in the valley which lies between the Euphrates and the Tigris rivers.

Leading settled lives, the farmers in these river valleys built their homes close together in villages. Some of these villages grew into towns.

In time all the farms and towns in the land of Egypt were united as a nation under a single ruler called the Pharaoh. 

In the towns, supported by the stores of food raised on the farms, there lived soldiers who defended the land; artisans who made pots and cloth and other things for daily use; artists who created things of beauty; merchants who gave their time to trade; priests who devoted their lives to religion and to learning.

So, with town building, modern civilization began; for although we sometimes speak of the civilization of tribes of hunters or of herdsmen, the word "civilization" is usually used to mean the life of town-building peoples. 

Aided by Metal Tools, Civilization Fights Wilderness. 

Ever since the days of Egypt and Mesopotamia farmers and townsmen have been fighting the wilderness. Hunters and herdsmen might be content that the wilderness should remain a wilderness. But it was different with the farmers and the townsmen. They were eager to clear more of the wild lands and to master the streams. To do these things they needed new tools.

At all times, whether as hunters, as herdsmen, as farmers, or as townsmen, people needed tools.

The hunters and the herdsmen had invented tools of wood and bone and stone-stone scrapers, stone axes, stone arrowheads.

The farming and town-building people invented tools of copper, then of bronze and iron.

With the new tools to help them the farmers and townsmen were able to win against the wilderness. Metal arrowheads helped to destroy the wild animals which endangered the farmers and their live stock. Metal axes aided in clearing forests for farming. Battle-axes, spears, and lances. made of metal gave the civilized peoples an advantage in their wars with the less advanced hunting and herdsmen tribes.

Ships and Roads Extend Civilization. With the aid of metal tools men built ships. Ships helped to bind the villages and towns along the rivers into nations strong enough to carry their civilization to new frontiers. Ships carried the wares of the farmers and the town builders to the hunters and the herdsmen in the wilderness beyond the frontiers.

To reach the inland country away from the shores of rivers and of inland seas, some of the ancient nations built roads. Along these roads wheeled chariots carried soldiers to defend the trading posts in the wilderness. 

Ships Carry Civilization 

Toward the Atlantic. So, from the days of Egypt on, farmer and townsman conquered more and more of the outlying wilderness, and each advance of civilization was bringing nearer the day when Europe would be able as well as eager to reach across the Atlantic to the lands which lay beyond. 

The Egyptians in their boats sailed the whole length of the Nile. 

The Phoenicians sent ships westward along the Mediterranean to trade with the people in Greece, Italy, Carthage,

Spain, and even out along the 

Atlantic coast of Europe northward to England.

The Alphabet Records New Faiths and Learning. 

To help keep records of their trade, the Phoenicians used 

The Bow

The Ship The Road The Pen Devices Which Helped in the Conquest of the Wilderness

an alphabet instead of the earlier picture and syllable writing used by the Egyptians and the people in Mesopotamia. Through their trade, the Phoenicians helped to spread the use of alphabetic writing.

By means of an alphabet, the Hebrews who lived in Palestine wrote the Old Testament the story of their lives and of their faith.

The New Testament, with its account of the life of Jesus Ptolemy and of the teachings of the Christian religion, was written with the letters of an alphabet. 

In the wonderful cities of Greece, handsomely decorated with colonnaded temples and marble statues, Greek poets used the alphabet to write their poems and plays; and 

Greek scholars used it in writing about their study of the earth and of the stars.

One Greek scholar named Ptolemy, after reading the books of other Greek scholars and after many talks with travelers, wrote a geography in which he declared that the

earth is not a flat plane as many people believed. He claimed that the earth is round like a sphere and he gave reasons to support his view.

Roman Empire Reaches from India to the Atlantic.- 

Ptolemy wrote his book about the year 150. 

By the time of Ptolemy, the Roman people who lived in 

Italy had conquered Greece, Phoenicia, Egypt, Carthage, and all the other Mediterranean lands. They had conquered Asia Minor and had won victories as far east as 

EGYPT GREECE 

ROME r 

ANCIENT CIVILIZATIONS 

India. They had conquered the wild lands in western 

Europe as far north as England.

The Romans did not excel in the fine arts. These they had borrowed largely from the Greeks. In the practical arts, which had to do with government, the Romans had gifts of their own to make to civilization. They were great builders of roads, bridges, and aqueducts. They gave to the peoples over whom they ruled a common law, the 

Roman Law. 

The Romans established a fair measure of peace throughout their empire, which in the west reached to the shores of the Atlantic. Yet the Romans never mastered the ocean itself.

Northern Tribes Overrun Roman Empire. About three hundred years after the time of Ptolemy, the Roman Empire began to crumble. There were many weaknesses within the empire. Besides, there were raids by the unconquered Germanic tribes to the north of Rome, even by nomad Asiatic tribes. The northern peoples, whom the 

Romans called "barbarians," were for the most part herds-

Barbarians

ROME GREECE PHOENICIA PALESTINE EGYPT ARABIA INDIA The Barbarians 

The northern races overran the Roman Empire. For a while they held back the progress of civilization; then, with their fresh strength, they carried civilization forward. men with some knowledge of farming, outdoor dwellers who had little knowledge of the ways and arts of the Greek and Roman townsmen. They were physically hardy and courageous; they were independent and liberty-loving in spirit; they placed a high value on family life and family loyalty; they were deeply religious and loved to hear their tribal poets recite stories of the deeds of their gods. 

As the northern tribes overran the lands of Western 

Europe, the Roman Empire fell.

From about the year 400 to the year 1000, Europe was torn by almost constant warfare. Trade practically ceased. 

Wild grass grew in the old Roman roads. It seemed that in some lands the arts, the industries, the learning of the old Greek and Roman civilization might be forgotten; that the conquest of the wilderness was at an end; that the 

Atlantic might forever keep its secret. 

Northern Tribes Accept Civilization. Western Nations. 

Civilization did not die.

The time was coming when 

The Norsemen Brave the Ocean the invaders, mixing with the western peoples, would accept the ways of the older civilizations and, adding their own fresh strength to the struggle, would themselves help to carry civilization forward in its struggle against the wild lands and the wild waters of the earth. 

Some of the invaders settled in the lands which they had conquered: the Goths in Spain; the Franks in France; the Angles, the Saxons, and the Jutes in England. In each of the western lands of Europe, sooner or later a strong leader set himself up as king and governed the people under him as a united nation.

One band of Norsemen settled in northern France where their descendants became known as Normans. In

Greenland and Iceland. 

About the year 1000 a small band of Icelandic Norsemen under Leif Ericsson, sailing all the way across the Atlantic, reached a land of grapes which they named Vinland.

Here they built settlements. 

Europe seemed on the edge of solving the riddle of the 

Atlantic; but the time was not yet ripe. The settlements were abandoned. The memory of Vinland became little more than an idle tale which

the Icelanders told around their fires in the long winter nights.

Feudal Europe: Nobles, Serfs, Monks. 

In Ericsson's day Europe was settling down to a way of living known as feudalism.

In a few countries by A.D. 1000 the most powerful of the fighting chieftains ruled as kings. Under the feudal system, each king claimed all the land in his country as his own, but he permitted lesser chieftains, or nobles, to hold and rule over separate parts of the land on condition that they first take an oath of vassalage declaring themselves willing to support him in his warfare. Some of the nobles permitted a few trusted knights to hold and rule over different parts of their estates, provided these knights in turn took the oath of vassalage to the nobles. 

The actual workers on the land were for the most part serfs, who lived very much like slaves. While the nobles who lived in stone castles built on high hills defended the lands, the serfs tilled the fields in the valleys below. 

The home of the serf was a small stone cottage roofed over with cakes of straw and mud. Its one living room was dark. Cows, pigs, or goats shared the cottage.

Plagues often broke out in the land. Often, too, there were famines, when many died of starvation. 

The serf had no legal right to seek a better lot by leaving his lord's estate. Under the law he belonged to the land on which he worked and could be bought and sold with the land, like the trees and houses which stood upon it. Most serfs lived and died in the place where they were born with little knowledge of the world beyond their doors. 

In many villages where the serfs lived, there were small Christian churches, for the northern tribes had long since been converted to Christianity. Here and there in the land, there were Christian monasteries where peace-loving

monks, patiently copying and recopying old manuscripts by hand, were keeping alive something of the ancient learning. The Christian churches had helped to teach the barbarians a little of the arts and industries which the older Roman civilization had known. 

The nobles in their castles had little use for learning. 

Clad in suits of steel armor and mounted on spirited chargers, they spent much of their time fighting one another for 

Social Classes Under Feudalism 

In feudal times, the Christian monks tried to keep alive something of the ancient learning; the serfs tilled the soil; the nobles defended the lands. more land; or, sometimes jealous of the king's power, they joined forces against him. When the nobles were not engaged in warfare their sports were tournaments, hunting, feasting, and drinking.

The nobles despised trade as well as learning. Each castle with its outlying fields and forests was almost a little world in itself, supplying most of its own needs. For this reason the nobles did not have much use for the merchants except to plunder them as they passed by. Such few towns as there were did not prosper. 

However, the day when the towns and townsmen would gain the upper hand was not far off.

Feudal Europe Turns to the East. The Crusades. 

About the year 1100 the people of Europe suddenly turned their faces to the East. 

In Asia Minor, the town of Jerusalem had fallen into the hands of the Mohammedan Turks. These Turks were fierce warriors who had recently become converted to the religion first preached about the year 620 by Mohammed, an Arabian cameldriver.

For centuries Mohammed an armies had overrun Asia and Africa. Mohammedan

Moors had conquered Spain and Portugal. Now that Mohammedan Turks had taken 

Jerusalem, the Holy City of the Christians, and were persecuting Christian pilgrims in that city, the Pope at Rome, as head of the Christian 

Church in Europe, called upon the kings and nobles to cease their fighting among 

The Crusaders 

When the crusaders returned from their wars in the East they brought with them a desire for the wares of the East. themselves and to set out to rescue the Holy City. 

The crusades followed.

For two centuries, from about the year 1100 to 1300, Christian nobles, their trained soldiers, and great numbers of the common people went into the rich eastern lands to fight the Mohammedan Turks and their Mohammedan allies, the Arabs. For a time the crusaders triumphed over 

Turks and Arabs. Then the crusaders were defeated and had to withdraw.

Crusades Help Towns. But meanwhile in Europe the crusades had helped to bring about great changes. 

During this time the trade of the towns had increased. 

Mediterranean towns had furnished the crusaders with food, clothes, and weapons. To obtain money for their travels, the nobles had promised many a town a charter of freedom in return for a loan. This freedom and the growth of trade had strengthened the towns. 

During the crusades the kings had also grown in power.

With the nobles away the kings had been free to seat themselves more firmly on their thrones. The kings, profiting by the taxes on the growing trade between the towns, had encouraged the building of roads which aided trade. 

Europe Desires Eastern Wares. Trade with Indies. 

Even after the crusades, trade continued to increase. 

Old towns were prospering. New towns were growing. 

One reason for the increase of trade in Europe was the growing demand for the goods of the East. The crusaders, when they went into the East, had been little more than herdsmen in their tastes. In the East, civilization was much older than in the lands of Europe. People were more advanced in the knowledge of tools, in learning, and in many of the arts. When the crusaders returned from the 

East, they brought with them a desire for the wares of the East, luxuries of civilization which they had seen the 

Turks and Arabs enjoying.

These luxuries which the returned lords desired came out of Asia Minor, Persia, and Arabia, and the rich eastern lands that lay beyond-the Indies, men called them. There were drugs and perfumes, incense, silks, ivory, gold, and jewels. Desired by rich and poor alike were the spices of the East - pepper, cloves, and cinnamon.

In Europe nothing was known about the canning of food. 

Modern cold storage was unknown. When fresh meat was

scarce, the people depended on preserved meats which were often far from pleasant to the taste unless they were heavily spiced. Besides, in those days as in ours, spices added

The route by way of Alexandria was practically an all water route. The route by way of Antioch was largely by water. The route by way of Constantinople to Cathay was in great measure a land route.

Constantinople, Mediterranean ships carried the goods westward.

The eastern trade was filled with dangers. Many a caravan bearing wares across the desert was attacked by robbers. In the mountain passes of the East, plunderers often waylaid trains of pack animals. On the eastern seas and on the Mediterranean many a ship was captured by pirates.

But difficult and dangerous as all these routes were, the

trade with the East was profitable and the Mediterranean was lively with the sails of many trading ships. 

Towns Lead in Eastern Trade. In all this trade,

Venice, Genoa, and other towns in Italy prospered most, because of their closeness to the Mediterranean Sea which lies midway between the Indies and the western lands of Europe. The merchants in Nuremberg and other towns north of Italy reaped the profits of trade between Italy and a great part of central and eastern Europe. Close to the Atlantic, Ghent, Bruges, Antwerp, trading towns in the Netherlands, grew rich through exchanging the wares of northern Europe for goods which reached them from Italy. 

As the merchants and workers in these and other towns of Europe prospered, the towns grew stronger as against the nobles.

Three Inventions Help Towns. — What helped the towns still further after the crusades were three new inventions. 

It may have been through the crusaders in the East, or it may have been through the Mohammedan Moors who had carried eastern civilization into southern Spain, that at about this time there came into Europe the knowledge of three things long known in the East - the lodestone or magnet; the art of mixing an explosive powder; the art of printing patterns and pictures from carved wooden blocks. 

About the time of the last crusade, men in Europe, using these hints, invented the astrolabe, the mariner's compass, cannon, and movable type for the printing of books. 

The compass, which utilized the principle that a magnetic needle points to the North Star, made sea voyages easier.

In time the use of cannon helped the townsfolk gain the upper hand over the nobles, whose stone castles and steel armor could not withstand explosive gunpowder.

Printing from movable type made books less expensive and helped to spread learning among the townsmen.

Two Printed Books: Ptolemy's Geography; Polo's 

Travels. Among the books printed by the new printing presses was the geography in which Ptolemy had written that the earth is round. Another was the account of Marco 

Polo's travels, which was put into writing about the time of the last crusade.

Marco Polo, a Venetian, had gone with his uncle, a merchant, into Cathay, or China, as it is known to-day. 

After about twenty years, he TLDE 

Polo Tells His Story had returned to his home town, and then in a battle between the fleets of Genoa and Venice, he had been captured by the Genoese and thrown into prison. While in prison he spent many hours telling of his adventures in the East to a fellow prisoner who wrote them down and made a book of them. 

In this book, Marco Polo told of the wealth of Cathay, where princes and their ladies dressed in garments of gold cloth set with jewels. He described Cathay's rich market towns; its river, the Yangtze-kiang, rich in commerce; its ports on the China Sea, where great fleets of spice ships lay at anchor. He wrote that in the China Sea there were hundreds of spice islands from which the spice fleets came. 

East of China there was the large island of Cipango (Japan), which had a temple roofed with gold. He told strange tales of India too.

The growing trade with the East, the printing of Ptolemy's book, and of the book of Marco Polo's travels, all helped to increase interest in the lands of the earth.

The Renaissance. Towns Make New Gift to Civiliza tion. As the towns of Europe prospered, more and more men found time for learning. Universities grew and flourished, and scholars pored over the old manuscripts written by Greeks and Romans. They studied the newly printed books to learn what they could of the lands and the waters of the earth, also of the ancient civilizations. 

Because of man's great interest in the Greek and Roman civilizations, this period is called the Renaissance, or the "rebirth." In some ways this name is misleading. Civilization, of course, had never died; besides, the age of the Renaissance witnessed more than a revival of the old civilization. While some men were looking backward to the arts and learning of the past, the minds of other men were venturing out in new directions. The new tools created by inventors were destined to lead to ocean exploration, world trade, and the building of colonies in the far lands of the earth. Roger Bacon and other scholars who were studying nature to see what they could add to the knowledge of her laws were starting modern science on its way. 

The Renaissance was an age, not only of new inventions and new learning; it was also an age of great creative work in the arts.

Ever since Polo's day, Rome, Florence, Pisa, and Milan, and many other Italian towns, prospering by the eastern trade, had been vying with one another to see which could boast the greatest poets, painters, sculptors, and architects. 

Dante, Petrarch, and Giotto all lived in Polo's day. 

Two centuries later, Raphael, Michelangelo, DaVinci, and 

Titian were adding to the glories of the proud Italian cities.

Other towns in other lands were also proud of their craftsmen, scholars, and artists. During the century in which Dante wrote his Divine Comedy in Italy, Chaucer was writing his Canterbury Tales in England, and the

Sixty Centuries of Old World Civilizations. So, from the days of Egypt on, for six thousand years and more, the civilization of farming and town-building peoples had been moving eastward and westward.

In the East, men had built their towns in the valleys of the Nile, the Tigris, the Euphrates, the Ganges, and the Yangtze-kiang. 

In the West, towns had grown up on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, and on the rivers which flow into the Mediterranean.

Old World empires had risen. Old World empires had fallen. But with tools to help, civilization had been winning against the outlying wilderness; until by the year 

1492 the towns of men reached from the shores of the China Sea on the far eastern coast of Asia to the shores of the Atlantic on the western coast of Europe. 

A few outposts of European civilization had been established on Iceland and on Greenland, in the Azores and the Canary Islands. 

The Atlantic's Secret: A New World Wilderness for Civilization to Conquer. What lay in the Atlantic Ocean between Europe and Asia no man in Europe knew. 

Now the age of the Renaissance was about to make its greatest gift to man by disclosing the secret which the Atlantic had so long been hiding from the known world. 

Columbus's fleet was sailing across the Atlantic on a voyage which was destined to open up to Europe a vast New World, mostly wilderness, for civilization to conquer.

AMERICA CHAPTER II The Great Discovery 

Columbus, a Poor Sailor Seeking an Ocean Route to the Indies, Matches His Plan Against that of a Prince - Other Captains Sailing for 

Nations Facing the Atlantic Make Brave Voyages Which 

Prove that Columbus Has Found a New World 

Columbus Sails West to Explore the Atlantic. - On the morning of August 3, 1492, three ships sailed westward from Palos, Spain. The largest of the ships, the Santa 

Maria, was one hundred tons burden; the Pinta was sixty; the Niña, forty.

On board the Santa Maria was Christopher Columbus, brave and purposeful, a commanding figure, the admiral of the fleet. This seaman, the son of a poor wool-worker in 

Genoa, was about to guide his ships on the most memorable voyage in the history of civilization. 

For years, before the morning when he set sail from Palos, Columbus had cherished the hope of exploring the 

Atlantic to discover its secret.

Now after long years of waiting, years in which he had 23

pleaded with kings for ships and men for such a voyage, Columbus was to have his chance. The rulers of Spain, King Ferdinand of Aragon and Queen Isabella of Castile, victorious in their long wars against the Moors, had decided to grant his request.

Through their aid he had secured this fleet which he 

Columbus Pleading For Royal Aid planned to lead westward across the Atlantic. Who could tell what the ocean might reveal? 

Sailors Fear Edge of World. His sailors thought

Columbus a madman. True, men told legends of wonderful islands in the ocean - St. Brandon's, Atlantis, and other islands far out across the sea. But in spite of such legends, the sailors looked upon the Atlantic as a Sea of Darkness, guarded by dragons that would destroy the overcurious. 

Like most people in their day, the sailors believed that the earth was flat, and that ships sailing too far would fall over the edge of the world into a bottomless pit. 

Columbus Plans Ocean Path to Indies. - Columbus had no such fears. He believed that the earth is round and that he might reach the Indies by sailing westward across the Atlantic.

Ptolemy in his geography had declared that the earth is round, and ever since his day there had been scholars who agreed with him.

In Columbus's time, many university professors, reading the newly printed copies of Ptolemy's book, believed with Ptolemy that the earth is round. 

Columbus did more than believe. He was willing to risk his life to prove the theory. 

Columbus had also read the book of Marco Polo's travels, with its accounts of 

Cathay, the island of Cipango, and the China Sea; and he reasoned that since the earth is round, the China Sea and the Atlantic Ocean must be one. From his study of maps he decided that a voyage of four thousand miles westward across the Atlantic should bring him to Cipango, Christopher Columbus 

Matching his plan against Portugal's, he led his fleet westward across the Atlantic. and that beyond he would find Cathay, the Spice Islands, and the other rich lands of the East. 

If this guess as to the ocean's secret were true, the circle of civilization reaching eastward and westward for thousands of years would at last be completed.

Portugal Seeks Indies. Prince Henry's Plan. - Colum bus was not alone in seeking an ocean path to the Indies. 

From about 1430 on, Prince Henry of Portugal, whom men called the Navigator, had been sending ships southward on the Atlantic to explore the coast of Africa. Each time when his men returned they reported that the long coast of Africa seemed to stretch on endlessly.

EARLY EXPLORERS OF THE AMERICAN COAST 

The earlier explorers seeking a westward path to Asia were blocked by two great continents. Vespucci described the southern continent as a "New World." For a long time, however, geographers continued to believe that the northern continent was part of Asia. As late as 1535 Cartier expected to reach China by way of the 

St. Lawrence River.

Turks, turning on their Christian enemies, had captured Constantinople, which had been one of the chief gateways to the overland trade with the Indies. This was in 1453. 

In time the Turks might close all the old Mediterranean routes to the Indies, but whether or not the Mediterranean routes were closed, Portugal facing the Atlantic had every reason to continue its ocean exploration. If the Portuguese sailors could find the end of Africa, they might sail around that continent and on to the Indies. 

PRINCE HENRY 

When Prince Henry died, King John of Portugal took up the prince's task of ocean exploration, and in 1486

Columbus, waiting for help from the court of Spain, heard that Bartholomew 

Diaz, one of King John's men, had sailed the whole length of Africa to a point which he called the Cape of Storms.

The Portuguese, encouraged by the news, had renamed the point the Cape of Good Hope and were planning to send a fleet around that cape into the Indian Ocean to the very shores of India.

Men called Prince Henry of Portu gal the Great Navigator. He established a school of navigation and sent ships southward to explore the coast of Africa.

A Race for the Indies. Spain; Portugal. - Such was the situation on that memorable morning when the three ships, the Santa Maria, the Pinta, and the Niña, left Palos. Columbus knew that his fleet, sailing for the king and queen of Spain, was in a race with the fleets which would sail for the king of Portugal.

Which would be the first to reach the Indies, the first to bring back a cargo of the eastern goods? If Columbus succeeded by the westward path across the Atlantic, the

His sailors were not so confident. When the ships left the Canary Islands, which was the last of land on the outward voyage, his unwilling crew, many of them recruited from the jails of Palos, almost wept. They expected that they would never see their old homes again. 

Columbus Aided by New Inventions. Columbus, poring over his maps and books, examining his cannon, studying his compass, felt that Providence was guiding him. His printed books, guns, compass, and astrolabe added to his confidence. These inventions had played a great part in preparing for this voyage. Printing had spread the knowledge of Polo's travels and of Ptolemy's proofs for the roundness of the world and so had helped him win the aid of the king and queen and their learned council. His compass gave him courage to risk his ships on the vast ocean which had so long held its secrets from the eyes of men. The cannon gave him confidence that he could defend his fleet in the case of need. 

The Voyage. Days passed and the ships sailed westward. Then one day the compass no longer pointed to the

North Star. The men were terrified; Columbus himself did not know the exact reason for the deflection of the needle, but he made up an explanation to calm his men. 

There were other fears too: the Sargasso Sea, filled with tangled seaweed and alive with slimy, crawling fish; a calm; winds blowing steadily one way.

To keep up the courage of his men, Columbus offered a prize to the sailor who should first sight land.

A month passed and still the ships were sailing westward. 

The men muttered. They protested. Some even plotted mutiny, but Columbus, fearless, commanded, "Sail on!" 

And the ships sailed on.

At two o'clock in the morning, October 12, 1492, a cannon boomed out across the water. A sailor had seen land emerge out of the gray of the dawning day. ५॥ 

Land and the "Indians." Where is Cathay? - When daylight came, Columbus and his men landed on the shores of a little island, which he named San Salvador. Columbus, clad in armor and surrounded by his men, solemnly planted the standard of Ferdinand and Isabella upon the beach. The tall, copper-colored men and women, who had first run away in fear, came from behind trees to see these white beings, who seemed to have been borne to their island on three huge birds with great white wings.

Columbus studied the copper-skinned natives Indians, he called them, for he believed he had reached the Indies. But where were the visions which Polo had described the gilded palaces of Cipango, the harbors of Cathay with their large fleets bearing precious cargo? Where were the eastern princes and their ladies clothed in garments of gold cloth set with jewels? 

The Landing 

Columbus landed on San Salvador, one of the Bahama Islands. Although he did not know it, he had found a 

New World. 

They were nowhere to be seen. 

Columbus Visits Cuba and Haiti. Returns to Spain. 

Some of the naked Indians wore small ornaments of gold. When Columbus heard that the gold came from islands to the south, he sailed on to Cuba and then to 

Haiti. Here he sent messengers to bear greetings to the

Khan of Cathay. When the messengers returned they reported that they had seen only a poor Indian chief in a village of mud huts. 

More days and weeks of sailing all proved fruitless.

Now one of his ships was wrecked. Another had deserted.

Portugal Wins the Race. - Believing the ocean route to the Indies would be hers, Spain hailed Columbus with joy.

All that was needed was to search further until Cipango, Cathay, and India would be found. In 1493, in 1497, and again in 1502 Columbus led a fleet across the Atlantic.

DA GAMA 1498 INDIAN OCEAN PORTUGAL WINS THE RACE 

In 1498 Da Gama reached India by the Portuguese route, sailing around Africa and across the Indian Ocean. More than twenty years passed before Magellan's ship, the Victoria, reached India by sailing westward as Columbus had planned. even a southern continent which lay beyond. But each time he failed to find the Indies which were his goal. 

Meanwhile news reached the Spanish court that Portugal had won the race. By 1498 a Portuguese captain, Vasco da Gama by name, had sailed around the Cape of Good

Hope, across the Indian Ocean to the shores of India, from which he had brought back a precious cargo. Poor Columbus! Mocking men in the Spanish court called him "Ad miral of the Lands of Deceit and Disappointment." 

Other Kings Send Sailors Westward. The kings of other nations which faced the ocean were aroused by the news of the voyages made by Columbus and they sent captains to search for the 

Indies by the western path.

The lot of those who undertook these voyages was a hard one-poor food; stale drink; waves pounding wormeaten vessels, and sweeping the low decks; furious gales which threatened to founder the ships or to carry away their masts, leaving the men to drift aimlessly on lonely waters. Cabot, Verrazano, and Cartier Fail to Reach Indies. 

In 1497 Henry VII, king of England, agreed that John 

Cabot, an Italian sea captain in the employ of English merchants, might cross the Atlantic. Cabot, sailing due west from England, with one ship and eighteen men, reached an island which may have been Cape Breton 

Island or Newfoundland. When he returned, the news caused some little stir and the king rewarded him with a sum of money equal in present-day value to a few hundred dollars, for the finding of the "New Isle."

The next year John Cabot and his son Sebastian sailed again. On this voyage they may have reached the mainland of the continent, west of the "new isle," but nowhere did they see the splendors of Cipango or Cathay.

Verrazano, an Italian sea captain, to find them. Verrazano sailed for many miles along a mainland coast, but he too failed to find any sign of the Indies. 

Ten years later, the king of 

France sent Jacques Cartier, a French sea captain, westward. Cartier found the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The next year, on a second voyage, Cartier sailed up the St. Lawrence River hoping to pass through the continent and on to China. The rapids which barred his way are, to this day, called Lachine, or the China Rapids. 

Magellan's Ship Reaches Indies: Proves the World 

Round. Columbus, Cabot, Verrazano, and Cartier all failed to find a westward path to the Indies. But there was one man who did not fail. That man was Magellan, a

Portuguese sea captain in the service of the king of Spain.

In 1519, with five ships and two hundred men, Magellan sailed across the Atlantic and followed the coast line of the southern continent southward to Patagonia. There ice floes forced him to winter. Mutiny arose. He put it down. 

When spring came and the ice thawed, he continued southward until he found a narrow strait, since called the Straits of Magellan, leading westward into a calm sea beyond. 

Magellan named this calm sea the Pacific, and trimmed his sails to cross its waters. 

His crews dropped from scurvy brought on by bad food, then from weakness brought on by no food at all. 

The eating of rats, of worms, and leather straps from the ship's rigging kept some of the men alive until they reached a group of islands 

MAGELLANX 

Although he himself was killed in the Philippines, his flagship, the Victoria, completely circumnavigated the world. which they named the Philippines. Here they landed. 

In a battle with the Filipinos, while covering his men's retreat, Magellan was killed. His men continued westward to the Spice Islands. They reached India. Then sailing through the Indian Ocean, around the Cape of Good Hope, they entered the Atlantic and set their sails toward Spain. 

Of the five ships and all their crew after three years of voyaging, only one ship, the Victoria, reached home. 

Manned by eighteen haggard sailors, with twenty-six tons of cloves in the hull, the Victoria entered a Spanish

port, the first ship to have sailed westward around the world.

Columbus Had Discovered a New World. The claim of those who argued that the earth is round was proved. 

The dream of Columbus had come true. A ship had sailed westward across the ocean to the Indies.

VESPUCCI 

In a letter describing his voyages along the coast of a great continent, Vespucci called the new lands "Novus Mundus" which is Latin for the "New World." 

Columbus himself had not found the pathway. He had not brought the coast towns of Europe into touch with the seaports of Asia. He had not completed the circle of civilization.

But if he failed it was only because he had accomplished something far greater. He had blazed the path to two vast continents. He had found a new world wilderness for civilization to conquer. 

The New World is Named 

"America."- Columbus himself never learned the truth. 

In 1506, poor, neglected, broken-hearted, he died. No monument marked his grave. 

Through a strange chance the New World was not even named for Columbus. Another explorer, Amerigo Vespucci, an Italian in the service of Portugal, who had crossed the ocean several times about 1501, wrote an account of his voyage along the shores of the southern continent which he called "Novus Mundus," which is 

Latin for the "New World." A professor in a university, preparing a new edition of Ptolemy's geography, believed that the credit for finding this southern continent belonged

to Amerigo Vespucci, and he accordingly suggested that it be named for him, "America." Other writers used the name. When people in Europe learned more of the two vast continents which the Atlantic had so long guarded from Old World eyes, the name was extended until in time the whole of the New World became known as America. 

America a New Land of Promise. Since this America seemed to be little more than a wilderness, was the New World to be again forgotten as it had been after its earlier discovery by Leif Ericsson?

The Vinland, which Ericsson had discovered about the year 1000, was a part of this same America. Nothing had come of that earlier discovery, but something was bound to come of this one.

Now, with larger ships, with compasses to guide their ships, with guns for conquest, with printed books to keep alive the interest in the new lands, Europe was soon to become eager and ready to master the ocean, and to establish a foothold in the lands beyond. 

Now, moreover, the rumors which came from the lands across the ocean were not merely of a wild-grape country, but of a New World where all could find their heart's desire. To Europe, America was soon to be a new Land of 

Promise, where kings would seek empire, where nobles would seek adventure, fame, and fortune, where the Christian Church would seek converts, where merchants would seek profit from trade and colony building, where the rank and file of people, poor and down-trodden, would seek opportunity and refuge from oppression.

CHAPTER III The Spanish Conquerors Spanish Nobles Seeking Golden Cities Explore the New World Wilderness, Conquer Strange Indian Civilizations, and Win a Great Empire for Their King 

The Conquerors. -While brave sea captains were exploring the coast line of America, Spanish nobles, clad in armor and mounted on prancing horses, were leading bands of soldiers into the virgin forests. Alongside of the armed soldiers, priests robed in long black cassocks walked with measured steps. With banners flying, and gilded crucifixes reflecting the light and shade of the rich green woods, these cavalcades were setting out to seek fame, fortune, and empire in the great New World.

The Lure of Gold.- Columbus, returning from his first voyage, had brought back bits of gold. For tens of years after, the Spanish sailors who followed him to America brought back stories of gold, stories which they had heard the Indians tell; of native chiefs who drank from golden goblets; of Indian tribes so rich in gold that they stored it in huge baskets; of El Hombre Dorado, the Gilded Man, 39

who every day at dawn was freshly gilded with pure gold; of seven golden cities in a desert. 

Gold! Gold! Gold! For the nobles the thought of the 

New World's gold held a magic spell. Unlike the merchants

El Dorado the nobles despised trade; but they desired the gold with which men traded. To obtain gold they were prepared to undergo the most trying hardships, to fight against almost overwhelming odds.

Gold and Trade.-Through out the ages civilized men have had to trade. In the farming districts they lived by barter. The shepherd gave wool for his neighbor's grain. The foresters gave fagots for the miller's flour. Even in the towns merchants lived by barter, but the merchants long since had found that barter was too clumsy. They had to have some form of money, small, durable, precious. Such a thing was gold. 

The use of gold for money dates back to the time of 

Egyptian and Phoenician traders. At first gold was used by weight and had to be both weighed and tested at each new purchase. Then Croesus, king of Lydia, in Asia

Minor, had gold minted into coins, stamped with a seal. 

This seal attested the quality and weight of gold in each coin. The use of coins made trade still easier. 

Gold coins were minted by the Greeks and the Romans. 

All during the barbarian invasions and even after, when the nobles in their castles discouraged trade, men returned to barter. But when the towns began to grow and trade revived, the merchants again used gold.

For some time gold had been growing scarce in Europe,

The scarcity of gold in Europe had much to do with ocean exploration. Prince Henry's men, in their voyages

along the coast of Africa, were looking for the gold coast of Guinea from which the Moors obtained their gold. 

When Ferdinand and Isabella agreed to aid Columbus it was partly in the hope that he would find gold for them.

a tenth share of all the precious metals he might find. Small wonder then that the Spanish nobles, hearing rumors of New World gold, sailed to Spain's military settlements in the West Indies, where they waited eagerly for their opportunity to cross over to the mainland in search of gold.

Ponce de Leon Discovers 

Florida. One of the first of these expeditions started out seven years after Columbus died. The men were 

Ponce de Leon, searching for a mythi- seeking gold, but story has it that their leader, Ponce de

Leon, an old Spanish soldier, was seeking something far more precious, a fountain which would make him young again. On Easter Day, 1513, the Spanish "Pascua Florida" or Feast of Flowers, the Spaniards came to a bright sunny land which they named "Florida." When Florida revealed neither gold nor the fountain of youth, the general and his men returned to Cuba. 

Balboa Finds the "South Sea," the Pacific. - That same year, 1513, another Spaniard, Balboa by name, finding himself in debt, left Haiti as a stowaway on a ship bound for the mainland. Arriving at Darien,

Balboa set himself up as a leader and shipped the appointed captain back, a prisoner. Then, hearing from the natives that near the shore of a great sea, a few days' journey to the west, there lived Indians rich in gold, Balboa with one hundred and ninety men plunged into 

Balboa Discovers the Pacific (1513) 

the wilderness. Here was a double promise, gold and a great sea, which might be the path to the Indies. 

The way was rough and difficult. The days stretched into weeks. But Balboa and his men fought and hacked their way through the forests and up into the mountains. 

Near the top of a high ridge, Balboa halted his men while he climbed to the summit. There, gazing from the mountain peak, he saw what no white man had ever seen before him. Gleaming in the distance was an ocean. Balboa named it the South Sea. 

Another few days' journey brought the Spaniards to the water's edge where Balboa, wading into the waves, claimed for Spain the sea and all the lands touched by its waters. 

But the rich Indian tribes! Where were they? A few

POLE ARMS Cortez The Conqueror of Mexico, the land of the Aztecs. 

days' journey southward was the answer. Balboa was determined to find them. The boats which he needed lay on the eastern coast, but piece by piece his Indian slaves carried the ships' timbers over the mountains to the South Sea, where they were rebuilt and launched. At last Balboa was ready to sail southward, but he never made the journey.

The new governor of Panama had him arrested on a false

CANNON METAL ARMOR Spanish Armor and Weapons charge of treason. He was tried, convicted, and executed at a place facing the ocean which he had discovered. 

Shortly after, when Magellan crossed this same ocean which Balboa had named the South Sea, Magellan renamed it the Pacific.

Cortez Conquers Aztecs in Mexico. Still the search for gold continued.

One day a Spanish ship, returning to Cuba from the Gulf of Mexico, brought back rumors of rich inland cities ruled by Aztec Indians. 

Soon Cortez, with a band of several hundred soldiers and some horses, sailed for Mexico. At Vera Cruz he built a fort. Then, destroying his ships, he led his men inland to the Aztec capital. This he found to be situated on an island in the middle of a lake. Three great roads led over the lake into the capital. 

There, Montezuma, the Aztec king, ruled over a land of farms and towns much as the Pharaohs had ruled in ancient Egypt. In the city there was a pyramid with a temple to the god of war; there were other temples with stone images carved by sculptors; there was a calendar stone by which the Aztecs divided time into years, months, and days. Within the palaces of Montezuma and in the temples there were skillfully wrought ornaments made of gold taken from the beds of Mexican mountain streams. 

Among the Aztecs there were master weavers of linens and of cotton cloths.

Montezuma was friendly. He welcomed Cortez and his men, and even proposed to offer up human sacrifices in honor of his guests. But Cortez had not come for idle show. His heart was set on conquest.

Shut within the city where thousands of Aztecs swarmed, Cortez strengthened his position by making Montezuma his captive. Before long, the aroused Aztecs attacked the 

Spaniards. Montezuma, forced by the Spaniards to plead for peace, was shot by the arrows of his own men. That night the Spaniards fled from the city but not before they had lost half their number in fighting their way across the lake. As the Spaniards retreated toward the coast, other

Aztec Gold Jewelry Aztec Warrior 

His armor was made of quilted cotton, his shield overlaid with feathers, and his wooden club set with small stone blades. battles followed. But finally, aided by tribes of Indians who hated the Aztecs, Cortez returned to the city and after a long and bloody siege the city fell. The Aztecs with their spears and lances were no match for the reënforced Spaniards with their charging horses, their guns, and cannons. The conquering Spaniards ruled in Mexico. Its treasure was theirs to plunder. 

Pizarro Conquers Incas, in Peru. Soon Pizarro and another small band of Spaniards made the voyage which Balboa planned to make. In Peru, on the west coast of 

South America, they found Indians, the Incas, living in a narrow fertile river valley of well-tilled fields and towns

far richer in gold and silver than the Aztec towns. The 

Spaniards, matching their wits and guns against the forces of the Incas, conquered them. 

Searching for More Golden Cities. When galleons bearing the loot from Mexico and Peru reached the seaports of Spain, the lust for New 

World plunder and adventure spread through the land. 

The Spanish nobles no longer begrudged the Portuguese the profits from the eastern trade. 

Columbus's voyages had led

Spain to richer treasure. The 

New World wilderness was worth exploring farther.

So led on by the hope of finding gold and winning new lands for the Spanish crown,

Spanish expeditions searched 

PIZARRO 

The Conqueror of Peru, the home of the Incas.

South America for the land of El Dorado, the Gilded Man, and for the lake behind which gleamed two golden mountains. One party of Spaniards under Narvaez landed near Tampa, Florida, and plunged northward into the wilderness.

Except for the news of the inland country which the survivors brought back, these expeditions came to nothing. 

The men suffered hardships beyond description. They died terrible deaths of tropical fevers, of hunger, and of thirst. Often those who lived had to eat their horses and even their leather harnesses. Sometimes they had to eat their own dead. Too weak to wear their armor, they wandered on in rags. Their Indian guides led them into impassable jungles only to desert them. Again and again

they were assailed by the Indians who shot poisoned arrows at them. Such few Indian tribes as seemed friendly enough to the Spaniards to give them lodging spent the nights plotting to destroy them. 

Of Narvaez's men, only Cabeza de Vaca and three others, after eight years of wandering among half-starved

Indian tribes, found their way to Mexico and shelter. 

De Soto Discovers the Mississippi. Still the lure of gold led the Spaniards on. 

De Soto was buried by the light of torches in the waters of the Mississippi, which he had discovered. 

Now it was Hernando de 

Soto, one of the conquerors of 

Peru, who, in 1539, set out to find new golden cities. De

Soto had returned to Spain, a hero, with half a million dollars' worth of Inca treasure. 

There he had wed the most beautiful lady of the land and spent his treasure lavishly. When his fortune was half spent, he recruited a band of nobles to try again in Florida. These Spaniards came well provided for a long search. They had droves of hogs for food, chains to bind the Indian slaves who would carry their packs, and bloodhounds to track down deserters.

After almost two years of wandering through swampy forests, De Soto came to a broad stream which the Indians called the Mississippi, the Father of Waters. He and his men crossed this stream in a raft of their own building and continued westward, only to return again to the banks of the river. Here De Soto died, and his followers, wishing to conceal his death from the Indians, buried him by the

light of torches at night beneath the waters of the river which he had discovered.

The three hundred men who were left now drifted down the Mississippi to carry back the news.

While the 

Coronado Marches North from Mexico. fate of De Soto was yet unknown, other Spaniards set out from Mexico City, Montezuma's former capital, to explore the lands north of Mexico, where, according to De Vaca, they would find the Seven Golden Cities of Cibola. The seven cities turned out to be the villages of the Zuñi Indians. 

Their dwellings, built of adobe or sun-dried cakes of mud, gleamed in the sun like golden walls, but within the dwellings the Spaniards found only pots of clay and woven baskets.

Still Coronado and his men journeyed on. They explored the deserts west of the Zuñi villages and gazed upon the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River. They wandered northward into prairie lands where they saw herds of roaming buffalo. When they reached the Kansas plains without seeing golden cities, they returned to Mexico. 

Spanish Missions; Spain's New World Empire.

After the failure of De Leon, Narvaez, De Soto, and Coro nado, the Spaniards lost much interest in the lands to the north. Here and there a solitary priest wandered alone into this region to carry the Christian faith to the Indians and to teach them the ways of civilization. Except for a few missions which Spanish priests built in New Mexico, and later in California, the Spaniards did nothing to plant settlements north of Florida and Mexico. Nevertheless 

Spain claimed the whole of North and South America except Brazil, which by Portuguese explorations and a decree of the Pope belonged to Portugal.

Spain had paid for the voyages which led to the discovery of America. Spanish nobles seeking gold had

explored the islands, the mainland coast, and even inland country as far as the Pacific. While Spanish conquerors were destroying the native civilizations of the Incas and the Aztecs, Spanish priests were introducing Christianity 

A Spanish Mission 

The Spanish priests brought to America the architectural beauty of old Spain. among the Indians in the missions which they built. The priests also taught the Indians something of the Old World crafts and ways of farming. In a few Spanish towns in 

America, Spanish priests introduced libraries and even printing presses. All told, the Spaniards had done much to establish the claim of their king to this New World.

Since it belonged to him, the king of Spain meant to keep his New World empire for himself. He ordered that none but Spaniards might trade or settle in America. To defend the New World against invaders, he stationed soldiers in the Spanish mainland settlements and in the West Indies, where Spanish nobles owned large plantations on which Indians worked as slaves. 

Spain Plans to Hold North America Against All Rivals. — 

A Spanish captain, Menendez, hearing that French Huguenots had settled in Florida, built a Spanish fort at St. Augustine, from which he marched north against the 

French and destroyed their settlement. So the warning was given that Spain intended to hold North America against all rivals.

As the news of Spain's rich New World possessions spread, the other European nations facing the Atlantic began to look out upon the ocean and the lands which lay beyond with a keener interest. Men were wondering whether Spain could maintain her advantage over other nations.

ENGLAND NETHERLANDS FRANCE SPAIN MEDITERRANEAN CHAPTER IV Rivals for Ocean Power 

Mighty Spain is Challenged by the English Who See in the Atlantic a

New Highroad to Trade, Wealth, and Power - The Defeat of the 

Spanish Navy Opens the Way for England, France, and Holland to Plant Colonies in America Europe's Mightiest Monarch Philip II of Spain. - After the conquest of the Aztecs and the Incas, each year a fleet of the high-decked Spanish galleons crossed the ocean to America and then returned to Spain with gold and silver from the mines where the Incas and the Aztecs worked as slaves.

This gold and silver helped to make Spain the richest country in all Europe and for a time Philip II, king of Spain, was Europe's mightiest monarch. 

Philip, crowned in 1555, ruled over Spain, Naples and

Sicily, and the Netherlands. He claimed the whole of 

North America and all of South America, except Brazil.

His armies, supported by New World gold, took possession of Portugal and so fell heir to Brazil and to the Portuguese trading posts in the East Indies. His armies waged 53

war against France and against his own subjects in the 

Netherlands. 

England under Queen Elizabeth Turns to the Sea. Yet with all his wealth and power there was one country which worried Philip. That country was England, whose captains were aiding his enemies and challenging his mastery of the 

Atlantic, the key to all his riches. 

Philip II 

Aided by gold and silver from world mastery.

When John Cabot, sailing for England under Henry VII, had failed to find the Indies, the 

English for the time being lost interest in the new lands to the west.

But during the reign of Queen 

Elizabeth, the granddaughter of Henry VII, the English became a thousandfold more curious about the world, more enterprising, more bent on large adventure. They were determined to win a place for themselves upon the ocean, and fortunately for their purposes the Spanish wars were playing into their hands.

The cruelty of Spanish armies Mexico and Peru, Philip II planned in the Netherlands was ruining the trade of Antwerp and Bruges, and much of this flourishing trade was passing into the hands of the English merchants. The wars in the Nether-

lands were also driving Netherland weavers into England where they were helping to build up the clothing industry. 

To provide wool for the weavers, many of the English landowners were raising sheep instead of crops; and the 

English cities swarmed with country lads who, since tilled fields were being turned into untilled pastures, were no longer needed at home. These fellows, their ears tingling with stories of the heroes of the past and the New World across the seas, swelled the number of those who were ready to hire out as seamen and to embark upon any adventure which promised fortune as well as excitement. 

Printed books, travelers who visited on the Continent, sailors whose ships had carried them to many shores, all were bringing back stories of the wealth and luxury of the trading cities to the south. 

QUEEN ELIZABETH. 

During the reign of Queen Eliza- In the London theaters plays beth, the English people, stirred up by of bold adventure were stirring the people. Before many new conditions at home and abroad, turned to the ocean for profit and adventure. years William Shakespeare, a youth who had come up to London from the provinces, was writing plays for these theaters, and in his plays we can see, as in a mirror, the spirit of the island people looking out upon the world. 

Just as in Shakespeare's play, the Tempest, the ocean and the strange lands in it are the stage on which the actors play their parts, so now the sea became the stage on which England itself was soon to play a leading rôle. 

With many ships which needed trade to keep them busy, with woolen cloth to sell, with thousands of men, driven

from the land, seeking employment, England now turned to the Atlantic. The day when the Mediterranean was the path to empire had passed. The centuries to come belonged to those who could master the Atlantic, the new highroad of empire. The Atlantic had led the Portuguese to the profitable trade with the Indies. The Atlantic had led the Spaniards to the rich mines of America. 

And now 

English leaders saw that the Atlantic must lead them to wealth and power. 

English Sea Dogs. - Before Philip was king of Spain many years he heard of the deeds of the English captains and sailors who were roving the ocean in the service of their queen and country.

Frobisher, Davis, and Hudson were seeking the northwest passage around America in search of China, as a possible market for English woolen cloth. These northwest voyages led the English explorers into icy waters, later named after them - Frobisher Bay, Davis Strait, Hudson

Bay - but nowhere did they find a strait such as Magellan had found to the south.

While these captains were guiding their ships and men through northern seas, other English captains set out to win what profits they could from trading with the rich Spanish settlements in the West Indies, and with the seaports on the "Spanish Main" - the mainland washed by the Caribbean Sea. The Spanish king forbade such trade but the English worried little about his laws. One of the English seamen, Hawkins, sailed southward to the coast of Africa where he captured a cargo of negroes to sell as slaves in the Spanish settlements. The adventure paid so well that he repeated it, but on the third trip, while at dock in the Mexican harbor of Vera Cruz, his ships were attacked by a Spanish fleet and he and his men narrowly escaped slaughter.

Plundering the Plunderers. - Baffled in their search for 

China and in their trade with the Spanish colonies, Sir John 

Hawkins, his nephew Francis Drake, Davis, Cavendish, and many another roving captain turned their ships to swifter ways of winning fortunes on the seas. They knew that 

Philip II was plotting to place Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots, cousin to Queen Elizabeth, on the English throne. They believed that if Philip won his war in the Netherlands, he would use his New World plunder in a war against England. 

What better adventure, then, than to plunder the plunderers by capturing Spanish galleons and their gold? Thus the 

English captains would strike at Philip II where it would hurt him most, both in his sea power and in his treasury. 

To weaken Philip II, therefore, as well as to gain booty for themselves, the English sea dogs scoured the seas searching for prey. Many battles followed as ships ran close and boarding parties fought hand to hand on the decks; and many a captured cargo of American gold and silver was brought to port in England. 

The boldest of the English sea captains was Sir Francis

Drake. Not content with taking Spanish ships at sea, he crossed the ocean to storm and rob the towns on the 

Spanish Main. 

One time he landed secretly at Panama, and marching inland waylaid the Spaniards as they were bringing their bags of Peruvian gold and silver across Panama to the eastern coast. On another raid in Panama, Drake climbed a high tree from which he looked down upon the waters of the Pacific. Then and there he decided to make the voyage which Magellan had made and to strike at the Spanish towns on the western coast of South America. 

Sir Francis Drake Sails Around the World. In 1577 

Drake left England with a small fleet bound for Alexandria; at least so the ship's clearing papers read. On the flag-

ship, the Pelican, the table service was of silver, and fiddlers played while Drake and his officers dined in merriment.

They were bound not for Alexandria but for Peru. 

Like Magellan, Drake led his ships southward to Patagonia and there they wintered. But unlike Magellan, in passing through the Straits, he found the waters dark with storms. 

Before those storms ceased, two ships, lost from the rest, turned their prows back to 

England; one went down with all on board; only Drake's ship, the Pelican, remained.

Undaunted, he renamed it the Golden Hind and continued northward to Peru. 

Sir Francis Drake

Along the Peruvian coast everything turned out as he had planned. The harbors were open and undefended. 

Treasure ships greeted the 

Golden Hind as a friend and were boarded almost before their officers or crew could realize that these were foes. 

Exploring parties from the 

English ship found a Spaniard sleeping in the woods. By his side were bars of silver. Walking farther, they found another Spaniard and an Indian boy driving sheep. On the backs of the sheep were swollen bags which sagged heavily. The bags were filled with silver. 

Drake led a fleet around South America to raid the Spanish coast towns of Peru. Then after wintering at New Albion (or California), he crossed the Pacific and completely circumnavigated the earth. He took part in the defeat of the Spanish Armada which was carrying troops to invade England.

The treasure galleon of the year was well on its way northward to Panama. But pursuing swiftly, Drake captured the ship before it put into harbor.

Now to avoid the Spanish ships which would be sent to block his return, Drake sailed north as far as Oregon, seeking for a passage back into the Atlantic. Failing in this, he stopped in California - New Albion, he called it; and then with copies of Magellan's maps, he guided his ship westward across the Pacific, around the Cape of 

Good Hope, and back to 

Plymouth, completing in 1580 the second voyage ever made around the world.

Gilbert and Raleigh Plan Settlements. Roanoke. - 

Philip was furious. Yet this was not all. For word reached him that the English were claiming a share in America and that they were trying to plant colonies north of Florida. 

Sir Walter Raleigh 

Raleigh was an English courtier and adventurer who had great faith in the future of America. A fleet sent out by him explored Virginia. His attempts to settle Virginia failed. 

Philip may not have known all the facts but this report was true. Sir Humphrey 

Gilbert had tried to plant an 

English settlement in Newfoundland. His plan had failed, and on the return voyage Gilbert had gone down with his ship which foundered in a storm. Then the queen had granted the right to take up the task of colony building to Gilbert's half brother, Sir Walter Raleigh, a courtier who had won her favor by his gallantry. Raleigh had sent a fleet under Amidas and Barlow to explore the coast in search of a new site. When they returned they gave such a good account of the land they saw that the country was named "Virginia" for Queen Elizabeth, the Virgin Queen.

Raleigh, who had a vision of this new country as a new home for Englishmen, undertook to plant a colony in Virginia.

Raleigh's first settlement on the small island of Roanoke, off the coast of North Carolina, failed; but the members of his second band of settlers were at this very time in Roanoke waiting for the return of their governor, John White, whom they had sent to England to bring them fresh supplies.

Philip II Sends Armada to Crush England, 1588. — Philip now felt that he must openly attack England. 

English soldiers sent by Queen Elizabeth were aiding his enemies by fighting his armies in the Netherlands. 

Englishmen were planning to build forts and settlements in America. English captains were robbing him of the gold and silver which he needed for his armies and his navies. His plots against Queen Elizabeth had failed. 

Accordingly Philip gave orders that his men should build many ships and that everything should be made ready for a naval attack on England.

When news of this reached England, the merchants and sailors in the seaport towns rallied to the colors, and every ship that could be used was gathered into Plymouth Harbor in readiness for the coming battle. The tension continued. Finally about one hundred fifty ships, Spain's "Invincible Armada," appeared in the English Channel. The 

English ships sailed out to meet the Spanish fleet. 

The battle was swift and decisive. The huge unwieldy galleons of the Spaniards, which were little more than transports bearing soldiers, were no match for the English sail-ships handled by captains who knew how to take every advantage of the wind in order to harass the enemy. 

After a struggle which lasted days, some of the Spanish ships were sunk; others were beached off the coast of

Holland; the rest, fleeing from fire ships, which Drake sent into their midst, sailed northward. Storms completed what the English ships had only begun. The coast of Scotland was strewn with Spanish wrecks. Less than half of the "Invincible Armada" ever found its way back to Spain.

A Relief Ship Starts for Roanoke. Soon after the defeat of the Spanish fleet, a ship was on its way to Roanoke to rescue Raleigh's colony. On board was John White, who had left the struggling settlement three years before.

During all that time he had been unable to get supplies to the settlement. Among those whom he had left in 

Roanoke were his own daughter, his son-in-law, and their child, Virginia Dare, the first child born of English parents in America. Now he wondered if he would ever see them again.

At last the ship reached Roanoke. The island was deserted. A few tumble-down shacks, a broken chest, and some scattered books were the only signs of the settlement except the word "CROATAN" carved upon a tree.

Croatan was the name of a friendly tribe of Indians, but the settlers were never found either with the Croatans or anywhere else. They had disappeared as though the earth had swallowed them, and their fate is one of the unsolved problems of history. It was another tragedy to add to that of the French settlers who had tried to settle in Florida. Thus the building of settlements in America was from the first a hazardous undertaking.

Spain's Defeat Opens Ocean to Rivals: Merchant 

Companies. -The defeat of the Armada in 1588 marked a turning point in Spain's power. 

During the next few years Dutch and English captains destroyed more of the Spanish navy. By 1609 Spain signed a twelve years' truce with Holland. By 1640 Portugal won

back her freedom. By 1648 Holland was acknowledged free. 

Although Spain's New World colonies were growing, her short day of ocean mastery was over. Spain's rivals on the western coast of Europe now found the way clear to extend their ocean trade and to build colonies in the new lands. 

Something of the stately dignity of the old Spanish kings and nobles can still be felt in the masterful paintings of 

Velasquez, court painter to Philip IV, grandson of Philip II. 

But by Velasquez' time, much of the Spanish gold had passed from the king's palace and the castles of the Spanish nobles to the counting houses of the merchants in France, England, and the Netherlands. With this gold these merchants had formed companies which applied to their kings for charters or legal papers guaranteeing to them the exclusive right to trade with and to plant colonies in some given part of the world. 

Raleigh's Prophecy 

"I shall yet live to see it an English nation."

From about 1600 on, there were formed the Dutch, the French, and the English East India companies. 

The Dutch, French, and English merchants also organized companies for New World trade and for the building of American colonies. In applying for their charters the companies explained that New World colonies and New World trade would bring profit to the home country, build up empire, and carry the Christian faith to the Indians north of New Spain. The English made the further claim that New World colonies would provide an outlet for Englishmen who were finding conditions in England difficult.
