Cartagena Raleigh's Prophecy. - Raleigh, who had lost a fortune in his attempts at colony building, relinquished his rights in America to two companies of English merchants, the London Company and the Plymouth Company, which now received a charter from James I, the new king of England. 

Raleigh, cast into prison for political reasons, retained his faith in America. He wrote, "I shall yet live to see it an English nation."

CHAPTER V The Indians The Indians, the Ancient Owners of America 

the Lives Which They Live in the Wilderness to Which the Home Builders Are Coming-Their Fate After the White Men Come The American Wilderness Claimed by England. - The part of America in which the English were about to build their colonies was a vast wilderness. Along the Atlantic coast the English claimed the land from the mouth of the 

St. Lawrence, southward to Florida. Back of the Atlantic shore the coastal plain rises gradually to the Appalachian Mountains. In these mountains many rivers have their source. Some flow eastward across the Atlantic plain to empty into the Atlantic Ocean; some flow westward into the valley of the Mississippi River. To the south of the 

Mississippi Valley is the Gulf of Mexico; to the north of the valley lie the Great Lakes. West of the Mississippi 

Valley stand two imposing mountain ranges of the West, the Rockies and the Sierra Nevadas. Some rivers rising in the western mountains flow eastward into the Mississippi; 65

others flow westward across a Pacific coastal plain into the Pacific Ocean. 

A Rich Unexplored Land. - The English people had little notion of the extent of the wilderness which they claimed or of its character. 

A great part of the country from the Atlantic to the Mississippi was covered with forests. West of this eastern woodland area there was a large stretch of level treeless plains on which herds of buffalo grazed. South of the plains there were deserts where the cactus and sagebrush grew on the hot dry soil. From the Rockies to the Pacific there were dense forests and fertile river valleys. 

Except for the desert areas, most of the soil throughout the land was productive. The forests were rich in wild game. The waters of the land abounded in fish. The mountains of the east were rich in coal and iron deposits. 

In the western part of the country there were great stores of copper, lead, tin, gold, and silver. Centuries were to pass before the vastness and the riches of the new land were fully realized. 

The Indians Who Owned the Land. A Divided People.— 

The failure of Raleigh's colonies at Roanoke left all of America north of Florida in the hands of the Indians who were the ancient owners of the land. 

These Indians numbered only a few hundred thousand scattered over millions of square miles of hunting ground. 

Yet if Raleigh's dream of an English nation in America were to come true, the English would have to reckon with the natives.

Fortunately for the English who were soon to seek homes in America, the Indians were very much divided amongst themselves.

In the eastern woodland area of North America which extended from Hudson Bay to Florida, there were three

THE INDIANS 

67 great groups or families of Indians: the Algonquian, the Muskhogean, the Iroquoian, each group speaking a different language. These families were divided into separate tribes.

On the plains, on the deserts, and in the far west, there were other families and tribes, following their own customs and adjusting their lives to local geographic conditions. 

Stone hoe

Indian Farm Implements 

Stone axe

Of all the Indian families and tribes, only the Iroquois had been able to form themselves into a confederation, the "Five Nations" (later the "Six Nations"), who fought as one. But between the Iroquois and other families and even between the tribes within the other families there was almost constant warfare. 

Indians are Hunters; Also Farmers. The Indian tribes who lived north of Mexico and Florida were not nearly as advanced in the arts and learning of civilization as were the Aztecs of Mexico, the Mayas of Central 

America, or the Incas of Peru.

The Indians living in the land claimed by England lived largely by hunting. The waters provided them with

fish. Wild animals provided them with meat. Wild fowl added to their store of food. The skin of the animals which they caught helped to clothe them.

Yet the life of these Indians was not entirely that of a hunting people. Many of the Indian tribes gave some time to farming. They raised tobacco and corn, two plants which had been unknown to European farmers. Between the rows of corn, the Indian planted squash, beans, and pumpkins. The Indians who lived on the deserts understood the art of irrigation and raised good crops. 

Indian Tools and Weapons. -The Indians did not know the art of making metal tools. In spite of the riches of the land in copper, lead, and iron, the Indians made their tools of stone, bone, wood, and shells. Stone axes, stone arrowheads, stone hoes, wooden war clubs, and wooden bows were among their most important tools and weapons. 

Travel and Transportation: Canoes, Trails, Portages. 

The natural roads through the wilderness were the inland waterways. Along these the Eastern Indians paddled, either in dugouts or in bark canoes. Some of the plains tribes crossed the western rivers in circular bull-boats, which they made of buffalo skins. 

When the woodland Indians traveled afoot, they walked single file along narrow trails, which usually followed the older trails formed by animals treading their way to water. 

Some of the Indian trails were portages, along which Indians could carry their canoes and packs from one stream to another.

The Indian tribes in the eastern woodland area lived in houses made of a framework of branches covered over with strips of bark. Some of these houses had a long hallway down the center, on each side of which there were small compartments. In each of these compartments a family lived; and in the winter the cooking, which was done

THE INDIANS 

69 over wood fires in the hallway, smoked up the whole of the house.

Indian tribes on the great plains lived in tepees, which were made by covering a framework of wooden poles with buffalo skins. 

Indian tribes in the desert region lived in houses built of sun-dried mud and rocks. 

The Spaniards called these large community houses of several stories "Pueblos," which is Spanish for "town."

Indian Women.-The care of the Indian home and farming were the tasks of the Indian women. They plowed, they sowed, they harvested. 

Some of their corn crop they ground in stone and wooden hand-mills. The rest they dried and stored for winter. 

They cooked their meats over an open wood fire. Their corn and potatoes they roasted in the ashes of the fire. Meats they broiled on a spit suspended above the fire. They heated water by dropping hot stones from the fire into bowls of wood or clay or skin.

Indian Children Learn Forest Ways. 

While the mother was busy with her many duties, her baby, snugly bundled up, was left hanging from the branches of a tree, or it was carried on a small cradle board strapped to the mother's back.

Grown children, instead of going to school, obtained their education by watching their fathers and mothers at their tasks and by listening to the stories which older folk told. 

They heard stories of the spirits which were in the winds, in the thunder and lightning, in the sun and the moon and the stars. They heard of the spirit of the dew and the spirit of the rain. In some of the tribes the children heard of 

Manitou, the Great Spirit, who is above all spirits. 

But children had more to do than to watch and to 58 vilk 

Indian Moccasins listen to stories. They had to learn the ways of the forest. 

The girls learned to farm and to prepare food; to dress animal skins and to make them into articles of clothing; to gather the wild herbs and fruits and prepare the family meals. They were also taught how to behave themselves when in the presence of older people, how to care for the younger children, and in all ways prepare themselves to take up their duties as good members of the tribe. 

The boys were taught to observe the ways of the birds and beasts, and to imitate their calls. They learned to shoot birds on the wing, to trap the otter, the mink, and the beaver, to stalk and capture deer or other large game. 

Along the shaded forest trails the sharp-eyed Indian lad could soon read as well as his father the many signs which, although they were hardly noticeable, were filled

with meaning. Here a deer had passed, there a bear. 

At this point some Indian had camped. Not far away the carcass of a deer had been dragged. 

The Indian's Hunting Grounds. It has been said by white men that the Indian's idea of the after life was a Happy Hunting Ground where he could find plenty of 

PD Indian Weapons 

Among the Indian weapons were the stone war club and the bow and arrow. After the coming of the white men they learned to use guns. game and fowl. While on earth, however, his hunting ground often failed him.

When the crop from the garden patch was good, when the fish were in the streams, when the hunter brought in the deer and many brace of fowl, the Indians enjoyed the bounty of nature and feasted gluttonously. But when winter came, if their stock of dried corn and other food ran low and if game was scarce, the Indians faced months of famine. At such times a band of Indians might go prowling into the hunting grounds of their neighbors in search of game to save themselves and their fellow tribesmen from starving. A poaching expedition usually caused much anger in the hearts of the hunters whose grounds had been trespassed upon. 

War Councils. started trouble.

Forest Fighting. - Poaching often 

At a council of the head men, warriors and sages alike, the wise men of the tribe, some of them fiery orators, would arise and heap denunciations on the head of the enemy. Old wrongs would be recalled and recounted.

THE INDIANS 

73 The spirit of revenge would seize upon the men and they would declare for war.

To prepare for battle the warriors of the tribe painted themselves in lurid colors and danced a war dance to the sound of a beating drum. The rhythm of the drum beat, the shouting, and the leaping steps of the dance, made the men feel ready and fit for the conflict. 

Once on the warpath the

Indians fought in their own way. The plains tribes, for example, often fought pitched battles. However, the usual style of Indian warfare was a surprise attack, either shooting from ambush, or a sudden and unexpected raid. 

As a proof of their triumphs in battle, the Indian warriors carried off the scalps of their victims. 

The Fate of the Indians. 

Such were the Indians who 

The Indian Trail 

The woodland Indians walked single file along trails. These trails in many cases had been first made by animals treading their way to water. lived in the land to which the English were coming. They had much to teach the newcomers about the ways of the wilderness, how to fish and how to hunt, how to raise corn, tobacco, and other native crops, how to build canoes, and where the white men would find the most convenient portages. These things and much more of wilderness woodcraft the Indians were able to teach the white men, but almost from the beginning there was conflict between the two races. 

The white men won. Swiftly they increased in num-

bers, and steadily they pushed the red men back across the continent. Most of the Indians in the land to-day have accepted the white men's ways and live on a few reservations set aside for them by the white men's government. In recent years the Indians have been made citizens of the United States.

Civilization vs. the Wilderness. A Summary. A 

Glimpse Ahead. - Ever since the days of Egypt and 

Mesopotamia, civilization in Europe, Africa, and Asia had been advancing against the wilderness. Now that the 

Old World, aided by the tools and learning of civilization, had discovered America, the fight between civilization and the wilderness was to be carried into the land claimed by 

England. 

The explorers, the discoverers, the gold hunters, and the sea captains had only prepared the way. Now Old

World settlers were coming as home builders to make over the red man's hunting grounds into well-tilled fields and pastures. They were coming to build towns in which 

Old World civilization might be carried forward. They were, in fact, destined to lay the foundations of a nation which would make its own gifts to civilization.

CHAPTER VI Jamestown, A Pioneer Settlement 

English Men and Women After Many Hardships Plant Their First 

Successful Settlement in America at Jamestown, Virginia 

The Home Builders. In the story of our nation we will again and again read the name of famous leaders such as 

Columbus, Cabot, Balboa, De Soto, and Raleigh, but we must never lose sight of the fact that the true founders of our country were the men and women who, coming simply as home builders, planted the colonies which were one day to join hands as the United States of America. Common men and women living their lives from day to day, doing each task as well as they knew how, they were serving their new country better than they realized. In our nation today, in the millions of homes which the early colonists helped to make possible, other men and women performing their daily tasks are also serving their country. To those millions of men and women and to their children the story 77

of the first home builders, the founders of the American colonies, will always be interesting.

Leaving Civilization for Wilderness. -On December 20, 

1606, one hundred and fourteen years after Columbus sailed out of Palos on his first voyage, another fleet of three ships sailed out from England on an almost equally memorable voyage.

On board were about one hundred passengers who were leaving a country of towns and tilled fields, pasture lands and well-kept forests, broad roads and hospitable taverns, to enter a wilderness where only a few years before a whole band of settlers had disappeared as though the earth had swallowed them.

These passengers, gathered by the London Company, were a strange mixture. 

Some of the men were younger sons of the English nobility, back from the wars on the Continent. As the feudal law provided that a lord's title and land must go to his eldest son, the younger brothers were as a rule adventurers who had to carve out their own fortunes. 

They were called gentlemen, which in those days signified that they were men who did not engage in trade, or work with their hands. About one-half of the passengers were adventurers of this type. The rest were from humbler walks of life. A brave band they must have been to put out from England in such flimsy ships to win for their native land a foothold in America. 

Plan of the London Company. Common Storehouse. - 

The London Company, eager for quick dividends for their stockholders, had ordered the colonists to seek for gold and also to explore the rivers for a path to the Pacific and to China. Whether or not they found gold or a path to China, the men were to build a settlement, to produce whatever they could, to put their produce into a common

storehouse, and to ship to the company anything which might help the company to pay dividends. Food and tools were also kept in the common storehouse maintained by the company.

Such was the plan which the company hoped to see realized in Virginia, "Earth's Only Paradise," as one 

English poet called their goal.

Settling Jamestown. Hardships.-Sailing by way of the 

Canary Islands the ships reached the West Indies. From these islands they sailed northward to the mainland where they found a river which they named the James River. 

Thirty miles upstream the settlers landed on a marshy peninsula which they called Jamestown. This was in 

May, 1607. The land, for all its wildness, seemed a paradise.

The next day the settlers began to hew wood for the building of a fort. The site of Jamestown was well chosen for defense against the Indians. The river surrounded 

Jamestown on three sides and the fort was built on the fourth side at the neck of the peninsula.

The Jamestown settlers did not forget to provide a place for religious services. Their first "church" was simply a shelter made by stretching one of the ship sails across some poles. They built a better church as soon as they were able. Robert Hunt, their first chaplain, was a particularly devout man, much loved and respected by the people. The Jamestown settlers were Anglicans that is, members of the Established Church of England. 

To-day we would call them Episcopalians.

Long before the fort was finished, the Indians disturbed the settlers in their paradise. Gliding through the high grass near the settlement, the Indians shot down stray settlers with their stone-tipped arrows. 

Other hardships followed. When the summer rains fell,

the ground of Jamestown became a swamp. 

The days were much hotter than the settlers had known in England. 

Searching for gold and a path to China, the settlers had planted nothing to sustain them. They did not know how to hunt. The ship's supply of food had run low. When the ships left, each settler had as his day's portion only one ladleful of wormy wheat and barley from the common kettle." 

JOHN SMITH 

John Smith, although a boastful man, was also a practical leader who helped to save the colony of Jamestown. 66 Soon the men were so weak that they could not stand on their feet. By the end of the summer half the men were dead and just as it seemed that all must die, the company ship arrived with fresh supplies and more men. The colony was saved. 

Finding some yellow earth the newcomers set to work with a will to send back a cargo of the worthless stuff. 

Again food ran low. Again fever and famine did their deadly work and the settlement might have failed as Roanoke had failed if it had not been for Captain John Smith, who had come over among the first settlers. 

John Smith 

Braggart, Hero, or Both. John Smith was a soldier of fortune who enjoyed telling of his adventures. According to his stories he had been through hairbreadth escapes on the Mediterranean. In eastern 

Europe he had led two hundred fifty cavalrymen in a war against the Turks. Taken prisoner and forced to labor in a treadmill, he had slain his master, escaped by

horse through Russia, and traveled across Europe to England, which he had reached just in time for the Virginia adventure which promised fresh excitement. 

In his True Narrative of Virginia, John Smith tells how in Jamestown he soon had other hairbreadth escapes.

While he and two others were exploring the river seeking for China as the company had ordered, his men were slain by Indians, he was wounded and taken a prisoner to the village of the chief, Powhatan, who condemned Smith to death. The Indian warriors were raising their clubs to kill him when Pocahontas, the chieftain's daughter, rushed from her father's side and begged for his life. Her wish was granted, and Smith was returned to his people where he now became the leader of the settlement. Pocahontas 

Hers was a strange life. This 

Indian maiden, who helped save the 

Jamestown Colony, later married 

John Rolfe and visited England, where she was received as an Indian princess.

There are some people who doubt the story of Pocahontas as Smith tells it, but there is no doubt as to the value of 

Smith's leadership in the days that followed. He explored the rivers and the bays and he made careful maps of his explorations. He forced the men to work at useful tasks by denying food to idlers. He traded with the Indians for corn with which to feed the settlers. But above all he tried to secure for the colony a supply of men willing and able to work at those simple tasks which count in winning a foothold in a new country.

The Starving Time. In 1609, wounded in a gun powder explosion, Captain Smith returned to England, leaving five hundred men in the settlement. The following winter, known as the "starving time," saw much suffering in Jamestown. Supply ships sent from England with fresh recruits had been caught in a hurricane off the West Indies. One ship was wrecked and went down with all on board. When the others after many adventures and much delay arrived at Jamestown, they found only sixty gaunt and famished men. The rest had died. 

It was decided to abandon the settlement. The men all embarked and their ships were in sight of the ocean when they met an English fleet bringing provisions and still more settlers. All sailed back to Jamestown. colony was saved again. This was in 1610. 

The 

A New Drive in England. By this time back in England ministers were preaching sermons and writers were issuing tracts urging religious and patriotic reasons for supporting the colony by buying shares in the company. 

Within two years many lords, small landowners, merchants, shopkeepers, lawyers, masons, and others all subscribed.

The king granted the colony a new charter in which he agreed that the affairs of the colony should be managed by the shareholders. 

Common Storehouse a Weakness. Still the prospects of the colony were poor. Here were settlers depending for their food upon hostile Indians and upon a country three thousand miles away; many of them idling because all they produced would go into the company storehouse; because all shared alike in the common supplies. 

Three Acres to a Man. After a few years the company changed its plan. Each settler received several acres to till. Part of the corn he raised went into the common storehouse. The rest he could keep for himself. This

rule led many men to work with enthusiasm. Soon the colonists no longer depended on the unwilling Indians, or upon England, for their food. They cleared ground to raise more corn and vegetables. New settlements were built. 

Tobacco Their Gold. - Still the settlers faced a serious problem. What could they send back to England in exchange for the wool, cloth, and other things which they needed? The answer came when the settlers began to raise tobacco, the plant whose large leaves the Indians cured and smoked in pipes. 

Columbus had brought tobacco back from one of his voyages. Raleigh, who had received some of the leaves from his settlers in Roanoke, helped to introduce into England the habit of smoking.

Now it was this habit of smoking that saved the day in Jamestown. John Rolfe discovered how to cure tobacco. By 1619 tobacco grew in the streets of Jamestown and twenty thousand pounds were shipped to England. 

The Effect of Private Property 

When the colonists at Jamestown were given their own land and allowed to put their crops into their own storehouses, they worked with a new will. 

King James denounced the habit of smoking. He even wrote a treatise called "A Counter-blast Against Tobacco." 

But in spite of the "Counter-blast," the English people smoked and the colony in Virginia thrived. 

What gold and silver were to the Spaniards, tobacco became to the Virginia settlers. 

1619. Slaves. Land Grants. Self-government. The 

---

year 1619 was an important one in the life of the colony. 

In that year a Dutch man-of-war arrived from Africa with a cargo of negroes, who were sold as slaves. 

That same year Yeardley, the governor, arrived from England bearing news. At a meeting of the London Company it had been agreed that each colonist who had paid his way over should be granted fifty acres of land. The company had also voted that the colonists should have Virginia tobacco was shipped to England in exchange for goods which the colonists needed. representative government in America as Englishmen had in the mother country. 

Representative Government in England; in Virginia. 

In England in the year 1215, the nobles combining forces with the townsmen had forced the king to sign an agreement, the "Magna Charta," in which he promised to respect the rights of Englishmen to trial by jury, to freedom from unjust taxes, and from an illegal confiscation of property.

Later when kings continued their acts of tyranny, one of the nobles, Simon de Montfort, had called upon the nobles and upon two representatives from each of the towns and counties to meet in London in a Parliament. 

This Parliament was divided into the House of Lords composed of nobles and the House of Commons representing towns and counties. Parliament was to have the

right to pass upon the taxes demanded by the king. In time Parliament secured power to suggest new laws. 

In spite of the Parliament, the English kings continued to have very much their own way. In 1619 those members of the London Company, who believed in more power for the English Parliament, decided to grant a parliamentary form of government to the English colony in America. 

Yeardley had orders that each of eleven large "boroughs" or plantation centers along the James River was to elect two representatives to sit in a House of Burgesses corresponding in a way to the English House of Commons. 

These burgesses were to assist the governor and his council in making laws for the colony. 

At the first meeting of the House of Burgesses, which was held in the church in Jamestown, the institution of representative government was introduced into America. 

One of the acts of this first colonial legislative assembly was a declaration that the colonists could be taxed only by their own consent. 

1619: Homes.- Now with plantations of their own, and a voice in their own government, this new life in a new land promised to become worth while. 

Only one thing more was needed. Few women had crossed the water. If the planters in America were to become true home builders, they must have wives. 

Accordingly that same year the London Company sent over a boatload of ninety women with the provision that each of the planters whose courtship won him a wife should pay for the passage of his bride, the cost being one hundred twenty pounds of tobacco.

The ninety were soon married and sent home such good reports that others followed and soon the fields and forests of Virginia rang with the laughter of children — the first generation of the new Americans.

The First Permanent English Settlement in Amer ica. At Jamestown then a beginning had been made. 

The settlements on the James River supported by tobacco crops were growing; and in spite of an Indian massacre in 1622, which destroyed three hundred and fifty of the twelve hundred settlers, the colony continued to grow. 

The London Company gained little from the venture. 

In 1624 King James took the charter from the London Company and declared Virginia a royal colony. From that time on he appointed the governor and the council. 

Whether or not he would have permitted the planters to keep their House of Burgesses we cannot tell, for the next year King James died.

Before James I died the success of the colony in Virginia encouraged other Englishmen to plant a settlement many miles to the north of Jamestown. The story of that settlement is told in the next chapter.

CHAPTER VII Plymouth: A Refuge from Oppression 

A Brave Band of English Men, Women, and Children, Persecuted for Their Faith, Move to Holland, then to America, Where They

Pilgrims Land at Plymouth. Winter Hardships. 

a day in December, in the year 1620, almost one year after the first meeting of the House of Burgesses in Virginia, a handful of Englishmen stepped out of a small boat on to a rock in Plymouth Harbor. While a few stood on watch to guard against Indians, the others set to work to lay out plans for some log houses. The houses were to shelter not only themselves but also their fellow settlers men, women, and children who were aboard the Mayflower, which lay at anchor a half mile from shore.

So, on a bleak and wintry coast, three hundred miles from 

Jamestown, began the settlement of Plymouth. 

For months the men, rowing back and forth each day, carried on their work. They built a storehouse on a hill which commanded a view of the adjacent woods. On this house they mounted their cannon. At the foot of the hill they laid out ground for nineteen homes, and when enough 88

of these were completed, the men brought their wives and children to the shore.

Soon sickness broke out among them. The long and stormy voyage on the overcrowded ship with its one cabin, the stale water and the poor food, had weakened them. 

During the months of waiting in the harbor, the short rations and the cold winds, much colder than the wintry winds of England, weakened them still further. Before the winter was over, more than fifty were dead. eighteen wives, only four were living.

When spring came and the ship lifted anchor to return to England, the captain and the crew sailed with her. 

The rest, a score of men, a few women, and the children, remained.

Why Did the Pilgrims Remain? Old World Persecution. 

Who were these settlers? Why had they determined to build themselves homes in this wilderness which had used them so cruelly?

For answer we must turn to England in the year 1603, when James I was crowned king of the land. In that year there lived in the little village of Scrooby a small number of farmers, simple folk who were known as Separatists, because, disliking the services in the king's church, they preferred to worship by themselves under the guidance of their own ministers.

When Columbus was still a young man the Christian churches of western Europe were all Catholic and were ruled by the Pope who lived at Rome. Since Columbus's day, there had been a division in the church. Italy, Spain, Portugal, and France remained Catholic. England, Holland, Switzerland, parts of Germany, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark turned from the rule of the Pope and became known as Protestant countries.

In almost every one of the European lands the ruler

considered it his duty to force his subjects to worship as he did and to contribute to the support of the church which he favored. The kings persecuted those who differed with them. In some countries they put to death those who would not conform. 

THE KING FORBADE THEIR SERVICES 

In many European lands, small congregations met in secret in order to escape persecution. — - 

English Separatists Meet Secretly. At the time when these farmer folk in Scrooby turned from the king's church, which was the Established Church of England, Englishmen were not put to death for holding independent views in religion. However, royal officers were ready enough to find other punishments for those who refused to worship in the king's church or to help support it. For

PLYMOUTH: A REFUGE FROM OPPRESSION 91 

this reason the Separatists held their meetings secretly in the home of William Brewster, the young postmaster.

The Separatists suffered none the less from their neighbors who found many petty ways of persecuting them.

Brewster Suggests Holland as a Refuge. Things went on in this way for some years when William Brewster suggested a change. Years before, Brewster, who had been a university student at Cambridge, had been in 

Holland as secretary to Queen Elizabeth's secretary of state. In Holland he had seen how the Dutch permitted people of many different sects to worship as they pleased, and he now suggested that the small congregation should move to Holland, which was prospering. The farmer folk, none too well off at home, agreed.

The first time they tried to leave the country they were prevented by the king's officers and Brewster was sent to jail. Their second effort was more fortunate. A ship carried them to Amsterdam, where they remained a year. 

From Amsterdam they went to Leyden. In 

Troubles in Holland. Pilgrims Turn to America. 

Leyden they lived according to their faith; but now new difficulties beset them. The Separatists were village folk trained to till the soil. The Dutch among whom they lived were merchants, skilled craftsmen, fishermen. The Separatists, strangers in a strange land, unskilled in the callings which would bring them a good livelihood, labored long and hard at work which paid them very poorly. They saw their children falling from the faith for which they themselves had made such sacrifices. To make matters still worse, a twelve years' truce in the long war between the Spanish and the Dutch was drawing to a close; soon the country would be torn by war. 

Now, once again, Brewster suggested moving-this time to America. But where? Some spoke of Guiana, where

Raleigh had twice sailed up the Orinoco in search of El Dorado. But in Guiana they would be at the mercy of the Spanish. There was talk of joining the settlers on the James River, but this plan found few supporters. 

Dutch merchants offered to advance them money if they would settle at the mouth of the Hudson River, which was claimed by Holland, but this plan also had a serious weakness. In the approaching war with Spain, a settlement under the Dutch flag might prove poor refuge. 

Merchants Help. Mayflower Voyage. The Compact. 

Brewster helped to make the decision. He went to London where he received from the 

London Company the right to plant a settlement within the boundaries of its land grant. A group of London merchants offered to supply funds for the chartering of a ship and for all other necessary expenses, provided the 

Separatists would agree to certain terms. By these terms the value of all that the settlers would build and produce for the first seven years would be divided with the mer- 

Signing the Mayflower Compact chants. The Separatists, determined to let no obstacle stand in the way of the new life which they were planning for themselves and for their children, agreed. 

As a beginning, therefore, thirty-seven Separatists from the congregation at Leyden left for England, where they were joined by others, some of them strangers to their faith; and together they embarked on the Speedwell and the Mayflower. A short distance out, the Speedwell proved

A stormy voyage brought the Mayflower to Cape Cod, north of the grant of the London Company. As rocks and shoals made sailing southward difficult, the Pilgrims, after weeks of searching, chose Plymouth for their settlement.

Pilgrims on a Lonely Shore

When the Mayflower started back for England, the small band of Pilgrims in Plymouth felt themselves completely shut off from their Old 

World homes. 

heard mutterings among the strangers that in this land which lay outside the patent granted to them, each man would be free to do as he pleased and no law would bind any man. Through the cabin window, as they discussed this danger, the men could see the rocky shores, the gray skies, the dark forests of the New England coast. 

They knew that the wilderness would prove their grave unless they stood together. So there in the cabin they drew up a compact, combining themselves into a government to enact laws and to elect officers for the general good and to obey such laws and officers as should be chosen. This compact was an agreement and not in any way a constitution of an independent state, as has sometimes been said.

In the spirit of that compact the Pilgrims had stood together through the first few months at Plymouth, and when the Mayflower returned the rest remained, because here in the wilderness, far from the king's officers and from the alarms of the Old World wars, they were free to live according to their faith.

Standish was in command of the Pilgrim militia who guarded Plymouth against the Indians. The story of his suit for the hand of

Helpful. Treaty. Now with spring in the air, the Pilgrims, under the leadership of their governor, John Carver, prepared for the planting. 

Fearing Indian raids, Miles 

Standish, the captain of the

Pilgrim militia, trained his men for the time when battle should come; but in this, things turned out much better than he expected. 

One day an Indian, Samoset, walked into Plymouth and greeted the settlers in English which he had learned from fishermen who had come to Maine. The next day he brought Squanto. These two 

Indians taught the Pilgrims many things about Indian ways of getting food. Among other things the Indians showed the English how to plant corn by using small fish from the brook to fertilize each seed hill.

Once, after Samoset had been off in the woods for a few days' absence he returned with Massasoit, the chief of the Wampanoag Indians, and sixty of his men. When 

Samoset explained that they had come to make peace with

the white men, the Pilgrims invited Massasoit and a few of his men into the town for a conference. Carver, followed by the town drummer and the town fifer, paraded to the meeting in state. Together the Wampanoag Indians and the white men agreed to a treaty and smoked the pipe of peace. Their peace lasted fifty years.

The First Thanksgiving. - Soon after the visit of the 

Wampanoags Governor Carver died and William Bradford was chosen in his place. With the coming of autumn, the fields having yielded good crops, Governor Bradford set aside a day of Thanksgiving, as the President does to-day.

Together with Indian guests, the Pilgrims feasted for a week on corn, squash, and pumpkins, on wild fowl, and on deer. 

Private Property. Pilgrims Pay Debt. So the first year passed. More settlers came and the settlement grew slowly. But the debt which they owed to the merchants weighed on them heavily and they were held back by the habit of planting their fields in common as the Jamestown settlers had done. After a few years they changed this plan by dividing the land according to a new agreement with the merchants in England. This agreement permitted a number of the Pilgrims to assume the full debt of Plymouth on the condition that they have the sole right to the fur trade with the Indians. In time the debt was paid and the Pilgrims received clear titles to their land. 

Town Meetings and Representative Government. — In all these things the Pilgrims continued in the spirit of the 

Mayflower Compact. From time to time the Pilgrims met in town meeting to elect town officers and to decide on laws and taxes. When there were some other towns near 

Plymouth, the townsmen in their meetings elected not only their own town officers but also the governor of the colony as well as two deputies to represent each town..

By the election of town deputies to a general court, representative government was planted in New England as in Virginia.

Pilgrims Honored to This Day. 

Plymouth never grew very prosperous. poor people who lived simply off the fields, the furs of the forest, and fishing. But to this day the Pilgrims are honored for their simple faith in God, their courage, and their devotion to their form of religion. 

At last, then, in Jamestown and in Plymouth beginnings had been made. Jamestown proved that for the poor, America could be a land of opportunity. Plymouth proved that for the persecuted, America could be a place of refuge and freedom.

Taking heart from the success of the Pilgrims, thousands of men and women were soon to leave their old homes to lay in America the foundation of four New England colonies.

CHAPTER VIII The Great Migration. Four New England Colonies 

A Tyrant King Claims the "Divine Right" to Rule England As He Pleases.

Twenty Thousand English Men and Women, Led by Puritan Ministers, Migrate to the American Wilderness, Where They Plant Four 

New England Colonies - Massachusetts, Rhode Island, 

Connecticut, New Hampshire 

A Divine Right King and the Cavaliers. In the year 

1629, eight years after the Pilgrims ate their first Thanksgiving dinner at Plymouth, Charles I, king of England, disbanded his Parliament. Charles I was the son of 

James I. He had been on the throne only a few years, but like his father he believed in his divine right to rule England as he pleased. And because Parliament had angered him by trying to increase its political power, he 98

decided to disband Parliament and to rule England without its aid.

The members of Parliament returned to their homes as they were ordered, but the struggle between the king and his people continued.

On the side of the king in this struggle were many owners of the large estates, lords and sons of lords. These aristocrats who gave much of their time to hunting were such excellent horsemen that men called them "Cavaliers." Unlike the hard fighting lords of old who dressed in armor, the 

Cavaliers dressed in silks and satins; they wore their hair in long, flowing locks, and when they were not at their estates enjoying the pleasures of the hunt, they often were in London enjoying the pleasures of the royal court. 

Charles I Puritan Roundheads Per secuted by the King. - On the other side, among those who were fighting for more power, were the Puritans who included among their number town merchants, owners of small country estates, and yeomen who owned small farms. A few of the Puritan leaders were powerful lords. 

His tyrannical rule was one of the causes of the Puritan migration to 

America. 

These Puritans, like the Separatist Pilgrims, objected to the services in the Established Church, which they regarded as too elaborately ceremonial, but unlike the

Separatists they wished to remain in the Established Church. It was the hope of the Puritans that they could use their power in Parliament to compel the king to agree to changes in church services, as well as to grant their political rights.

To show their contempt for the long curls of the Cavaliers, many of those who were opposed to the king cropped their hair so close that men called them "Roundheads." 

Cavalier 

Parliament (to-day)

Roundhead 

In the struggle for political power the Cavaliers sided with the king against Parliament; the Roundheads sided with Parliament against the tyranny of the king.

The disbanding of Parliament enraged the Roundheads. 

But that was not all. Soon the king's officers were forcing 

Puritan ministers from their churches; they were flogging, fining, and even jailing Puritans who would not attend services in the king's church. To make matters worse for the Puritans the king, who was so oppressing them, was sending men to their homes to collect "loans" so that he could continue his rule without calling on Parliament to vote him taxes.

Sheep Raising Makes Life Hard for Farmers. - To add still further to the troubles of the times, the nobles were taking from the yeomen or small farmers the right to use

the village "commons" "commons" or village pasture land for their sheep and cattle.

The raising of sheep for wool had long been an important industry in England. For centuries English wool had been shipped to the Netherlands to be woven into cloth by Flemish weavers. Then during the war between Spain and the Netherlands many weavers had come into England, Urob blow 24400

Farms Became Pastures 

When English landowners turned their farms into pastures, many farmers without employment at home migrated to Puritan New England. and the wool which in the past had been shipped to the Netherlands for weaving was now woven and sold for a good price in London.

Because of the increased profits in sheep raising, the nobles were enclosing the village pastures for their own sheep. They were also using every opportunity to take over the farms of the yeomen for sheep enclosures. This. policy which hurt the yeomen hurt the poor landless farm laborers still more, since now one shepherd watching over his lord's flock took the place of many farm laborers.

The increased gold from America had caused prices to rise. The increased cost of living made life hard for those who were not prospering through England's growing trade and industry. 

Puritans in Massachusetts Bay Company Receive Charter. Seeing these hard conditions in England, a group of Puritans decided on a new plan. While some of their fellows would continue the good fight for liberty at home, they would lead a migration across the waters to a new England which they would make a Puritan land.

In the year 1628, even before Parliament had been disbanded, these men had founded the Massachusetts

Bay Company and had received a land grant in New

England. The following year 

Charles I granted them a charter which gave them the right to plant a colony in 

America. 

Governor Winthrop 

Winthrop was the first governor of

Massachusetts. He brought the colony's charter with him from England. 

In 1628, also, John Endicott and some forty settlers had built a settlement at Salem. When good news came from 

Salem, a few of the Puritan leaders in the Massachusetts Bay Company agreed to leave for America and to take the company charter with them so that they could rule their colony as they chose. 

John Winthrop, a country gentleman, was made the governor of the colony. A number of other landowners were appointed to act as his Assistants. Puritan ministers

were asked to come along and to bring with them as many of their congregations as possible. 

The Great Migration, 1630-1640. In the year 1630 eleven ships set sail. On board were John Winthrop and the Assistants with the precious charter. There were 

Puritan ministers and their congregations of farmers and other workers, with their wives and children. 

When the ships reached America and the passengers saw the wild unfriendly land, two hundred grew discouraged and returned to England. The rest landed at different points along the coast to build towns which they named Boston, Dorchester, Roxbury, and Newtowne (later renamed Cambridge), after their old homes in 

England. 

The following year thousands more came from England to New England.

Between 1630 and 1640 over sixteen thousand men, women, and children came to New England. This movement of the people from England into the wilderness is sometimes called the "Great Migration."

Towns and Town Meetings. The Town Church. 

Coming together as fellow townsmen the Puritans settled together in towns; and they decided their affairs in town meetings, as the Pilgrims were doing at Plymouth. In these meetings the leaders apportioned the land, giving a fair amount to each man who had paid for his passage. 

They also set aside a common pasture and woodland and agreed on a site for their church. 

The church, generally located on a hilltop, was the center of town life. In the beginning no house was built more than half a mile from the church where the settlers gathered on Sundays to listen to the sermon and on Thursdays for prayer. The ministers, who were learned men graduated from English universities, were looked to as advisers and

leaders. Both the people and the ministers regarded the 

Bible as their guide.

number of the Massachusetts towns combined to protest

Rhode Island. He was one of the early American champions of the ideal of religious toleration. against taxes imposed by the 

Boston officials. They asked for the right to elect deputies to represent them in Boston. 

In time they won the right, and so representative government was established in Massachusetts as it had been in Virginia.

Roger Williams Founds Rhode Island. - Not all of the twenty thousand English settlers who came to New

England remained in Massachusetts. 

When Boston was only a few years old, Winthrop and his Assistants found that there were colonists who objected to their rule. Some of those who were dissatisfied with the rule of the Governor and his Assistants left Massachusetts and laid the foundations of new colonies in the wilderness beyond.

One of those dissatisfied with Puritan life in Massachusetts was Roger Williams, who preached in the church at Salem. Williams did not believe that it was right to unite the church and the state. To his mind it was wrong for

the Puritan officers to pass laws demanding that all settlers attend Puritan churches, just as it was wrong for the king of England to demand that all Englishmen attend the Church of England. Williams argued that a man's religion should be no concern of the state, that his faith rested between him and God. 

Williams also argued that the English king had no right to give away land which in his opinion belonged to the Indians. He insisted that colonists could become rightful owners of the land only through purchase from the Indians. 

The Puritan leaders were outraged. They saw the greatest danger to their colony unless the people were held together by a common worship. Accordingly they ordered 

Williams banished to England but he fled into the woods. 

It was winter and icy cold, but a friendly Indian tribe sheltered him until the spring when he continued southward and founded a new settlement which he named 

Providence. 

Besides Roger Williams, the Puritan leaders expelled

Mrs. Anne Hutchinson, who angered the officers at Boston by the sermons she preached in her own home. Anne 

Hutchinson went south from Boston and settled at Newport. Soon more people of many different faiths came to settle in the region around Providence and Newport. 

Religious Toleration in Rhode Island. - In time Roger 

Williams secured a charter for all these settlements which were united under the name of the colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations. 

The colony of Rhode Island prospered and its success proved that people could live and work together, serving their common land in peace and good will, even though they worshiped God in different churches. In the Old 

World there were few places outside of Holland where religious freedom was permitted by law. Roger Williams

will ever be remembered in American history for his part in helping to establish in America the principle of religious toleration. 

Thomas Hooker Helps Found Connecticut. The Fron tier Moves Westward. In the summer of the same year that saw Williams banished from Massachusetts, still 

Moving into Connecticut 

Puritan settlers, attracted by news of the fertile Connecticut Valley, pushed westward to found a new colony. 

another minister showed his dissatisfaction with the rule of the Boston officials. Winthrop frankly enough said that the best government is by the few. But Hooker, who was the minister of the church at Newtowne, believed that all who had paid for their passage to America should have the vote. The Assistants refused. When news reached 

Hooker that the land in the 

Connecticut Valley was fertile, he led his congregation out of Newtowne. Driving their sheep and cattle before them, this little band went westward through the forest to the banks of the Connecticut River, where they built the town of Hartford.

In the English colonies, that march of a small band of men and women toward the western frontier marked the beginning of the winning of the West. 

Connecticut Constitution Sounds Principle of Democracy. In 1639 there was a meeting at Hartford. At that meeting the people of Hartford and of the neighboring towns of Wethersfield and Windsor drew up a constitution

for their colony. Their document, the first constitution made by colonists in America, expressed in almost every line the spirit of democracy, the desire of the people to rule themselves.

Before the constitution was adopted, Thomas Hooker preached a sermon in which he said, "The foundation of authority is laid in the free consent of the people." 

According to the constitution the settlers were to be ruled only by a governor and deputies of their own choosing, answerable to them.

Under this constitution, the towns on the Connecticut

River, together with settlements founded at New Haven, Stamford, and other towns along Long Island Sound, later received a charter which established them as the colony of Connecticut. The foundation of government is to be found in the consent of the governed. 

Every government building in the United States is dedicated to the democratic doctrine preached by 

Hooker in 1639. 

New Hampshire Becomes a Separate Colony. - The year 1636 was an exciting year for the leaders in Massachusetts. Roger Williams, banished, had gone south where he and his followers founded 

Rhode Island. Hooker had led his followers westward where they had founded Connecticut. About this same time word came from England that Sir Ferdinando Gorges, one of the owners of the land to the north, was urgently pressing his claim to the land which Massachusetts held, and that the king had upheld the claim of Gorges and was demanding the return of the Massachusetts charter.

When a similar report had come a year or so before, the Massachusetts men had voted funds for the building of a fort on the sea-front facing England and the troop ships which the king or Gorges might send over. But the troop ships never came. Now once more the colonists were anxious. But there proved to be no need to fight. The king and his followers soon had troubles enough at home without borrowing trouble in Massachusetts. Gorges never gained control of Massachusetts, but Massachusetts succeeded in gaining control of Maine, and governed it for many years; in fact, until some time after 1800. Settlers went north to build towns in New Hampshire, which, for a time, was governed as part of Massachusetts. After about fifty years of this rule New Hampshire became an independent colony. 

Pequot Indians Wiped Out. The year following 1636 

brought more excitement. Word came from the Connecticut Valley that the Pequot Indians were attacking the settlers in Connecticut and were plotting with the Narragansetts to attack the colonists in Massachusetts. 

Until this time the Pilgrims and the Puritans had had little trouble with the Indians. The Wampanoags had observed their treaty with the Pilgrims. The Narragansetts had once sent the Pilgrims a snakeskin filled with arrows; but when Governor Bradford had returned the skin filled with powder and ball, the Narragansetts had a change of heart. Now again when Roger Williams went among them to plead for peace, the Narragansetts yielded to his urging. The Pequots were left to carry on their war alone; but it did not last long. Puritan soldiers, aided by several hundred Indian allies, marched through the wintry snows to the Pequot encampment, a palisaded fort in the middle of a swamp. In the battle the Pequot fort was set afire and their force destroyed.

Daily Life in New England. The Sea. Now, with peace restored, let us turn to see the everyday life of the settlers in Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and New Hampshire. The long coast line of New England is indented with many harbors. The east coast is washed by the Atlantic Ocean, the south coast by Long Island Sound. Swift flowing rivers come rushing into the ocean and the Sound from thickly wooded mountains and hills covered with stubborn stony soil. The New England summers are short, the winters are much colder than the winters of old England. 

In the beginning the land was the sole support of the settlers. Clearing the ground of trees took time. Ridding the fields of stone was a huge task. Plowing the stony earth with wooden plows was not much easier. But vegetables were raised in the small gardens and corn grew in the cleared fields. Very early, too, cattle and sheep and hogs were brought over from England and the town shepherd watched over them as they fed. To add to the supply of food, the settler who learned how to use his gun and nets had bear meat, venison, wild fowl, and fish.

But how were the settlers to pay for clothes, tools, and other things which they would have to buy abroad? Although New England had no gold ore such as Spanish nobles found, and its stony soil yielded no such golden crop as Virginia tobacco, the New Englanders did have good harbors and the ocean offered them an added means of livelihood. The ocean had an abundance of fish which could be sold for coin. There was profit to be made by sailing the sea in New England ships as ocean carriers. 

For these reasons many yeomen trained as farmers in England took to the sea in New England. They became shipbuilders, fishermen, sailors, or ocean traders dealing with Virginia, England, Europe, and the West Indies.

MAP OF THE N. J. 

LONG ISLAND New York NEW ENGLAND COLONIES 

New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut were the four New England colonies. Plymouth, which had been independently founded, became part of Massachusetts. New Haven, which also started as an independent colony, was later joined with Connecticut. The disputed territory between New York and 

New Hampshire became the present state of Vermont. The present state of Maine was a part of Massachusetts all through Colonial times. 

The many harbors along the New England coast and the forests of oak which grew along its shores favored shipbuilding and ocean trade. Ocean fishing was also an important New England industry. 

Much of the New England country is either mountainous or hilly. There are few long navigable rivers, but many small swift streams. In Colonial times the smaller streams furnished power for grain and lumber mills. To-day this power is used for manufacturing. Colonial New England was almost wholly English in population. 

To-day the population of New England is largely of non-English stock. 

New England Immigration Decreases. When the colony of Massachusetts was about ten years old immigration to New England fell off for a while. In old England there was a turn in the struggle between the king and the

Puritans. The Puritans gained the upper hand and there seemed no reason for them to leave England. On the contrary, before many more years passed, the Cavaliers were leaving England to find refuge in America. 

When they left England, these Cavaliers turned to the royal colony of Virginia and to the other colonies which were growing up around Virginia.

CHAPTER IX Planters and Plantations. The Southern Colonies 

Five English Colonies- Virginia, Maryland, Georgia, North and South 

Carolina-Flourish South of Chesapeake Bay; Lordly Cavalier

Planters Hold Choice Lands Along the River Banks; Hardy Yeomen Till Their Fields in the Back Country 

Cavaliers Arrive in Virginia. - During the year 1649, and for some time after, the ships which sailed up the James River to Jamestown and beyond brought as passengers young English Cavaliers. Accustomed though they were to the pleasures of the king's court and to the excitement of the chase on the large wooded estates of their native land, the Cavaliers were coming to America to begin life anew among their friends. 

Tell of Civil War in England. -The planters listened eagerly to the news which the Cavaliers told of the turn of events which had led them to leave England. 113

At home the long struggle between King Charles and the Parliament had ended badly for the king. When the king, lacking funds, found himself compelled to call a meeting of Parliament in 1640, the king's enemies were numerous enough to have their own way. They ordered that two of the king's chief officers be put to death. They abolished special courts which the king had created for the persecu- They finally demanded that the king's army should take its orders from Parliament. 

The Cavalier tion of his enemies. The result of all these demands brought war which broke out in 1642. The king's troops were aided and led by the Cavalier lords. One army raised by Parliament to oppose the king was led by Oliver 

Cromwell, a Roundhead. 

Charles I Executed. Prince Charles Flees to France. 

England Becomes a Commonwealth. The war ended with the defeat of the king's forces. King Charles was taken prisoner, tried for treason, and executed. His son, Prince Charles, took refuge in the court of France, where many of the Cavalier lords joined him. Oliver Cromwell soon became the head of the new English government, which was called the Commonwealth. 

As for themselves, the newcomers in America told their hosts, being younger sons with little to look forward to either in Puritan England or in France, they had decided to try their fortunes in Virginia, where they knew that they would find friends.

Cavaliers in Virginia Receive Large Estates. - For twenty-five years Virginia had been a royal colony.

King

James, angered by the London Company, had taken away its charter and from that time on, English kings had appointed the governor. At the time when the Cavaliers arrived they found Governor Berkeley and his council ruling the colony with the aid of the House of Burgesses. 

These now made the Cavaliers liberal grants of land. 

Virginians Mostly Yeomen. 

The Cavaliers and wealthy planters were few but very influential. They maintained in Virginia the lordly and aristocratic traditions of England. A large proportion of the Virginians came from the class of English yeomen or farmers who had been attracted to Virginia by reports of its fertile soil. 

Indentured servants and slaves helped on the large tidewater plantations on the banks of the broad rivers which flowed through Virginia into the ocean.

Maryland. He championed religious toleration in the colony. 

Maryland a Refuge for

Toleration Act.-Just as Massachusetts was the center of the New England colonies, so in time Virginia became the center of a group of southern colonies. When the 

Cavaliers came to Virginia in 1649 there was a colony to the north named Maryland, in honor of Henrietta Maria, the wife of Charles I. King Charles had granted this territory to George Calvert, the first Lord Baltimore, a

Catholic noble, who was free to rule the colony almost as

a king except that the settlers were to be granted a representative assembly. 

Lord Baltimore died soon after the grant was made.

It was his son, Cecil Calvert, the second Lord Baltimore, who, late in 1633, sent out an expedition which built St. 

Mary's, the first permanent settlement in Maryland. 

Charles II Charles II, King of England, granted the Carolinas to eight nobles known as the Lords Proprietors. 

Calvert, as lord proprietor of the colony, declared that there was to be no established church in Maryland and that settlers of all Christian faiths were to be welcomed. In 

1649 he had the Assembly pass a Toleration Act which promised equal rights to all settlers of Christian faith. He hoped that Maryland would continue to be a refuge for his fellow Catholics, worshiping freely alongside of Anglicans, Puritans, and Separatists. 

Maryland Prospers in Spite of Troubles. - Maryland, like

Virginia, is a land of broad rivers. Chesapeake Bay cuts into the land for more than a hundred miles. Along the waterways of Maryland, the settlers raised tobacco as the Virginians did. Maryland had many trials and troubles: Indian wars; quarrels with the Virginians about the boundary; open warfare with 

Claiborne, a Virginian who laid claim to Kent Island; even civil war between the Puritans and the Catholics within the colony. Yet Maryland prospered. 

Charles II Rewards Friends. North and South Caro lina. Before long England was again a monarchy.

PLANTATIONS. THE SOUTHERN COLONIES 117 

Cromwell, who had ruled England, died. For a short while his son ruled and then the English people welcomed Prince Charles, who in 1660 returned from his exile in the French court to rule England as Charles II. By this time the English settlers in the colonies numbered about sixty thousand. The New England colonies were prospering, Virginia and Maryland were firmly planted, and Charles, looking to America, was well pleased because its wild lands gave him an opportunity to repay some of the nobles who had stood by him in the days of his troubles. 

Accordingly, he granted to eight nobles, the "Lords

Proprietors," a tract of land south of Virginia.

This land, like Virginia and Maryland, was well watered by long, slow-moving rivers. 

The northern part of Caro lina was thickly wooded, while 

The Yellow Pine the southern part had great stretches of open lowlands. 

Partly as a result of this difference in geography these two sections ultimately became separate colonies, known as 

North and South Carolina.

In North Carolina the settlers raised tobacco along the rivers, but the forests of pine served to build up a flourishing trade in such naval supplies as lumber, pitch, tar, and turpentine.

In South Carolina, the settlers, after trying many things, found that rice would grow in the moist lowlands, and for

this labor they bought so many slaves that in time there were more negroes than whites in the colony. The leading settlement in South Carolina was at Charleston, a wellprotected harbor on the coast. The proprietors at first tried to govern the Carolinas by a lordly rule, ill-fitted to the independent spirit of the colonists. Later the Carolinas became royal colonies, gaining steadily in population and in wealth. 

The Buffer Colony. Geor gia. After the settlement of 

Charleston, sixty-two years passed before the last of the Southern colonies was planted. This last was Georgia, which was in a position to serve as a buffer colony against the Indians and the 

Spanish in Florida. To people this colony, Oglethorpe proposed that men confined in prison in England for no other crime than their inability to pay their debts be freed from jail and helped to a new start in America. Parliament agreed; a new company was formed; and people gave money to aid the philanthropic cause. At the same time there was hope in England that the new colony with its hot climate might yield silk, olives, wines, figs, and other goods which England was buying at high prices from the countries of southern Europe. 

Old World Debtors 

In Europe people who could not pay their debts were jailed.

In 1733 Oglethorpe himself with about one hundred settlers built the port settlement of Savannah. Efforts to raise silk failed, and the colony after beating off an attack of the Spanish, who came up in force from Florida,

PLANTATIONS. THE SOUTHERN COLONIES 119 

finally settled down to the raising of rice with slave labor.

Life in the Southern Colonies. Planters and Yeomen. 

All told, there were five Southern colonies - Virginia, Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia all with very warm and lengthy summers, all well watered by rivers rising in the mountains more than two hundred miles back of the coast, all with rich black soil, so fertile that the earth hardly needed plowing. The principal products of these colonies were tobacco, rice, indigo, and naval stores. 

Along the banks of the rivers the wealthy planters lived almost like feudal lords. 

Back from the river stood the planter's spacious mansion. Behind the mansion were the cabins for the negroes and the other plantation buildings. 

James Oglethorpe In founding Georgia, Oglethorpe created a buffer colony between the 

Carolinas and Spanish Florida. 

Along the wharves at the river's edge ships were loaded with hogsheads of tobacco, as well as rice, indigo, and naval stores to be carried to England. On their return voyages, the ships brought back to the colonies furniture, silver, pewter, wines, and fashionable clothes.

Living in this manner, most of the Southern planters had little need for towns. Except for the two seaports, Savannah, Georgia, and Charleston, South Carolina, there were few large towns. Outside of the towns, the center of

MAP OF THE SOUTHERN COLONIES 

The Southern colonies were Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. Observe how Maryland is served by Chesapeake Bay. Note the long navigable rivers in these colonies; also the divide between the rivers flowing to the East and West. This divide marks the region of the Appalachian Mountain range. 

All through Colonial times, Charleston was an important seaport. 

In the East the population of these colonies was largely English, but on the frontier to the west and south the pioneers in the battle against the wilderness were mostly Scotch, Irish, and, to an extent, German. To this day, except for its negro population, this region is settled largely by the descendants of the original colonists. political life was the county court, and there from time to time the settlers gathered on election day to vote for their county officers and for the burgesses. 

A number of the wealthy planters, having plenty of

PLANTATIONS. THE SOUTHERN COLONIES 121 

time, gave much of their lives to politics, serving either on the governor's council or as burgesses. Through their agents in England they helped to market the tobacco of the smaller planters. They and their ladies kept open 

A Southern Ball Room. Eighteenth Century house, attended dances at the governor's court, and went fox hunting. As the South had few towns there were few schools, and the planter's sons were either educated at home by tutors or sent to England to study law so that they might better take their places in the life of the colony. The planter's wife was kept busy overseeing the work of her servants; and she and her daughters spent several hours each day embroidering, sewing, reading, playing the spinet, and chatting with their guests. 

In each of the Southern colonies the wealthy planters

numbered only a few hundred, and even with the aid of their many servants could have made small progress in the conquest of the wilderness.

Farmers, thousands in number, owned the less choice lands back from the river. As the years passed, new settlers who arrived had to go into the western country above the falls where the land was not at all suited to tobacco and where they had to be contented with the raising of corn, pigs, and cattle for themselves and for sale to the planters. Many of these new settlers were 

Irish and Scotch-Irish.

In the earlier years much of the plantation work was done by indentured or bond servants who had sold themselves into service for a number of years in order to pay for their passage to America. As the slave traffic increased, the number of slaves grew rapidly in all the Southern colonies, and the number of indentured servants was proportionately lessened. The use of indentured servants became far more common in the other English colonies, where, for various reasons, slave labor proved less profitable than in the South.

The Call of Free Land. Attracted by land free or almost free, fresh bands of settlers continued to pour into the Southern colonies and into the New England colonies as well.

How the territory between New England and the Southern colonies grew into four English colonies is another story which will be told in the next chapter.

Different Languages and Different Faiths English Fleet Sails for New Netherland. - Shortly after coming to the throne Charles II, looking at the map of his growing possessions on the coast of North America, saw that there was one weakness in his colonial empire. To the north lay the New England colonies. From Maryland 124

to the south lay the Southern colonies. These two groups of colonies were separated by hundreds of miles and in this intervening territory, the Dutch, who were the leading rivals of the English, were in possession. 

Without much ado, Charles made plans to take this territory from the Dutch so that the English colonies would spread in one long line along the coast. Accordingly he gave the territory to his brother, the Duke of York, and a fleet left England with orders to take over New

Netherland, which was the name of the territory held by Holland.

Buying Land from the Indians 

In some cases colony builders paid for Indian lands. In 1623 the Dutch governor, Peter Minuit, purchased Manhattan Island from the Indians for about twenty-four dollars' worth of wares. to-day; and here the Iroquois who hunted in the Mohawk 

Valley exchanged their furs for Dutch knives and hatchets, liquors, beads, and blankets. 

From New Amsterdam some traders went into the Connecticut River valley, but when the Puritans built Fort Saybrook at the mouth of the Connecticut River the Dutch withdrew from this region. 

Patroons Along the Banks of Hudson. To strengthen its hold on the Hudson Valley, the Dutch West India Company now tried to induce settlers to occupy New Netherland as the Cavaliers were occupying plantations

99 in Virginia. To this end, they offered the title "patroon and a great tract of land on the banks of the Hudson to any Dutchman who would take with him to the colonies at least fifty settlers, tools, seed, cattle, and all other things necessary for the beginning of a community of true home builders. These patroons ruled over their estates like feudal lords. 

Tenants ground their grain in the patroon's mill, and in many other ways lived after the fashion of feudal tillers of the soil.

Dutch Conquer New Sweden. New Amsterdam Grows.

By the year 1650 Spain had fairly well established her claim to territory reaching across the continent from Florida on the Atlantic to California on the Pacific. England had colonies in Virginia, Maryland, and New England. France (as we shall read in 

Chapter XIV) had established her claim to Newfoundland and New France which included the valley of the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes. Sweden claimed the territory bordering on Delaware Bay. Holland had settlements in the Hudson 

River valley and territory to the south. 

Within a few years after 1650 the Dutch conquered New Sweden and included it in their colony of New Netherland. In 1664 the English took over New Netherland. 

After that the rivalry for North America narrowed down to England, France, and Spain (except for Russia which appeared on the scene more than a century later to lay claim to Pacific coast territory from Alaska southward). 

Note how much of the territory which England, Spain, France, Holland, and Sweden claimed in 1650 is included within the present boundaries of the United 

States. 

this people who numbered only about a million. Living on low, marshy, thickly wooded ground which was little more than the mud deposited by the Rhine as it flowed into the ocean, chilled by cold winds, in constant danger of being flooded by the surrounding seas, the Dutch had mastered wind and ocean. They had harnessed the winds to windmills. They had built dykes to keep out the ocean. They had transformed their forests into ships and sailed the seas as traders and as fishermen. When the

Atlantic Ocean became the chief highway to trade and the planting of colonies, the Dutch, trained to the sea, were swift to take advantage of their seamanship. 

Dutch shipowners became carriers of the eastern spices which came to Portugal; Spanish gold flowed into Holland in return for lumber and grain and fish, for wool and cloth and leather, and the many other things in which Dutch merchants traded.

When the Dutch rose in revolt against Philip II, their ships traded directly with the East Indies. After the defeat of Spain, Holland with her great fleet of merchantmen became the carrying nation of the world. 

England's Reasons for Wanting New Netherland. 

In England the merchants and nobles who were advising King Charles in colonial matters pointed out that by sending the fleet to take over New Netherland he would not only give the English colonies in America a continuous coastline, but he would also weaken Holland, whose ships might some day become a menace to the whole of the English empire. One thing more they pointed out. With the middle harbors in English hands, it would be easier for England to enforce the laws which England had passed to prevent Dutch smuggling and to regulate colonial trade and navigation.

Colonists Dissatisfied with Stuyvesant Yield to English. In all of New Netherland at the time when the 

English fleet left on its important mission there were only a few thousand settlers and they were dissatisfied with Peter Stuyvesant, their governor, who ruled them in the name of the Dutch West India Company. The company had given them no share in the management of their colony; Peter Stuyvesant was even trying to interfere with their freedom of worship by demanding that all settlers must attend the Dutch Reformed Church.

The easy-going Dutch in New Amsterdam therefore paid no attention to Stuyvesant's demands that they resist the English fleet. They were few in number. The island was poorly fortified. The settlers, who had been informed by the English that they would enjoy more selfgovernment as an English colony than as a trading post for a Dutch company, refused to fight. New Amsterdam was surrendered, and with it the whole of New Netherland passed into English hands. 

Under English rule this middle territory was ultimately divided into four colonies New York, New 

Jersey, Delaware, and Pennsylvania.

When the Duke of York appointed a governor to rule over the colony, the people appealed to him for the right to have a representative assembly. The governor agreed rather reluctantly. Then, when King Charles II died, and the Duke of York ruled England as James II, he broke his promise. Later James 

II planned to unite New York with New England as a single dominion under a common government, and it was not until after he lost his crown in England that New York was granted the right to have an assembly. From that time forward the colony grew rapidly.

and to Lord John Berkeley the Duke of York gave a stretch of land south of New York which was named New Jersey, after the island of Jersey in the English Channel. 

When these proprietors sold their claims, the colony was divided for a time into East Jersey and West Jersey.

The Colony of Delaware. South of New Jersey lay 

Delaware, first settled by the Swedes, then taken from the Swedes by the Dutch, then from the Dutch by the English. 

This colony the Duke of York later sold to William Penn, who soon had Quaker settlements growing up beside Dutch and Swedish towns. 

Delaware, although one of the smaller colonies, proved most attractive to the farming type of settler, who found its rich, level land easy to cultivate and remarkably productive.
