William Penn Founds Colony of Pennsylvania. fore William Penn bought Delaware he had founded the colony of Pennsylvania. 

This Quaker aristocrat was the son of Admiral Penn, who had been a close friend of Charles I. As commander of a fleet, the admiral had helped to win for England the island of Jamaica in the West Indies, and he had every reason to be confident that his son William, studying at Oxford, would fare well at court. One day William returned home from college, having become a member of the Quaker sect with its gospel of equality, brotherly love, and peace.

Parliament, in the hands of the Cavaliers, was intolerant of Quakers and all other "Dissenters" who were preaching new ideas in church services or church creeds and were regarded as enemies of the king. The members of the king's party were determined to defend the Established Church against the teachers and followers of new sects. 

To the old admiral it seemed certain that his son's career would be quite ruined unless a change of scene should bring him to his senses. William was therefore persuaded to travel on the Continent, where he saw the pleasures of the continental capitals. He also saw the sufferings of the poor and the persecution of worshipers in

forbidden faiths. Shortly after his return to England, he was once again in the Quaker fold, only now as an active worker - preaching, writing pamphlets, conducting street meetings, even serving prison terms, as did many other 

Quakers. 

When the Quaker merchants bought a share in West Jersey, as a refuge for people of their faith, William Penn gladly joined in the venture.

From this it was but a step to his next plan. 

William Penn 

As the king owed his father a large sum of money, Penn asked Charles I for a grant of land. The king granted him forty thousand square miles west of New Jersey and named it Pennsylvania, or 

Penn's Woods, in honor of the old admiral.

Penn immediately proceeded with his plans to make 

Pennsylvania a Quaker col- 

William Penn, the Quaker pro- ony. The faith of the Quakers prietor and founder of Pennsylvania, championed the new social ideals: religious liberty and political democracy. was one which needed a New 

World for its trial. 

In 1682 Penn himself sailed up the Delaware River to a point where he helped to lay out the town of Philadelphia. The "Great Law," which his assembly adopted that same year at his recommendation, had many progressive features. It provided that there should be freedom of worship for all who believed in one God, that death should be the penalty only for murder and for treason, and that prisons should be workshops in which the condemned should be taught useful trades.

Penn Welcomes Poor and Persecuted. 

To help build up his colony Penn extended a welcome to the persecuted and the poverty-stricken whom he had seen on his travels. 

By printed handbills translated into French, Dutch, Swedish, and German, he let it be known on the Continent that in Pennsylvania the newcomers would be given land on easy terms and would be given a share in the government.

The news spread swiftly, and wherever the words were heard they brought new hope to men. Here was a promised land within a promised land, a colony where the disinherited of the earth would be given an opportunity to own land, where tillers of the soil, who had been oppressed by feudal laws, would be given the rights of freemen, and where men and women would be free to observe their faith without fear of persecution. To the poor toiling

Mennonites of Germany the words were flaming torches pointing the way to happier days. They lived in the Palatinate, east of France, and their land had been fought over for one hundred years. When the news of Penn's offer reached them, their unfortunate land was the scene of fresh horrors. 

Villages were burning. Fields were being trampled by contending armies. The cattle of the land were being devoured by the troops of friend and enemy alike. Whole towns, captured and put to the sword, were silent as the grave. 

How eagerly those who had saved a little money from the wreck and who were living as refugees in Holland rushed to the seaports to engage passage to America! How gladly those who had no money agreed with ships' captains to be sold into service for a term of years as a means for paying their passage. Other Germans besides the Mennonites came, as did also emigrants from Wales and Ireland. 

Many died on the ships which greedy shipowners overcrowded; but those who arrived joined with large numbers

of Quakers who came from England to transform Penn's

Woods into a region of busy towns and well-cultivated farms. 

The English, for the most part, remained in the East. 

It was largely through the pioneering courage of the Irish, the Scotch-Irish, and the Germans that the frontier of the

ATLANTIC OCEAN 

New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Delaware were the four Middle colonies.

Note the many long navigable rivers in this area and observe the location of mountain ranges. See how the Hudson River and its branch, the Mohawk, served the colony of New York. Observe the value of Delaware Bay to New Jersey, Delaware, and Pennsylvania. From the beginning, these Middle colonies with their splendid shipping facilities and their fertile river valleys attracted settlers from many parts of Europe, and to this day the population of this region is a blend of many nationalities.

This dispute was not settled until 1767, when both colonies accepted the Mason and Dixon Line, named after the surveyors. 

The Middle Colonies: America's First Melting Pot. 

New York, New Jersey, Delaware, and Pennsylvania were

four Middle colonies midway between the New England and Southern colonies in position and also in other respects, as we shall read in the next chapter. 

In the Middle colonies, Dutch, Swedes, Germans, Swiss, French, English, Irish, Scotch-Irish, and Scotch met on common ground. Many of these groups settled near the coast in small communities of fellow countrymen, or still clinging together they went into the back country. Others, groups of settlers drawn together as neighbors by common needs and common dangers, mingled and intermarried. 

This mingling of Old World peoples marked the beginning of what has since been called the New World "melting pot."

The Americans: Founders of a Nation. To the north in the New England colonies and to the south also, in Maryland, Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia, newcomers from other lands lived in peace with the English settlers. It was to be only a question of time when here, too, the home builders, intermingling, would produce a blend of Old World stocks. 

99 These Americans in their colonies on the frontier of civilization, living three thousand miles from the shores of Europe, were laying the foundations of a new nation which was one day to lead the world. In the next section we shall observe more closely the life and problems of the colonists in their New World homes.

The Good News: America

Where Jarm and Wilderness Meet  CHAPTER XI Character and Geography Play Their Part The Colonists, Though of Different Faiths, Have a Common Character and 

Spirit;

Their Colonies, Although Varying in Soil and in Climate, Possess Common Advantages The New Americans Differ in Race, Faith, and Rank. - 

The men and women who settled in the English colonies differed in a number of ways.

They were of different races. There were English, Scotch, Irish, and Welsh colonists - all from the British Isles. There were colonists from Germany, Holland, Sweden, Switzerland, and France.

The colonists belonged to different religious sects. There were Catholics and Episcopalians; there were Congregationalists, Presbyterians, Quakers, and members of many other Protestant sects. In the Southern seaports there were French Protestants, known as Huguenots, seeking refuge from the persecution of French kings. In a few of the seaport towns there were Jewish colonists. 141

The colonists differed in social rank. The leaders in the colonies were the wealthy planters in the Southern colonies, the lordly proprietors and patroons in the Middle colonies, the merchants and the ministers in the New England colonies. Below these in rank were the owners of small farms. Farther down in the social scale were free laborers who owned no land. Still lower in rank were the indentured servants who had been sold into service to pay their passage to America. Lowest of all were the slaves. 

The Common Spirit of the Colonists. -In spite of these differences in race, nationality, religion, and rank, the colonists who had come to America of their own free will were not entirely unlike. 

The majority of the colonists were English; their common language was English; their government was English. 

In religion the Bible was the common guide of the colonists.

In social rank the colonists were largely of the farmer type, free men who owned their own homes and land. The indentured servants and the free laborers in the towns could both look forward to the day when they too would be farmers tilling their own fields.

Almost all who had come to the colonies of their own free will were possessed of a common courage. Some had come because of the opportunity to own land; others had come to find religious freedom. Still others may have come for the sheer love of adventure. But one and all, they were brave men and women willing to risk the task of beginning life anew in America. They were also determined men and women, with their hearts set on making the most of their new environment. 

Geography Plays Part in People's Lives. To appreciate the way in which the colonists solved their problems, we must first know the geography of their new homes. In

CHARACTER AND GEOGRAPHY 

143 Egypt, with its long, slow-flowing rivers, the people had lived by farming. In Phoenicia and Greece, small countries with good harbors, men had turned to the sea and trade. Rome, midway between the rich countries of the 

Mediterranean and the wild lands of western Europe, had turned to soldiering and enjoyed the fruits of conquest. 

With the discovery of America the countries facing the 

Atlantic - Spain, France, Holland, and England — rose to power. At every turn the geography of the Old World lands had helped to mold the lives of the people. 

So, too, in America.

The Coastal Plain. The Soil. The Forest. The Ocean. 

- The colonists made their homes on a coastal plain, well watered by rivers, with excellent harbors, with a climate ranging from the long cold winters of New England to the long warm summers of South Carolina and Georgia, and with a good average rainfall.

This plain, with its long coast line on the east and shut in on the west by the Appalachian Mountains, was thickly wooded. In the forests the deer, the beaver, the marten, the mink, and other animals valuable for their furs abounded. 

The forests also yielded good timber for fuel and for the building of ships and homes. 

The ocean served all the colonies as a common road which connected them with one another and with Europe. The ocean also led to the fishing banks, off the coast of Newfoundland, and to the West Indies where the French, the English, the Spanish, and the Dutch owned sugar plantations worked by Negro slaves. As these West Indian planters found sugar growing very profitable, they neglected to cut lumber for building. Nor did they take the trouble to grow food. Thus, the mainland English colonies soon began a lively trade with the West Indian planters, supplying them with the things which they needed.

Colonial Industries FARMING FUR TRADE PITCH-TAR-TURPENTINE FISHING AND SEA TRADE SHIP BUILDING 

Although this was in general the geography of the colonies, the New England group, the Southern colonies, and the Middle colonies differed from one another in character. 

The New England Colonies. Hilly Country. Swift Rivers. Harbors. In the 

New England colonies outside of the fertile Connecticut River Valley, the Puritans found stony hill country. The slope of the coastal plain is fairly steep and small rivers flow swiftly to the coast which is indented by many harbors. 

In these harbors or inland on the banks of the rivers, particularly near waterfalls where mills could be built, the New Englanders lived in small villages or towns. 

Because of the broken country and the stubborn soil, the

New England farms were small, and the New Englanders, like the Greeks and the Phoenicians, turned to the sea to add to their income by fishing and by trading. The 

West Indies, which were much closer to the colonies

CHARACTER AND GEOGRAPHY 

145 than to England, furnished the New Englanders with a good market for their fish, their lumber, and the lath and barrel staves which they made around their fires during the long winter nights. The barrels made from these staves came back to New England filled with West Indian molasses which was made into rum. This rum, carried to 

Africa, aided in the purchase of slaves who were carried to the Southern colonies, and to the West Indies where they were exchanged for fresh cargoes of molasses. 

The Southern Colonies. Slow Rivers and Level Fertile 

Fields. In the warm Southern colonies, the coastal plain was level for miles inland, the rivers were long and slow-flowing as in Egypt, and the soil was fertile. Here the wealthy planters owned large tobacco, rice, and indigo plantations which their help was able to work the year round. In the low hill country above the waterfalls, farmers raised corn and live stock. The forests of the 

South yielded furs as well as pitch tar and turpentine. 

The many navigable rivers of the South made it easy for population to spread far inland. 

The Middle Colonies. Combines Features of North and South. The Middle colonies were in all things midway between the New England and the Southern colonies. 

The winters in the Middle colonies were not so cold or so long as the New England winters. The summers were not so warm or so long as the Southern summers. 

In the Middle colonies a number of rivers, the Hudson, the Mohawk, the Susquehanna, the Delaware, flowed through fertile river valleys where the farms were large. 

In the Middle colonies there was also broken hill country, with swifter, shorter streams suitable for mills. Along these streams the farms were small. The good crops of wheat and corn raised in the Middle colonies furnished a surplus which was ground into flour for the West Indies trade.

Also in the Middle colonies a few seaports and river towns near the ocean shared with the New England and the Southern seaports in the profits of ocean trade. 

The Backwoods.- From New Hampshire to Georgia, in the great backwoods which lay west of the coast settlements, there lived many colonists who gained a livelihood directly from the soil and forest.

Such, then, was the geography of the wilderness in which the colonists were now finding food and clothes and shelter, and all unaware of their mission were laying the foundations of a great nation which was to carry forward the arts of civilization.

CHAPTER XII Civilization's New Frontier The Colonists Bring Into Their Wilderness Homes Many of the Old World Ways, Ideas, and Ideals Wilderness Conditions Favor the Development of New Ideals: Political Democracy, Religious 

Toleration, and Spirit of Brotherhood The Common Land. A New Frontier of European Civilization. By the year 1733 the British colonies stretched along the Atlantic coastal plain, from New Hampshire in the North to Georgia in the South. To the east the ocean three thousand miles broad separated them from Europe. On the west the Appalachian Mountains shut them in.

The colonies which the settlers from Europe planted on this coastal plain marked a new frontier of that civilization which had been moving westward across Europe ever 148

since the day of Greece and Rome. The colonists brought with them to America many of the tools, the industries, and the habits of thought to which they had been accustomed in their old home. The ways of European civilization were being transplanted westward to American soil.

Getting Food. Farming in the Old World Way. The colonists learned many things from the Indians; but as they had brought with them the Old World tools they did not farm in Indian fashion.

For their first clearings, the colonists girdled the trees as the Indians did and in these clearings they raised Indian corn. Soon Old World axes were hewing down the trees

to make larger clearings in which the colonists planted wheat, rye, oats, and other Old World seeds.

In tilling their fields the colonists used Old World plows. 

They reaped their crops with Old World scythes. At an early date they built flour mills to grind their corn in the 

Old World way. 

The North American Indians depended for their meat upon wild game. ད་ The colonists brought into America cattle, sheep, pigs, and goats. 

They also brought over horses and oxen to help them in their farming.

Farming became the principal occupation in the colonies, but hunting and fishing helped to lend variety to the colonial diet. 

Old World Clothes. In clothing themselves, as in farming, the colonists intro duced Old World styles. Al though farmers in the back country wore deerskin clothes as the Indians did, colonial clothes as a rule were made of woolen cloth and linen. 

Spinning Wheel and Winder 

Farmers raised sheep for wool and flax for linen. Women spun woolen or flaxen thread on a spinning wheel, an invention which had only recently come into use in Europe. In many homes women wove thread into cloth and made the finished garment as well. Some farmers prepared leather for aprons, shoes, or breeches, as well as for harness.

In a few towns men set up shops in which they made hats from beaver skins. 

Wealthier colonists often imported their clothes from

England coats of velvet and plush, silken knee-breeches, 

---

silk hose, shoes of fine leather trimmed with silver buckles.

For their wives they bought gowns of chintz, calico, and brocaded cloth, fashionably made with hooped skirts supported by a wire frame. MonLog

Types of Colonial Homes 

Building Homes. Sawmills. Brickyards. In building their homes, as in feeding and clothing themselves, the colonists brought with them Old World standards of comfort. Their first homes were, as a rule, made of logs which they hewed from the forest and trimmed so that they would fit into place. With the aid of neighbors a colonist was able to raise his log cabin in a few days.

Then as their settlements prospered, the colonists introduced the Old World sawmills, with metal saws which cut the logs into boards for the building of handsome frame houses. A type of colonial home developed later in the 

South was the stately planter's mansion, with its broad 

Betty Lamps porches and its balconies built all the way around the house. 

Both in the North and in the South some homes were built of brick imported from 

Europe or made in colonial brickyards. 

Heating and Lighting the Home. Cooking. The colo nists heated their homes by burning logs in stone fireplaces which had outside chimneys such as they had known in Europe. As matches had not been invented, the colonists tried to keep their fires from going out each night by covering the live coals with ashes. To start a fire the colonists used flint and steel, or they had to borrow live coals from a neighbor. The fireplace served as a stove and oven. It also helped to light the house. Occasionally home-made candles were burned. In some homes lamps burning whale oil were used. 

A type of lamp in which whale oil was used as fuel

Paper dipped in fish oil served as windows, except in the homes of those who could afford to import clear glass, a new European luxury.

Furnishing the Homes. Colonial Cabinet Makers. — 

Most colonists, in coming to America, brought little furni-

ture with them, except bedding and chests. The first new pieces of furniture they made in a rough-and-ready way like their log houses, but soon there were chairs and tables, beds, and finely carved chests made by colonial cabinet makers. When clocks and mirrors, writing boxes and writing tables came into fashion in England, the local cabinet 

Early Colonial Chest makers used similar designs in manufacturing furniture to compete with that imported from the mother country. 

Transportation. Canoes, Ships, Pack Horses, Coaches. 

-The Indians, who traveled either by canoe or on foot along forest trails, knew the country well and the paths they took pointed the way for the white men. 

Many of the settlers who moved inland went afoot, following the Indian trails. Others followed the waterways in canoes, built in Indian fashion. The white men introduced into New World travel the Old World sailboat, which sailed on the navigable rivers and along the coast. In overland

Canoe Pack Horse 永​康 ​Stagecoach Sailing Vessel travel the colonists introduced riding horses and pack horses.

After the colonists had widened the Indian trails into roads and had built bridges across the streams, stagecoaches came into use between the principal cities. 

One stagecoach, advertising itself as the "Flying Machine," boasted that it could cover the distance between 

New York and Philadelphia in two days. This was accomplished if the roads were not too muddy. 

Within the cities wagons were drawn by oxen or by horses. The wealthier citizen rode in horse-drawn chaises or coaches.

Colonial Newspapers. 

Communication. 

Mail. In 

colonial days, the colonists had no means of communicating with one another swiftly.

In America, as in the Old World, there were no telephones, no telegraphs, no wireless. These things had not yet been invented. Communication therefore could be only as swift as transpor-

tation. The colonists along the coast depended for their news on the arrival of ships from Europe or of coastwise sailing vessels from the other colonies. When the stagecoaches came into use, they helped in spreading news. 

In the year 1704 a newspaper appeared in one colonial city. In time there were newspapers in all the larger towns. 

These papers unlike the papers of to-day usually contained little real news concerning conditions in America and little important European news. They had many advertisements which help to give us a picture of life in colonial days advertisements of ships and their cargoes, of rewards offered for the capture of runaway slaves or bond servants; and other such items. 

Rougher Life in Backwoods Settlements. - As inland travel was still difficult and dangerous, few of the luxuries of civilization were carried into the backwoods settlements. 

In the backwoods, settlers depended for much of their food upon hunting. The men wore deerskin trousers, hunting shirts, and moccasins, all made more or less Indian fashion. 

Within the palisaded walls of their settlements, the backwoodsmen and their families lived in rough log cabins. The furniture was home-made and simple. Fields were cleared outside the settlement wall; and here crops of grain and vegetables were raised, not so much for sale as for the needs of the settlers themselves.

Colonial Industries. Beginnings of Manufacture. 

In all the colonies farming was the principal industry. At least nine out of every ten people worked on farms or plantations. New England and the Middle colonies yielded a surplus of foodstuffs, grain, and meats for export. The 

Southern colonies produced tobacco, rice, and later, indigo and naval supplies.

We have read how, side by side with farming, the colonists were carrying on other industries — fur trade, fishing,

Tobacco Furs 

Corn (נננננט 

Wampum shipbuilding, commerce, and even a small amount of manufacturing. In New Eng land during the long winters colonists made wooden pegs, laths, and barrel staves. In 

Pennsylvania metal workers smelted iron ore and made iron implements for sale. In all the colonies artisans made shoes, hats, cloth, furniture, wagons, harness, and other things of daily use. 

Barter. Forms of Money. 

- Because the goods which the colonists imported were mostly manufactured articles costing more than the raw materials which they exported, they could get little surplus money in exchange for their wares. For this reason they had to trade by means of the old method of barter.

In paying for services as well as in trading, the colonist used farm products or fish in place of money. A minister might be paid in potatoes or corn or tobacco. A teacher would be paid largely in board. In some colonies taxes and bills could be paid in

corn, tobacco, or fish, with values fixed at so much a measure or a pound.

As the wampum shell, carefully ground down and drilled through in the shape of a bead, was highly prized among the Indians, the Dutch colonists manufactured wampum which they used for trading with the Indians. Furs also had a fixed value and were used as money.

Colonial Women. So far, we have read mostly of the colonial men. Now let us see the part which the wives of the colonists played in conquering the wilderness. 

Without their wives the men would have been little more than adventurers. The women colonists were the true home builders.

The Colonial Woman 

In the new country colonial women played a vital part. The establishment of permanent colonies and the victory against wilderness conditions would have been impossible without their unremitting toil. 

The wives of the Southern planters and the wives of the Dutch patroons had slaves and bond servants to help them, but the rank and file of colonial women did their tasks without the aid of servants. They cooked and they

baked, they scoured and they polished, they laundered the clothes which they had spun and woven, they planted the vegetable gardens, they preserved fruit and vegetables for the winter months. They looked after the barnyard fowl. They cured the sick. They educated their children. 

They gathered and dried herbs and berries. They compounded drugs. They made candles of bayberry or tallow.

They made their own brooms. They mended the clothes of the family. Most important of all they cared for their children who in many cases numbered twelve or fourteen to a family. 

Colonial Boys and Girls. The children of colonial parents were very helpful about the home. 

For the boys there was wood to chop, the cows to fetch and milk, errands to run, the setting of traps in the woods, even fishing and shooting of game. Boys learned how to handle a jack-knife for cutting lath and barrel staves, and for making other things of home manufacture. 

When they were scarcely in their teens, boys who lived near the sea signed up each winter with the fishing fleets. 

Some went out to the fishing banks off Newfoundland. 

Others sailed away in whalers which carried them into the 

Arctic waters. Through the spring, summer, and fall boys worked in the fields with the grown men.

A Colonial Cradle 

The girls also learned to help. They shared in the household tasks, helping their mothers with cooking, baking, soap-making, cleaning, candle-dipping, laundering, and mending. They helped with the garden and chickens. They brought water from the spring. They gathered berries, herbs, fruits, and

nuts - tasks which were none the less useful for being pleasant. 

Colonial Schools and Education. All during the years when colonial boys and girls were helping their fathers and mothers with their tasks, they learned many things to prepare them for the time when they, too, would be home builders. The fathers and mothers knew that for further education, schools which would teach at least reading and writing were necessary. 

In the South, where towns were few and far between, schools were not common.

The children of the planters were taught at home by private tutors or were sent to England to complete their education. Here and there the children of the poorer colonists were taught by their minister in classes connected with the parish church. 

In the Middle colonies the Dutch churches provided classes for the education of the children in their congregations. In a few towns elementary and grammar schools were introduced, but in the Middle colonies, as in the Southern colonies, many children were privately tutored. 

In New England the Puritans decided that it was the duty of every town to provide for the schooling of the young. In Massachusetts, at an early date, the General 

Court passed a law ordering every town of fifty householders to engage a teacher to instruct the children in writing and reading. A township of one hundred householders was ordered to support a school to prepare boys for college. 

Laws providing for free schools were soon passed in other 

New England colonies. 

One reason for the interest in schools and education was the desire of parents to have their children able to read and to write so that they could become more familiar with the Bible. The colleges which were established in the colonies were intended to help prepare students for the

ministry. The earliest colonial college was Harvard, established in 1636 by the General Court of Massachusetts. 

It was built at Newtowne, which was renamed Cambridge after the English university in which many New England ministers had been trained. The second oldest college in 

America, and at least equally famous for its long line of TH 

The College in the Wilderness 

It is a remarkable fact in American history that men built colleges in wilderness country, even before the danger from the Indians was well past. 

From these colleges there have come many of the nation's leaders. distinguished graduates, is William and Mary College, founded in Williamsburg, Virginia.

All through the colonial period girls were not admitted into colleges; girls were not as a rule encouraged to learn more than writing and reading; arithmetic was not for them. For the boys, reading, writing, and arithmetic made up the greater part of school studies. 

We must not think of all the children of the Northern and Middle colonies as going to school nor of all the Southern children as privately tutored. The fact is that with the hard conditions of life, many, particularly the poor

and those who lived on the farms, had to do without the privilege of schooling. Nevertheless it must be remembered that the early colonists did lay the foundation for the public school, the high school, the college, and the university of to-day. 

Sciences and Arts in the Old World. The colonists then had schools and even colleges; but did the arts and sciences flourish in the colonies as they did in the Old 

World? This could hardly be expected.

Since the beginning of the Renaissance, the Old World had seen some of its greatest triumphs in the sciences. 

With the aid of the newly invented telescopes, Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, and Newton had been exploring the heavens, adding immeasurably to all that men had learned before their time. In England Lord Bacon had written his Novum Organum, which was a trumpet call to all scientists to observe and experiment more and to base their theories only on the results obtained in their laboratories. Harvey had discovered the true function of the heart, and by his discovery gave the studies of anatomy and physiology a new start. So in other sciences men learned more of nature and her laws. 

During the time of Columbus, of the gold hunters and colony builders, Europe had been excelling in the arts. 

In Spain the art of the story teller reached its climax in the work of Cervantes in his Don Quixote, and the art of painting found great masters in Velasquez, Murillo, and El Greco. In Flanders after the war with Spain, Peter 

Paul Rubens painted his canvases of the abundance of life, pictures of powerful men and beautiful women aglow with the color of health, pictures of wild animals in luxuriant landscapes. And while he painted this abundant life in which kings, queens, merchants, angels, satyrs, and goddesses cross the stage, Teniers the Younger painted

scenes picturing workers and their wives, soldiers back from the wars, the village fiddler, and the village dance. 

So in Holland, Rembrandt and Hals, masters of portraiture; Hobbema and Ruysdael and Cuyp, lovers of the

Dutch fields and forests; Ter Borch, De Hoogh, Vermeer, and Metsu, who sang in color of the beauty of the homeall painted their canvases. 

In England at about the same time, Van Dyck, pupil of Rubens, painted his portraits of the family of Charles I and of many Cavaliers. Shortly before Van Dyck's time 

William Shakespeare carried the old art of drama to new heights in plays which have found an audience ever since his day.

And while Shakespeare was giving to spoken English a new richness of meaning and of pattern, scholars were translating the Old and New Testaments into an English version, the King James Version. The Bible, even more than Shakespeare's plays, helped to shape the language of the English people, giving form to their thoughts and expression to their feelings. 

Sciences and Arts in the Colonies. - Now when we turn from the Old World to the colonies in 1689, we see that America is after all still a wilderness, where men are struggling to maintain Old World comforts, but can hardly aspire as yet to Old World culture. In literature men like 

John Smith, Governor Bradford, and many others, writing the records of their colonies, had made something of a contribution to the world's readable books. In 1636 a printing press was established at Harvard. Other presses followed. For the most part the books printed were volumes of sermons written by the ministers. 

From 1607 to 1689, while Europe had a host of great artists and scientists, the colonies had no great poet, no great playwright, no theater, no painters, no sculptors.

But the home builders did not lack for good literature, since almost every English-speaking home had a copy of the Bible.

What a part the Bible played in the lives of these colonists! Differ as they might about the way in which they understood its meaning, almost all looked to it for guidance. 

The early colonists naturally had little time for either the sciences or the arts. But toward the end of the colonial period there was one colonist, Benjamin Franklin, who won fame among the scientists of the world by a kite-flying experiment through which he proved that lightning and electricity are one.

Toward the end of the eighteenth century there were able colonial painters, most of whom received their training in England. A few colonists had private libraries which contained plays, poems, essays, and novels, written in England at the time. Benjamin Franklin started a subscription library which helped to prepare the way for the public libraries of our own time.

In the main, the colonists read little except their newspapers. Franklin was a newspaper publisher; he also published Poor Richard's Almanac, a farmer's calendar into which he introduced proverbs containing homely wisdom. 

Franklin also wrote an Autobiography, which was an interesting contribution to world literature. 

We have seen

Religion in the Life of the Colonists. 

that the one book which could be found in almost every colonial home was the Bible, and that religion had played a large part in the lives of the colonists. 

In Virginia, and in some of the other Southern colonies, there were many members of the Church of England. In 

Maryland there were many Catholics. In the Middle colonies the sects were more numerous. In New England the 

Puritans attended their Congregational churches. On Sun-

days and on Thursday nights the Puritans held services, and in many towns all were forced to attend. Sermons often lasted two hours. In the summer the beadle woke those who fell asleep by tickling them with a rabbit's foot attached to a rod or by poking them sharply with a stick. In the winter it was not difficult to remain awake, for the churches were very cold and only by the aid of foot warmers and wood stoves could the congregation keep from freezing.

The church was not only a place for worship; it was a meeting place where the people could gather as neighbors to talk over their troubles and their joys. In New England for a long time the

Puritan ministers had considerable influence in holding the settlers united for their common good and against common enemies. Many of them, however, were intolerant of any but members of their own faith. In Massachusetts a few Quakers who tried to arouse feeling against Puritan forms of worship were hanged. There was far less intolerance in other colonies. As we have seen in Rhode Island, in Maryland, and in Pennsylvania, colonial leaders had pleaded for religious toleration.

A Colonial Church A Witchcraft Scare in New England. The colonists had brought with them to America a strange Old World superstition. It was quite commonly believed that a

woman who had sold herself to the devil as a witch could put the spirit of the devil into others and so cause them to have fits and convulsions. At one time there was a witchcraft scare in the town of Salem. The fear of witches suddenly seized the people of the town. About twenty persons, mostly women, were accused of being witches, tried by court, found guilty, and put to death. At last, however, the townsmen regained their senses. The scare passed. 

The charge of witchcraft was hardly ever heard thereafter. 

Colonial Crime and Punishment. The severe punishment of the witches in New England was on a par with the punishments for other crimes. For in the matter of trying to check crime by punishment, the colonists had brought with them Old World notions. In England, at the time, there were scores of offenses for which the punishment was death. It was considered less costly to kill the criminal than to jail him at the public expense. When killing seemed a trifle harsh, the court might order the cutting off of an ear, a hand, or a foot. For slight crimes the prisoners were sentenced to the ducking post, the pillory, the stocks, or even to whipping at the cart's tail. These punishments were to be found in the colonies. Punishment was in the open where all might see and profit by the lesson. The criminals, with hands or feet stuck through the stocks, or standing with head and hands through the pillory, were visible to the passersby. The whipping cart was driven through the town so that all might see the flogging. Hangings were public holidays. 

Colonial Holidays. Fortunately the colonists had other holidays. In the South there were days of fox hunting when the planters rode to the chase like the English 

Cavaliers on their estates. Christmas was celebrated in the spirit of Old England, with the yule log and the mistletoe.

Drinking and card playing, cock fights and horse races were common in many of the colonies. 

In New England Thanksgiving days, set aside from time to time, were days of feasting and family reunion, not unlike Christmas in spirit. Training days also were gala days, when men from many towns gathered to compete in marksmanship, yet found time for feasting, for prayers, and psalm singing.

There were few set holidays, but since people must play, they made play of work. Men gathered at one another's homes for log rollings and for the raising of new barns and houses. The young people gathered for corn huskings and the women for quilting and candle dipping.

The New American Ideals. Being far from European influences the colonists were able to grow in the new spirit of a new land. Here in America, on the frontier of civilization, in the face of common dangers, they learned brotherhood; they gained in the religious toleration which is born of the spirit of brotherhood; they grew skillful in the art of self-government. Brotherhood, toleration, self-government these three ideals were destined to become the basic democratic ideals of the new Americans.

CHAPTER XIII Colonial Governments and Frontier Dangers 

The Colonists, Through Their Representative Assemblies, Face Three 

Dangers on Civilization's Frontier - Danger from the Indians, Danger from Old World Rivals, Danger from Tyrannical and Oppressive Laws 

Colonial Government. In all the colonies from the beginning there was some form of local government. 

Sooner or later the government of each colony came to resemble the English form of government. In each colony there was a legislative or law-making assembly elected by the voting colonists. This assembly resembled the House of Commons in the English Parliament. 

In each colony there was a governor who was aided by a council chosen from among the more influential colonists. 

In the royal colonies which belonged directly to the king, the governor was appointed by the king. 

In the proprietary colonies, such as Pennsylvania, Maryland, and the Carolinas which belonged to one or more lords, the proprietors acted as governors or they chose the governors. 169

In Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut, which had received charters of self-government, the colonists chose their own governor as well as their own legislative assemblies.

In the New England colonies the unit of local government was as a rule the town. Town officers were chosen in town meetings and the representatives in the colonial assemblies came from the towns. In the Southern colonies the unit of local government was almost without exception the county. County officers were chosen in an annual election held at the county court. The members of the colonial assemblies represented the counties. In the Middle colonies the unit of local government, in some cases, was the town; in other cases, the county. 

Colonists Face Three Dangers: Indians, Tyranny, 

Rivals. The colonial assemblies in their meetings often found it necessary to consider the dangers which beset the colonists. Foremost was the danger from the Indians who looked upon the land as theirs. Then there was the danger from Old World rivals, the Spanish and the French, eager to crowd the English out of their new possessions. Finally there was the danger that England, the mother country, knowing the weak position of the colonies, would try to tyrannize over them.

The Indian Danger. -The danger from the Indians was nearest to them. From the day the colonists landed, the white men felt the presence of the red men. After the Virginia massacre of 1622 and the Pequot uprising of 1636, the Indians had been held in check both in the North and in the South; but the danger of an outbreak grew greater each year.

As the English home builders increased in numbers, the square miles left to the Indian tribes became all too few for their hunting. Yet the English farmers, hungry for land, moved ever on and on, and the red men,

COLONIAL GOVERNMENTS 

171 caught between the advancing colonists and hostile Indian tribes in the rear, felt that they had to fight the English colonists in defense of their hunting grounds. 

We have seen how the Pilgrims in Plymouth, the Quakers under William Penn in Pennsylvania, the Catholics under Lord Baltimore in Maryland, all made treaties of peace with the Indians. So in other colonies assemblies tried to come to terms with the Indians in order to insure peace. The smoking of the peace pipe was the Indian way of ratifying a treaty of peace.

But sooner or later as the Indians watched the advance of the white man across their lands, they would rise in an attempt to destroy him. From Georgia to New Hampshire, at different times, there were Indian attacks, the burning of farms and farm houses, massacres, and the torturing of prisoners. The immediate cause of the Indian wars might be a misunderstanding between an Indian tribe and a white trader; or a drunken frenzy brought on by bad liquor given the Indians in exchange for furs. But the deeper reason for the Indian wars was to be found in the fact that the English colonists, being farmers, were taking over and conquering the red man's wilderness the wilderness which the red man needed for his hunting grounds. 

King Philip's War. The one thing which the Indians

lacked was leadership and union among themselves. And it was not until 1675 that this came on a large scale in New England where King Philip, an Indian chief, led an 

Indian uprising against the whites.

From 1643 on, a number of the New England colonies had been joined in a New England Confederation prepared to unite against Indian attack. Years passed and the 

Carrying Guns to Church

On the frontier the danger from the Indians was always present. fears of the colonists seemed groundless. Suddenly in 1675 

King Philip's War broke out. 

King Philip was the chief of the Wampanoags, the son of that same Massasoit who had signed a treaty with the 

Pilgrims in Plymouth. For forty years the Wampanoags had kept the peace, but now that peace was ended; the 

Wampanoags joined the

Narragansetts and other tribesmen on the warpath.

The colonists immediately put troops in the field, but these troops did not act together under a single leader. Their campaign was for the most part badly planned, poorly provisioned, and badly equipped in its weapons. 

The Indians, bearing guns and ammunition which they handled as skillfully as the white men, seemed to be everywhere at once. Villages, surprised by night, were burned to the ground; settlers were killed or carried away to be tortured. Colonial troops sent to the aid of towns were trapped in ambush and destroyed almost to the last man. 

Yet all the fierce courage of the Indians could not save

COLONIAL GOVERNMENTS 

173 them. The whites outnumbered them. The whites with their superior farming had larger stores of food to carry them through. They could get fresh stores of ammunition from England. As events proved, time was bound to play into their hands. In a battle against the Narragansetts, who held a fortified position in the middle of a swamp, the colonists repeated the victory of forty years before against the Pequots. They captured the fort and set fire to the wigwams. Some time later, Philip was shot dead by an

Indian, and the power of the New England tribes was completely broken.

Many of the Narragansett Indians had been killed. 

Many, captured, were sold into slavery in the West Indies. 

The rest signed a peace pact and lived as best they could in the small holdings which were left to them. 

A Tyrant Royal Governor. Bacon's Rebellion. — In the year 1676 an Indian uprising in Virginia led indirectly to a revolt against the governor. Governor Berkeley was ruling the colony with his council composed of his own favorites among the planters. For years he had refused to call a meeting of the Burgesses. This grieved the Virginians.

When in addition he refused to send militia against the hostile Indians on the frontier, many of the colonists suspected that he was sacrificing their interests because of his own profit from the Indian fur trade. It was at this point that Nathaniel Bacon, a planter in the back country, took matters into his own hands. Although refused an officer's commission by the governor, he led a small force of Virginia militia in counter attacks against the Indians. When 

Berkeley declared him and his men outlaws, Bacon turned on the governor, captured Jamestown, and burned it. 

Bacon died, possibly through poisoning. The rebellion collapsed. Berkeley took a swift revenge by hanging most of Bacon's lieutenants.

When news of Berkeley's action reached England, the governor was recalled and so the incident of Bacon's Rebellion was closed. Nevertheless, it gave proof of a spirit of independence in the colonies. Just one hundred years after the death of Bacon that spirit was destined to flame up into the American Revolution.

James II Sends Andros to the Northern Colonies. 

In the year 1687, the new king, James II, alarmed the 

Northern colonies by appointing Andros governor of the

New England colonies. Soon after, James went a step farther and ordered Andros to take over the government of New York and New Jersey as well. All these colonies were to give up their independent charters and to lose their right to elect assemblies.

When a New England town meeting protested, Andros ordered that town meetings cease. In fact, taking advantage of the carelessness of the Massachusetts company in its land grants to the townships, Andros even attacked the land titles of many of the Massachusetts colonists. 

He claimed that the land on which the colonists lived belonged to the king, and he brought suit for recovery in the courts. 

Governor Andros 

Acting under orders from James II, Andros took steps which threatened the liberties of the Northern colonies. 

Serious as were these moves by Andros, the most dangerous to the security and well being of the colonists was the king's plan to enforce a set of acts which Parliament

COLONIAL GOVERNMENTS 

175 had been passing for the control of colonial trade and navigation.

English Acts of Navigation, Trade, and Manufacture. 

In planting their colonies the rulers in England, France, Spain, and Holland were interested in adding to the wealth and strength of the mother country by controlling colonial navigation, trade, and manufacturing.

Each nation naturally wished to see its colonial exports and imports carried only in its own ships. This would add to its strength upon the sea.

Each nation wished to see the colonial trade in both imports and exports pass through its own home ports. 

This would add port duties to the national treasury. It would bring profit to the merchants at home. Above all it would give the mother country the first choice of the colonial raw materials.

Each nation wished to prevent the colonies from manufacturing those goods which the home merchants had for sale. This would oblige the colonies to exchange their own low-priced raw materials for imported high-priced manufactured goods and so leave a balance of trade in favor of the mother country.

To the European mother countries this scheme of things (called the Mercantile System) seemed the means by which colonies could be made profitable enough to be worth planting and defending.

Of all the mother countries, England was the most liberal in her navigation, trade, and manufacturing acts. The 

Navigation Acts passed by England encouraged colonial shipbuilding and increased colonial as well as English shipping.

Some of the trade acts passed by England were a direct aid to the colonists. Although it was true that the Southern colonies could not sell tobacco directly to any other nation,

it was also true that England did not permit the raising of tobacco at home. Furthermore England, eager to encourage the colonial production of pitch, tar, turpentine, and other supplies for her navy, added a bounty to the price paid for such colonial goods. 

Nevertheless, many colonists felt that the Navigation Acts were unjust, since these acts compelled them to pay the freight rates demanded by English or colonial ship owners free from competition. There were colonists who felt that the Acts of Trade were unfair since they obliged the colonies to sell to English merchants and to buy from English merchants at any price which these merchants chose to put upon the wares. That the English laws were more liberal than the Spanish or the French was no answer to those who were discontented with the English Mercan tile Acts. To their minds the Navigation and Trade Acts were unjust because they tried to deprive the colonists of the fruits of their labors and their sacrifices in a new land. 

Many a colonist therefore resorted to the smuggling of goods in or out of port as the only way to evade the hated laws.

It was partly to enforce the Mercantile Acts that King James II planned to unite the colonies under his rule through a single royal governor like Andros.

James II Dethroned. Leisler's Rebellion. Andros De ported. Fortunately for the colonists James was not able to maintain his rule even in England. The old struggle between Parliament and the Stuart kings was still on. Parliament won.

In 1689 Parliament offered the throne to William of Orange, who was the ruler of Holland, and to his wife Mary. 

William crossed the channel and placed himself at the head of the army. James fled.

William and Mary were crowned king and queen. The

COLONIAL GOVERNMENTS 

177 rule was not theirs, however, but Parliament's; for in order to win the crown, William and Mary had to sign a "Bill of Rights" by which they agreed to give the major part of their governing power to Parliament. 

When news of the fall of James reached the Northern colonies, the rejoicing was great. In New York a German merchant, named Leisler, rose against the lieutenant governor and acted in his place. For two years Leisler ruled the colony, but finally a governor appointed by William and Mary took over the government. He was persuaded by Leisler's enemies to sign a warrant ordering Leisler put to death. So ended Leisler's Rebellion. 

Meanwhile in Boston, when the leaders heard of the fall of James II, they removed Andros from power and shipped him back to England in chains. Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and New Hampshire were once again separate colonies. William and Mary granted Massachusetts a new charter which provided that the old rights of town meeting and assembly be restored, but that the governor should be appointed in England. From this time on the colony of Massachusetts remained a royal colony. 

The Colonists' Third Danger. War with Neighbors. 

After the fall of James, the struggle concerning the Acts of 

Trade and Navigation might have continued under William and Mary if it had not happened that the colonists and England now came face to face with the third of their dangers. This was the danger from Old World rivals. 

When William and Mary were crowned, France declared war on England. The war in Europe led to a war between the French and English colonists, which was only one of four bitterly fought intercolonial wars.

CHAPTER XIV A Rival to the North. New France French Soldiers, Traders, and Priests Lay Foundations of a New France, an Empire of Furs Held by Forts, Trading Posts, and Missions - The Rivalry of England and France Leads to Three Inconclusive 

Wars Between the French and English Colonists, with Indians as Allies on Each Side English Attacked. In the year 1689, about the time 

Andros was sailing back to England a prisoner, the Count de Frontenac was sailing from France to Canada with orders for the capture of the Hudson River Valley and the harbor of New York. Nothing came of the plan but almost 179

immediately after his arrival in Quebec, French soldiers with their Indian allies were marching swiftly down frozen rivers and across ice-covered lakes to strike at the frontier towns of New York and New England. One such war party, coming down from the St. Lawrence, followed the 

Mohawk Valley westward to within striking distance of the little palisaded village of Schenectady. They waited for night and when the people in the town were sleeping and only a snowman made by an overconfident sentinel stood guard at the open gate, the raiders entered the town to burn and slay. A few of the settlers escaped through the open gate and walked through the snow to Albany. The other survivors were carried back to Canada to be sold as slaves.

This and other frontier massacres marked the beginning of a series of wars between the English colonies and their rivals to the north, wars which it seemed could not end until either the French or the English had made themselves masters of the continent.

Before turning to the battlefields to see the outcome of the struggle, let us first see how France had gained her foothold in America. 

Champlain Founds Quebec. St. Lawrence River the 

Highroad of New France. In the year 1608, one year after the English came to Jamestown, a French explorer, Champlain, and twenty-seven other Frenchmen, sailed up the St. Lawrence to Quebec where they built a settlement. 

Champlain and his men had come with orders to hold the land for a French nobleman who had received from the king the right to the fur trade of this region. 

Champlain saw that the St. Lawrence and its network of branches would give France the control of the heart of the continent. Along these rivers the French explorers could paddle their way in search of the path to China. Along the

same rivers French missionaries could carry the gospel to the inland Indian tribes. In this way, too, the Indians could bring their furs to the French. The key to all this vast empire was the high hill of Quebec, a natural fortress, which a few men could hold against an army. 

Champlain's vision came true. While French fishing smacks were sailing each year to the fishing banks off Newfoundland, and while a few French settlements built in 

Nova Scotia north of Maine were becoming rivals of the New England fishing towns, the true New France which 

Champlain foresaw grew up inland; Quebec was its principal stronghold

Champlain Helps the Al gonquians against the Iroquois. 

In New France, as in the 

English colonies, the wilderness claimed many victims before the colonists gained a firm foothold. During Cham- Champlain 

As founder of Quebec, as explorer, "Father of New France." plain's first winter at Quebec and as governor. he earned the title, all but eight of his men died; and it became clear that without the good will of the Indians, a handful of French in the middle of a wilderness could carry on no missionary work, no fur trade, no exploration. 

But how was the good will of the Indians to be won? 

With gifts? Gifts helped, but gifts were not enough as 

Champlain soon learned. That very spring, a tribe of the

Algonquian Indians appealed to him for military aid against their enemies, the Iroquois, who dwelt in the valley of the

Mohawk. Champlain agreed to help. Together with two other Frenchmen he joined the Indians, who paddled up the St. Lawrence and then marched southward to a large lake since known as Lake Champlain.

Here the battle took place. All night long the Algonquians in their canoes and the Iroquois on land taunted one 

A New Faith 

French missionary priests, unarmed and unguarded, went among the Indian tribes to teach them the Christian faith. 

They won the good will of the Indians for New France. another. In the morning the 

Algonquians landed and the

Iroquois with their three plumed chiefs in the lead were advancing against them when the Frenchmen dressed in full armor stepped forward.

The Iroquois, startled by this strange apparition, stopped a moment. The 

Frenchmen fired. A few Iroquois warriors fell. The rest fled pursued by the exulting

Algonquians. 

Champlain had won the friendship of the Algonquians, but the Iroquois became the deadly enemies of the French.

It was only a few weeks after this defeat of the Iroquois that Henry Hudson, sailing up the Hudson River, drank and feasted with the Iroquois, who later became the fast friends of the Dutch and the English with whom they traded.

New France Grows. French Explore Great Lakes. - 

Returning to Canada, Champlain, reënforced by new settlers from France, strengthened Quebec.

Years passed. The colony grew, but slowly. The crafti-

ness of the Iroquois prevented the French from following the St. Lawrence beyond the Lachine Rapids. Instead the traders and the explorers and the missionaries, and those who came after them, followed the Ottawa River and then crossing overland reached the waters of Lake Huron, Voyageurs 

The voyageurs, or French explorers, paddling along the shores of the Great Lakes and down the rivers of the Mississippi Valley, were thrilled by the beauty of the virgin wilderness. 

Lake Michigan, Lake Ontario, and Lake Superior. But for a long time the Iroquois prevented the French from entering the Mohawk and Hudson Valleys, the Lake Erie country, or the valley of the Ohio. 

When Champlain died, there were about two thousand Frenchmen in New France and the colony passed into the hands of a company which held it until King Louis XIV took it over as a royal colony. During this time explorers pushing farther and farther inland heard rumors of a great

river, the Father of Waters, the Mississippi, which flows southward from the Great Lakes into a "Crimson Sea." 

Joliet and Marquette Paddle Down the Mississippi.

At the news of a great waterway through the Continent to the Crimson Sea, which might prove to be the China 

Sea, Joliet, a French fur trader, and Marquette, a French

La Salle

missionary, started out on an exploring expedition. They set out from the trading post at Michilimackinac on Lake Michigan, and with the help of Indian guides they followed the canoe routes and portages from the Great Lakes to the headwaters of the Mississippi. 

They then paddled down the 

Mississippi to within seven hundred miles of its mouth where they learned that they were close to Spanish settlements, and thought it best to return.

La Salle Reaches Mouth of River. Claims Louisiana for France.

The task which 

Joliet and Marquette had set for themselves was completed by La Salle. This young nobleman was determined to explore the Mississippi River to its mouth. 

After a number of trials and many mishaps, La Salle and a small group of fellow explorers paddled the full length of the Mississippi and emerged into the Gulf of 

Mexico. Here in April, 1682, they planted a cross, and with the firing of muskets and loud huzzas, La Salle claimed the Mississippi and all the lands washed by its

waters for King Louis XIV, in whose honor the land was named Louisiana.

That same year, while Penn was gathering Quakers to lay the foundations of Philadelphia, the French built a

fort on a high bald cliff on the Illinois River near the present site of Ottawa, Illinois. This fort they named St. Louis. 

La Salle himself returned to France to organize an expedition for the building of a settlement at the mouth of the Mississippi. Once again misfortune attended his efforts. The ships sailing through the Gulf of Mexico missed the outlet of the Mississippi and the settlers landed in 

An Empire of Furs 

Each spring after the waters thawed, the Indians carried their furs in canoes to the French trading posts.

Texas where their sufferings were so great that La Salle set out north hoping to find Canada and to bring back reenforcements. On the way La Salle was fatally shot by one of his own men. Most of his followers in Texas perished miserably. 

Indian Canoes Bring Furs to French Trading Posts. 

Nevertheless the French did hold the Mississippi and the St. Lawrence, and each spring when the ice thawed, the 

Indian tribes came paddling down the forest streams bringing their canoes filled with furs to the trading posts in the Mississippi Valley, on the Great Lakes, and along the St. Lawrence. Every spring the French traders gath-

ered to meet the Indians, offering knives, hatchets, silver rings, bracelets, colored beads, bells, woolen blankets, and brandy in exchange for the furs. And every spring an ocean fleet sailed up the St. Lawrence bringing supplies from France and then sailed away again laden with furs.

The Iroquois Sell Furs to Dutch and English. — There was only one weak link in this chain of exchanges by which the French were planning to obtain the furs of a continent. 

This was the colony of New York, the home of the Iroquois. 

Ever since the Iroquois had made friends with Henry Hudson they had been trading first with the Dutch fur traders and later with the English fur traders. 

France Desires Hudson Valley. Frontenac's Orders. — 

The French saw that with the Iroquois conquered and the Hudson River in French hands, their hold on the continent would be strengthened. The St. Lawrence is frozen about half the year. Sailboats found it impossible to ascend the swift-flowing Mississippi from the Gulf. The St. Lawrence and the Mississippi gave them command of the inland forests; the Hudson and its harbor would give them an all-year-round outlet to the sea. And with the Hudson in their hands, the Iroquois could be forced to terms. 

It was for this reason that when Louis XIV, king of France, declared war on England in 1689, Count de Frontenac sailing for Canada was ordered to conquer the Hudson Valley and to break the Iroquois power. When Frontenac arrived at Quebec, however, he found that the Iroquois had been ahead of him. They had crossed the St. Lawrence and burned the French settlement of Lachine. 

Without waiting to organize a force large enough for the capture of New York, Frontenac sent raiding parties to strike at the frontier towns of New England and New York. 

It was one of these raiding parties which attacked Sche-

nectady. This same party then continued westward up the 

Mohawk to the Iroquois encampments where they burned the Iroquois villages and fields. 

Three Colonial Wars Begin in Europe. - From the year 1689 on, for almost seventy-five years, the settlers who looked upon the New World as a new home suitable 

Louis XIV 

It was because of fear of the plan of Louis XIV for world empire that

England fought two wars with France. 

Each of these wars involved the French and English colonists. for farm lands found themselves in conflict with French settlers who looked upon 

America as a wilderness which would serve them best as long as it was kept a wilderness, the home of 

Indians, and of the otter, the marten, and the beaver. 

Nevertheless, the the first three of these wars between the English colonies and 

New France did not begin in 

America; they were part of a larger struggle which 

France and England were waging for world power.

King Louis XIV. Ver sailles. - In 1689, when 

Frontenac left for America, Louis XIV was the absolute ruler of France. While the peasants on the land lived and toiled very much as did the serfs in feudal days, French nobles lived as courtiers in gorgeous court buildings at Versailles where they danced attendance on the king, intriguing for his favor. Here they saw such luxury and splendor in palace architecture, in furnishings, in clothes, as the world had

rarely known before. The spacious rooms of Versailles were lined with marble and hung with wall mirrors, paintings, and tapestries; they were lighted by candles set in chandeliers from which hung showers of finely cut crystals; the floors were covered with rare eastern rugs; the chairs were richly upholstered, gilded, and carved with scrolls and ribbons. The nobles and ladies of the court dressed in gowns and mantles of the finest weaves of silk and velvet, gold cloth, damask, and brocade, trimmed with furs or fine laces.

The money which paid for the splendor of the king's court came partly from the far-flung empire of France which, since the defeat of the 

Spanish Armada, had been a close third to England and Holland in the race for ocean trade and colonies. France had posts in India and a number of choice sugar islands in the West Indies.

France had the fur trade of Canada and Louisiana. But in spite of all these sources of wealth Louis XIV was not satisfied. He planned to make himself master of Europe by extending France to her "natural boundaries." He believed that in this way France would be in a stronger position to forge ahead of England and Holland in the race for world trade and world colonies. 

A Louis XIV Chair

England and Holland Unite Against France. 

- To keep the English from interfering with his plans in Europe, Louis XIV gave money to Charles II and James II. But by the year 1689 the English, seeing that Louis' plans threatened their safety, took action. As they had a number of other grievances against King James, the English drove him from the throne. England then united with her old enemy, Holland, against France.

The union of England and Holland against France held throughout the four wars which followed. In the first war (1689-1697) Louis XIV tried to drive William of Orange, the former Stadtholder or President of Holland, from the English throne. In the second war (1702–1713) the enemies of France fought to prevent Louis XIV from uniting the empires of France and Spain, through his grandson, who had been crowned king of Spain. It was during this war (in 1707) that England and Scotland were united in the single kingdom of Great Britain. In 1715 Louis XIV died, and his greatgrandson, Louis XV, ruled in his place. In the pictures painted in the court of this pleasure-loving king, we can see the French courtiers and court ladies of the period, human butterflies fluttering about in lovely groves near shaded fountains, seeking the pleasure of the moment. Yet, under the surface gayety and gallantry of court life, there was still the ambition to extend French power in Europe. 

The year 1740 saw France and Great Britain fighting each other in Europe in the third of these struggles, known as the "War of the Austrian Succession." The fourth of these wars began not in Europe but in America. 

King William's War. Queen Anne's War. King 

George's War. Indian Allies.- The first three wars were known in America as King William's War, Queen Anne's

War, and King George's War. In the English colonies each of these wars was marked by much suffering among the

frontier dwellers. Each time the woods were the scene of marches and counter marches, midnight attacks and burnings, in all of which the Indians, armed with guns and powder as well as bows and arrows and tomahawks, were reënforced by English rum or French brandy. 

New Englanders Take Louisburg. Great Britain Re stores It to France. During King William's War, a New 

England fleet of fishermen and sailors trained to the sea captured Port Royal in Acadia, only to see Great Britain return it to France at the close of the war. 

During Queen Anne's War, Charleston, South Carolina, repulsed an attack by combined French and Spanish forces; and New England ships again took Port Royal. This time when the treaty with France was signed, Great Britain retained Acadia (renamed Nova Scotia), Newfoundland, and the whole of the Hudson Bay territory. Nor was this all. By her victories Great Britain wrested from Louis

XIV part of the French West India Islands; she won from 

Spain the Straits of Gibraltar, commanding the entrance to the Mediterranean; and Louis XIV had to promise for 

France that never would the same king rule over France and Spain.

During King George's War, New Englanders, aided by farmer lads from New York, provisions from Pennsylvania, and British ships, captured the fortress of Louisburg which the French had built on Cape Breton Island to guard the St. Lawrence River. Here was a victory which might have ended the struggle. With Louisburg in British hands, Great Britain might well have asked France to surrender Canada, at least so thought the colonists. But when the treaty of peace was signed at Aix-la-Chapelle, Great Britain restored Louisburg to France. This was in 1748. 

Seven years later, Great Britain and France were again at war.

CHAPTER XV Furs Versus Farms. Seven Years' War British Colonists Seek New Farm Lands and French Colonists Seek New Fur Posts - They Clash Over the Ownership of the Ohio Valley- George Washington, a Youth of Twenty, is in Command at the First Battle of the War Which Wins the West and Canada for Great Britain 

French Build Forts in Ohio River Valley. In 1755, the 

British colonists learned that the French had added to their chain of forts by building three new forts on the Allegheny River, which unites with the Monongahela to form the Ohio 

River. 

The French forts on the Mississippi had worried the colonists very little, but when they learned of French forts in the Ohio Valley, only a few hundred miles beyond the 

Alleghenies, they were alarmed.

The British wanted this Ohio Valley for themselves. 

Their population, increasing steadily, had been slowly pushing westward toward the Alleghenies. Traders who 194

crossed the mountains brought back word of the beautiful Ohio Valley with its forests rich in furs, its fertile soil, its broad flowing rivers. Here was an empire in itself. 

A company of Virginians, eager to profit from the land in the Ohio Valley, had formed the Ohio Company, and received a grant of six hundred thousand acres on condition that they get settlers to cross the mountains.

One of the members of the 

Ohio Company was Lawrence 

Washington, and one of the surveyors of the company was his half-brother, George Wash- 

Surveying the Ohio Valley ington, a strapping youth of twenty, the descendant of one of the early Virginia Cavaliers. 

The True Issue. Furs versus Farms. The conflict between the French and the English colonists was now taking on its true character. It was to be a struggle between two groups of colonists, each with its own idea as to the uses of the new continent. 

On the one side were the French who, in spite of their settlements which reached from New Orleans to the mouth of the St. Lawrence, looked upon the New World primarily as a wilderness which should be kept a wilderness for its furs. On the other side were the British who looked upon the New World as a new home for men, where settlers from many lands could clear away the forests, till the soil, and build homes and towns.

Washington Carries Message to the French. Builds 

Fort. To protect the claims of the British colonists who were preparing to push into this western land as farmers, Governor Dinwiddie of Virginia sent George Washington to carry a message to the commander of the French fort warn-

ing him that he was on British ground. The way was long. 

It was the dead of winter. But Washington and his aides delivered the message, and after many adventures returned with the commandant's courteous answer, which stated that he was at his post by order of the governor of Canada.

Conditions in New France, 1755. The French colo nists, who numbered about one hundred thousand, lived widely scattered along the rivers which had helped to carry them inland. They had little share in the government. They received their laws from the king through the royal governors, and the king's officers planned the lives of the colonists in almost every detail, frequently telling them when to plant, what seeds to sow, what tools to use. This dependence on 

France the settlers could scarcely throw off, since they depended upon the French fleet which came up the St. 

Lawrence once a year for the sale of their furs and for

the receipt of the things which they needed in exchange. 

In all New France, which was by this time almost one hundred and fifty years old, except in Montreal and Quebec, there were few signs of the Old World civilization — no schools, no colleges, no printing presses, and very little of the luxuries in home furnishing which were becoming more common both in Europe and in the English colonies. 

Conditions in English Colonies, 1755. — In the English colonies all these things were different. The English who numbered more than one million lived as true home builders in a compact group of colonies between the Alleghenies and the coast. Nearly all of the English colonists were tillers of the soil who had cleared vast stretches of the wilderness. In their town meetings and in their assemblies they enjoyed a large share of self-government. Even in the royal colonies, with royal governors, the assemblies had ways of keeping power in their own hands. 

While the French depended on one stream, blocked by ice about half the year, and on another which was almost impassable, the English colonies had many navigable rivers and fine harbors open the year round. They were therefore able to trade furs, provisions, tobacco, lumber, and even manufactured goods with one another, with the 

West Indies, and with Europe.

All this prosperity had helped those who lived in the more thickly settled parts of the English colonies to enjoy schools and colleges. Harvard was the first college to be founded. Others which had followed were William and 

Mary in Virginia, King's College (now Columbia) in New 

York, and Princeton in New Jersey.

Printing presses, books and newspapers, well-built homes, were additional signs of progress in the English colonies. 

Furniture making flourished. There were laces made by 

French Huguenot weavers, andirons and lamps made
