CHAPTER XIX Planning the Law of the Land 

The Representatives of a People, Seeing Their Government Weak, Peacefully 

Draft a New Plan to Bind Their States Into a More Perfect Union The Need of a Strong Tie. Steps Toward Union. - 

After the War of the Revolution was over, it became clear to many of the patriot leaders that the states which had just won their independence were in need of some strong bond of union. 

The colonies had been separately founded. They had been separately governed. And before the Revolution the people in the different colonies had felt their separateness more than they had felt the things which bound them. 

Only in time of danger had they seen that one could help the other. The New England Confederation, 1643-1684, was a union of colonies against Indian dangers. In the 257

first war against the French and their Indian allies, New York had joined forces with the New England colonies. In the second, third, and fourth wars with France, more of the colonies had joined in the common cause. But all through these wars with the French there was no real 

THE COMPANY 

1724 

CARPENTERS HALL Carpenters' Hall 

It was in this building, in Philadelphia, that the first 

Continental Congress met. 

union of the colonies. In 1754 the "Albany Plan" for such a union had been rejected. 

Ten years later, in the face of a new danger, some colonial assemblies sent representatives to speak for them in a 

Stamp Act Congress. Then as the danger from the tyranny of the British king grew greater, Committees of Correspondence helped to keep the colonies in touch with one

another and so prepared the way for the First and Second Continental Congress, in which representatives from the various colonies gathered and acted in the name of all. 

Second Continental Congress Drafts Articles of Confederation. The Second Continental Congress issued the Declaration of Independence. The Second Continental 

Congress called for troops, appointed military officers, and in all ways acted as the representative of a united nation in the carrying on of the war. 

Throughout the war, however, the representatives in this Congress found themselves hampered at every turn because they had very little real power. Before they could vote on any really important matters, they had to refer back to the colonial assemblies for advice. They might request from the state assemblies funds for troops, for ships, for supplies, but the separate states had never entered into any agreement to do as the Congress asked. 

Even before the signing of the Declaration of Independence Virginia had drawn up her Constitution as an independent state and soon the others took similar action. 

There was need for a real Union. A plan of national government was drawn up in Congress for the confederation of the states. By the year 1781 the states had all agreed to this plan, called the Articles of Confederation, but the Articles did not improve conditions very much. 

Weak Congress Under Articles of Confederation. The 

Articles of Confederation still left the Congress weak. 

Congress could request funds of the states, but had no right to enforce the collection of taxes for the support of the government and the payment of its debts. Congress was not given the right to regulate the trade between the states or to make treaties with foreign powers which would be securely binding on the states. The Articles of Confederation did not provide for a responsible head, as a president.

They did not provide for national judges to try offenders against the will of Congress.

In New England where the farmers were hard pressed for cash with which to meet their debts, some of them banded together and forced the courts to close, thus blocking legal action against their property. Finally, some two thousand farmers led by Daniel Shays, an ex-army officer, marched on Springfield, Massachusetts, hoping to secure NC NJ 

NY 

SC 

UNITE OR DIE Unite or Die 

NE This symbol of the weakness of disunion was invented by Benjamin Franklin at the time when the Albany Plan was being considered in 1754. 

Under the Articles of Confederation ratified in 1781, the states were joined, but events proved that they needed a stronger plan of union. arms from the Federal Arsenal. Congress had no available force to restore order, and seven months had passed before Massachusetts militia put down the uprising. 

In the face of such difficulties men began to wonder. 

Were rioting and hard times all that the war for independence was to bring them? Was liberty a delusion and a snare? Would people have to choose between anarchy and some form of tyranny set up by a military dictator?

Northwest Territory and Northwest Ordinance Strength ens Union Feeling. For a long time a number of the states had been quarreling with one another about the ownership of lands which lay beyond the Allegheny Mountains, north of the Ohio and east of the Mississippi. This rich territory which had once brought on a war between France and England, and which was later conquered for the Revolutionary cause by the victories of George Rogers

Clark, was well worth a contest. Massachusetts, Virginia, Connecticut, and New York all pressed their conflicting claims for the whole or some part of this Northwest Territory. Maryland insisted that the new territory, won through a common war, should belong to the whole nation, which would then own a vast empire as government land; and it was not until 1781, when New York and Virginia had agreed to cede their claims, that Maryland, the last of the states, ratified the Articles of Confederation. 

In 1787 there came the one great act of Congress under the Articles of Confederation, an act which proved that a central government might be trusted to pass laws intended for the common good of all the states in the nation. 

This act was the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. The 

Northwest Ordinance provided that in the great Northwest

Territory there should be no slavery, there should be political and religious freedom, and there should be public schools. 

An ordinance passed in 1785 had provided that in each township the income from one thirty-sixth of the land was to be set aside for the support of education. As states were formed from the territory, a portion of the state land was to be reserved for the support of a state university. Most important of all the provisions of the Land Ordinance to the land-hungry people in the states was the provision that the government land could be sold to settlers at low prices and on easy terms. The inhabitants of the North-

west Territory were not to be treated as subjects of a colonial empire. 

As soon as the population of a territory reached five thousand, the inhabitants had the right to choose a representative assembly. When there were sixty thousand inhabitants, a territory had the right to adopt a constitution and to apply to Congress for statehood on equal terms with the original thirteen states. (And out of this Northwest Territory there grew Ohio, Indiana, Illinois,

Michigan, and Wisconsin; a small section of the present state of Minnesota was also part of this Northwest Territory.)

The national ownership of the valuable Northwest Territory tended to strengthen the feeling of union. In the past the colonies had been drawn together only by common dangers. Now they were being drawn together by the possession of a common treasure.

Internal Trade Discussed. Mount Vernon and Annapo lis. As early as 1785 Maryland and Virginia, having a common interest in the Potomac River, sent representatives to meet in Washington's home at Mount Vernon to try to come to an agreement as to its use. They were interested also in plans by which a water route could be established from the seaboard to the western lands.

The following year representatives from five states met at Annapolis, Maryland, to talk over the western lands and other matters which might help to build up trade and commerce. At this convention Alexander Hamilton was the leading spirit. Hamilton was a young man who had been attending college when the Revolution broke out. 

He had then left college to join the army and served on Washington's staff during the greater part of the war. During this time the youth showed unusual ability for statesmanship, and now at the Annapolis Convention it was he

who strongly urged the members of the convention to consider changes in the Articles of Confederation. 

A Constitutional Convention in Session. Early in 1787 

the Congress of the Confederation called such a gathering, and by May the Constitutional Convention was in session in Philadelphia.

The men present, both from the North and South, were carefully picked for the task in hand; they were probably the ablest group of men to be found in all the nation. 

In almost all the Old World lands, the union of people into nations had come about not through peaceful deliberation but through long and bloody wars. In each case a united nation had been born only through the victory of one fighting chieftain who generally had to maintain a large army to keep his throne and to hold his nation together. 

Here in Philadelphia a different scene presented itself.

The colonies had grown up side by side in peace with one another. They had united from time to time to fight a common danger. They had fought the War of Independence as "The United States of America." Now, a people finding their plan of government too weak were peaceably gathered to draw up a plan which would bind them into a stronger nation. This Convention showed that the growth and spread of civilization in the New World was to follow a new course. Here people speaking, reading, and writing a common tongue, trained in self-government in their local communities, were gathered to solve through deliberation those problems which for thousands of years the people of Europe and Asia had been able to solve only through bloodshed.

The task which these men in Philadelphia were facing was no simple one. They wished to draw up a strong plan of government. Yet they represented states, each of which was jealous for its own power and its own liberty.

Washington was elected presiding officer and the delegates proceeded, not merely to revise the Articles of Confederation, but to draft a new document which would prove a stronger bond of union for the Republic, a supreme law for the new-born nation facing its great tasks and problems. 

The sessions were secret, but James Madison, who with 

Alexander Hamilton and Benjamin Franklin played a lead ing part in the Convention, kept minutes which were published many years later; in those minutes we can follow the trials of the Constitution makers. 

For weeks, for months in fact, the case looked hopeless. 

Some were eager for a Constitution which would establish a very strong central government. Others feared that such a government would interfere unduly with the separate states, which should be left free to look after their own separate interests. Besides, the small states feared that with a strong central government the larger states would be able to control lawmaking. The Southern states in which there were many slaves feared that the Northern states might use the power of the national government to abolish slavery. 

There were believers in democracy who wished to see the people trusted with the power to choose officers of the government by direct vote. There were men who feared that popular government might be rash; who believed that it was best to prevent the people's whims and fancies from expressing themselves too easily. 

Feeling in the Constitutional Convention must have run high as the different factions, apparently unyielding, faced each other. But finally, by September, through compromise, a plan of government or constitution was adopted. 

The Constitution Provided Threefold Government. 

Under the Articles of Confederation the nation had neither a President nor a judicial department. Congress consisted

of only one house and each of the states held only one vote in the Congress.

Under the new Constitution the government of the nation was to have three divisions or branches: (1) an executive department, headed by a president; (2) a legislative or lawmaking department -in other words, a Congress consisting of an Upper House called the Senate, and a Lower House called the House of Representatives; (3) a judicial department, consisting of the Supreme Court and of such other courts as the Congress might establish. 

Powers of the President or Chief Executive. - Under the Constitution the President or chief executive of the land was to be elected for a term of four years; he was to be commander-in-chief of the army and navy; to have power to make treaties and to appoint Supreme Court judges and other government officers upon the approval of the Senate. 

With the aid of the army, the navy, the Supreme Court, and all other branches of the government, he was to see that the Constitution was upheld and the laws passed by 

Congress enforced.

Powers of Congress. The Legislative Body. — Under the Constitution Congress had considerable power. 

Congress had the right to levy and collect taxes. Congress was given power to raise and to maintain an army and navy. Congress was granted the right to make laws regulating trade and commerce among the states, with foreign powers, and with the Indians. And, in addition, Congress was empowered to take any steps necessary to help it in enforcing its powers.

Judicial Powers. Under the Constitution, a Supreme 

Court consisting of a Chief Justice and associates to be appointed by the President with the consent of the Senate was given judicial power to interpret the meaning of the Constitution and the laws made by Congress. The Su-

preme Court in its various departments was to serve as a balance wheel in settling differences between states and in other disputes arising under the Constitution and the laws of Congress. 

Compromises Between Large and Small States. - To compromise the differences between the small states and the large states the Constitution provided that each state should be entitled to a representation in the House of Representatives which should be in proportion to the state's population, but that each state should be equally entitled to two members in the Senate. Since no act of the House of Representatives could become a law unless it was passed by the Senate, the smaller states had little to fear from the larger states. Since the larger states had more representatives in the House of Representatives, they could not complain that their larger population was not sufficiently represented in Congress. 

A Compromise on Slavery. — Concerning slavery there had been a compromise. The Southern delegates had agreed that Congress should have the power to regulate trade, but not until it had been stipulated that Congress could not prohibit the slave trade before the year 1808. In counting the population of a state to determine its number of representatives in the House, it was agreed that every five slaves would be counted as equal to three whites, as had been the custom in making assessments under the 

Articles of Confederation. 

A Compromise on Direct Government. In the Constitution as adopted by the Convention, the differences between those who favored direct popular government and those who feared it were also settled. 

The Constitution provided that the President should be chosen not by the people directly, but indirectly by "electors." The judges of the Supreme Court were to be chosen

by the President whose choice must in turn be ratified by the 

Senate. 

The Constitution provided that senators, two from each state, were to be chosen not by direct vote of the people but by state legislatures. An amendment, the Seventeenth, passed many years later, provided that senators be elected by a direct vote of the people.

Constitution Voted on by States. Hamilton is Champion. When the Constitution was completed, it came up for the vote of the state conventions. There was great excitement in the land as some men pleaded for the Constitution while others attacked it as a menace to state liberty. 

Chief among the champions of the Constitution was Alexander Hamilton, who joined with James Madison and

John Jay in issuing papers explaining the Constitution and its advantages. Later these papers were gathered together in one volume called the Federalist. 

The people, stirred by all this argument, studied every provision of the proposed law. Anxiously they awaited the news of its acceptance. Would nine states ratify the 

Constitution, making it the law of the land? 

Constitution Ratified Becomes "Supreme Law of the

Land." Gradually word came from the state conventions. Delaware was the first to agree; Pennsylvania came next; New Jersey third. Then came two more,

Georgia and Connecticut. There was a long pause when it was feared that the plan would fail to please any other states. But Massachusetts agreed, then Maryland, and 

South Carolina. Only one more state was needed. On 

June 21, 1788, New Hampshire sent in her answer. She too had accepted. There was great rejoicing. The victory was won, and was made doubly sure within the next few weeks by the ratification of the Constitution by the powerful states of New York and Virginia.

Bill of Rights. A number of the states in accepting the 

Constitution recommended that amendments be added to more thoroughly safeguard the rights of individuals against the danger of tyrannical laws and of unjust practices such as had been common under Old World kings. 

Within two years, a Bill of Rights, consisting of eight amendments drawn up by Congress, was ratified by the states and became part of the Constitution. These amendments provided, among other things, for freedom of religion, for free speech, and a free press; for jury trial of citizens accused of crime.

Two additional amendments, the ninth and the tenth, placed limitations upon the power of the federal government over the state governments. 

Preamble States Objects of Fathers of Constitution. - 

"We, the people of the United States, in order to form a more perfect Union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquillity, provide for the common defense, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty to ourselves and our posterity, do ordain and establish this Constitution for the United States of America."

George Washington, First President, Sworn In. - 

With these objects before it the new Constitution was on trial. Elections were held. The electors unanimously chose George Washington for President. On April 30, 1789, in the city of New York, Washington was inaugurated, taking the oath of office which every President has taken from that day to this: "I do solemnly swear that I will faithfully execute the office of President of the United States, and will, to the best of my ability, preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States."

THE NEW NATION FEUDAL IDEAS OF THE OLD WORLD  CHAPTER XX 

A Nation Among the Nations, 1789 In the New Nation, the United States of America, the People North, South, and West Face Serious Problems 

The New Nation Has Broken with the Old World Monarchism. — In 1789 the United States of America, reorganized under the Constitution, was ready to take its place among the nations of the earth. 

The discoveries of Columbus, the voyages of the explorers, the conquest of the Spanish gold hunters, the sea victories of the English had all served their purpose in the building of this new nation. The home builders and those who came after them had laid the foundation of the nation. 

They had tamed the wilderness. They had fought off the 

Indians and the French. By their victories during the 271

Revolution they had overthrown the rule of the Old World kings and had set up a republic. 

In the new republic, where almost every trace of Old World feudalism was dead, the common people were coming into their own as lords of the land. Here there was no king with notions of his divine right to rule over the people. Here there were no nobles claiming feudal rights in the land and refusing to share in the expenses of the government. Here, according to the Constitution, the President and the lawmakers were to be chosen by the action of the voting citizens. Rich and poor were to share in the support of the government.

New states could be carved out of the government lands, and local governments controlled by the people could establish schools and other agencies to promote their welfare. 

Congress was drawing up a series of amendments to the Constitution, known as the Bill of Rights, which guaranteed to all such rights as religious freedom, free press, and trial by jury.

Those Old World kings and nobles who still ruled their lands in a feudal way no doubt believed that this new-born nation, with its strange plan of government, could not last. 

They certainly had every reason for wishing to see the failure of this new contender in the race for world power. 

For if government by the people could succeed in America, the crowns of the kings in Europe might be in danger.

Population Mostly Farmers. Leading Cities. At this time the people of the United States numbered about 4,000,000, most of whom lived on small farms. Along the seacoast, or near it, there were a few cities, Philadelphia, New York, Boston, Charleston, Baltimore, and

Savannah, with populations ranging from 13,000 in Baltimore to 42,000 in Philadelphia.

Ocean Trade of North. Fishing, Whaling. Voyages

to Indies. In the Northern states farming was the principal industry, but the presence of good harbors and of forests for shipbuilding had caused people to turn to the sea for added income. Fishing vessels manned by New 

England sailors went to the fishing banks off Newfoundland. Whale hunters sailed into the Arctic and even into 12 

Population Distribution: Town and Country 

The Constitution of the United States provides that there shall be a census or counting of the population every ten years. The first census taken in 1790 showed that for every one person who lived in a town or city, nine lived on farms. the Antarctic Oceans. Trading vessels carried cargoes of lumber, furs, grain, and fish to the West Indies and to 

Europe. Some trading vessels sailed around Cape Horn at the far end of South America across the Pacific to China and the East Indies.

In the year 1791 one such ship, the Columbia under Captain Gray, sailed up the west coast of the American continent to Oregon. There Gray exchanged trinkets for the furs which the Indians obtained in the Pacific Coast forests. Then he continued to China where he added tea to his cargo. The following year returning to Oregon he

discovered the waters of a mighty river flowing into the 

Pacific. This river he named the "Columbia."

South Raises Some Cotton Besides Other Crops. — In the Southern states as in the Northern states there were wealthy shipbuilders and ocean traders. There was also a lively lumber industry. But in the main, the South was devoted to farming. Planters raised tobacco, rice, and indigo. They had also been raising a little cotton. The 

Population Distribution: East and West 

According to the census of 1790 there were about twenty people east of the Alleghenies for every one person west of the mountains. planters shipped their surplus to market in the vessels which, coming down from the north, sailed up the sluggish rivers to the plantation wharves. 

Population Beyond Alleghenies. Small Farmers. 

West of the Allegheny Mountains there were about two hundred thousand settlers living on small farms along the banks of the rivers which drained into the Mississippi. 

On their farms they raised mostly corn, and hogs which thrived on corn. 

Pittsburgh, on the site of old Fort Duquesne, and Detroit were little more than villages. The site of Chicago was still virgin wilderness.

Tasks and Tools Hardly Changed Since Colonial Days. 

-On the farms of the North and West and on the plantations of the South life was still very much the same as in the earlier days. The men worked with the same old hand

tools. The women looked after their homes in the same old way. In those places where there were schools the children attended them for a few weeks or months each year.

Travel and Communication Slow. Stagecoaches. 

Newspapers. Traveling was still difficult. There were neither railroads nor steamships. Coastwise sailing vessels connected the Atlantic seaports. By stagecoach it took

three days to go from New York to Philadelphia; eight to ten days from New York to Boston. There was some inland trade along the rivers flowing into the coast. Those who lived away from stagecoach and water routes depended upon pack horses to carry their goods along forest trails which were turned to mud by the spring and summer rains.

In some of the cities there were newspapers; but without telephones, telegraph, or cables to serve them, these often reported an important item of national or European news weeks after it had happened. 

North, South, and West not Closely Bound. - Because their means of communication and travel were slow, the people had little opportunity to understand the problems of the nation as a whole. However, each section of the country felt that it had enough cause for worry in its own problems.

At every turn, the North, the South, and the West found that the Old World nations were all too ready to put obstacles in the path of their prosperity. 

North Finds Ocean Trade Hampered by Foreign Duties. 

Those people in the Northern states who depended largely on ocean trade for their prosperity found the ports of England, France, and Spain, and of their colonies in the West Indies practically closed by foreign navigation and trade acts to United States ships and goods. This made life difficult for the Northern shipbuilders, ship owners, merchants, sailors, and fishermen. It made life difficult for the Northern farmers who had to sell part of their crops abroad in order to obtain the money with which to buy manufactured and other goods which the nation imported from abroad.

The Northerners, who had made a beginning in the manufacture of woolen cloth as well as iron tools and im-

Southern Planters Blocked by Spaniards and Indians. —

In the Southern states the tobacco planters were heavily in debt and there seemed to be no way for them to meet their debts. Their old lands, exhausted by many years of tobacco raising, were less productive. They were therefore in a mood to seek new lands to the South and West.

Western Settlers Face Freight Problem. Unfriendly 

Neighbors. The Western settlers who were almost shut off from the east by the Allegheny Mountains had the problem of shipping their produce to markets. The way over the mountains was far too costly for such freight as bulky grains and meats.

Room Interior of the Period 

The prosperous town homes of the period were handsomely furnished. 

Most homes, however, both in town and country, were much plainer. 

West of the Alleghenies pioneer conditions prevailed in the rough log cabins. the American settlers the port of New Orleans, which was the one outlet by means of which the river settlements in the Mississippi Valley could secure a continuous water route to the West Indies and the rest of the world. The

Indians of the Southwest sided with the Spaniards, who held the land thinly, rather than with the American settlers, whose farms would crowd them. The old struggle between furs and farms, between civilization and the wilderness, still continued and the settlers in the Southwest as in the Northwest suffered from frequent Indian raids. 

The Nation in Debt. In addition to these local problems of North, South, and West the republic as a whole faced the serious problem of the lack of funds. The nation had, as yet, no source of income with which to pay the expenses of government. It had no funds with which to make payments on the money which had been borrowed during the struggle for independence. 

Such, then, was the state of affairs in 1789. The American people found themselves more or less blocked in their freedom of trade, handicapped in their manufacture, endangered in their freedom to settle the frontier lands, while the government which had the duty of promoting their general welfare was heavily in debt. 

We shall see in the next chapter how the new nation, reorganized under the Constitution, solved its problems.

CHAPTER XXI The Ship of State Sets Sail 

Shortly After Washington Becomes President, European Autocracies Begin to Fall-The European Wars which Follow Help to Solve Some of America's Problems but Create Others - Hamilton's Domestic Policies Strengthen America - Two Political Parties Arise Differing in Their Interpretations of the Constitution Washington's Task. Starting the Republic on Its 

Course. As the first President of the new republic, it was Washington's duty to help start it on its course-a difficult task in which a false move might spell disaster. 

Years before, when Washington had been chosen to lead the armies of the Revolution, he had wondered whether his untrained farmer soldiers could stand and win against the trained troops of England. 

That question had been answered on many a battlefield. 

The soldiers of the Revolution had set their faces toward 282

liberty. Through all the dark days and the doubts he had seen them fight their way to victory.

The citizens of the new nation desired a lawful and orderly self-government under the Constitution. Would they hold together and win? Would the new republic under its Constitution hold its own against the Old World nations and their kings?

European Autocracies Fall. As events turned out it was not the new republic which failed, but the Old World autocracies.

In 1789, the very year in which Washington took the oath of office, Louis XVI, king of France, seeing his nation bankrupt, called a meeting of the Estates General or French parliament, a body which no French king had consulted for hundreds of years.

From the day when Louis XVI issued his call, events moved swiftly toward revolution. The old feudal system, suited to a day when stone castles were the centers of so many separate little worlds, had lasted centuries beyond its usefulness. In the new age of world trade the feudal laws, which were made to specially benefit the kings and nobles, were holding France back; and now feudalism fell. 

France was declared a republic. The king and queen were guillotined.

The old feudal laws concerning land ownership and taxes were ultimately abolished.

Soon after the revolution in France all the old rivalries and fears which existed among the European nations again flamed into war. In 1792 France declared war on Austria and Prussia. In 1793 England declared war on France.

The French leaders in Paris, alarmed for the safety of the republic, guillotined without mercy all whom they suspected as enemies of the new government. This "Reign of Terror" lasted almost a year. By 1795 five directors

were ruling the republic. In 1799 Napoleon Bonaparte, returning from a campaign in Egypt, deposed the directors and became First Consul of France. Later he had himself crowned Emperor and led his armies through Europe deposing kings, setting up rulers of his own choosing, wiping out the old feudal laws, and giving to the people his own laws, the "Code Napoléon.' 

The Napoleonic Wars shook all Europe until 1815, when the Battle of Waterloo ended Napoleon's career. 

Europe's Need of America Solves Many Problems. 

As the European wars drew masses of men from their work, the European nations had to turn to American farmers for foodstuffs and to American ships as ocean carriers. European and colonial ports were thrown open to the United States ships and American ocean trade increased by leaps and bounds. In 1795 Spain signed a treaty which granted to the Western farmers the "right of deposit" in New Orleans; or, in other words, the right to unload their riverborne goods in New Orleans for reloading on ocean-going vessels. Western lands boomed in value as cotton, grains, and meats brought high prices. 

So, because of Europe's need of American farm products and shipping, many of the problems of the North, South, and West were solved. In time the European wars even led to the acquisition of new territory by the United States. 

Washington Declares Neutrality. The Case of "Citi zen" Genêt. Almost immediately after England and 

France went to war, France tried to bring the United States in as her ally. Many Americans sympathized with her cause and felt that we should repay France for her aid during the Revolution. Other Americans sided with 

England. Washington issued a "Declaration of Neutrality" 

which made it clear that the United States planned to keep out of the European mix-up.

Meanwhile "Citizen" Genêt had come from France to ask for aid. The French sympathizers welcomed him most cordially, but Washington and Congress held to their course. Genêt decided to appeal to the people over the heads of their leaders. His appeal was not heeded. The people stood by the federal government and the Constitution. Washington asked France to instruct Genêt to stop his meddling. France yielded. 

Differences with England. Confiscation at Sea. Impressment. Forts. - The European wars and the sudden opening of foreign markets helped to solve some American problems. They brought prosperity. They also brought irritation and created new problems. 

Great Britain and France each took the stand that they had the right to capture United States ships trading with the enemy nation and to confiscate the American cargoes. 

To add to American irritation Great Britain, needing many men for her navy, her main defense, held up United States ships and impressed into service any sailors born in Great Britain, even when these men had taken out citizenship papers. She did this on the claim that no British subject could change his allegiance. "Once an Englishman, always an Englishman." This idea of citizenship was held by most European nations.

The British, moreover, were occupying a number of the Western forts which, according to the Treaty of Paris, should have been turned over to the United States government. 

Washington Sends Jay to Make Treaty. Washington was eager to settle these matters peacefully, if possible. 

In 1794, one year before he succeeded in getting Spain to sign the treaty opening New Orleans for the Western farmers, he had sent John Jay to draw up the terms of a treaty with Great Britain. Jay returned with a treaty in which

Great Britain agreed to give up the Western forts but did not promise to stop impressing English-born sailors on 

American ships.

When Congress accepted this treaty, the sympathizers with France were furious. In New York Hamilton was 

Alexander Hamilton 

Hamilton was born in the British West Indies, and was, therefore, in a sense an immigrant. He served in the American Revolution. He was a guiding force in the planning and adoption of the Constitution. As the first Secretary of the Treasury, he formulated policies which went far toward establishing the financial security and future of his adopted country. 

Hamilton's brilliant career was cut short when Aaron Burr, a political rival, killed him in a duel. stoned. Washington was vilely abused in the pro- 

French newspapers. 

Washington's Cabinet. 

In all the trials of the Euro pean situation Washington was supported by a Congress of able men. In addition he had as his advisers three secretaries, whom he had appointed to head the War, State, and Treasury departments, which Congress had created as branches of the 

Executive department. Gen eral Knox was Secretary of 

War; Thomas Jefferson was 

Secretary of State; Alexander 

Hamilton was Secretary of the Treasury.

Congress also created the office of Attorney General, to which Edmund Randolph was appointed. Randolph and the three secretaries formed a Cabinet, or presidential council. 

Hamilton Plans Debt Bonds, Bank, Tariff. - Almost. 

as soon as he entered office Alexander Hamilton planned a series of acts by means of which he hoped to win for the

Constitution and the republic the faith of the people at home and of statesmen abroad.

He proposed to Congress an act by which the United States government should take over all the debts of the separate states as well as those of the previous national government.

Hamilton also advised the Congress to create a United 

States Bank.

To establish a bank was easy enough. But how would the nation obtain money for the expenses of government? 

Here, too, Hamilton had a plan. He advised that Congress put a tariff on certain manufactured goods imported into the country. 

Hamilton Wishes American Manufacture to Increase.

Great Britain in Lead. At a time when most people could see little in America but farming land, Hamilton was looking ahead to the building of American manufactures. 

Hamilton did not wish to see America remain a farming country dependent upon Great Britain for her manufactured goods. He saw something of the part which manufacturers were going to play in the future of the nations of the world, and he was eager that the United States with its splendid resources should develop its manufactures so that it would not depend too much on Great Britain or other European nations.

In cloth making, English manufacturers were aided by the invention of new spinning and weaving machinery. 

With England's coal and iron mines, and with her newly invented steam-engine pumps to keep the mines free from water, Great Britain's iron workers had much the better of their rivals. English ironware as well as English woolen and cotton cloth led in the world's markets. 

Besides the advantage which the new inventions gave to English manufacturers, all the Old World manufacturers

had the further advantage of cheaper labor. In America, where land for farming was plentiful, men had to be paid more to be induced to work in mills, mines, or factories. 

Tariff for Revenue: Also for Protection of Manufac tures. These facts did not discourage Hamilton. He was convinced that if given a chance American manufactures would grow in quantity and quality. He advised that UNITED

Hamilton's Policies 

Hamilton proposed: (1) That the nation issue United States bonds to help pay off foreign and domestic debts. (2) That a tariff law be passed mainly to raise revenue and partly to protect American manufacturers. (3) That Congress charter a United 

States Bank.

Congress help build up American manufactures by collecting a tariff on manufactured goods imported from other countries. This tariff would first and foremost be a tariff for revenue, providing the government with needed funds, but it would also help to protect the young manufacturing industries against the cheaper goods from Europe. 

For a tariff to be fully a protective tariff it would have to add enough to the cost of the cheap European goods to make these at least as expensive as the American-made goods.

In addition to the tariff Congress considered a direct tax on whisky to increase the government revenue.

Jefferson Opposes Hamilton; Yields When South Wins

Capital. — All of Hamilton's plans aroused a good deal of criticism. One complaint was that the state debt certificates had been bought up by speculators, many of whom would now reap fortunes through the government's payments in full. Jefferson and other Southern statesmen who opposed Hamilton's measures were finally won over when Hamilton promised to support an act moving the

United States Capital from 

New York to Philadelphia for ten years, and then to 

Washington in the District of Columbia. The District of 

Columbia was a tract of land which Virginia and Maryland agreed to set aside for the nation's use. 

Rebellion against Whisky

Tax. Federal Power Wins. 

In western Pennsylvania a few thousand men who manufactured and sold whisky took up arms against the government tax-collectors.

Finding it too costly to send their corn across the mountains to the East, they had been turning their bulky crops into whisky which could be shipped more easily. They felt that the tax was an unfair burden on them. 

Here was a test of the willingness of the people to support the Union under the Constitution. Would the other Western settlers rally to the rebels and break the power of the new government, or would the Federal power prevail? 

The question was answered immediately.

Washington called upon Pennsylvania and neighboring states to furnish him with fifteen thousand men. These volunteers advanced to meet the rebels, who dispersed. 

The rebel leaders were arrested, tried, and convicted. 

Washington, however, was lenient toward them. He knew that the trouble-makers had learned that the people were going to stand by the government.

As the taxes and duties were collected, money began to flow into the government treasury. 

Funds from Western Lands. New States: Kentucky and Tennessee. The sale of government lands in the 

West was also bringing money into the Treasury. In spite of the difficulty in moving farm produce from the Western farms into the East, many Easterners bought government land in the Northwest Territory. This Western movement was made with less risk when Washington sent troops against the hostile Indians in the Ohio Valley. 

To the south, so many settlers had moved into Kentucky and Tennessee that these two territories were ready for statehood. They were soon admitted as states on equal terms with the thirteen original states. 

Whitney's Cotton Gin Helps South. During Wash ington's administration Southern planters who had been worried by the decreasing fertility of their tobacco fields heard good news.

In 1793 a young man, Eli Whitney by name, had invented a cotton gin, a small hand machine which could swiftly and inexpensively remove the seeds from the boll of the cotton plant. This meant that Southern planters who had been raising a little cotton would find it profitable to raise large quantities for sale to the manufacturers of cotton cloth.

A short time after Whitney's cotton gin came into use, cotton became an important crop in the South, and

Southern planters saw themselves on the way to a new prosperity.

Washington's Farewell Address against Alliances and 

Party Spirit. - When his second term expired Washington refused to run for reëlection. Before retiring, he delivered a farewell address in which he advised the people against alliances which would entangle them in European politics, and he urged that duty to country should be placed above party spirit.

Political Parties. Federal ist and Republican. - Washington's advice concerning entangling alliances was heeded. His advice about party spirit fell upon deaf ears. During his second term of office the leaders of the people had built up two parties. 

A Political Argument 

Should the Constitution be interpreted as giving the federal government any powers not specifically mentioned? This was a subject of constant dispute between the Federalists and the Anti-Federalists. 

The members of the Federalist party, led by Washington and Hamilton, were eager to see a strong central government. They claimed for the government many powers which were not always stated in so many words in the Constitution; in other words, they favored "Loose Construction" of the Constitution.

The members of the Republican party were jealous for the power of the separate states; and they insisted that the national government should exercise no powers which were not definitely given to it by the Constitution. They favored "Strict Construction" of the Constitution.

The Federalist leaders were accused of being aristocratic, pro-English, and eager for kingly power. The Republican party was frankly pro-French and wished to see the people have a larger share in the government. 

Federalists Win. John Adams President. - All through 

Washington's second term these two parties had divided on almost every issue, and more than once one side or the other had shown the bitter party spirit against which 

Washington had counseled.

When Washington retired the Federalists still held the 

John Adams

John Adams was the second president of the United States (1797-1801). 

The leading events of his administration were: X, Y, Z demands; battles with French ships; Alien and Sedition 

Acts; Virginia and Kentucky Resolu tions. upper hand. They had elected John Adams to the presidency. 

French Directors Demand 

Bribes. Shortly after Adams took the oath of office, the

Directors of the new republic of France began to show open hostility to the United States. 

From the first days of the war with England, the 

French officials had counted on United States aid. The failure of Genêt's mission angered them. Still further angered by the Jay Treaty, they manifested their hostility by refusing to receive the American minister. 

When Adams sent special envoys to France to discuss the difficulties which were arising, the French Directors sent three representatives to meet the American envoys. These 

Frenchmen demanded a United States loan to France; they

demanded personal bribes for the Directors, and they threatened that unless the bribes and the loan were handed over they would make war on the United States. 

Adams Resents Demands. War With France. - Presi dent Adams announced to Congress the demands and threats made by the three men whom he called X, Y, and Z. 

The President wrote, "I will never send another minister to France without assurances that he will be received, respected, and honored as the representative of a free, powerful, and independent nation." "Millions for defense; not one cent for tribute," became the slogan of the nation. To the new tune of “Hail Columbia," companies of men marched to drill on the village greens. Many of them were dressed in the cast-off uniforms of the Revolution, which they had taken down from their garrets. Although there were no formal declarations of war, fighting began at sea. It did not last long. In 1800, after Napoleon had driven the French Directors from power, he made peace with the United States. 

Alien and Sedition Acts to Suppress Critics. — During this brief outbreak there were critics in the land, many of them foreign-born, who, through newspapers and other means, found fault with the government and its officers for fighting France instead of helping her. Congress, seeing danger to the republic in this wartime criticism, passed the "Alien and Sedition Acts," which were aimed to silence these men either through deportation or imprisonment. 

The Alien Acts empowered the federal government to deport non-citizens for the slightest of causes. 

The Natu ralization Act increased the term of naturalization from five to fourteen years. The Sedition Acts empowered the government to imprison editors, public speakers, and others who criticized the government or its officers. Many of those arrested under the Sedition Acts were Republicans.

Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions Against Acts. — The 

Republicans claimed that the Alien and Sedition Acts proved the danger of tyranny under the Federalist loose interpretation of the Constitution. According to them, under a strict interpretation of the Constitution, Congress had no right to enact such drastic laws. In Virginia and

The Alien and Sedition Acts were passed during the administration of John Adams, Federalist. Anti-Federalists criticized these acts as proofs that a strong federal government may prove as tyrannical as any king. The 

Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions denounced the Alien and Sedition Acts. in Kentucky, the state legislatures, jealous of their states' rights, passed resolutions against the Alien and Sedition 

Acts. 

In the second Kentucky Resolution of 1799, the stand was taken that the states have the right to declare an act passed by Congress null and void. The Virginia and 

Kentucky Resolutions had no effect as regards the Alien and Sedition laws, but they became the basis upon which rested the many subsequent declarations of the right of secession and of nullification by both Northern and 

Southern states.

The popular opposition aroused by the Alien and

Sedition Acts may have helped to strengthen the cause of the Republican party, which, in 1800, succeeded in electing 

Thomas Jefferson as President. 

Washington Dies. -That same year Washington, who had been called from his retirement to lead the American army, gave up his command and retired to Mount Vernon, where he died. In Congress Henry Lee spoke those words which have lived as the best expression of the esteem in which Washington has been held by a grateful people, "First in war; first in peace; first in the hearts of his countrymen.' 99 He had lived to see his country, strengthened by its 

Constitution, survive ten years of stress and storm.

Thomas Jefferson Third President of the United States 

(1801-1805) 

CHAPTER XXII Buying an Empire 

Thomas Jefferson, Republican President, a Believer in Economy and

States' Rights, a Strict Constructionist, Agrees that the United States 

Pay Fifteen Million Dollars for the Purchase of Louisiana- 

He then Sends Lewis and Clark to Explore the New 

Government Lands President Jefferson Cuts Expenses. Reduces Navy. 

On the fourth day of March in the year 1801 there walked through the streets of Washington, the nation's new capital, Thomas Jefferson, who was on his way to be inaugurated as third President of the United States. 

Thomas Jefferson, like George Washington, was a Southerner, one of that large body of able political leaders and statesmen born and raised in the atmosphere of a large plantation. His home at Monticello was one of the handsome mansions of the South.

Jefferson was a well-read scholar and a fine writer, as his ringing words in the Declaration of Independence prove. 297

He who had written that all men are created equal had a deep faith in the judgment of the people. 

As the leader of the Republican party, which had won its first victory in the presidential election of 1800, he did not wish to see Congress exercise kingly power. Nor did he wish to see Congress indulge in any kingly extravagance. 

It was the policy of his party to help pay off the nation's debt by cutting down the expenses of the government wherever possible. He dismissed unnecessary officeholders. He even cut down on the small allowance for the army and navy.

Jefferson and the party he led had no sympathy with Hamilton's plans for promoting American manufactures. 

He wanted to see the republic remain a nation of farmers, and it seems to have been his belief that a farming nation could, if it wished, gain all its aims by peace. 

New Orleans Closed. West Clamors for War. Then, as though to prove Jefferson wrong, bad news came from the West where the farmers were clamoring for war. Since the treaty with Spain in 1795 the Western settlers had been shipping their grain and meats by flatboats down the Mississippi through New Orleans. Now the Spanish officials suddenly closed New Orleans to United States trade.

This act came as a thunderbolt to the Western farmers, who demanded from Jefferson a war which would once and for all win New Orleans for their own. 

Jefferson Sends James Monroe to Buy New Orleans from France. But Jefferson knew that if there were to be a war for New Orleans, it would not be with Spain but with Napoleon. He had learned through the United States minister in France that by a secret treaty with Napoleon Spain had returned Louisiana to France. 

Louisiana under the rule of Napoleon might become an even greater menace to the United States than Louisiana

under Spain. Jefferson, eager for peace, had decided on action even before the closing of New Orleans.

As soon as he had heard of the secret treaty, he had sent James Monroe to sound out Napoleon about the sale of 

New Orleans and the western part of Florida.

TO EUROPE Napoleon's Plan for French Empire in America Fails. - 

It seemed a strange thing to ask. Why should Napoleon yield New Orleans, the key to Louisiana? Nothing seemed less likely. In fact for some time Napoleon had been planning to build in Louisiana a powerful French empire. To that end he had sent troops to put down a revolution in

San Domingo, one of the French Indies. With this island as a base he planned to have French troops enter Louisiana, where they could help make real La Salle's old dream of a vast French empire reaching from the Gulf of Mexico northward to the Great Lakes and westward to the Rockies.

But an island revolt, led by a negro patriot, Toussaint l'Ouverture, had checked Napoleon's troops. And now 

Great Britain was once more on the verge of declaring war on France. Great Britain, with her many ships of war, might easily capture New Orleans and take over the undefended Louisiana territory. 

Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed. So chance fa vored the United States.

Napoleon did not refuse the American offer. To save 

Louisiana from Great Britain and to raise money for war, Napoleon now offered to sell to the United States, not only New Orleans, but all of Louisiana, from the Mississippi to the Rockies. The offer was accepted. A payment equaling about fifteen million dollars was the price agreed upon. 

James Monroe, Robert Livingston, the American minister to France, and Napoleon's agent, signed a treaty for the purchase of Louisiana which was to add approximately eight hundred seventy-five thousand square miles to the government lands, thus practically doubling the territory of the United States. 

Jefferson Favors Purchase. - Jefferson was more than a little worried when the purchase treaty arrived.

As a Republican standing for a strict interpretation of the Constitution, how could he agree to the purchase?

There was nothing in the Constitution about the right of 

Congress and the President to buy an empire. 

What was he to do? 

Wait for an amendment? There was no time. Napoleon

might change his mind before the amendment could be passed upon by the people. 

Should he refuse to purchase? That might leave Louisiana to become a battle ground of European powers, fighting endless wars into which the United States might be drawn.

Jefferson, therefore, considering all things, favored the purchase. The Senate rati fied the purchase treaty and he signed it, thereby establishing a national policy of territorial expansion by treaty-making power. Through a peaceful business transaction, the United States doubled its size, and the federal government became the owner of an area far greater and richer in natural wealth than most of the empires for which Old World kings had fought long and bloody wars. No one to-day questions the wisdom of the purchase of Louisiana.

Louisiana was still an almost unbroken country. The shipping center at New Orleans with its eight or ten thousand people, the trading center at St. Louis with its twelve hundred inhabitants, were its two main towns. 

Here and there along the Mississippi were small villages which were hardly more than trading posts where the Indians could barter their furs for the white man's goods. The little which was known of the interior of Louisiana came through the vague reports of trappers and traders who had ascended the swift-flowing rivers in canoes.

There were critics who called the purchase of all this unknown, unexplored country a waste of public funds. "What is the value of an empire of wild land beyond man's reach? The

For seven months they worked their way against the swift current of the Missouri, using both sail and oars, laboring unremittingly and overcoming the endless obstacles of the wilderness, until they finally had traveled six-

teen hundred miles upstream. But the source of the river was still not in sight.

Value of Louisiana to Nation. - Lewis, Clark, and Pike wrote careful reports of all they saw, but they could give

little more than a hint of the wealth which this great West was one day to yield to an eager world.

Exploring the Far West 

No picture can do more than merely suggest the varied beauty of the Far West with its high snow-capped mountain ranges, its deep canyons, roaring waterfalls, strange geysers, dense forests, and sun-baked deserts aglow with brilliant desert flowers. To-day millions of people live in the states carved out of the West; millions more tour the West to enjoy its scenic beauty. 

Louisiana provided reckoned in terms of mere wealth. new farm lands for millions, who, coming out of the East and out of Europe, helped to build new states in the West.

While other nations were to fight with one another for markets in distant parts of the world, the farmers who went into Louisiana provided the United States with a great home market for its manufactured goods. While other nations turning to manufacturing needed colonies from which to get food supplies, wool, cotton, lumber, metals, and minerals, the United States discovered in Louisiana a great source of foodstuffs, of metals, minerals, and other raw materials needed for the trading and manufacturing cities of the East, as well as for the mighty cities which grew up in the West.

All of these things were scores of years off. There were pressing problems nearer home. Jefferson had avoided war on the New Orleans issue, but other issues more difficult now confronted the nation.

Monticello 

The stately home of Thomas Jefferson is still standing and has become a national shrine, dedicated to the simple philosopher, statesman, planter, lover of the arts and sciences, who wrote the Declaration of Independence, served his country as President, and founded the University of Virginia.

Pirates and Paper Blockades

The United States Fights Sea Pirates in the Mediterranean; English and French Interfere with Neutral Ocean Trade; The United States Declares War against England 

Trade on the Seas. Danger from Pirates. When 

Lewis and Clark returned to the East in 1806 they found the people alarmed over the freedom and safety of their sea trade.

Long ago, when men first learned to sail the inland seas, ship captains seeking goods in foreign lands frequently robbed the natives instead of buying from them. The natives naturally tried to defend their goods. There were battles, and men were killed. Slowly, very slowly, neighboring peoples learned that it was better to exchange goods peacefully rather than to sacrifice human lives in the attempt to rob property or to defend it. So sea trade began. But with the development of sea trade, piracy, or, in other words, sea robbery, continued to flourish. Pirates setting 310

out to sea attacked many trading ships and robbed them of their goods.

For centuries after the Mediterranean became the highway of European trade with the East this sea was the scene of piracy. Later when ships learned to sail the oceans, sea robbers also turned to these new avenues of trade. 

Ocean piracy was common all through the colonial days. 

After the beginning of the nineteenth century, piracy on the Atlantic was less common. 

The United States Brings Pasha of Tripoli to Terms. 

As late as Jefferson's day, the Mediterranean Sea was still infested with pirate ships. On the Barbary Coast of North 

Africa there were four Moorish kingdoms - Algiers, Tripoli, Morocco, and Tunis. Pirates sailing out of the harbors under the master pirate, the Pasha of Tripoli, captured many Mediterranean ships and their cargoes. 

The pirate captains then demanded ransom for their prisoners on threat of selling them into slavery. Often there were collections in the churches at home for money to be sent to the Moorish kingdoms for ransoming poor captives. To buy protection for their Mediterranean trade, many of the European nations, even Great Britain with her mighty navy, paid tribute to the Moorish kings. So did the United States for a time. 

In his first year as President, Jefferson, peace-lover though he was, refused to pay these disgraceful bribes and decided that the United States would do what Great

Britain and the other European nations had not done. He sent a few warships to besiege Tripoli. It was difficult to carry on naval operations so far from home, and against such freebooters as these pirates. But after a series of encounters, extending through several years, the Americans brought Tripoli to terms in 1805. Ten years later, after another display of force by the American navy

under Stephen Decatur, Mediterranean piracy practically ceased.

New Danger. Great Britain and France Restrict Ocean 

Trade. For those Americans who depended on the freedom of the seas for their prosperity, the old danger from 

Napoleon Bonaparte the Continent. 

piracy was nothing compared with a new danger which the United States was facing in her sea trade. Word reached the United States 

Gio that both Great Britain and

France were determined to prevent American ships from enjoying the freedom of the seas.

The struggle between Napoleon and Great Britain had reached a deadlock. On land Napoleon had defeated the Russians, the Prussians, and the Austrians, all allies of Great Britain. In so doing he had made France master of 

On the sea Lord Nelson, commanding the

British fleet, had defeated the French fleet at Trafalgar. 

Some one has said that from this point on, the war between Great Britain and France was like a fight between a whale and a lion. It seemed that so long as each was master in its own element, there could be no victory for either France or Great Britain.

Great Britain now decided to use her sea power to break Napoleon's land power by cutting off the supplies which reached France by way of the ocean. In 1806, the same year in which Lewis and Clark returned from the West,

Great Britain issued Orders in Council which declared the northern part of the coast of France blockaded; neutral ships were ordered not to carry goods into these French ports. Napoleon retaliated with the Berlin Decree which declared a blockade of all British ports, and asserted that if ships of neutral countries entered British ports they forfeited their rights to trade with French ports as neutrals.

Great Britain issued further Orders in Council, which demanded that United States or other neutral ships trading with any ports on the Continent must first enter a British port, register there, and make heavy payments. Napoleon, by another edict, the Milan Decree, declared war against all ships which complied with the British orders. 

These acts if enforced were bound to seriously menace 

United States trade and shipping and impair American prosperity. In order to obtain funds for many of the things which they needed, American farmers, planters, and fishermen all had to sell their surplus in foreign markets. 

To deny them the freedom of the seas would choke their economic life and rob them of economic independence. 

During the few centuries of trade on the Atlantic, nations had more or less agreed upon a body of international laws concerning ocean trade. It had been understood that a nation at war might use her navy to blockade the coast of an enemy and take all neutral ships which tried to break through. But these blockades of Great Britain and France were not real blockades maintained by a navy patrol. 

They were paper blockades; the mere fact that Great 

Britain and France wrote on paper that the United States ships must keep out of the enemy ports was supposed to constitute a blockade of the enemy coast. "Free ships make free goods" was the answer of the irritated Americans.

Great Britain Impressing American Sailors. Leopard 

Stops Chesapeake. - To add to American ill-will against 

Great Britain, British ships were still stopping United States vessels to search them for sailors born in the British empire. In one case, the captain of a British frigate, the Leopard, had even gone so far as to stop a United 

States frigate, the Chesapeake, from which he removed four sailors, three of whom were United States citizens. 

British Impressment of Sailors 

British ships stopped American vessels to search them for sailors born in Great Britain. Even when these sailors had proof that they were naturalized citizens of the United States, British captains forcibly impressed them.

Great Britain justified her action by the claim "Once an Englishman, always an Englishman." 

Clearly conditions at sea called for action. 

What was the United 

States to do?

While Napoleon was master of the Continent, war against France would close the ports of continental Europe to those farmers who were depending on this market for the sale of much of their grains and meat stuffs. 

To make war against Great

Britain would bring a vigorous attack by the powerful 

British navy against United 

States ocean trade. It might cause the destruction of the American merchant fleet. 

Jefferson Hopes Embargo Act Will Bring Victory 

Without War. - To Jefferson, who was determined to preserve peace yet eager to serve the nation, the situation was a difficult one.

It seemed to him that there was one peaceful way of striking back at both Great Britain and France. 

He would ask Congress to pass an Embargo Act ordering no vessels to leave an American port except those engaged

WEST The Embargo 

During the embargo, ships lay idle; goods intended for export filled the warehouses to overflowing; crops rotted in the fields. Without ocean trade and foreign markets the country faced ruin. in coastwise trade. He hoped that Great Britain and 

France, shut off from American supplies, would be forced to grant to American shipping the freedom of the seas.

Embargo Act Choking Sea Trade Causes Suffering. 

Congress passed the Embargo Act but the plan did not work as well as Jefferson had hoped. The shutting down of the export trade was a blow to Great Britain and France; but it also hurt the United States severely. 

With ships idle in the docks, thousands of sailors and other men who lived by sea trade were suddenly thrown out of employment. Farmers and planters also suffered; their crops rotted in the fields. Merchants lost heavily; their warehouses became choked with cotton, wool, and tobacco. Shops, mills, and factories were forced to close. 

Throughout the country people felt the sudden cutting off of trade.

Congress Repeals Embargo Act. Passes Non- 

Intercourse Act. At the very end of Jefferson's administration, after a little more than a year of the Embargo, Congress withdrew the act and passed instead a Non- Intercourse Act. This act which forbade trade only with 

Great Britain and France did not help matters very much. 

Since most of the United States trade was with these two countries, the Non-Intercourse Act differed very little from an Embargo.

The New England states managed to scrape along with the greatly reduced trade of those years. The Southern planters with little outside market for their tobacco, rice, indigo, and cotton were in sore straits. The Westerners with their unsold stock of corn, wheat, wool, and meat were the hardest hit of all. 

Despite national unrest Jefferson held the nation back from war during his second term. When his party offered him the nomination for the third term, he refused. Like 

Washington, he did not wish to see the presidency of the United States tend to become a life job as a kingship. No president has ever been elected for more than two terms.

President Madison for Peace. - James Madison, the

Republican candidate, who along with Hamilton had played a large part in drawing up the Constitution, succeeded Jefferson as President and served for two terms. 

Madison, like Jefferson, wished to keep the path of peace, but during his term of office the trouble with Great Britain, which had been brewing ever since 1793, finally came to a head. 

West Angered by Indian Uprising. Harrison and Tippecanoe. In 1811 the Indians in the Northwest Territory, under the lead of Tecumseh, planned to win back their lands from the Western settlers. On the day when Tecumseh would give the signal, the Indian tribes were to fall upon the unsuspecting white men, destroy their towns, burn their fields, and kill as many as possible. 

General William Henry Harrison met the Indians at

Tippecanoe near the Wabash River. He and the armed forces of the frontier put the Indians to flight and burned the Indian village.

As many of the Indians had British guns and ammunition, the Western settlers believed that they were urged on in their plot by the British in Canada. 

South Blames England for Indian Raids. — In the South, too, where the frontier plantations had suffered and were suffering from the Indians, men laid the blame partly to British interference. Spain's indifference to the border raids conducted from her Florida territory were likewise charged to the influence of Great Britain, now her ally. 

So South and West attributed their Indian troubles to 

Great Britain. 

Madison Yields to "War Hawks." In the spring of 

1811 a United States warship, ordered out to protect the coast against annoyances at sea, fired upon a British warship. Many Americans greeted this act with enthusiasm.

When Congress met in December, 1811, a group of younger men from the South and West arose and pleaded for war. Among these new leaders in Congress were Henry 

Clay from the new state of Kentucky and John C. Calhoun from the state of South Carolina. 

These "War Hawks," as they were called, insisted that the day for talking peace had passed. They claimed that the British had been encouraging the Indians in the West; that the British blockades had been ruining United States trade; that the search of the United States ships by 

Great Britain was an insult to the United States flag; that the impressment of United States citizens into the 

British navy was illegal.

According to the "War Hawks" all these things called for one answer, "War!" The object of the war would be to force Great Britain to respect the rights of neutral nations at sea and to make Great Britain pay for the damage she had done, by American conquest and annexation of Canada. 

Congress voted for war. 

President Madison signed the declaration.

CHAPTER XXIV Freedom of the Seas 

After Unsuccessful Campaigns against Canada, a Few Brilliant Naval Victories and an Unnecessary Battle at New Orleans, the 

War Ends - The Treaty Mentions None of the Causes of the 

Struggle Even so, the Conflict Has Important Results 

War Finds United States Unprepared. What a fool hardy struggle the War of 1812 must have seemed to the nations of the world! Under Jefferson and Madison, both lovers of peace, the United States had economized in its army and navy expenditures until the country now was almost totally unprepared. The nation was divided; New 

England and New York did not want war. The small, untrained army of the United States was being pitted against the British army of veterans trained in the long 320

struggle with Napoleon. The tiny American navy was to face the thousand fighting craft which Great Britain had at her command.

In spite of these figures the American leaders went into the war expecting to win. They counted on Great Britain's conflict with Napoleon to keep the British army and navy busy in and around 

Europe. They were confident that the American army could conquer Canada. 

Canada not Taken. British in Northwest Territory. 

Those who hoped for the conquest and annexation of 

Canada were sorely disappointed. The campaigns of the United States against 

Canada all failed. One of the armies which was counted upon to overrun Canada was so poorly led by its general that the British and their 

Indian allies were able to bottle it up in Detroit. The general surrendered his army without striking a blow. The

British entered Detroit and
