Madison was the fourth president of the United States (1809-1817). 

The leading events of his adminis tration were: Non-Importation Act; 

Indian uprising led by Tecumseh;

Battle of Tippecanoe; War of 1812, largely forced on the country by the 

War Hawks; Hartford Convention. 

soon held practically all of Michigan. For a time it seemed. that the United States was in danger of losing the Northwest Territory.

British Capture Washington. Bombard Baltimore. 

British troops landing in the South captured the American

Capital at Washington. The government buildings were

burned. The British excuse for this act was that American troops in Canada had set fire to a town. The British next struck at Baltimore, bombarding the city from the fleet of warships in the harbor. It was during this bombardment that the "Star-Spangled Banner" was written.

Francis Scott Key was on board a British ship arranging for an exchange of prisoners when the bombardment began. 99 

Through the porthole he saw the American flag above the fort. Would the Americans fall and lower that flag? 

Eagerly he waited for morning to see whether the banner would still be waving over the city. When the morning came, he saw the The "Star-Spangled Banner' flag and wrote the words of the song which millions of 

Americans have been singing ever since. 

American Victories at Sea. On land the United States armies paid for their lack of preparedness by the loss of practically every campaign. At sea the story of the War of 1812 was different. On the ocean, on the Great 

Lakes, and on Lake Champlain, United States sailors won against Great Britain in hard-fought battles. Although 

Great Britain with her many ships finally succeeded in establishing a crippling blockade of the American coast, the record of American naval victories thrilled the country.

In the very first sea fight the United States frigate Constitution, or "Old Ironsides," as the people later called it, defeated the British frigate, Guerrière.

In the first six months of the War of 1812 the British lost every sea fight with the American ships. Five of her

fine ships were captured or destroyed in a series of brilliant American naval victories. 

Perry on Lake Erie. Saves Northwest Territory. In the second year of the war, in a battle on Lake Erie, Captain Oliver H. Perry de feated a British fleet of six vessels and captured them. 

His message read briefly," We have met the enemy and they are ours.' 99 

Perry's victory prevented a British army from over running the Northwest Ter ritory. It also helped make possible General Harrison's advance into Canada. There in the battle of the Thames, Harrison defeated the British and their Indian allies, whose chief, Tecumseh, fell in battle. This triumph, together with the earlier victory of Tippecanoe, broke the power of Tecumseh and of the Indian tribes who had been terrorizing the Northwest. 

The Constitution ("Old Ironsides") MacDonough's Victory on Lake Champlain Saves Hudson Valley. The following year, Commodore 

MacDonough won a victory on Lake Champlain similar to Perry's. By his defeat of a British fleet, MacDonough prevented an army of British veterans, fresh from victories over Napoleon, from coming into the Hudson Valley. 

Privateers Attack Enemy Commerce. At sea, American privateers added to Great Britain's losses by their steady attack on British trade. Within two years they 

---

captured well over a thousand British merchant vessels and brought their cargoes into United States ports. During the third year of the war, when British armies gained the upper hand in Europe, Great Britain sent a fleet to completely check American ocean trade by an effective blockade of the American coast. 

This blockade lessened the activities of the privateers. 

Dolly Madison 

As "first lady of the land "Mrs.

James Madison, known to history as Dolly Madison, became famous for her grace and beauty. 

New England Federalists Against War. Hartford Con vention. In New England, where merchants and ship owners who had been reaping large profits from European conditions had all along been opposed to war with Great Britain, the blockade was the last straw. 

Before the war, Federalists in New England had complained that a struggle with 

Great Britain would ruin their section of the country. 

New England commerce had grown by leaps and bounds since 1809. The spindles in American cotton mills largely located in New England had increased rapidly since 1807, growing from 8000 to 80,000 spindles in only two years and mounting to 130,000 by 1815. In spite of acts limiting trade, the commerce of New England practically held its gains. Consequently when the British blockade closed the ocean to American trade, a group of delegates gathered at a convention in Hartford, stated their grievances, denounced the war, and threatened secession. Even

before the war, New England had taken action to nullify federal laws. Clearly, the idea of the nation as an indivisible union had not yet taken shape. It seemed to be the view of the states that if the federal government did not suit them, they could set aside its laws or might freely secede from the Union which they had joined. 

New Orleans. The Battle after a Peace Treaty. 

At the time of the Hartford Convention the war was practically over.

Before the war ended, an American general won fame in a remarkable battle. News had reached America that an army of veteran British soldiers was on its way to capture New Orleans as a first step toward winning 

Louisiana for Great Britain. General Andrew Jackson, an 

Indian fighter, was sent to defend the city.

Hastily organizing an army of excellent riflemen from the outlying states and territories, Jackson prepared them for the British attack, which came on January 8, 1815. In less than half an hour the sure aim of the Americans repulsed the British. Of the British, over two thousand were killed or wounded. Only a few of Jackson's men lost their lives.

Had communication between Great Britain and America been swifter, the battle would never have been fought. 

Sixteen days earlier, on Christmas Eve, 1814, peace had been signed at Ghent. The fact of the matter is that if we had had cable service in those days the whole war might never have been fought, since the British had withdrawn the hated Orders in Council and had dispatched a messenger to carry the news across the Atlantic shortly before Congress issued its declaration of war. 

Treaty Ignores War Issues. Good Will Since. 

Strangely enough, the treaty of peace said nothing about the rights of neutrals to freedom of the seas; it did not

mention the issues of impressment or of British friendship with the Western Indians. Since the war was over these issues were dropped. The treaty was practically an agreement to stop fighting and let bygones be bygones. 

Since 1815 the few difficulties which have arisen between the United States and Great Britain have, in all cases, been settled peacefully and in a spirit of friendship. Neither the United States nor Canada has built a fort along three thousand miles of boundary. Not until the year 1914 was the question of our right to freedom of the seas challenged by Great Britain or by any other foreign power. The issue of impressment never again came up. In time Great

Britain and other nations agreed with the United States that immigrants to this country had the right to change their allegiance and become United States citizens. 

The War of 1812 is sometimes referred to as the Second War of Independence, the thought being that in the Revolutionary War the United States won its political freedom, and that in the War of 1812 the nation won economic freedom from England. 

War Stimulates Manufacture. An unlooked-for result of this war for ocean freedom was the more rapid development of American manufactures. The Embargo Act of 1807, shutting out foreign goods, had helped the growth of American manufactures. When the war further shut off the United States from its supply of British-made goods, the American people were forced to buy their own homemade goods. New England ship owners and others who formerly had profited from ocean trade now put their money into cotton and woolen mills. In Pennsylvania men built iron mills for the manufacture of farming tools and other iron implements. Hats, shoes, glassware, furniture, and many other wares were manufactured in greater quantities in this country than ever before.

CHAPTER XXV The Monroe Doctrine: A Wall Against Autocracy 

All of Spain's Mainland Colonies, Excepting Florida, Fight for Independence; Florida Is Purchased by the United States; the Monroe

Doctrine Warns Old World Powers against Interference or 

Aggression in the New World, and Thereby Preserves the

Western Hemisphere for New Ideals 

Old World Kings in "Holy Alliance" to Suppress 

Democracy. - After the War of 1812, the Old World kings who hated democracy began to change their minds about the weakness of the United States government. 

They had not seen the New World republic fail. Instead, they had seen the spirit of the Declaration of Independence spreading through Europe. Even their own subjects 329

were demanding more and more of the rights of free men. 

It was largely because of the spread of this new spirit of revolt against the old feudal order that the rulers of Russia, Prussia, Austria, France, and most of the other European powers pledged themselves to stand together in what they called the Holy Alliance. In the name of this alliance, they issued many noble and high-sounding declarations about peace and justice and religion, but their main object seems to have been the suppression of revolutions against kingly power.

Many Spanish-American Colonies Revolt. - Meanwhile the Napoleonic Wars had aided in the spread of republicanism in North and South America. In 1808 when 

Napoleon, invading Spain, set up his brother Joseph as ruler, the Spanish-American colonies made this an excuse for revolting against the mother country. After Waterloo, a Spanish king again sat upon the throne of Spain, but the Spanish-American colonies continued their fight for liberty. 

Florida Does not Revolt. A Thorn in Our Side. - One of the few Spanish-American colonies that did not revolt was Florida, which continued to be a thorn in the side of the United States. Even in early colonial days Florida had been a source of disturbance to the Southern planters. 

In later colonial days the harbors of Florida were the nesting places of pirate ships and gathering places for runaway slaves and outlaws. During the War of 1812, Spain, which was an ally of Great Britain in the wars against Napoleon, permitted Great Britain to use Florida as a naval base. The Indians in Florida also took advantage of this war to repeat their old raids against the 

Southern border. 

Jackson Invades Florida. Spain Sells Florida to United

States. In 1818, when the Indians again broke loose,

THE MONROE DOCTRINE 

331 General Andrew Jackson pursued them into Florida and took over the capital. 

President Monroe, who had succeeded Madison in 1817, supported this move on the ground that since Spain, apparently, was too weak to prevent these raids, as it had promised to do by the treaty of 1795, it was the duty of the United States government to protect its citizens. 

To prevent further trouble, Monroe offered to buy Florida for the United States. Spain, after some argument, agreed. The purchase price of about $5,000,000 added the territory of Florida to the growing nation. 

Holy Alliance Plans Interference in America. - Mean while the other South American countries were still struggling for their freedom from Spain, and the people of the United States were watching the struggle with sympathy. 

The independence of the Spanish republics would open ports long closed to United States trade by Spanish navigation acts; it would remove from the American continent a rival 

European power which had used its colonies in time of war to aid the enemies of the United States. 

Then news reached the United States that the king of Spain was appealing to the Holy Alliance to aid him in suppressing the rebellion in his colonies. And members of the Holy Alliance gathered at Verona were considering 

Spain's plea. 

Great Britain Suggests Joint Action. Adams Advises 

Independent Action. Great Britain was not at all pleased by this turn in affairs, which might close the Spanish-American ports to her trade, as well as to ours. 

Accordingly, Canning, the British Prime Minister, let President Monroe know that Great Britain would be willing to act with the United States to check the plans of the Holy Alliance.

The secretary of state, John Quincy Adams, persuaded

President Monroe that there was no advantage to be gained by acting with Great Britain. He knew that the 

United States had good and sufficient reasons on its own account for wishing to see the Holy Alliance prevented from carrying out its plans in America. 

If the Holy Alliance were successful in suppressing revolutions in Spanish America, France would, in all likelihood, receive a share of the Spanish colonies as a reward for her help. Quite independent of the Holy Alliance, Russia in that very year had laid claim to the Pacific Coast lands from Alaska southward to California. Adams felt that there was danger to the United States in any moves which would make the whole of South America, Central America, and the western coast of North America a battle ground for foreign powers eager for colonies. 

"Monroe Doctrine" (1823), a Message Warning

Europe to Leave New World Alone. Accordingly, 

Monroe, sensing the situation and acting on Adams's advice, in his annual message to Congress, announced the stand of the United States in this matter. This doctrine has since become famous to all the world as the 

Monroe Doctrine. 

In his message, Monroe declared that just as the United States proposes to keep out of European politics, so it expects the European nations to keep out of American politics; that no foreign powers are to build new colonies in America; that the United States would regard as an unfriendly act any "interference for the purpose of oppressing the governments which had declared their independence and maintained it."

In other words, the Monroe Doctrine requested European kings and diplomats to refrain from interfering with the New World. 

In the thirty-five years since Washington first took the

THE MONROE DOCTRINE 

333 oath of office as President of the United States, the nation had won the respect of European powers, so that this simple message of the President of the United States to the kings of Europe was not unheeded.

Monroe Doctrine Prevents Wars. Brings Responsi bilities. By means of the Monroe Doctrine the United 

States helped to win for the 

Spanish-American republics the right to lead the kind of political life they chose without interference from the Old 

World. In this way, also, both of the American continents were taken out of the realm of European politics and warfare. While Old 

World kings and their diplomats continued to wage war for territory in Europe, in 

Africa, and even in Asia, their contending armies with one exception have never since entered the New World. 

James Monroe 

Monroe was the fifth president of the

United States. The leading events of his administration were: revolts of the Spanish-American colonies, the formation of the Holy Alliance in 

Europe, and the issue of the Monroe

As we shall read later on, when the United States was engaged in the Civil War, a foreign power used its troops Doctrine. to establish a European as emperor in Mexico, but soon after the Civil War was over the United States took action which resulted in putting an end to this defiance of the Monroe Doctrine. 

The Monroe Doctrine brought the United States peace, but it also brought responsibility. In later years this country learned that in order to feel justified in asking

European powers to keep out of the new republics, it would be necessary to see that the New World republics gave European powers no excuse for warfare. This has not always been easy. Boundary disputes in the Spanish- 

American republics, the destruction of foreign property by revolutionists, nonpayment of debts to foreign merchants and investors, have been given as grounds for war by foreign powers. To prevent those powers from sending their armies into the Spanish-American republics, the United States has occasionally insisted that the opposing sides settle their differences by arbitration. For a hundred years this policy has been successfully maintained.

The Pioneer EMPIRE BUILDERS CHAPTER XXVI Across the Alleghenies 

American Pioneers, Frontiersmen, and Settlers Push Their Way West ward across the Alleghenies Into the Wilderness Beyond 

- In the year

The Winning of the West a Gigantic Epic. 

1829, when Andrew Jackson was inaugurated to succeed 

John Quincy Adams as President, the United States held undisputed title to land as far west as the Rocky Mountains. The nation even shared with Great Britain a claim to the territory of Oregon, which reached beyond the Rockies to the Pacific coast, from 42° northward to Alaska, which was claimed by Russia. 

To own all this vast wilderness was one thing. To have citizens living there was another. The story of the 337

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

men and women who went into the West to carve new states out of the wilderness can never be fully told. It is a story of pain and sacrifice, of defeat and victory. It is an epic of humanity, the westward march of a people, matching their wills and tools, their brawn and brain against wild lands, wild animals, and wild men. 

Slowly the empire builders advanced. First a few here, toiling through the wilderness, starving, fighting, some falling in battle, others fighting on; a few there plodding onward, fighting, soulsick, weary, still pushing westward, farther and farther westward. Then more and more advanced fighting the Indians, fighting rival nations, breaking new ground, holding their gains, until the broad continent was alive with swarming millions, living on prosperous farms, on sheep and cattle ranches, in mining towns, or in towering cities.

Explorers and Traders Prepare the Way. - The first to enter the New World wilderness were Spanish conquerors seeking gold and Spanish priests eager to convert the Indians. Their wanderings carried them far across the continent. In time the Spanish priests built their missions as far west as California.

French and British traders, who came to America to exchange trinkets for furs, built their trading posts far into the Western wilderness. The adventures of the Spanish gold hunters and the French and British fur traders were many and picturesque, but these men were not bent on mastering the wilderness.

Those who did most to make a beginning in conquering the wilderness were the settlers who came to build themselves homes and to live by farming in the thirteen colonies along the Atlantic coast.

Westward Movement Begins Soon After First Settlers 

Arrive. The coastal plain did not hold all the newcomers.

Soon after the coming of the first home builders, many began to push westward. Just as the Eastern coast lands of America promised liberty and opportunity to the poor and oppressed of Europe, so the free lands of the West held forth a new promise of liberty and opportunity to those who were not happy in the Eastern settlements. 

In New England the settlers moved westward from Massachusetts into Connecticut, and northward into New Hampshire, Maine, and Vermont. In New York they went northward up the Hudson toward Albany, and westward into the Mohawk Valley. In Pennsylvania and the colonies to the south they pushed their way westward until their homes reached to the base of the Allegheny Mountain range.

In backwoods homes life proved far more dangerous than in the coast settlements. During the wars with the 

French and the Indians many frontier towns were burned to the ground, and many frontier families were completely wiped out by Indian raids. Those who escaped with their lives built new homes above the smoldering ruins, and the frontier towns served as a defensive wall in the battle against the wilderness.

Alleghenies Block the Way. Call of New Land! 

Freedom! Adventure! To the British colonists, the 

Allegheny Mountains seemed like a wall blocking further progress. The lofty mountains covered with thick forest and heavy undergrowth were difficult to cross. The wild animals and the savage red men who roamed through the mountain forests made the way dangerous. To live on the other side of the mountains would shut one off from the growing comfort and safety of the older settlements. 

For many years very few even of the bravest ventured to cross the forbidding mountains; but from beyond there came the call of freedom, adventure, and fertile land.

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

Daniel Boone Crosses Alleghenies. One of the first to cross the Alleghenies was Daniel Boone. 

For years

The Mountain Wall 

For a long time the Alleghenies stood like a wall blocking the westward movement of the English colonists. 

French coureurs de bois, missionaries and traders, following the Great Lakes and the rivers of the Mississippi Valley, entered the West easily. But 

English colonists remained shut within the Atlantic Coastal plain until about 1750, when land companies began to turn to the trans-Allegheny country, and pioneers of the type of Boone went 

West to hunt. before the Revolution, Boone had lived with his family in a little log cabin in the western part of North Carolina.

There on the very frontier of civilization after the French and Indian War in which he served, Boone tilled the soil. 

Behind him, to the east of his home in Carolina, lay the growing settlements of his fellow colonists. To the west stretched the Alleghenies. On the other side of the mountains were the river valleys. 

When Daniel Boone heard the stories of the good hunting in the Ohio Valley, he and a few companions went through Cumberland Gap into Kentucky, where Daniel spent a year hunting deer, bear, and other animals while 

Indians hunted him. Cumberland Gap was a mountain 

pass a gap in the mountain wall. Soon settlers were pouring through this and other gaps into the valleys beyond the mountains. 

Planting Settlements in Kentucky and Tennessee. 

In 1775, leading a party of settlers, Boone again entered

Kentucky, where he helped plant a settlement at Boonesborough.

In the same year some hunters were encamping in the wilds of Kentucky when news came of the Battle of Lexington. Accordingly, they named the place of their encampment Lexington, a name adopted by the settlement later established there. In 1775, too, the little settlement of Harrodsburg, first settled the previous year, was being rebuilt. 

In Tennessee Sevier and other heroes blazed new paths as Boone had done in Kentucky. 

During the Revolution, Kentuckians, fighting under the lead of George Rogers Clark, won the Northwest Territory from Great Britain. 

Pioneers Like Boone and Sevier Advance Runners of

Civilization. Throughout the winning of the West, pioneers of the type of Boone and Sevier were the advance runners of the westward march. Fur trappers, traders, hunters they lived almost like wild men in their closeness to nature. Some of them slept each night under a different sky, with no shelter from storms but the hollow of a tree or a cave; with no food but the meat which their rifles and swift aim won for them.

Many of the pioneers were rough-hewn men who hated towns and the crowded life of the civilization which had grown up behind them. Yet as they forged ahead across the continent to escape this civilization, they blazed the paths along which civilization marched. 

Frontiersmen and Families Follow Pioneers. After the pioneers, often led by them, went the frontiersmen, men like the founders of Boonesborough and Lexington. 

In the early days some went afoot with their packs on their backs; others guided a pack horse or a canvas-covered wagon loaded with their belongings. Like the pioneers

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

these early frontiersmen followed the Indian trails and the paths made by the deer in the forest. 

The frontiersmen did not move singly or in pairs, as did the pioneers. They went with their families or in groups of several families. Once across the Allegheny Mountains, they built canoes, rafts, or flatboats, in which they floated 

The Frontiersmen 

The frontiersmen were those men and women who went to live upon the edge of civilization. They had to face many dangers and overcome great hardships, but in the end they triumphed and became the founders of great states. down the many streams which flowed westward toward the Mississippi. Wherever they stopped a while and built their homes they helped to prepare the way for those who came after them.

These frontiersmen who came into the West with their families were the first true builders of the Western states which had their beginning when women and children crossed the mountains with the men. 

A "Raising" on the Frontiers. The first of the frontiersmen built their homes themselves. The frontiersman who came later often had the aid of his neighbors who

came from many miles around to help him build his rough log cabin. Following the old colonial custom, they made a holiday of the day and called it a "Raising." While the men wielded their axes and plied saws, the womenfolk prepared the ample meal and often before the day was done the cabin would be ready for the newcomer. 

Frontier Axes and Guns. Frontier Hardships. — The frontiersman was seldom without his ax or gun. His ax helped to build not only his cabin but also his chairs and tables. His ax helped to feed his family; its lusty blows made a clearing of a few acres where corn and garden vegetables soon grew in the stump-dotted field. His gun defended him against the surrounding Indians. It brought down the game of the forest; the skins of the deer were made into clothes; and the meat, salted and put away for the winter, added to his store of food. 

It was in many ways a hard life. For years the frontiersmen who left the East to follow in the footsteps of Boone suffered untold agonies. The cold piercing winds of winter blew through the chinks of their cabins. The undrained swamps were breeding places for mosquitoes which spread malaria in summer. Men and women, weakened by the life they lived, grew old before their time. Cold and fever carried off the weak. Of the strong, many met death at the hands of the hostile red men who hated these invaders of their hunting grounds.

The frontiersman and his wife had little time for book learning or the idle pleasures of the city. All day long they and their children worked hard to earn their living. Ken-

In Kentucky and Tennessee the growth in population was so rapid that both were ready for statehood before the end of Washington's second (See map, page 277.)

Settlers Enter Northwest 

Territory. As early as 1787 the Ohio Company in New England bought from the government a million acres. 

Soon after, Rufus Putnam led a band of New Englanders out of their stubborn stony fields across New York by the way of the Mohawk Valley, and down the Ohio to a point which they named 

Marietta. There, on the fertile banks of the river, they built the first flourishing town in the Northwest Territory. 

Settlers 

After the building of roads through the mountain passes great numbers of settlers followed the solitary pioneers and the small bands of frontiersmen into the West. Many went West in covered wagons. Once across the mountains they built flatboats, and with their livestock and their household goods floated down the river to choose a site for their new homes. 

When the United States offered to sell government land in sections of six hundred forty acres for as little as one dollar an acre, with time to pay (the price was later raised to two dollars and then dropped to one dollar and a quarter), thousands of workmen in the Eastern towns, Eastern farmers who owned poor lands, hired men who owned no land at all, and immigrants fresh from

Europe, where few but lords could own such farms - all longed for the day when they might go into the Northwest Territory to clear land for themselves. 

They went West. They cleared the ground. They built log cabins. They planted seed. They made a living for themselves. They provided increased opportunity for their children; they brought nearer the day when the Northwest Territory would furnish the nation with new states. 

Western Settlers Face Border Problems. European 

Wars Affect Them. In the West, as we have seen, the newcomers as well as the old settlers had to face many problems. United States troops helped the Western settlers to defeat the border Indians. The purchase of Louisiana settled their problem of an outlet to sea trade. Then, for a while, the British "Orders" and the French "Decrees," the Embargo and the Non-Intercourse Acts shut off their markets. After the War of 1812 the sea was again opened for Western shipments. 

Northwest Territory Carved Into Five States: Ohio, 

Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin. During the

War of 1812 the suffering caused in the East by the British blockade of the Atlantic coast forced many families to seek a living in the lands of the West. For the next two years, when the British poured their manufactured goods into the country, and New England's shops were forced to close, thousands more turned to the West and population in the Northwest Territory increased rapidly. Soon this territory was carved into five states, each reaching the necessary sixty thousand population. Ohio had been admitted to statehood in 1803. Following the end of the 

War of 1812 Indiana became a state in 1816. Two years later Illinois received statehood. Within the next thirty years Michigan and Wisconsin both entered the Union as states. The Northwest Territory was no more.

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

Most of the citizens in these new states were farmers, who according to the requirements of the Northwest 

Ordinance owned no slaves.

The survey system used made it easier to locate land accurately. It divided the whole territory into townships six miles square. Each township was divided into thirtysix sections one mile square and these sections were then subdivided into smaller parcels of land. 

The sixteenth section in each township was set aside for the support of public schools and other land grants were made for institutions of higher learning. Many of the large universities in this section started as "land grant colleges.' 99 

New States in the South: Louisiana, Alabama, Mis sissippi. - In the South the invention of the power loom and of Whitney's cotton gin helped in the winning of the wilderness to the Mississippi and beyond. Because of the new tools, cotton cloth could now be manufactured at a low cost; and as the wearing of cotton clothes increased, cotton planters turned to the southwest to help meet the increased demand which came from the cotton mills in England and New England for raw cotton. 

Southern plantation owners whose lands were exhausted, and Southern farmers who owned no land, turned to the rich bottom lands of Tennessee, Louisiana, Alabama, and Mississippi. There in the fertile river valleys with slave labor, they cleared great plantations and were soon raising hundreds of millions of pounds of cotton. Kentucky had been admitted to the Union in 1792; Tennessee in 1796; Louisiana, which had some sixty thousand French and Spaniards in 1803, was admitted to the Union in 1812. Mississippi and Alabama followed in 1817 and 1819, respectively. By 

1820 the population of Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana had reached more than a quarter of a million.

In the Southwestern states, the cotton growers lived very much like the planters of the old South. The best plantation lands lay along the banks of the rivers which flowed either into the Mississippi or the Gulf of Mexico. 

The planter and his family lived in a stately mansion near the river front. Back of the mansion were the slaves' quarters, where hundreds of slaves lived in small shacks. 

River craft carried the cotton down to Mobile or New Orleans where cargoes were reloaded on gulf and oceangoing vessels bound for Great Britain or New England. 

The grains and other products of the Northwest, which had been floated down on the Mississippi rafts and flatboats, also found their way to New Orleans where they were put aboard ocean and coastwise sailing ships. 

Can the West Be Bound to the East? Although the rivers of the West helped to carry the Westerner and his goods, the great problem of the West was transportation. 

Unless the East and West could be more closely bound, there was danger that they might part company politically; that the Western states might leave the Eastern states and set themselves up as a separate nation.

CHAPTER XXVII Binding East and West 

In Spite of Mountain Walls, the East and West Are United by Natural Waterways, by the Building of Roads and Canals, by the Invention of the Steamboat, the Railroad, and the Telegraph 

East and West Must Be Bound. Roads Are Built. 

In many ways the Appalachian Mountains separated the West from the East much more thoroughly than the ocean separated the East from Europe.

To prevent the West and East from parting company they must be bound in some way. The first and most likely way was the building of roads. Roads would help to carry settlers into the West. Roads would help to carry tools, clothes, and other manufactured goods from the East into the West. Roads would help to bring the produce from the West to the East. In case of need, roads would enable soldiers to rush to the defense of the distant 349

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

lands. In all ways, roads would strengthen the tie between the Western settlers and the national government. 

Roads were built. Some were built by private companies, some by states. The national government also helped. The military road to Fort Duquesne, which the colonists had commenced, was now finished as a broad highway from the town of Philadelphia to the town of Pittsburgh, which had grown up near the ruins of the old fort. 

The famous Cumberland road reached from Cumberland, Maryland, over the mountains to Wheeling, West Virginia. 

Then in time this road was continued by the government as the National Road which ran from Wheeling through Ohio and Indiana, to Vandalia, at one time the capital of 

Illinois. 

The National Road was used by thousands of families who went West out of Virginia, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Maryland. Ever broadening trails in the Mohawk Valley in New York were followed by many settlers who went West out of New York and New England. Along these roads, teamsters driving ox-drawn wagons carried manufactured goods into the West and then returned with 

Western farm products. 

Cheaper Transportation. Flatboats. All Water Route. 

But the roads at first were few and the way was long and it still cost very much to carry freight back and forth. 

The cost of sending the farm products of the new West into the East was particularly high. The cost averaged about ten dollars a ton which was often as much as onethird of the price which the load would bring. If the West was to prosper, the farmers in the new country would have to find a less costly way to send their grains and other goods across the mountains.

So the farmers in the new states asked themselves: "Why should we send our goods across the mountains to

the cities of the East? Why not send them in flatboats down the streams which flow into the Mississippi, and then down the Mississippi itself to New Orleans? From

New Orleans the cargoes can be sent in coast sailing vessels to the Atlantic seaboard. Carrying goods by water would be cheaper. It would be safer; it might even be swifter than the overland traffic."

To meet the needs of river traffic, flatboats were built, many of them large enough to carry sixty or eighty tons. 

The rivers beyond the Appalachians resounded with the calls of the boatmen, while the river wharves were crowded with the traders who brought their goods for shipment. 

In its early days the river trade was not wholly without danger. Indians on the shore often shot arrows at the boatmen; and marauding parties even put out in canoes to give open battle to the passing vessels. In New Orleans, while the Spaniards ruled, the officials, fearful of the pushing frontiersmen, were eager to close the port to the trade of the United States. As we have seen, that danger did not last long. In 1803, when the United States purchased

Louisiana from the French, New Orleans became part of the nation's domain. 

After the pur

To float downstream was easy. The return was difficult. It took weeks of the hardest toil of man and beast to pull the boat northward against the current. That is why many boatmen abandoned their boats at New Orleans and

returned north on horseback. Some signing up with coastwise vessels would sail from New Orleans to an Atlantic seaport. Those who chose the latter route could then travel overland as teamsters. 

"Fulton's Folly." A Steamboat Moves Upstream. 

If only a way could be found by which heavily laden ships could move upstream, all 

Robert Fulton 

Fulton was the inventor of the Clermont, a steamship which opened up a new era in river and ocean transportation. However, many people regard 

John Fitch as the inventor of the steamboat. His boats undoubtedly were built earlier; and at least one of them was successfully operated for a time. this roundabout traffic would be unnecessary. 

A way was found. 

For years after the invention of the steam engine, men had been trying more or less successfully to make a ship which would use the power of steam to move against the wind and tide. 

As early as 1787 John Fitch succeeded in driving a small steamboat on the Delaware, and for some time his boat continued to give service as a ferry. For some reason, his boat was not completely practical and the ferry was abandoned. It was left for another to show the world the way.

In 1807 Robert Fulton finished a steamship. He called it the Clermont. The doubters called it "Fulton's Folly." 

When all was made ready, Fulton tried out his ship from a New York City dock on the Hudson River. As the crowds watched, they saw the Clermont, puffing, snorting, and belching flame, leave its dock and move slowly up the Hudson.

The power of a steam engine was turning the side paddles of the boat, and as the paddles were turned the ship plowed through the water. In thirty-two hours the Clermont reached Albany. This meant a speed of over four miles an hour.

By 1812 the steamboat was carrying freight from Pittsburgh to New Orleans. Within a few years a steamboat had succeeded in moving northward against the current of the Mississippi from New Orleans to Pittsburgh, and there were steamboats on the Great Lakes.

These steamboats, carrying men and women into the West and also carrying goods back and forth, all helped in the winning of the West.

Steamboats Cause Rivalry. New Orleans and Atlantic 

Seaports. The use of steamships brought a problem to the East. Eastern merchants and ship owners began to be worried when they saw the West growing up as an almost independent country, increasing in population with its own highways and its own seaports. With steamboats which could carry goods upstream as well as down, New Orleans would become the greatest port in the country unless the East could find new means of bringing Western goods across the mountains to the Atlantic coast. 

Erie Canal a New Water Route from West to Atlantic. - 

Almost immediately after the first steamboat carried a cargo northward from New Orleans, Governor Clinton suggested a way by which the produce from the farms in all the country fronting the Great Lakes might be sent to 

New York instead of to New Orleans. 

He favored the cutting of a canal through New York State from the Hudson River to Lake Erie. In this way the freight of the West could be sent across the Great Lakes to Buffalo, by canal from Buffalo to Albany, and southward down the Hudson to New York.

When Clinton proposed the building of this Erie Canal, three hundred and sixty-three miles long, some men laughed at his plan as men had laughed at Fulton when he explained his steamship. The doubters called the canal "Clinton's Ditch."

Clinton was determined. The people of the state voted the necessary money, and in 1817 the work began. Men set to work with picks and shovels to build the artificial waterway. The doubters kept on doubting until the Erie

Canal was finished and officially opened. In 1825 a boat carrying a distinguished company made the long voyage across the state. To symbolize the welding of the inland waters and the ocean, a bottle of the waters of the Great Lakes was poured into New York Harbor. The West now had a new way to send its produce east. 

The Canal Boat 

Canal boats carried passengers as well as mail and freight. Since transportation by canals was cheaper than transportation by land, these artificial waterways helped trade between the East and the West. They also served to open up new territory to settlers. 

Canals Reduce Freight Rates. The canal proved to be an immediate success. The carrying of freight from 

Buffalo to New York had been costly and had taken twenty days. The cost now dropped and the time was at once reduced to eight days and less.

Western farmers who were too far from the Lake region to take advantage of the Lake and Erie Canal route to the East urged their states to build canals from the local rivers to the Great Lakes. Along the shores of the Great Lakes, Cleveland, Detroit, and Chicago grew rapidly. sprang up along the line of the Erie Canal. 

Cities

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

Merchants in Philadelphia, Baltimore, Boston, seeing how the Erie Canal was benefiting New York City, applied themselves vigorously to the building of canals which would bind them directly with the Western country. They believed that only in this way could they secure for their cities some of the trade which was passing through New 

Orleans and New York.

Canals soon connected Philadelphia with Pittsburgh, except for a short break in the mountain country. 3 4 2 

Canal Lock

The canal boat enters the lock through gate A, with the water on the lower level. Gate A closes, and water enters the lock through the sluices (ss) in Gate B. The inrushing water raises the boat to the higher level. Gate B opens and the boat proceeds upstream. When a boat is coming down to a lower level, this process is simply reversed. 

Massachusetts was planning a canal to connect the Hudson River with Boston. Baltimore was at work on a canal. Many of the canals which were planned were never finished because of new ideas in the field of transportation.

Cheaper Land Transportation. - Inventors were seeking to add new ways of carrying goods across the country. 

Steamboats could serve only those parts of the country lying along waterways. Canals were artificial waterways.

There were still vast stretches of land in the West which did not lie along waterways of any kind. Even where these places had roads to serve them the freight charges by land were too high. If produce from these places could be carried to market at a cost which would leave some profit to the farmer, these lands would become valuable for settlement.

In order to find a cheaper form of transportation for such inland country as had no convenient waterways, inventors were seeking a new type of road and a new type of horse. 

A New Road: the Railroad. A New Horse: the 

Locomotive. In England for some time the mine owners had been hauling their loads of coal in wooden cars drawn by horses along tracks made of wooden rails. 

These railroads, as they were called, made the hauling of heavy freight much less costly. When Fulton succeeded in using a steam engine to propel a ship upstream as well as down, his success encouraged inventors to believe that a steam locomotive could be used instead of horses to draw cars along these railroads.

Soon, both in England and in the United States, inventors were experimenting with the railroads and steam-drawn wagons. The first steam locomotive railroad was opened in England in 1825. 

Railroads Bind East and West. In 1828 the Baltimore and Ohio Company decided to lay a short road of rails out of Baltimore to Ellicott's Mills, about twelve miles away. 

Charles Carroll of Carrollton, who was one of the signers of the Declaration of Independence, turned the first spadeful of earth for the laying of the rails. As he did so he said that he considered the act one of the most important of his life, second only to the signing of the 

Declaration of Independence. 

Carroll spoke truly.

The first cars to run along the

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

railroad tracks were drawn by horses; but only a few years after the laying of that road in Baltimore, a steam locomotive pulling cars carried freight and passengers from Baltimore to Ellicott's Mills. That short haul gave promise of the great railroad systems which were destined to unite all parts of the nation. bowhead bo

A Wooden Railroad 

The first American railroad was a road of wooden rails, along which a wagon was drawn by horses. Such a track was laid from Baltimore to Ellicott's Mills, twelve miles out. In 1830 a steam locomotive drew a train of coaches along this same track. Pioneer trips of this kind marked the beginning in this country of steam transportation on land. 

Soon builders were laying hundreds and thousands of miles of railroads, some of which connected the cities of the East with the towns which were growing up on the other side of the Alleghenies. In time these railroads extended to the banks of the Mississippi and even across the Mississippi into the new states which were growing up beyond.

One man who became interested in this possibility was 

Samuel F. B. Morse, an excellent portrait painter, who

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

turned from his canvases to experiment with electromagnetism. When he succeeded in making an instrument by means of which he could send messages three miles by electricity, he appealed to Congress for financial aid in order to make a larger and more convincing experiment to prove the usefulness of his invention. Telegraph companies were soon building lines to carry personal messages, business messages, and political news north and south between the large cities on the Atlantic coast, as well as east and west across the 

Alleghenies.

The Iron Horse 

This early American railroad train (about 1830) consisted of a number of stagecoaches drawn by a steam locomotive, the "iron horse." The tender carried wooden fuel for the steam engine which belched smoke and cinders. 

Crude as this early service was, the value of this new type of transportation was so great that soon companies were building thousands of miles of railroads from the Eastern cities inland to the growing cities of the West.

Westward Toward the Pacific CHAPTER XXVIII 

From the Mississippi to the Pacific 

The Missouri Compromise Shuts Slavery Out of Northern Louisiana Slave Owners Enter Texas and Make It a Republic Texas Is Annexed to the United States Texas Boundary Dispute Leads to Mexican War and Acquisition of Great Southwest - To the North Free Farmers Cross the Con tinent Into Oregon - "Gold Rush" Makes 

California Ready for Statehood

Northern Farmers and Southern Planters Cross Mis sissippi Into Missouri. - Even before 1803, when Louisiana was purchased, Boone had crossed the Mississippi into the territory of Missouri and its fertile prairie land. Only a few years later, settlers who had pushed their way across Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois found themselves on the banks of the Mississippi with the Missouri lying on the other side. Many crossed the river. Farmers without any slaves entered Missouri from Illinois. Planters bringing their slaves with them entered Missouri from Kentucky and Tennessee.

Timber for the building of homes was scarce. Malaria 362

FROM THE MISSISSIPPI TO THE PACIFIC 363 

was common. Drinking water was obtained only by drilling deep wells. Yet the urge to the land was so great that settlers in Missouri were soon of sufficient number to apply to Congress for admission as a state. 

Free State or Slave State. The Missouri Compromise 

(1820). There was one difficulty in the way of admitting 

Missouri. Missouri applied for admission into the Union as a slave state. A minority in Missouri wished that slavery should be prohibited. 

The issue, however, was not only local. There was a national side. 

Thomas Hart Benton 

Back in the East farmers and laborers who were looking toward Louisiana territory, as desirable land to which they might some day wish to go, wanted to see the spread of slavery checked in the West. They opposed the admission of Missouri as a slave state. In fact they wished to see slavery prohibited in all of Louisiana, just as it had been shut out of the whole Northwest Territory by the Ordinance of 1787. 

In 1821, the new state of Missouri sent Benton to represent it in the 

United States Senate. There he became a fiery champion of westward expansion, prophesying the day when the nation would reach from coast to coast.

The Southern planters, who were looking to the West for new cotton land, and for more congressmen favorable to slavery, were eager to see Missouri admitted as a slave state. They wished to see all of Louisiana territory and the states which would be carved out of it kept open to slavery. 

Congress debated the issue and the matter was settled

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

by the Missouri Compromise, in which, as in all compromises, each side yielded something to the other. 

The state of Louisiana, which was in Louisiana territory, had been admitted in 1812 as a slave state. By the terms of the Compromise, Missouri was admitted as a slave state. 

On the other hand, it was decreed by the Missouri Compromise, that except for the state of Missouri, all of Louisiana territory north of the southern boundary of Missouri would be held as free territory, and slavery would be allowed only in the land south of Missouri. (See map, ch. XXXIV.) 

As most of Louisiana territory lay north of Missouri this was regarded as a victory for those who opposed slavery in the lands west of the Mississippi. In the hundreds of thousands of square miles which the Missouri Compromise set aside as free territory, there was ample opportunity for all farmers seeking homes in the West. 

Planters Welcomed in Southwest.-What were the

Southern cotton planters who were eager for new lands to do? Since the demand for cotton goods was increasing the world over and the owners of cotton mills were in the market for hundreds of millions of pounds of cotton, the Southern planters looked about for new lands. 

The purchase of Florida in 1819 gave them hope of a new slave state. Their opportunity to obtain more land suited to cotton growing came very soon. As early as 

1821 settlers from the United States began entering Texas. 

In 1823 Mexico, which had just succeeded in winning her independence from Spain, offered large tracts of land in 

Texas to planters at a very low price.

Texas Thinly Occupied by Mexico.-Texas, at the time a part of Mexico, was poorly settled. Many of the 

Spanish colonists who had settled Mexico had come to America as adventurers, traders, or soldiers, and in most cases they counted on returning to their old homes in

FROM THE MISSISSIPPI TO THE PACIFIC 365 

Spain. Naturally they had done little to clear the land or to build towns and cities. Except for a few towns where the officials and the high church officers lived, almost all of the land was wild with only an occasional fort and its garrison of soldiers guarding some trading post, some mine, or a mission where a few brave priests lived among the Indians.

Bull Boats on the Missouri River

The life of the plains Indians affords an excellent example of the red man's adaptation to geographic conditions. Great herds of buffalo grazed upon the treeless plains. The Indians ate buffalo meat. They wore buffalo robes. 

They used buffalo hides to cover their tepees, or houses. They built boats for the fording of rivers by covering a circular framework of thick rushes with dried buffalo skin. province of Texas by offering land at twelve and one-half cents an acre, many Southern planters took advantage of the offer.

Within a few years there were twenty thousand American colonists in Texas. 

Texas Revolts Against Mexican Rule. Soon there were differences between the Mexican officials and the Americans in Texas.

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

In the early days of the Mexican republic Mexico suffered from violent political disputes and even from civil warfare. 

One of the factions which came into power was far from friendly to the Americans in Texas.

Finally there was an uprising of the Texans who drove the

mission, the Alamo, resisted Santa Anna's troops for thirteen days, until all but six men fell. When at last

The Mexican Congress re fused to do what Santa Anna had promised, but within a year the United States Con gress recognized Texas, under its President, Sam Houston, as an independent state. 

Sam Houston

The career of Houston was highly picturesque and in a way resembled that of Washington. After leading the 

Texans in their war for independence, Houston became the first president of the republic of Texas, and served it well. He favored the annexation of 

Texas by the United States and saw his wish come true. 

Texas Admitted Into Union. Soon Texas applied to

Congress for admission into the Union and many men favored what they called the re-annexation of Texas. They pointed out that Texas was in fact a part of Louisiana and should have become part of American territory with the purchase of Louisiana. 

President Van Buren and Congress saw reasons for hesitating. Antislavery congressmen objected to the annexa-

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

tion of Texas because it would increase the number of slave-holding states. Besides, Mexico insisted that Texas was not really free, and so it seemed to them that it would be just as well to wait.

In the year 1845 Texas was still a separate government, and Mexico had done nothing to reestablish her power. 

Mexican leaders still threatened that if the United States annexed Texas, they would declare war. Congress paid no attention to the threat.

In the presidential campaign in 1844, one of the election slogans for James K. Polk, the democratic candidate, was the "Re-annexation of Texas." When Polk was elected, President Tyler decided that the vote of the people proved that they favored the annexation of Texas. Accordingly, President Tyler, on the last day of his term, March 3, 1845, sent a special messenger to the Texan government with the signed resolution of Congress admitting Texas into the Union.

Again the nation grew in area and in wealth. The purchase of Louisiana in 1803 had virtually added an empire. The purchase of Florida in 1819 increased the area of the country by eighty thousand square miles. 

The annexation of Texas in 1845 added almost four hundred thousand more square miles and extended the United States coast line on the Gulf of Mexico for hundreds of miles.

Treaty with England Fixes Oregon Boundary. - Be yond the Rockies, the boundary line of Oregon had long been an unsettled question. Since 1818, by agreement, Great Britain and the United States had left the ownership unsettled, but both claimed the territory extending south from latitude 54° 40', the southern boundary of Alaska, to the northern boundary of California. Mountains. The states of Oregon, Washington, Idaho, and part of Montana and 

Wyoming were carved out of the Oregon Territory. Consult a statistical almanac for a description of the geographical advantages and industrial development of this region, which because of its wealth of natural resources is called "The Inland Empire."

The boundary question was settled by the peaceful treaty of 1846, running the line to fortynine degrees north latitude westward to Puget Sound. All of Oregon territory north of this line, as well as Vancouver Island which lies partly south of the line, went to Great Britain and extended her dominion in Canada to the Pacific. 

All of Oregon south of this line became part of the United States. The United States reached from ocean to ocean. 

Polk Seeks Boundary Treaty with Mexico. - Still the nation grew this time through war.

One month before Great Britain and the United States signed the treaty establishing the dividing line between Oregon and Canada, war broke out between the United 

States and Mexico.

Mexico was angered by the annexation of Texas, and her statesmen were still disputing with the Texans about the southern boundary. Did the Texan line end at the Nueces 

River or at the Rio Grande? The Mexicans insisted on the strip of land which lay between the two streams. Polk claimed that this was American territory. 

The President felt, with many of the people, that the trouble with Mexico could be ended only by the purchase of Mexico's holdings in the far Southwest from New Mexico to California, with its splendid Pacific harbor at San

Francisco. As long as the Mexicans held this territory so thinly, the United States settlers were bound to enter the territory, and he believed that the United States should, if possible, secure it by peaceful purchase.

Polk sent a commission to Mexico to talk over the Rio Grande boundary dispute and to offer to purchase California and New Mexico. The commission was also empowered to adjust with Mexico the question of the claims

FROM THE MISSISSIPPI TO THE PACIFIC 371 

of the American citizens who had suffered losses in Mexican territory during the Mexican disorders. He hoped that in this way all could be settled peacefully. 

The Mexicans were in no mood to consider the President's purchase offer. They refused to discuss the settle-. ment of the American claims. 

Mexican War Begins. When General Zachary Taylor in command of the United States troops took up his post on the north bank of the Rio Grande, on land which the 

Texans claimed as theirs, Mexican soldiers crossed the stream and attacked a scouting party of United States soldiers, killing a few and capturing the remainder.

When President Polk heard this, he immediately wrote to Congress. "Mexico... has invaded our territory and shed American blood on 

American soil!" Congress then recognized that a state of war existed. 

John C. Frémont 

Frémont was an army officer and 

Western explorer. During the Mexi can War Frémont, who was on an exploring tour in the West, joined with 

Commodores Sloat and Stockton of the

United States Navy in helping to establish the Republic of California.

Our Troops Occupy Cal ifornia and New Mexico. 

Directly after the opening of the war in May, 1846, General Taylor proceeded against the Mexicans and defeated them in battle after battle. At

Palo Alto, at Resaca de la Palma, at Monterey, at Buena 

Vista, he defeated the Mexican forces.

Meanwhile, President Polk took advantage of the war to secure possession of California and New Mexico. A United

States fleet anchored off the Pacific coast, and aided by

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

John C. Frémont, an explorer, and some American settlers in California, took possession of that territory. At about the same time, Colonel Stephen Kearney marched with eighteen hundred men from Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, through the arid lands of the Southwest and captured Santa Fe in New Mexico. He then marched on through the valley of the Gila to the Colorado River and thence to San Diego on the California coast. 

The next year, American Army Captures Mexico City. after cannonading Vera Cruz for days, a fleet under Commodore Conner landed a United States army in the city. 

This army, under General Winfield Scott, now set out to repeat the journey which Cortez had made three centuries before him. The line of march ran from Vera Cruz to 

Mexico City, the capital of the Mexican republic, as it had once been the capital of the Aztec kingdom. 

The Mexican army tried to block the advance of the American troops. Cannon shelled them from the mountain heights. On the passes there were fierce skirmishes. At 

Cerro Gordo they stormed the steep heights and drove the 

Mexican army from its ground.

Twice Scott stopped in his campaign to permit peace negotiations, in which Polk's purchase offer was renewed. 

Each time the Mexicans refused to yield to the United States terms. Peace negotiations failing, Scott's men resumed their forward march which brought them to Mexico 

City, where Santa Anna's thirty thousand soldiers were strongly intrenched.

Before the United States troops stood the rock of Chapultepec, a fortress one hundred fifty feet high, which seemed to defy capture. Five days later Scott's men stormed the place, and on the sixth day the keys of Mexico City were surrendered to the American troops. This victory brought the Mexicans to terms.

Through annexation, the republic of Texas (389,166 square miles) came into the Union on December 29, 1845. Parts of the states of New Mexico, Colorado, and 

Wyoming lie within the original boundaries of Texas. By the treaty which ended the 

Mexican War in 1848 and the Gadsden Purchase in 1853, the United States acquired from Mexico almost 550,000 square miles. Within the Mexican accessions there grew up the states of California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and part of New Mexico and Colorado. This region now leads the nation in many fields of production. Consult a statistical almanac for a description of the geographical advantages and industrial development of the states carved out of the Texas annexation and the Mexican accessions.

EMPIRE BUILDERS Terms of Peace Treaty. Far Southwest Becomes United 

States Territory. Despite the conquest of Mexico, the treaty of peace in 1848 contained the same terms as did the earlier offers made by the United States. The Rio 

Grande was to be the boundary line of Texas. The United 

States was to retain the territories of New Mexico and California, but the offer of fifteen million dollars as the purchase price still held good and would be paid. The 

United States also agreed to pay three and one quarter million dollars to American citizens who held claims to that amount against Mexico for damages incurred. 

By a later treaty, known as the Gadsden Purchase (1853), the United States bought from Mexico a small additional strip of land which straightened out the boundary of the 

United States in the Southwest.

One result of the Mexican War, then, was to add more than five hundred thousand square miles to the government lands, giving possession of the far Southwest from Texas to the Pacific coast. This new territory, together with the Oregon territory, to which the nation obtained clear title in 1846, gave the United States a continuous coast line on the Pacific. It was not long before this far 

Western country was furnishing the nation with new states. 

Empire Builders in Far Northwest. In the far Northwest, for many years before the upper Mississippi Valley was well settled, the empire builders were reaching out beyond the Rockies even to the Pacific coast. 

Soon after Captain Gray discovered the Columbia River flowing out of Oregon into the Pacific, John Jacob Astor, an Eastern fur merchant, established a trading post at Astoria, in Oregon. This post was a rival of the British 

Hudson Bay Company for fur trade of the Pacific coast, and it marked the first move of actual occupation of the Pacific coast territory by the United States citizens.

FROM THE MISSISSIPPI TO THE PACIFIC 375 

Great Britain also claimed Oregon, but the question of final ownership of this territory would depend very largely on actual settlement, and a small fur post was hardly enough to make good the United States claim. Fortunately, other Americans followed the fur traders into Oregon. For years American missionaries went into the territory, 14 

Missionary Settlement in Oregon Territory traveling almost single-handed to their appointed task of winning the Indian tribes to Christianity. 

Dr. Marcus Whitman, an American missionary leader, in the year 1835 made his first trip across the continent to Oregon. From that time Whitman was an enthusiastic lover of the far Western country, and on his return to the East spread reports of the beauty and fertility of the Oregon River valleys. He himself recrossed the continent several times and led parties of men and women out of the 

East across the Oregon trail.

When the United States sat down at the treaty table with Great Britain to decide the ownership of Oregon, the United States claim on the valuable territory was strengthened one hundredfold through the fact that United States citizens

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

were actually living as home builders in the disputed territory. Consequently, a few hundred men and women braving the wilderness helped to secure for their country a vast and precious territory.

Eleven years after the close of the Mexican War, one section of Oregon territory was sufficiently well populated to be admitted into the Union as the state of Oregon. 

Empire Builders in the Far Southwest. For about three centuries before the Mexican War, Spain held claim to the territory in the far Southwest. After Coronado had explored much of this territory in his search for gold, Spanish missionary priests built their missions among the Indian tribes. The mission at Sante Fe, New Mexico, dates back to 1605 and there were also Spanish missions in 

California at very early dates.

Along the trails which led to these missions in the Southwest there were deserts, yet even this territory saw the advance of Americans. For years before the outbreak of the Mexican War, American traders had been following trails to Sante Fe and to San Francisco, to deal with the Spaniards in their forts and missions. These traders were soon followed by American settlers in small numbers, who went to live among the Spaniards. When the Mexican 

War came the American settlers in California and New Mexico were glad to see the Red, White, and Blue unfurled above the territories which they had chosen as their homes. 

Mormons Settle in Utah. Irrigate Desert. Many of the immigrants into the West did not march on to the Pacific. 

In 1847, one party, a band of Mormons, a religious sect, seeking new territory in which to establish a colony, crossed the desert to a salt lake in Utah which was Mexican territory. The site of this lake, beautiful though it was, did not seem promising for a settlement. The soil was sandy and rain was scarce. Nevertheless, the Mormons decided 

---

FROM THE MISSISSIPPI TO THE PACIFIC 377 

to build their settlement by the shores of the lake. By the use of irrigation on a large scale, they turned the barren desert into a garden of plenty. Salt Lake City thrived and when the treaty with Mexico made Utah United States territory, this Mormon refuge was on its way to statehood. 

California Gold Causes Rush into West. Forty-Niners.

Shortly before the treaty between the United States and Mexico was signed, an 

American carpenter, supervising the making of a mill race at Sutter's Mill not far from San Francisco, discovered shining particles of metal near the edge of the rushing stream. It looked like gold. When tested in 

San Francisco it proved to be gold. 

The word spread, but the treaty granting California to the United States was signed before the treaty makers learned the news. The precious metal for which the 

Spanish explorers had attacked empires with a handful of men, for which English sailors had fought Spanish galleons, had been found on 

United States soil. 

Bret Harte 

Harte was a writer who won fame through his short stories of Western life. His stories of mining camps and frontier towns showed a keen feeling for the fact that the Americans in the 

West were living through romantic adventures at least as thrilling as the adventures of Old World nobles and knights in the feudal days.

As the news traveled through the territory, sailors left their ships in the harbor, farmers left their plows, and shopkeepers abandoned their stores. All set out for the mountains to search for gold.

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

Land was free, and men had only to stake out their claims and work them.

It was before the day of the telephone, the telegraph, or the wireless. News could not move faster than horses or 

Cradling Gold

The gold found in the California fields in the days of the "Forty-niners" was largely of the nugget form, and lay close to the top soil or in the beds of streams. Spadefuls of stone and earth were put into a wooden cradle, and water was then used to wash out the fine earth, leaving only rocks, gravel, and nuggets above the sieve. boats. It was months before word reached the East. But wherever it reached, men caught the gold fever.

In every city, every town, even in the hamlets and the villages, there were men who started for the land of treasure. Within two years from January, 1848, when the gold was first discovered, over ninety thousand fortune hunters called "Forty-niners" had streamed into California.

FROM THE MISSISSIPPI TO THE PACIFIC 379 

Journey Westward. Covered Wagon. Indian Fighting. 

Hardships. In their westward march, most of the 

Forty-niners, like the empire builders who went into the Far West before them, journeyed in canvas-covered wagons. 

Long lines of these wagons drawn by oxen or horses moved like caravans across plains and deserts, through river valleys and over mountains.

The more fortunate immigrants had cattle and oxen, horses and sheep, which they drove before them. 

At night and during the day, if there were signs of hostile Indians, the wagons were formed in a hollow square or circle. Then, using the wagons for protection, the men awaited the assault of the Indians. 

Sometimes the Indians, mounted on swift horses, finding the white men prepared for attack, would gallop away as suddenly as they came. At other times they would give battle in their own way, circling around and around the encampment during the exchange of shots. If the immigrants won, they could continue to drive their wagons westward.

On the deserts which lay across the Western trails the immigrants faced many hardships from the terrific heat, from thirst, and from violent wind storms. Sometimes, after a wind storm had blown sand over the trails, whole parties would lose their way and perish of thirst.

The crossing of the Rocky Mountains was also dangerous, especially so if the travelers lost their way or were caught by unexpected snows.

In fording broad rivers, immigrants had to risk the loss of their household goods and even the danger of drowning. 

In many cases they drove their loaded wagons into the streams trusting that the wagons would remain afloat while the horses tugged steadily toward the opposite shore. 

Fortunately they did not have to construct rafts to bring

EMPIRE BUILDERS 

their cattle across. These plunged into the rivers, breasted the current, and then, rounded up on the other side, were ready to continue with the men and women on the long trail toward the Pacific.

Such was the nature of the overland journey taken by the home-building farmers as well as the Forty-niners. 

Some of the Forty-niners, impatient to reach California, went by other routes. They either sailed down the Atlantic to Panama, crossed the narrow isthmus, and then sailed up the Pacific to California; or they went all the way by water, sailing down the Atlantic around Cape Horn at the southern end of South America, into the Pacific, thence northward to San Francisco.

California Seeks Statehood (1850). -The century had only half passed. There were still great stretches of the 

West which were thinly settled. Yet the empire builders had completed their march across the continent. Along the 

Pacific coast, in Oregon, and in California, the citizens of the republic were building new states to add their strength to the strength of the nation.

In the year 1850, when California applied to Congress for admission as a state, the old question of the extension of slavery into the West came to the fore. The question was settled by a compromise, but the debate in Congress proved that during the time that the empire builders had been carving new states in the West, sectional feeling had grown so bitter that the spirit of union within the nation was in danger.

A Clipper Ship 

This type of sailing vessel with its pointed prow and its wealth of square rigged sails was designed by American shipbuilders to make possible greater speed and ease in sailing with or against the wind. American sailors, profiting by the design of their clippers, performed marvelous sailing feats, making unheard-of speed in long trade voyages across the Atlantic to Europe, or down the Atlantic and around Cape Horn to California and Oregon, and even across the Pacific to China.
