SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS CHAPTER XXIX High Tariff or Low Tariff The North, South, and West Divide on Political Issues - The Tariff Presents a Problem to North and South as to Whether the Nation Is an Indivisible Union or a Confederation of States A Threat of Nullifica tion Forces the Issue-President Jackson Supports the Union - A Compromise Settles the Question for a Time 

The Era of Good Feeling Passes. - 

-During the years when the United States was growing steadily from east to west, there was every sign that the nation was dividing into separate sections with separate interests. 

Since the War of 1812 the North, with few interruptions, had developed steadily as a manufacturing country. The 

South, including the Southwest, continued as a plantation country. The Northwest, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and later, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Iowa were for the most part developed as farming and grazing countries. 384

At one time, during Monroe's administration, after the question of admitting Missouri as a slave state was settled by compromise, there seemed to be not a single issue to divide the people of North, South, and West, and men spoke of the time as the Era of Good Feeling. 

Nevertheless, at this very time sectional issues regarding important matters were coming to the front.

Sectional Differences. 

The people of the North, the 

South, and the West were beginning to look upon all questions which they had to solve from a sectional point of view; the Northern manufacturer, the Southern planter, and the Western farmer, each had his own ideas as to the kind of laws which the government should pass. 

John Quincy Adams 

John Quincy Adams was the sixth president of the United States (18251829). Leading events of his administration were: opening of Erie 

Canal; tariff of 1828 called "Tariff of Abominations." 

In the election of 1824 there was only one party, but sectional differences showed themselves in the choice of the candidates - John Quincy Adams, William 

H. Crawford, Henry Clay, and Andrew Jackson. Adams represented the North, Crawford the South, and Clay of Kentucky and Jackson of Tennessee both represented the 

New West. Another Southern leader but not a candidate was the forceful John C. Calhoun.

In the election Andrew Jackson received a larger number of votes than the others, but as no one received a majority

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

of the electoral votes the decision was left to the House of 

Representatives. There Henry Clay threw the weight of his influence to John Quincy Adams who was chosen 

President. 

The Protective Tariff a Sectional Issue. During the 

Adams administration which lasted from 1824 to 1828 the issue of a protective tariff on imported manufactures and other goods became a subject of violent debate, with the people of the North, South, and West taking different positions. 

As far back as 1789 Congress, on the advice of Hamilton, had passed a tariff bill putting a low duty on manufactured goods brought into the country. 

After the War of 1812, when English manufacturers began sending large quantities of goods into the country to sell at any price, Congress passed a new tariff act, this time a protective tariff act, raising the amount of the duty so that the English would not be able to undersell the American manufacturers and so destroy the infant American industries. 

The tariff measures of 1789 and 1816 had found some enemies both in the North and in the South. They also had many friends on both sides of the Mason and Dixon Line. In 1824, when Congress passed a new tariff act still further raising the duties on imported goods, the North, for the most part, agreed with the South in opposing it. 

But by 1828 they divided clearly on the issue. 

Manufacturing North Wants Protective Tariff. Since the Revolutionary War many men in the North had been putting their money into mills, shops, and factories, where they wove cotton and woolen cloth, made hats and shoes, farming tools, and machinery. Tens of thousands of farm hands had gone into the new manufacturing towns to work as laborers. As many of the laborers had no homes

or land of their own, they depended upon their work for the money which they needed for rent, clothes, food, and 

To the Northern manufacturer and to his laborers the importation of cheap foreign goods seemed dangerous. 

Cheap imports might force the owners to close their mills and factories and so leave the workers without their means of livelihood. 

The people of the North saw only one way to avoid these dangers and to safeguard their growing industries. It was the way Hamilton had pointed out. Let Congress place a protective tariff on imported goods, a tariff which would protect the United 

States manufacturer and be high enough to make it impossible for the Old World manufacturer to undersell the 

American products. 

A New England Mill Jown 

The introduction of cloth-making machinery into New England led to the growth of factory or mill towns along the banks of swift-flowing streams. These streams furnished water power to operate the machine looms and spindles.

Agricultural South Objects to High Tariff. —A high tariff was very well for the North.

The South saw the tariff from a different angle. The fertile soil, the warm climate, and the use of slaves, all tended to keep the South an agricultural region. The large plantations yielded bountiful crops of cotton, rice, and tobacco, and the planters who had their funds invested in slaves and land found themselves unable to develop manufactured goods.

As the planters manufactured nothing, they had no such products to protect. They had to buy their clothes and

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

farming implements and other tools, and wished to buy these goods as cheaply as possible. 

Therefore the South looked upon the tariff of 1824 as sectional legislation, passed in the interest of the Northern manufacturers at the expense of the Southern planters. 

Western Stand on the Tariff Question. 

John C. Calhoun 

Calhoun, a Senator from South

Carolina, was one of the War Hawks who urged the War of 1812. Later he became the leading spokesman of the Southern planters in their demand for recognition of the principle of "states' rights"; in their opposition to high tariff rates; in their defense of slavery. It was he who urged South 

Carolina to pass the Nullification Act. 

Calhoun, Webster, and Clay were the three leading orators of their day. 

Although the 

West, like the South, was primarily agricultural and wished to buy manufactured goods cheaply, Western leaders wanted to see a high tariff on wool so that the mills of the North would buy Western wool rather than imported wool. In planning protective tariff legislation the North had to yield to this wish of the West in order to secure 

Western votes. 

Tariff of 1828 Angers South. South Carolina Threatens Nullification. In 1828 

Congress passed a new tariff act which placed very high duties on imported goods. 

The South boiled with indignation at this "Tariff of

Abominations," as they called it. Vice President John C. Calhoun of South Carolina did not hesitate to send a letter to the South Carolina legislature protesting against the tariff.

In this letter Calhoun claimed that as the act passed by Congress was for the benefit of the manufacturers of one section of the country it was unconstitutional, and he

urged that South Carolina should hold a state convention to consider some way of declaring the tariff law null and void within the limits of the state. 

How could South Carolina nullify a law passed by 

Congress? 

Quite simply, according to Calhoun. He, like many another statesman of his time, clung to the idea of "states' rights." As a believer in "states' rights," he insisted that the Union was a compact into which each state had entered of its own free will and that therefore the people of each state were free to nullify or to set aside any law passed by Congress if it appeared to them that Congress had gone beyond its constitutional rights in passing the law.

About thirty years earlier the legislatures of Virginia and Kentucky had passed resolutions declaring the Alien and Sedition Acts passed by Congress unconstitutional. 

Jefferson himself had drawn up the statement of the Kentucky Resolutions. Madison had drawn up the Virginia Resolutions. During the War of 1812 some of the 

Federalist leaders in the Hartford Convention, who themselves professed to believe in strong federal government, nevertheless had gone so far as to threaten a separation of the New England States from the rest of the Union. 

Nothing had come of the Hartford Convention or of the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, or of the many other threats of nullification or secession which had been made both in the North and South. But now with Calhoun, the vice president of the country, advising his own state legislature to call a convention for the purpose of nullification, the fate of the republic seemed to be hanging in the balance. 

President Jackson, "A Man of the People," Faces the Nullification Issue. - John Quincy Adams did not have to face the issue of nullification, for at this point an

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

election brought his old rival, Andrew Jackson, to the presidential chair. 

At the election of Jackson, or "Old Hickory" as his friends called him, the "plain people" throughout the country were overjoyed. They looked upon Jackson as a "democrat," a man of the people; and they flocked to see their hero inaugurated.

Jackson was a Westerner, a poor man, the son of hardworking Scotch-Irish immigrants who had settled in South Carolina. As a lad he had moved into Tennessee, where later his victories as an Indian fighter, his defense of New Orleans, and his raid into Florida had made him a popular idol.

As President, Jackson practiced a political policy which has since been called the "Spoils System." He rewarded many of his followers among the people with government jobs.

The "Spoils System" caused many trained employees to be turned out of their positions to make way for political supporters of the President, who were not nearly as capable. The system was very much criticized by Jackson's enemies, but his friends answered, "To the victors belong the spoils." The "Spoils System" offered an opportunity to build political power and it continued to grow through many of the administrations after Jackson's day. 

Jackson soon had more pressing matters to occupy his mind than the filling of government positions. 

Senators Webster and Hayne Debate Nullification. 

Shortly after Jackson's election as President, the discussion of nullification was carried to the Senate. John C. Calhoun as vice president could not take part in the debate. 

However, Senator Robert Hayne, of South Carolina, in a speech attacking the New England manufacturers, took the same stand Calhoun had taken in his letter to the

South Carolina legislature. He defended the right of a state to nullify an act of Congress, even to secede. 

The answer to Hayne came from Daniel Webster, the senator from Massachusetts. The South has always been famous for its great orators, whose speeches in many cases helped to make history. In Daniel Webster the brilliant 

Southern oratory of Hayne met an able opponent. There were many occasions on which Webster's oratory stirred the Senate, but his reply to Hayne was destined to become famous as the clearest statement of the position of those who opposed nullification and secession. 

In his speech Webster argued that only the Supreme Court could declare a law unconstitutional; that the Union could not legally be broken; and that no single state had a right to pass on laws made by Congress or refuse to obey them.

His stand against secession can be summed up in the oft-repeated words of his speech, "Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable."

Jackson Takes Strong Stand for Union. - Webster's words went ringing through the country, but the leaders in South Carolina were not to be so easily silenced. 

They still held to the idea that a state has the right to set aside a law of the republic. Their one hope was that 

Andrew Jackson, who was politically a believer in “States' Rights," would stand with them on the nullification question.

Yet they were not certain, and they therefore planned a means of finding out how he would act. They invited 

Jackson to a dinner given in memory of Thomas Jefferson, who had himself drawn up the Kentucky Resolutions. At that dinner, one speaker after another talked in favor of states' rights and nullification. 

Finally, the time came for Jackson to speak. There was

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

a hush as he arose. Slowly and deliberately and in a voice clear enough for every man in the room to hear, he proposed a toast, "Our Federal Union; it must be preserved!"

Jackson was the seventh president of the United States (1829-1837). He had won fame as an Indian fighter, and 

Still the South Carolina leaders held to their course.

In 1832 a new tariff act was passed which lowered the rates but still left them high enough to cause a special convention to be called by the legislature of South

Carolina. This convention, acting on Calhoun's suggestion, passed the Nullification Act, thus setting aside the 

Tariff Act of 1832. 

President Jackson now proved that he meant his words. Even before the

He was the founder of the Democratic party of to-day, which inherited much of the traditions of the older Anti-Federalist or Democratic Republican party which had been led by Thomas Jefferson. There was a feeling of tension all through the land. For both North and South those were anxious days. Would

the other Southern states which sympathized with South Carolina rush to her aid, declare for nullification, and oblige the federal government either to use force or to yield? Would South Carolina alone bring the issue to a head by resisting collection of the tariff? Neither happened. 

99 

Henry Clay, Champion of the "American System

Proposes Tariff Compromise. The tariff issue was settled not by the Force Act but by a compromise proposed by Henry Clay and passed by Congress at the same time. 

Henry Clay, who represented Kentucky in Congress, had long been a leader in national politics. While other leaders in Washington were contented to look upon most issues from a purely sectional point of view, Clay believed that the interests of the North, South, and West could be harmonized. He became the champion of a plan of political action which he believed would benefit all sections of the country. The plan was known as the "American System." 

This plan provided for a protective tariff which would encourage the manufacturers of the North; for the sale of government lands in the West at a reasonable figure which would help in its growth; for a policy of internal improvements at government expense, or in other words the use of government funds obtained from land sales and from the tariff to build roads and canals into the West. If, however, the high tariff rates should prove harmful to the South, he was in favor of lowering such rates. It then was part of the "American System as he saw it that no section of the country should profit at the expense of any other section, but that all should enjoy a steady growth and increase in prosperity. 99 By the terms of Clay's compromise tariff rates would be gradually reduced until, by the year 1842, the rates would be quite low but still protective.

South Carolina claimed that she had won a victory in

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

the reduction of the tariff. Jackson's show of force proved that the doctrine of nullification and secession would lead to a struggle.

The Tariff Issue to Our Own Day. -The tariff has continued to be a political issue through many political administrations down to our own day, but never again did the tariff bring a threat of nullification. In most of the legislation after 1842, even when the tariff rates were high, there was some regard for the special needs of the various sections of the country, some attempt to compensate in one way or another for any increased burden laid upon the people in the North, West, or South. The old division of sentiment continued. There were champions of high tariff. There were champions of low tariff, or a tariff for revenue only. In the main, the tariff rates continued to increase as the country turned more and more to manufacturing interests, and political leaders were getting more and more eager to protect the manufacturers of the country by means of a tariff wall against cheap foreign goods. 

Finally, Congress found the problem of deciding on a fair tariff so difficult in each of the thousand and one industries which would claim protection, that a bill was passed creating a tariff commission which has the duty of making a special study of the problem. To-day the tariff question can hardly be called a sectional issue. There are leaders in North, South, and West alike, who are for high tariff, just as there are leaders in all sections opposed to high tariff. 

Another issue now happily adjusted with a fair degree of satisfaction to all parts of the country, but a cause of much sectional bitterness in Jackson's day, was banking. The tariff of 1832 had no sooner been settled by Clay's compromise than the issue of the United States Bank came to the fore, stirring up North, South, and West to fresh antagonisms.

Speculation Leads to Panic - All Sections Agree to Sounder Banking Methods Banks Extend Credit. Help Industry. The issue of the tariff was no sooner settled than a new issue arose to create bitterness of feeling within the Union. 

This time the controversy centered about banking. The charter of the United States Bank originally granted at Hamilton's suggestion in 1791 had been allowed to expire in 1811. In 1816 the United States Bank was rechartered for a period of twenty years. 396

Banking was a subject very close to the life of the people and the welfare of the nation. Just as barter, which had proved too clumsy for the needs of trade, had given way to gold, so in time gold proved to be insufficient for the purpose of trade and men had to resort to credit. A merchant would sell a farmer manufactured goods on credit expecting the farmer to pay for the goods after he sold his crops. Since the merchant and the farmer needed money from day to day to pay help and for other outlays, some men went into the business of banking and used their money to make loans to both merchant and farmer. As security for these loans the banks had a claim on the merchant's stock of goods or on the farmer's growing crops. 

Banks in the United States were of three kinds: private banks, which in certain states were chartered and in others operated without the supervision of the state government; state banks, which were depositories for state funds; and the United States Bank, in which the United States government kept its funds. 

United States Bank Has Many Enemies. This United 

States Bank, which was located at Philadelphia with branches in other towns and states, was a powerful institution. The fact that the United States government deposited its own funds in the United States Bank helped to give it a large working capital. That also won for the bank the confidence of many investors within the nation and in foreign countries, all of whom reaped rich dividends from the profits which the bank made through its loans.

But the United States Bank had many enemies, particu.. larly in the South and West. In these sections men complained that the United States Bank was making most of its loans to the Northern manufacturers and merchants, that the bank notes issued by the United States Bank were

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

not sufficient for the needs of the growing industries of the Southern planters and Western farmers, and that they found it difficult to obtain loans from the bank to help them carry out the improvements which they wished to make on their plantations and farms. 

South and West Favor State Banks. Southern plant ers and Western farmers believed that the improvements which they were putting into their own lands were creating wealth as real as gold, and they favored their own state

One Federal Bank or Many State Banks?

Jackson withheld government deposits from the United States Bank. He had the government's funds deposited in state banks, which his political opponents called "Pet Banks." When these "Pet Banks" made loans too freely, a wave of wild speculation followed. The panic which resulted proved that the banking and credit system of the country needed to be placed on a sound basis. banks which printed and issued notes on the basis of the wealth in the land. With state banks issuing such paper money, it was easier for them to obtain loans, and with these paper notes accepted as money they could still further improve their lands.

As the United States Bank often insisted upon gold in its dealings with the state banks, these were in constant danger of being forced into bankruptcy. The state banks found it difficult to thrive as long as the United States

Bank was being especially favored by the receipt of funds for government deposit. 

Congress Recharters United States Bank. Jackson

Destroys It. — Jackson opposed the United States Bank, not only as unconstitutional and as an unfair money power in its operation, but also as a danger to the Union, because of the influence which its directors, controlling so much of the government money, could have in elections. 

Henry Clay, who favored the United States Bank, decided that as election time was approaching he would force the issue to the forefront by asking Congress to pass a bill for the rechartering of the bank in 1836. This Congress did; and when Jackson promptly vetoed the bill, the question was carried to the polls for the people to decide. 

In the election of 1832, when Jackson was overwhelmingly reëlected, he took this as evidence that the people had disapproved of the United States Bank and, accordingly, set out to destroy it by shutting off its supply of government funds.

Government Deposits in State Banks. Easy Credit. 

Wild Speculation. - Jackson arranged that the federal funds be deposited in specified state banks, which because they were so favored were known as "Pet Banks." 

These pet banks and many other state banks which grew up like mushrooms began to print and issue bank notes in quantity. As this money increased the state banks made loans freely; business boomed and individual citizens, business companies, and even states began to take advantage of the easy money to embark in speculation. 

Many people speculated in western lands which they bought from the government at one dollar and a quarter an acre and held for a rise in value. The purchase of government lands increased rapidly. The government selling its lands was being paid with borrowed state bank

notes, which were redeposited in the state banks where they were loaned out again to be used in buying more government lands.

In early days land values in the West, as in other undeveloped sections of the country, usually rose quite rapidly with the swift increase in population and improved transportation. In some land-boom areas, when new developments in the form of roads, canals, or railroads were abandoned, prices fell more swiftly than they rose. In the main, however, land values throughout America have increased greatly. There are cities in which land sells for hundreds of dollars per square foot.

As many of these projects turned out to be successful, foreign governments loaned money to Western states.

These states deposited much of the borrowed money in their state banks, which issued more bank notes and multiplied loans out of all proportion to the actual amount of gold and silver, out of all proportions even to the increasing values of the lands, due to the building of canals and railroads.

With easy credit, the people in the South and West bought heavily from the Eastern merchants, the Eastern

merchants bought heavily from the European merchants. 

States, companies, and individuals all owed money, but all felt rich because of the value at which they placed their holdings.

Then a few men began to see that a day of reckoning must come. They realized that if people should suddenly be asked to meet their debts or should try to sell, values would drop, state banks would fail, government funds would be lost, and so would the visionary fortunes of the states, companies, and private speculators.

CLOSED 

A Panic

From time to time the nation has passed through one of these dark periods of business gloom and depression. In each case, however, after a few years of hard times the business of the nation bounded forward to new heights of production and prosperity. At present the nation hopes to avoid the worst phases of panics through sound banking and more easily, widely, and wisely distributed credit. banks and merchants who had extended too much credit to the boomers went down to ruin with the rest. 

The panic of 1837, as it is called, was a crisis in the life of the nation. During 1837, and for several years after, suffering was widespread, particularly in the Northern towns where the mill workers, who had no homes or lands of their own, found themselves without employment. 

A few of the states were overwhelmingly in debt. The government was without funds. It seemed to some that the nation had suffered a blow from which its industries and its credit would never recover.

Essential Soundness of Nation. Natural Wealth. Man 

Power. Fresh Immigration. In a few years the cloud of gloom lifted, for as a matter of fact the nation was rich by virtue of its great natural resources. Much of its soil was fertile. Its excellent ocean ports and inland waterways favored trade. Its swifter rivers furnished power for factories.

The man power of the country was increasing through fresh immigration. Between 1840 and 1850 there was a large wave of immigration from Ireland where there had been much suffering because of poor crops. When rebellions failed to develop better conditions in their own country, many German immigrants came to this country in search of the freedom which they had been unable to win at home. So now, as in the days of Jamestown and of 

Plymouth, the call of American opportunity and freedom brought new home builders to America and these like the earlier ones helped to conquer the wilderness and to develop American industries.

With increased man power the national wealth grew. 

After the panic years North, South, and West prospered beyond the dreams of the wildest speculators in the prepanic period. 

Regulation of Banks. Nevertheless the reckless loans which had been made by state banks convinced the people that "easy money" and " and "easy credit" could prove dangerous. For this reason the separate states passed laws regulating state banks as to the amount of paper money which they might issue and the conditions under which they might make loans. 

President Van Buren and the Independent Treasury

Act. The failure of state banks which had been intrusted with government funds led President Van Buren to favor the establishment of a government treasury at Washington

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

with branches or subtreasuries in different cities in which to deposit the nation's funds. In 1840 Congress accordingly passed the Independent Treasury Act, and practically ever since the United States Treasury has been the depository of a goodly portion of the government's money. 

In 1863 Congress passed the National Bank Act. This act provided for the establishment of banks which were permitted under the act to issue paper notes. As security for the value of this paper money, the banks were to purchase government bonds.

In 1913 Congress passed the Federal Reserve Bank Law which marked a great step forward in the attempt to aid the farmer and the planter as well as the merchant and the manufacturer to obtain credit. By the terms of this act 

Congress created a Federal Reserve Board and a system of twelve federal reserve banks, each serving a section of the country. These twelve banks and other banks which are members of the federal reserve system are permitted under certain conditions to issue paper notes, and so the problem of easier yet sound credit is somewhat nearer a solution. 

But this is carrying us ahead of our story. In the next chapter we will return to consider the general condition of the United States at about the time of Van Buren's administration.

A Force Strengthening Nationalism. John Marshall. 

Supreme Court Decisions. In spite of the panic of 1837 the national government had been growing steadily in power.

The spirit of nationalism had been greatly strengthened by the legal decisions handed down by the Supreme Court under Chief Justice John Marshall. Marshall, who had been appointed to office by President John Adams, served for many years during all of which time he inter- 406

NATIONALISM: PROSPERITY AND PROGRESS 407 

preted the Constitution as giving large powers to the federal government. 

Nationalism Aided by Growth of West. The influence of lawyers upon the political development of the republic in its early years was great. Many of the lawmakers in the state and national legislatures were trained to the legal profession, and they brought to the task of lawmaking the advantage of their professional training. 

John Marshall, as the Chief 

Justice of the Supreme Court, held the most honored position in the government to which a lawyer as a lawyer could aspire, and his decisions in favor of a loose interpretation gave a legal foundation to the growing spirit of nationalism. 

John Marshall

Marshall was a lawyer who served as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court for many years. Marshall interpreted the Constitution as giving great power to the federal government, and so helped nationalism. Lawyers have played an important part in American history. 

Many of our presidents were trained in the law. For a long time the majority of Congressmen were lawyers. 

Another factor in the development of the national spirit was the influence of the New West. The owner ship of the Western lands strengthened the hands of the federal government in many ways. In the West, whether 

Northwest or Southwest, the people facing frontier conditions felt a common interest in the national government. They had in many cases bought their lands directly from the federal government; federal troops had helped to protect them against the Indians; federal power had obtained for them the ownership of the

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

Mississippi River and the lands beyond it and an open path down the river into the Gulf of Mexico. The War of 

1812 waged by the federal government had removed all danger to the West from British forts in Canada. The federal government was in a position to help Western growth through the building of roads across the mountains. The Western states, being farther removed from 

Europe than the East, had less desire to emulate Europe; and in many ways the Westerners felt themselves to be and actually were much more American in spirit than the people in the East.

National Prosperity. The growing power of the national government went hand in hand with an increased national prosperity.

The sale of Western lands brought money not only into the national treasury, but also into the pockets of the men and women who went into the West to live. In the South as well as in the West farm production gained rapidly in quantity, and trade with the rest of the world increased. 

Ships from Northern and Southern states did much of the world's ocean carrying and Northern manufactures increased. Directly or indirectly, the strength of the nation as a whole, its successful foreign policy, and its success in meeting domestic problems had helped in building up the prosperity of the individual states and of the people within the states.

New Inventions Help Prosperity. Revolutionize Industry. One reason for the growth of national prosperity during the period from 1789 to 1850 and ever since was the inventive skill of the Americans and their readiness to make use of important foreign inventions. When England gave to the world the steam engine and new spinning and weaving machinery, America was swift to introduce these labor-saving inventions and soon added to these many new

ones.

The Bessemer process for making cheap steel, patented in England, was used in American mills. In farming, McCormick's reaper was one of a large number of American labor-saving devices. We have seen how the steamboat and the railroad, the telephone and the telegraph, revolutionizing transportation and communication, helped to build the nation. In like manner the new labor-saving tools began to revolutionize farming and manufacture. 

The cotton gin helped to develop cotton growing in the South. New England became an important manufacturing center when the spinning and weaving machinery was installed in newly built mills. With increased production in the South, North, and West, the railroads carrying goods from section to section became a vital factor in America's industrial life.

Prosperity and Education. 

With the growth of prosperity there were many signs of progress in the social life of the nation. Necessity may be the mother of invention, but education, the arts, and the sciences are generally born of the greater leisure which usually comes with prosperity.

In education, the colonists had made a beginning, even when they were facing the first trials of wilderness life.

They had established schools and colleges, but well into the early years of the republic education was far from common. Schools were few and they were for the most part private or church schools. A student attending a free school was regarded as more or less the recipient of public charity. demand for public tax-supported schools. To-day practically every community in the United States provides for free public education. 

We have seen how the election of Jackson marked a triumph for the common people in political life. Side by side with political victory the people demanded and won other victories for democratic ideals in education.

NATIONALISM: PROSPERITY AND PROGRESS 411 

For a long time labor organizations in the cities of the East had joined with the democratic leaders of the West in demanding free public schools supported by public taxes. 

In the East there were leaders outside the labor movement, such men as Horace Mann, Henry Barnard, and De Witt

Clinton, who gave much time to the fight for free public schools. They believed that free education was a good investment for the government as well as for its people. 

Since the plain people were going to run the government, it was, in their opinion, advisable that they should be prepared for the tasks of citizenship.

During the years of the new prosperity which followed the panic of 1837, the free public school system was developing in many states, not only for elementary grades but also for high school grades.

During the same period the establishment of colleges and universities continued, often under circumstances as picturesque as the founding of the early colonial colleges. 

In communities which were little more than wildernesses, where Indian tribes still lurked, a handful of men of one religious sect or another built colleges which grew with the years. This same period witnessed an increasing number of state universities both in the East and in the West. 

Progress in the Arts. With growing prosperity and increased leisure, a few cities, especially in the East, became noted for their activity in the arts. 

In painting, sculpture, and in literature European masters exercised a strong influence over style; but in many cases the subject treated by Americans gave proof of an increased national feeling and interest in things American. 

During the early decades of the nineteenth century, one small group of men, known as the Hudson River School, painted Adirondack Mountain scenery. A few American sculptors of European training executed statues of Amer-

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

ican heroes. But the new national note was more evident in the field of literature. In the North, Washington Irving's 

Sketch Book, his Knickerbocker's History of New York; 

James Fenimore Cooper's novels, The Spy, The Pilot, and his Leatherstocking Tales; a good portion of the works of the New England writers, Whittier, Longfellow, Bryant, Lowell, and Emerson, belong to the middle period of the nineteenth century. There were many others in the 

North and South, who, although not so well known to-day, were helping during this same period to create an interested audience for literature dealing with American themes. The chief of the Southern writers, Edgar Allan Poe, was a poet and writer of mystery tales, which marked the beginning of the American short story. 

In the field of music, apart from popular ballads and church hymns, there were about this same time occasional performances of European grand opera in a few cities; some of the most noted of the European musicians began to tour America, and orchestral societies and other musical organizations were founded. 

Progress in Science. Agassiz. -As the American colleges benefited by increased endowments from wealthy citizens, they offered positions on their faculties to distinguished European scientists. The chief of these

European scholars in America was Louis Agassiz, who helped to train many a young American in the methods of scientific study and research. 

Prosperity and Social Reforms. Laboring Conditions. 

Manhood Suffrage. Because of the new inventions and the growth of manufacturing industries, the ways of living were changing somewhat, especially in the factory towns.

With the building of factories the cities soon had a large class of laborers, many of them immigrants. As a rule,

NATIONALISM: PROSPERITY AND PROGRESS 413 

mill and factory laborers worked for many hours each day; they were poorly paid and poorly housed. Eager to improve their lot, men formed labor unions which agitated for free schools, for the workman's right to vote, for government gifts of land to actual settlers. A few men and women in the East, believing in the justice of labor's claims, became champions of social reforms which labor desired, and pleaded for those reforms in public speeches and sermons.

The reformers won in the field of education. They also made progress for white manhood suffrage. In many of the democratic Western states every white male citizen had the right to vote. In the Eastern states where the vote had been restricted by property or religious qualifications, reformers gradually succeeded in having laws passed granting the vote to all male white citizens. The election of Jackson was helped by the vote of the "plain people," and it was during Jackson's term of office that politics were still further reformed, in the direction of democracy, by the introduction of national conventions of the political parties. Before Jackson's day a group of congressmen of each party picked the party candidate for President. During Jackson's term of office he helped to introduce the custom of choosing the presidential candidate in a national convention of party delegates. 

Women Demand Political Rights. During this period of social reform in education and in politics, leaders appeared as champions for reforms in the social and political status of women. 

It had long been an axiom concerning women that "woman's place is in the home," and that she could safely trust to men the management of the other affairs of life. School education was not supposed to be for her, except, possibly, a knowledge of reading and writing.

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

According to this notion, voting and the affairs of government were certainly not for her. 

However, leaders now appeared upon the scene who wished to see women as a class benefit from the new democratic tendencies. They argued that if the plain people were to come into power, it should be remembered that

Women Gain Higher Education. Leaders of the 

Woman's Movement wished to see women share equally with men in the opportunity to get an education. Since most schools of higher education were closed to them, a few women established schools of their own. A few women, among them Emma Willard and Mary Lyon, established seminaries where girls could receive competent schooling. The West, by introducing coeducation, again proved its democratic spirit when Oberlin College, Antioch College, and in time state universities admitted women students.

Women Leaders in Reform Movement. Women played a leading part in the humanitarian movements which were organized to promote social welfare. One woman, Dorothea L. Dix, devoted her life to the cause of social reform. 

Women leaders played a large part in organizing temperance societies which aimed to check drunkenness. The drinking of strong alcoholic liquors was a part of the tradition of many of the people who had come to America. They had taught this evil to the Indians upon whom it had had the most disastrous results, and although they themselves seemed more inured to strong drink, many suffered from alcoholic excess.

The temperance societies tried to bring about legislation, prohibiting the sale and use of alcoholic liquors. 

They won their first important victory when the state of Maine in 1846 adopted prohibition.

CHAPTER XXXII 

Slave or Free

The Nation, Although Prospering and Progressing, Finds the Issue of 

Slavery Difficult and Dangerous to Its Peace 

Among

Slavery Issue Disturbs National Good Will. 

the sectional issues which tended to divide the nation, the most dangerous was the issue of slavery. The tariff issue caused bitterness, but it was safely compromised. The banking issue caused some ill-will between the sections, but the panic of 1837 taught people that North, South, and West alike needed sound business methods in money dealings and credit arrangements. Neither the tariff nor the banking issue ever again seriously threatened the safety of the nation. 418

The slavery issue was different. On this problem North and South each took a stand which became less and less yielding as the years went on. In time, the issue of slavery created so much bitter sectional feeling that it threatened to destroy the Union.

Negro Slavery before Invention of Cotton Gin (1793). 

-The story of negro slavery begins far back in history. 

Negro slaves were first introduced into Europe by Prince Henry of Portugal. His ships, exploring the coast of 

Africa, captured negroes and sold them in Portugal to help pay the cost of the expeditions. Slavery was introduced into the English colonies in 1619 when a Dutch ship brought negro slaves to Virginia. Negroes were not brought into the English colonies in great numbers until the wealthier planters in the South began to use slaves on their large plantations. For more than a century negroes were used generally throughout the Northern and Southern colonies, but in the North they were used as house servants rather than as farm or shop workers. In Europe, nations fought with one another for the profits of the slave trade, and New England merchants as well as British kings and lords invested heavily in the traffic. 

During colonial times the Quakers had raised their voices against slavery, and later many a man and woman both in the South and North began to look upon slavery as an evil. 

At the convention which drafted the Constitution there were men who wished to take steps toward ending slavery, but a few of the delegates insisted that their states could not run plantations without slaves. Accordingly the drafters of the Constitution compromised on the issue by guaranteeing no prohibition of the importation of slaves before the year 1808.

Those men who opposed slavery hoped that by 1808 slave owners would feel convinced that slavery was neither

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

right nor profitable and that slavery would gradually disappear. Such might have been the case had it not been for the impetus given to the cotton industry by invention. 

Cotton Growing and Slave Labor. When new spinning and weaving machinery and Whitney's cotton gin made it 

possible to make cotton cloth at 

The Cotton Gin 

In the cotton gin, invented by Eli Whitney, wire prongs on revolving rollers comb the seeds out of the cotton bolls. These mechanical combs cleaned more cotton in an hour than a slave could clean by hand in many hours. 

With the cotton gin to reduce the cost of cleaning cotton, and with the mills of England and New England demanding raw cotton for the manufacture of cotton cloth to help clothe the world, cotton eventually became the leading Southern crop. little cost, the planters turned to cotton raising. 

Cotton raising was profitable, but the cultivation of new lands and the raising of valuable crops required a plentiful supply of labor.

This the South ern planters obtained through the use of slaves. 

The free laborers of the country preferred to work in Northern mills or to go West to clear farms of their own. Many of the white immigrants who came from 

Europe also chose to live in the manufacturing centers of the North. Immigrants who were eager to work on farms went to those parts of the West where they could work on land of their own and would not have to compete with slave labor.

Nor could the wealthy Southern planters obtain their labor from the poorer farmers in the South. These men and

women, although they owned little or no land and had no slaves, preferred to live in poverty rather than to work with slaves.

In the absence of any other available supply of cheap labor, the planters increased their stock of slaves and the number of negroes increased rapidly. 

By the year 1808, when the Constitution permitted the ending of the foreign slave trade, there were sufficient slaves in the Union, even without the influx of smuggled slaves from the West Indies, to make it most unlikely that the slavery problem would solve itself. 

Still hopeful of solving the slavery question peaceably an organization called the American Colonization Society, headed by Bushrod Washington, a justice of the Supreme Court, and many other prominent men, including Henry Clay, attempted to interest the people in their plan. Both 

Washington and Clay were Southerners as were most of the members of the society. 

The object of this organization was to promote the emancipation of the negro by sending to Africa those freed by their owners. Through the interest of the government in the activities of the society, the colony of Liberia on the west coast of Africa was established as a refuge for freedmen, but the plan did not succeed. The negroes did not go to Africa in large enough numbers to affect the problem in the United States.

By 1820, when the question of the admission of Missouri as a slave state was settled by the famous Missouri Compromise, the number of slaves in the country had increased materially.

Antislavery Men Want Free West. Missouri Compro mise. When the nation acquired Louisiana, the question which was sooner or later bound to arise was, "Shall the new territory be 'free soil' or open to slavery?" This

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

question was settled temporarily by the Missouri Compromise, which admitted Missouri into the Union as a slave state, but set up a line dividing the Louisiana territory into free soil and territory open to slavery. 

For a time the Missouri Compromise seemed to work. 

As we have read in the story of the winning of the West, while farmers from the North were pouring into the Western free soil, Southern planters and their slaves were developing Tennessee, Kentucky, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana. Those who wished to move still farther west had, with others, gone into Texas and set up an independent republic.

The Abolitionists Want All Slaves Freed. Although the 

Missouri Compromise seemed to work, there were men who were determined that the slavery problem should not and could not be settled by compromise. These men, who were called abolitionists, were not content with the limitation of slavery in the West. They wished to see slavery abolished throughout the land by the emancipation of all slaves.

These abolitionists began to publish magazines. They agitated by handbill and newspapers, they mailed circulars, held street-corner meetings, and extended their efforts through abolition societies which they organized. 

William Lloyd Garrison, Abolitionist Leader. Move ment Alarms North and South. - An early American who devoted himself to this abolition propaganda was Benjamin Lundy, a New Jersey Quaker, who, beginning in 1821, published in Ohio and elsewhere the Genius of Universal 

Emancipation. Seven years later, William Lloyd Garrison, a young compositor who worked in Boston, joined Lundy. 

In 1831 Garrison returned to Boston where he issued the first number of his magazine, the Liberator, in which he denounced slavery in fiery terms.

That same year Virginia saw a slave uprising led by Nat Turner which resulted in the massacre of over sixty white people. The South claimed that Nat Turner, who could read and write, had been aroused to insurrection by his reading of the Liberator and demanded that the North take steps to prevent the abolitionists from stirring up abolition sentiment. The Northern leaders, who feared the abolitionists because of their open attacks on the Constitution for its toleration of slavery, turned on the abolitionist leaders as dangerous fanatics and troublemakers.

Garrison was attacked in Boston and dragged through the streets of the city to be tarred and feathered on the Common. Only the interference of the police saved him. 

Elijah Lovejoy, an abolitionist editor, was shot dead in 

Alton, Illinois. In Cincinnati, James G. Birney, another abolitionist leader, had to flee for his life from a mob which wrecked his office. Southern postmasters refused to deliver abolitionist petitions which were sent to Congress by mail. Northern congressmen voted with Southern congressmen (1836) to prevent the abolitionist petitions from being read. Although ex-President John Quincy

Adams, now a congressman, fought this "Gag Rule," as it was called, on the floor of Congress, eight years passed before he succeeded in having it repealed. 

Antislavery Leaders Seek to Limit Slavery by Law. - 

John Quincy Adams was not an abolitionist. He, Daniel 

Webster, and Charles Sumner were congressional leaders of the antislavery or "free-soil" men.

Adams objected to "Gag Rule" because he believed that it violated the constitutional rights of people to petition Congress. He opposed the abolitionists because he felt that the things which they proposed were as unconstitutional as the "Gag Rule."

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

Adams, Webster, Sumner, and the antislavery followers whom they represented, wanted to see slavery disappear through some agreement between the North and the South. 

Since the Southern planters insisted that they could not manage their crops without slavery and that slavery was even a desirable institution, the antislavery leaders aimed 

Daniel Webster 

Webster, who represented Massachusetts in the United States Senate, is most famous for his "Reply to 

Hayne." In his answer to Hayne's brilliant defense of the doctrine of states' rights, Webster claimed that the Constitution had created an indissoluble union. only to prevent slavery from spreading beyond the boundaries fixed by the Missouri 

Compromise. 

Northern Reasons for Trying to Limit Slavery in West. The people of the 

North had at least two reasons for being against the extension of slavery into the 

West even if they did not oppose slavery in the states where it was established.

In the first place there was the question of the land itself; 

Northerners who looked to the West as a future home in case of need did not want to see the Western lands occupied by Southerners and their slaves. In the second place, there was the question of the West as a market for manufactured goods; the Northern manufacturers had much to lose and little to gain by seeing the West filled up by a slave population which would naturally be kept by the planters at a low standard of living. A West filled with free men would help to build up Eastern manufacturing more than a West filled with slaves. The Northern men

clung to their program of keeping slavery within its boundary.

South Plans New Slave States in the West. - To the antislavery leaders, the events which followed immediately after the lifting of the Gag Rule seemed to prove that the South was planning to increase its power by winning additional territory south of the Missouri line. Southern planters played a large part in colonizing Texas, in winning its freedom from Mexico, and in securing its annexation as a slave state in 1845. Southern planters were most active in the Mexican War which resulted in the acquisition of new territory south of the Missouri Compromise line. If this additional territory should be carved into slave states, the South would have more senators and so could strengthen its power in the national government. 

Wilmot's Proviso. The leaders in the North were worried. Before the end of the Mexican War, Wilmot rose in Congress and proposed what is called the "Wilmot Proviso," in which he urged that Congress declare in advance that any new territory acquired by the United States as a result of the war would be closed to slavery. 

The measure was defeated. The Purchase Treaty made no mention of slavery, but the question of the extension of slavery into the West was not to be escaped. 

California Slave or Free State? Clay Proposes Compromise. By 1850 the rush of gold miners to California brought the population of that territory up to one hundred thousand, and the Californians asked for admission into the Union with a state constitution forbidding slavery. 

The Southerners, who had counted upon the new territory to strengthen their side, objected. The antislavery men in the Senate and in the House of Representatives approved. Feeling ran high and there seemed no way of bringing the two sides to an agreement.

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

In the Senate there was a mighty debate. 

Henry Clay, by this time an old and feeble man, once again endeavored to patch up matters by a compromise. 

He laid his plan of give and take before the Senate, and for 

Henry Clay 

Clay, who represented Kentucky in 

Congress, was one of the War Hawks of 1812. He won for himself the title of the Great Pacificator through his share in securing the compromise of the Tariff of 1832 and the Compromise of 1850. As a leader of the Whig party he championed the American system, a high tariff to protect American industry, and the building of internal improvements, such as roads and canals, at government expense. two days he pleaded with his colleagues from the North and South to follow the path of peace by meeting one another halfway. 

John C. Calhoun, the champion of states' rights, who, in 

1832, had urged South Carolina to nullify the Tariff Act, being too weak to stand on his feet and deliver his speech, sat by while a friend delivered his address against the antislavery movement in the 

North. Passionately, he pointed out that the North had grown all powerful through its hold on the West, through the tariff, through its manufactures, and its increased representation in the 

Senate and House. He claimed that under the circumstances unless the South were given room to expand and to restore the balance, it had to make a desperate choice. It had either to face the day when its wealth would be destroyed by the antislavery forces or it would have to secede from the Union. 

For days the debate continued. Daniel Webster, still

devoted to Union above all things, pleaded that the South should not be driven to extremities. Then arose younger men like William H. Seward, the new leader of the antislavery men, and Jefferson Davis, who was soon to become the leader of the proslavery men. 

Compromise of 1850 Wins. Terms of Omnibus Bill. 

Clay's compromise plan finally won the day. An Omnibus 

Bill, as it was called, provided that, while California was to come in as a free state, the settlers in Utah and New Mexico were to decide the slavery question for themselves. 

The compromise provided also that slaves were not to be bought or sold in the District of Columbia, and a new and more stringent Fugitive Slave Law was passed. The Fugitive Slave Law of 1850 made it the duty of United States officers to help in capturing slaves who had escaped from their masters into neighboring states; and it provided fines and prison terms for any one found guilty of helping a fugitive slave or interfering with his arrest. 

The law about fugitive slaves seemed on its face to be a victory for the South. The provision that Utah and New

Mexico could settle their own slavery question was a partial victory. The admission of California as a free state and the stopping of slave trade in the District of Columbia were victories for the North. In Congress both sides felt relieved by the compromise Omnibus Bill, and back in the states many resolutions were passed to express the hope that the Compromise of 1850 would once and for all settle the differences between the slavery and the antislavery men.

Fugitive Slave Law Opposed. Underground Railway. — 

A vain hope! In the North the attempt to enforce the

Fugitive Slave Law kept the issue before the people. They saw officers pursuing slaves through country lanes and city streets. They read newspaper advertisements describing

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

slaves who were wanted. According to law it was their duty if called upon to help the officers capture the runaways.

Many Northerners made up their minds that they would not help in the capture of slaves. On the contrary they would do all in their power to help fugitive slaves escape to Canada.

For this purpose they laid out routes, along which night journeys would be safe. They chose as stopping points villages in which there were one or two families who agreed to shelter the slaves through the day and to send them on when night came. This line of flight was called the "Underground Railway." 

Uncle Tom's Cabin Stirs Abolition Sentiment. Just at this time, Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote a novel,

Uncle Tom's Cabin. This novel presented the author's imaginative notion of life on a Southern plantation in a very black picture of the sufferings of the slaves under their taskmasters. There was a cruel overseer, named 

Legree, with whip in hand ever ready to lay on the lash.

The Southerners, annoyed by what they regarded as a libel upon the South, pointed out that the book gave a wrong impression of life on a plantation. They insisted that most slaves were happy and cheerful and that their lot was not nearly so bad as the novel depicted. 

Nevertheless, the book was read far and wide in the North where it gripped the hearts of people and increased abolition sentiment. 

Douglas Proposes Kansas-Nebraska Act. - Soon men were realizing that the new Western lands were to be more valuable than any one had realized. In addition to the gold of California, gold, silver, and lead had been found in Colorado and Nevada. Just before 1860 there was talk of a Pacific Railroad extending west from St. Louis across

the prairies of Nebraska Territory through Colorado and 

Utah to the coast.

According to the terms of the Missouri Compromise, the Nebraska Territory was closed to slave owners, but shortly after the California Compromise was passed, the senator from Illinois, Stephen A. Douglas, offered a plan to Congress, which, if adopted, would practically set aside the 

Missouri Compromise. 

His plan, called the Kansas-Nebraska Act, provided that the territory of Nebraska be divided into two parts: 

Kansas to the South (as possible slave territory), and Nebraska to the North (as possible free territory). It provided further that the settlers who went into Kansas or Nebraska should be permitted to decide for themselves whether their new home should be free soil or open to slavery. 

This, he said, would make for "Popular Sovereignty" or the right of people while still in territories to settle the slavery question for themselves. In this way the dangerous question of slavery in the new territories would be taken out of the hands of the national government. 

In 1854 when Congress passed the Kansas-Nebraska 

Act a wave of joy went through the South. At last the hated line set up by the Missouri Compromise would no longer worry them. They could carry their slaves into the valuable Western lands. A wave of indignation went through the North when it was learned that the antislavery provision of the Missouri Compromise had been set aside. 

Bloodshed in Kansas. — Soon it appeared that the doctrine of "Popular Sovereignty," far from lessening the danger from the slavery issue, was transferring the fight for the West from the halls of Congress to the prairies. 

While Northern organizations were protesting in their mass meetings, groups of free-soil men and slave owners

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

were pouring into Kansas, each determined to win the territory for its own side. 

In Massachusetts, Eli Thurber, the head of the Emigrant Aid Society, furnished families with funds for settlement in Kansas. In Missouri thousands of border settlers crossed the line into Kansas. At Lecompton those who favored slavery drew up a constitution making Kansas a slave state. The free-soil men drew up a separate constitution shutting slavery out of Kansas.

Soon both sides passed from political maneuvering to lawless warfare. The proslavery men raided free-soil settlements. Free-soil men raided slavery settlements. One of the most violent leaders in this warfare was John Brown, an abolitionist.

After a series of raids, midnight murders, and even pitched battles, two hundred lay dead in "Bleeding Kansas."

Naturally, with "popular sovereignty" working out in this bloody way, it was not long before the slavery question was once again debated on the floor of Congress and with more bitterness.

By 1856 these debates were most bitter. The slavery issue had reached a point where Northern mobs were openly rescuing captured slaves from the officers of the law and thousands of citizens were secretly leagued together to aid in the escape of slaves. But the most ominous symptom of all was in Kansas where proslavery men and free-soil men were trying to settle by force the issue of the spread of slavery.

Was civil strife in Kansas to be only a foretaste of civil strife in the nation? Men and women pondered the question. They were eager for a peaceful solution, and turned to the political parties and their election platforms to search for signs of hope.

Washington to Buchanan

The Story of Political Parties from the Time of Washington to the Year 1856, When the New-born Republican Party Enters National 

Politics on an Antislavery Platform

Slavery, a National Campaign Issue. The New 

Republican Party. - In the year 1856, when the time came for the nomination of presidential candidates, every one looked forward to the convention of the political parties with great interest.

In the face of the slavery issue, and the loss of old leaders, old party lines were breaking down, and there was every reason to believe that a new national party was going to make the limitation of slavery its principal issue.

Early Political Parties: Federalist, Republican. — At this point it might be well to go back in our story in order to see the development of party politics, and to follow more closely the political careers of the Presidents. While 

Washington was still President, two parties came into 433

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

1 existence: one the Federalist, and the other, an opposition party soon known as the Democratic-Republican, and later as the Republican. The Federalist party stood for loose construction of the Constitution and a strong central government; the Republican party favored strict construction and states' rights. Washington favored the principles of the Federalists. John Adams was a Federalist; Jefferson, Madison, and Monroe were Republicans or Republican-Democrats. By the time of the election campaign of 

1824 the Federalist party completely disappeared as a party, although its faith in the principle of a strong federal government lived on. That same year, when John Quincy Adams, Republican, was elected, there were signs of a break in the ranks of his party.

Democratic Party vs. Whig Party. -After the election of Andrew Jackson in 1828, his followers reorganized the old Republican party as the Democratic party, which has lasted to this day. The Democratic party of Jackson's day was hardly a new party. It was really the successor of the 

Republican-Democratic party of Jefferson's time, and its platform was practically the same. The leaders of this party championed the cause of popular government; they stood for states' rights, they opposed government aid in internal improvements, and they favored a low tariff. 

Jackson's enemies, led by Clay, organized the "Whig Party." They explained that they called themselves 

Whigs because like the English Whigs in the reign of George the Third they aimed to check tyrant rule. They referred to Jackson's terms of office as the "reign" of Andrew Jackson. Clay as the leader of one branch of the 

Whigs urged the "American System," which advocated strong central government, government aid to roads, and a tariff high enough to protect manufacturers. 

Jackson was in office from 1829 to 1837, and during his

term he greatly increased the power of the executive department of the government by his strong stand in the case of the Nullification Act of South Carolina; in his deliberate destruction of the United States Bank; in his "Specie Circular," by which he took it upon himself to demand specie in payment of government lands. His personally chosen candidate, Martin Van Buren, was 

President from 1837 to 1841.

It was during Van Buren's administration that the panic of 1837 occurred and this panic gave the Whigs their opportunity. Campaign.

A Modern Whigs Elect Harrison. - In the election of 1840 the Whigs nominated the aged William 

Henry Harrison, the famous 

Indian fighter, for the presidency. When some Democratic paper, forgetting its democratic ideals, scoffed at 

Harrison as an old man who would like nothing better than to be left alone in his log cabin with a barrel of hard cider, the Whigs took up the challenge and made the most of this picture as election campaign material. 

Martin Van Buren 

Martin Van Buren was the eighth president of the United States. The leading events of his administration were: panic of 1837; "gag" resolution; establishment of independent treasury.

This was the first campaign during which party organizations in states and towns and villages held public parades, circulated campaign literature, displayed party banners, and adopted campaign slogans.

Whatever the cause, whether the people turned against the Democrats because of their suffering during the panic

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

or whether they were carried away by the spirited campaign of the Whigs, Harrison was elected. But his election profited the Whigs little; Harrison died one month after his 

William Henry Harrison 

Harrison defeated Tecumseh's forces at Tippecanoe in 1811 and won the Battle of the Thames in Canada in the War of 1812. In 1841 he was elected to the presidency, but he died shortly after his inauguration. The slogan of the Whig campaign for Harrison was "Tippecanoe and Tyler too."

That the people seemed to favor the move was indicated by the campaign of 1844 when they elected James K.

Polk, Democrat, on the double slogan of the Reoccupation of Oregon and the Reannexation of Texas.

Political Compromises on Slavery Fail to Satisfy. From 

1789 to 1850 men had tried to avoid the slavery issue. The drafters of the Constitution had compromised on the question of the slave trade when they agreed not to limit it until 1808. Congress had compromised on slavery when it agreed that slavery might exist in the Louisiana territory south of Missouri. Compromise of 1850. 

The Fugitive Slave Act, which was part of the Compromise of 1850, was opposed in the North, and the agreement to permit Utah and New Mexico to settle the slavery question for themselves did not satisfy the South. 

The underground railway was the antislavery answer to the Fugitive Slave Act. The Kansas-Nebraska Act gave the South an opportunity to carry slavery north of the Missouri Compromise line. When war broke out in

Kansas, the seriousness of the slavery issue was brought home to the people. In spite of all the compromises, events seemed to be carrying the nation toward civil war. 

Republican Party's First National Convention. As many men now began to see that slavery was a leading problem before the American people, old party lines rapidly 

To voice the disappeared. growing free-soil sentiment, the Republican party appeared in national politics. In its first national convention, held in 1856, the new party drafted a platform which attracted antislavery men among the 

Northern Democrats. It also drew great numbers of its members from the old Whig party. 

Franklin Pierce 

Pierce was the fourteenth president of the United States (18531857). The leading events of his administration were: Kansas-Nebraska Act; civil war in Kansas; introduction of many new inventions into daily life. 

When the convention came to naming a party candidate, the spirit of compromise again showed itself. The new party passed over Seward, who was the true leader of the antislavery men, and gave the nomination to Frémont, the explorer, who in the forties had blazed trails for the United States government across the Southwest to California.

The Democrats, also unwilling to stand squarely on the issue of popular sovereignty and the Kansas-Nebraska Act, which had stirred up so much trouble, passed over Douglas and nominated James K. Buchanan instead. Buchanan, having been minister to England during the discussion of

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

the Kansas-Nebraska Act, had neither said anything nor done anything in the matter to make personal enemies. 

Nominating Dark Horses. The practice of choosing a 

"dark horse" for the presidential nomination rather than a strong man who had proved his convictions by public stand or utterances was a habit which had been growing on the country after Jackson's time. The leading aim of each party seemed to be to win the election rather than to stand squarely for a cause or a principle. And, since strong men made enemies, it seemed safer to pass them over and to nominate instead some less well-known figure who had said little and done less on the stormy issues of the day. 

In all the elections up to 1856 the people may have preferred it so. They were not ready to face the slavery question. The issue had not come to a head, and to most people there seemed no reason for forcing matters to a crisis.

Minor Parties Oppose Slavery Before 1856. - Such minor parties as had come out strongly on the slavery issue before 1856 had polled small votes in comparison with the votes cast for the two leading parties. In 1840 the Liberty party, which opposed the extension of slavery, polled seven thousand votes. In 1844 the same party received 

62,000 votes of the more than 2,500,000 cast. In 1848 a new party, the Free Soil party, expressed its antislavery sentiment in the slogan "Free Soil, Free Labor, Free 

Men." With Van Buren as candidate, the party had polled 290,000 votes. In 1852 the Free Soilers dropped back to 156,000 votes.

Republican Votes in 1856 Point to Victory in 1860. 

The Republican party, which appeared in the field of national politics in 1856, inherited much of the platform of the Free Soilers. Because of the breakdown of the Whigs and the growing split in the Democratic party, the Republicans

polled an enormous vote. The Republican vote was 

1,340,000, as against the Democratic vote of 1,830,000.

The Democrats elected their candidate, James Buchanan, but it was clear that in the next election, only four years away, the Republicans might win the day upon their platform, which opposed the extension of slavery in the West.

Planters Alarmed by Republican Vote Await Dred Scott 

Decision. The Democrats won the election of 1856. 

Their President, Buchanan, sat in the White House, but the unexpected increase in the Republican party's vote alarmed them.

The Republicans had elected many representatives to Congress, and if they gained many more votes in Congress they could easily outvote the South. 

To the slave-owning planters there seemed to be only one ray of hope and to this they now turned. The Supreme 443

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

Court was trying a case which involved the question of the constitutional rights of Congress to limit slavery. 

The case which would bring a decision on this point was that of Dred Scott, a negro who had been carried by his master out of a slave state into a part of the Louisiana Purchase territory which had been declared free by the Missouri Compromise, and then back into the state of Missouri, which permitted slavery. Upon the death of his master, Dred Scott claimed that when his master had carried him into free territory, he became a free man. When a citizen of New York bought him and hired him out to work in Missouri, Scott again sued for his freedom, this time in the federal court of the district. Failing there, Dred Scott appealed his case to the Supreme Court of the 

United States. 

The South eagerly awaited the decision of the Supreme Court. According to their constitutional lawyers there was every reason to hope for an important decision in their favor.

Supreme Court Declares Missouri Compromise Uncon stitutional. - In 1857 the Supreme Court handed down. its verdict. The Court denied that Dred Scott was a free man and a citizen. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney of Mary land wrote the decision. He claimed that a slave is property, and he denied the right of Congress to interfere with this form of property by excluding slavery from United States territory as it had undertaken to do by the Missouri 

Compromise. 

To the antislavery men in the North and the West, the verdict came like a thunder bolt. It opened up all the 

Western territory to the slave owners. With these territories open to slavery, the South might be in a position to make its next move the opening of the Northern states to their slaves.

Douglas, a Democrat, Opposed by Lincoln, a Republican.

Debates. When Buchanan urged Congress to admit 

Kansas under a state constitution permitting slavery, Douglas attacked the move on the ground that he was convinced that the Constitution did not really express the will of the people of Kansas. 

Douglas, who had injured his standing in the North through the Kansas-Nebraska Act, now lost much of his hold in the South as well. As his term of office as senator was to expire, he hastened back to Illinois to stand for reëlection, and all eyes were turned to Illinois to see what would be the fate of the "Little Giant," as he was called. 

Stephen Douglas

In Illinois the men who still hoped for compromise on the subject of slavery were anxious to see Douglas, the

Democratic candidate, reelected. The antislavery men had put up a strong opponent, Abraham Lincoln, to to run against him on the Republican ticket -"Honest Abe," they called him. 

Douglas wanted to see the dangerous slavery question taken out of national politics. He was the author of the Kansas-Nebraska Act, which proposed that the question of slavery in 

Kansas and Nebraska be decided by the settlers in these territories.

Abraham Lincoln was a lawyer. He was a very tall, plain, gaunt man, slightly stoop-shouldered. The people liked him because he liked the people. He was one of them. 

He knew the lives they lived. He knew the meaning of poverty, of suffering, of hardship. He knew the struggle which men go through, for he himself had struggled very hard.

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

As a boy on his father's farm, he was able to do the work of a grown man for he was very strong. At the age of sixteen he was six feet four inches tall, and a neighbor said of him, "Abe could sink an ax deeper into the wood than any man I ever saw."

Born in Kentucky, he later lived in Indiana and when twenty-one he moved with his father to Illinois. There 

The Lincoln-Douglas Debates 

It was during these debates, that Lincoln, who was running against Douglas for the election to the United States Senate, won the nation-wide reputation which gained him the Republican nomination in 1860. 

Abe helped to build the cabin and plow the fields. The next year he was hired to take a flatboat down the Mississippi River to New Orleans. For a time he served as store clerk and even owned a country store. He also practiced surveying. Then he studied law, and was admitted to the bar as a practicing attorney. He had also served in the Assembly of Illinois and in Congress. 

Now his fellow citizens in the Republican party chose him as their candidate for the United States Senate. In accepting the nomination, Lincoln spoke the words which later aroused the nation: "A house divided against itself

cannot stand. I believe this government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free. I do not expect the 

Union to be dissolved, I do not expect the house to fall, but I do expect it will cease to be divided. It will become all one thing or all the other."

Lincoln challenged his opponent to speak upon the same platform. Douglas accepted the challenge. Debates were held throughout the state. In one of the debates Lincoln asked Douglas, "Can the people of a United States territory, in any lawful way, against the wish of any citizen of the United States, exclude slavery from its limits prior to the formation of a state constitution?"

It was a difficult question for Douglas. 

If Douglas supported the Dred Scott Decision which opened all the Western territory to slavery, he would lose the votes of the free-soil men. If his answer favored leaving the question of slavery in the West for Westerners to decide, he would antagonize the slave owners in the South. 

Douglas decided to stand by popular sovereignty. 

At Freeport, Illinois, in his answer, called the Freeport doctrine, Douglas said: “I answer emphatically ・・・ that in my opinion the people of a territory can, by lawful means, exclude slavery from their limits prior to the foundation of a state constitution. . . . It matters not what way the Supreme Court may hereafter decide as to the abstract question whether slavery may or may not go into a territory under the Constitution; the people have the lawful means to introduce it or to exclude it as they please, for the reason that slavery cannot exist a day or an hour anywhere unless it is supported by local police regulations."
