John Brown's Raid. Whatever the slave owners may have felt about Douglas and his Freeport doctrine, they soon had matters nearer home to alarm them. 

In October, 1859, John Brown of Kansas, with money supplied by New England abolitionists, crossed the 

Potomac River to Harpers Ferry, a military arsenal in

Virginia. It was Brown's plan to take the arsenal by force and with added weapons to set the slaves of the neighboring country free, and to arm them for a general uprising against their masters. 

The raid ended in failure. After thirty-six hours Brown and his little band were defeated. He and four of his men were arrested. Brown, charged with treason, was tried at 

Charlestown, found guilty, and sentenced to be hanged.

Brown's act was quite generally condemned in the North. 

In the South it was taken as further proof of the danger to life and property to which the growing abolitionist sentiment was leading.

The thought of an uprising of millions of slaves was a calamity which might well cause the planters to shudder.

Party Conventions and Nominations. Now came the time for party conventions and the nomination of candidates for the presidency. 

The Democratic party at its convention broke into two camps: those who were for outspoken insistence on the right of slave owners to carry slavery into the new territories, and those who favored Douglas and his stand for popular sovereignty. The Southern Democrats who were slave owners broke with Douglas and nominated an outand-out proslavery candidate. The Northern Democrats

James Buchanan slavery leaders and appealed to the powerful West by nom inating Abraham Lincoln. 

Lincoln in his speeches had shown none of the bitterness of the abolitionist. He had taken the stand that although slavery was wrong and must not spread, the Southern planters could not be deprived of their slaves without setting aside the Constitution. The South Secedes. Pres ident Buchanan's Stand. - Little more than one month after Lincoln's election, a convention in South Carolina declared that their state was no longer one of the United States. Soon six other states followed this lead. 

The day so long feared had come. Secession was no longer a threat. It was a reality. If South Carolina could secede, the Union was broken.

Buchanan was still in the presidential chair. Lincoln's inauguration would come come in March. What would

Buchanan do meanwhile? 

Buchanan had only recently delivered a powerful statement against secession in a message to Congress, but when it came he showed none of the spirit of Andrew Jackson. 

Instead of meeting secession with force, he gave it as his opinion that he could do nothing to prevent secession and he retained in his Cabinet men who sympathized with secession. 

On February 4, 1861, delegates from the seceding states gathered in Montgomery, Alabama. Here they adopted a provisional constitution for their states, which they organized as a new nation, the Confederate

States of America.

Abraham Lincoln 

In 1860 he was elected President of the United States. believed in the everlasting power of compromise were heard in the land. Compromise had won the day in 1820, in 

1833, in 1850. Why not in 1860? Many plans were proposed.

The leading one was the plan submitted by Senator Crittenden of Kentucky. The details of the compromise are of no importance to us now for the events proved that the hour for compromise had passed. 

On March 4, 1861, Lincoln, who had stood out against

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

compromise, was inaugurated President of the United States of America. Standing on the Capitol steps he said, “I consider the Union is unbroken." He felt that the Union is one and inseparable; that although the Southern states might say they had left the Union, no state can leave the Union; that as the Union had been created by the will of the people of the whole country it could not be destroyed by the will of the people of part of the country. He told the South that he did not want war. But he took the stand that if the Union was attacked by those who wished to destroy it, war would have to be accepted by those who wanted to preserve the Union. 

He said further that he would not take the first step nor strike the first blow. "The Union is unbroken." He had sworn to uphold its laws and to protect it. If it were attacked, he would defend it.

CHAPTER XXXV The Conflict A Long and Bloody War Finally Decides That Slavery Shall End and That the Union Shall Remain

Fort Sumter Falls. On March 4, 1861, Lincoln was inaugurated as President of the United States of America. 

On February 9, Jefferson Davis had been elected President of the Confederate States of America. Davis believed in the right of states to leave the Union. that the Union must be preserved. 

Lincoln believed

There were many men in the North who agreed with Davis. They were willing to see the Confederate States secede, but the matter was not destined to be settled as they wished.

In the South there were forts which according to the Northern viewpoint belonged to the United States government. 454

455 According to the Southern view, these forts being on the territory of the Confederate States of America belonged to the new government set up by the South. One of the disputed Southern forts was Fort Sumter, built on an island in the harbor of Charleston, South Carolina. The federal soldiers in the fort were running short of provisions. In the early days of secession, while Buchanan was still President, the Southerners had fired on the United States vessel

Star of the West to prevent its landing supplies at Fort Sum ter. South Carolina, however, had up to this time made no effort to take the fort by force. 

Now, Lincoln sent word to the governor of South Carolina that he was sending provisions to the fort.

Jefferson Davis 

Jefferson Davis was the first and the Confederates who regarded only president of the Confederate 

States of America, which fought for their independence in the Civil War.

He and the others who led the cause of secession were firmly convinced that those who drafted the Constitution of the United States never meant to create an indissoluble bond of union. 

This issue was decided on the battlefield by the victory of the Union forces. the fort as theirs fired upon 

Fort Sumter. For thirty hours the soldiers in the fort held out. 

At last, when food and powder were gone and the fort was aflame, the garrison surrendered. Firing a last salute to the flag, they marched out of the fort and were permitted to sail away to the North. 

When word went through the land that Fort Sumter had fallen, people felt that war must follow-war, civil war, a war of brother against brother. 

Call for Volunteers. -The country was aflame. Lincoln and Davis both called for volunteers. Lincoln's call was

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

for 75,000 state militia. He also ordered that the regular army and the navy should enlist more men. Soon afterward he called for 42,000 volunteers to serve three years. 

In the cities bands played military airs and the streets were gay with flags. But the hearts of men and women were heavy, for fathers, sons, and brothers were marching off to battle.

The Response.-Throughout the country, from North and from South, from East and from West, volunteers came swiftly to the call of their leaders. Clerks left their desks, carpenters left their work benches, storekeepers closed their shops, farmers dropped their plows in the field, machinists threw down their tools.

The Southern soldiers were determined to defend the right of the Confederate States to form a new union. The federal soldiers were equally determined that the Union founded in 1789 should live.

Now, when men were forced to declare themselves and to take sides, Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee joined with the seven states which had previously seceded. In the North, Douglas as the leader of the Northern Democrats called on the President to assure him of support and of the support of his followers. 

North Cries "On to Richmond!" Bull Run. Both sides were impatient. Each wanted victory to be swift. 

In the South the cry went up "On to Washington!" The 

Confederates believed that the capture of Washington would end the war at one stroke. In the North men urged, "On to Richmond!" Richmond, Virginia, was the capital of the Confederacy. Between Washington and 

Richmond lay the Potomac River. The North wanted the army to lose no time in marching on to Richmond. 

Many Northerners believed that with Richmond captured, the South would soon lay down its arms.

THE CONFLICT 

457 On April 19, 1861, as Union troops were marching southward through Baltimore on their way to Washington, they were fired upon by friends of secession. 

The next three months passed in drilling the green troops and strengthening the federal hold on Maryland, where many were for secession. 

Then the Northern soldiers crossed the Potomac, and were on their way to Richmond when they met the 

Southern army at Manassas near Bull Run, thirty miles from Washington. A battle followed. The Union troops were winning until Confederate reënforcements turned the tide of battle, and the Northerners, breaking ranks, fled in confusion all the way back to Washington. 

The Confederate troops exulting in their victory thought that the war was over. Many of them even returned to their homes.

The Armies. In the North, Lincoln, who saw that the task of saving the Union would be no easy one, asked the people to support him in the work which lay ahead. "The Union must be preserved." The day after the defeat at Bull Run, Lincoln called for a war appropriation of five hundred million dollars.

The Union army grew but it was untrained. It takes time to train clerks and mechanics, shopkeepers, and farmers to fight the battles of modern warfare. 

In the South the Confederate army had the advantages of able leadership. Many of the Southern officers had seen active service during the Mexican War and they were well prepared for their task. 

North Plans Offensive. Conditions in North and

South. The North, which undertook the task of subduing the South, could accomplish this only by taking the offensive. In the first place they had to make certain that the border states which might help to feed the South be

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

held loyal to the Union. In the second place, they would have to blockade the Southern ports, so as to make it impossible for the South to receive supplies or to sell their crops by sea. To bring the South to terms, the Northern armies would have to take Richmond and to push back the Southern troops all along the line from Richmond to the Mississippi and beyond. If they could capture the 

Mississippi and break the Confederacy in two, this task would be made much easier. 

The North was favored in this program by its large fleet of merchant ships; by its mills and factories which met the needs of war with a great increase in output; by an ample supply of grains, of live stock and wool, of coal and iron- all of which were produced by well-developed industries in the Northern states. 

The South had one advantage in that they were to fight in the main a defensive war. The South hoped to have another advantage. The Southerners were an agricultural people who depended to a large extent on the outside world for food supplies, for a market for their crops, for tools and machinery, even for guns and ammunition, but Great Britain depended on the South for eighty per cent of the cotton used in British mills, and the South was therefore hopeful that Great Britain would come into the war on the side of the Confederate States. 

Such were the conditions under which the North and South faced each other. Let us see how the plans of the 

North and South worked out during the four years of struggle which followed the Battle of Bull Run. 

North Wins Border States. The border states, Kentucky and Missouri, as well as the western part of Virginia, which was against secession, became the scene of serious fighting; fighting which must have been the more tragic and bitter because neighbors and even brothers,

THE CONFLICT 

459 dividing on the issue of loyalty to the Union, were enlisted in the opposing armies.

The result of the border fighting was a victory for the North, which was greatly strengthened by the fact that immigrants favored the federal cause particularly in Missouri, where the newly arrived Germans, devoted to the Union, helped to win the state. West Virginia, wrested from the secessionist planters, was admitted to the Union as a separate state in 1863.

Union Navy Blockades South. - The North also suc ceeded in its blockade. At first the blockade of the hundreds of miles of ocean and Gulf Coast was little more than a paper blockade, but the number of effective ships increased swiftly until most blockade runners found it very difficult to carry goods either into the Southern ports or out of them.

Toward the end of 1862, the South managed to have a little navy of her own, largely by building ships in British ports. These Southern warships caused havoc on the seas where they destroyed almost three hundred of the Northern merchant vessels and captured cargoes to the value of fifteen million dollars. The chief of these ships, the Alabama, built in Liverpool, alone captured more than sixty vessels before the Kearsarge destroyed her off the coast of 

France in June, 1864.

Iron Ships. The Merrimac and the Monitor. — In its effort to break the federal blockade the Confederate government converted a former Union steamboat, the Merrimac, into an iron ship, by covering its sides with metal plates. So armored, the Merrimac, or Virginia, as it was renamed, entered the harbor at Hampton Roads, Virginia, where it swiftly sank two federal warships and drove a third aground. 

The next day a second iron ship entered Hampton Roads.

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

It was a federal ship, the Monitor, a strange-looking craft, designed by a Swedish immigrant, John Ericsson. "A cheese-box on a raft" was the way one man described the Monitor. On a flat iron hull there were two cannon in a round iron turret which could be swiftly revolved. In the battle between the Merrimac and the Monitor, the Monitor, somewhat damaged, retreated into shallow water where pintar The Merrimac and the Monitor This battle of the iron ships, fought off Hampton Roads, Virginia, marked a turning point in the history of naval warfare. the Merrimac could not follow her. Neither ship succeeded in destroying the other, but the principle of the iron ship won the day and from that day to this the warships of the world have been built of iron or of steel.

John Ericsson 

Ericsson, who was born in Sweden, came to America at an early age.

He was the designer of the Monitor, an iron ship with a revolving turret; a type of design which marked the beginning of the modern navies of the world.

Neither France nor Great Britain yielded to the pleading of the Confederate commissioners. Because of the failure of her own wheat crops, Great Britain needed American wheat from the Northern states. Besides, in Great Britain, many of the working people favored the cause of the free North against the slave-owning South. As the war pro-

gressed and the North more frankly took a stand against slave labor, it became increasingly difficult for the South to win foreign aid.

With no danger of interference from Great Britain's navy, the Union blockade continued to tighten its grip on the South, choking off Southern supplies.

Fighting in West. Fort Henry, Fort Donelson, Corinth.-— 

So far, then, we have seen the Union forces winning and holding the border states, Missouri, Kentucky, and West Virginia; we have seen the Union ships establishing and strengthening their blockade. Now let us turn to see what was happening in the West. There, if you remember, the 

Union plan was to obtain possession of the Mississippi and so to divide the Confederacy in two parts. Success in this plan would give the North the added advantage of shutting off the traffic of blockade runners who were trading with the South by way of New Orleans.

This campaign in the West began early in 1862. In 

February Northern gunboats, under Commodore Foote, steamed up the Tennessee River and captured Fort Henry.

Ten days later soldiers, led by General Ulysses S. Grant, captured Fort Donelson on the Cumberland and continued up the Tennessee River to Shiloh in western Tennessee.

After a battle at Shiloh, the Confederate forces retreated into Mississippi, where the Union troops soon seized the 

Confederate position at Corinth. 

Fighting on Mississippi. Farragut Captures New 

Orleans. These victories so weakened the Confederate hold on the Mississippi that the Southern troops had to withdraw from Island Number Ten down to Memphis.

Now Captain Farragut planned his attack on New 

Orleans, the leading Southern seaport. 

The port was well defended: by forts below New 

Orleans, by heavy iron chains stretched across the river,

463 and by a fleet of gunboats to help guard the approach. 

But all these defenses proved of no avail. Farragut's fleet passed through all of them and the city fell. The Union fleet established control of the lower Mississippi to within two hundred miles of Vicksburg.

This was in 1862. Vicksburg fell on July 4, 1863, and a few days later the Union forces controlled the Mississippi 

Valley. 

Fighting in the East. McClellan Foiled by Stonewall 

Jackson. If we now turn to the East to follow the campaigns there, we find the picture not nearly so easy to understand because there the fortunes of war were much more varied.

All the Union campaigns in the East had one of two purposes. There were repeated attempts to take Richmond and there were campaigns planned to push back the Confederate forces all along the line. The Confederate side, fighting a defensive war, countered the Northern attacks on Richmond by thrusts at Washington and when an opening showed itself, carried the war even farther North. 

After the failure of the first attack on Richmond, when the Union forces were defeated at Bull Run, General McClellan, who commanded the Army of the Potomac, trained his troops for a second attempt. McClellan was a good drill master, but he gave his soldiers no fighting to do, and as month after month passed without action the North grew impatient.

When McClellan did start, he decided to strike at Richmond from the South. Accordingly gunboats and transports carried his troops to the Peninsula between the York and James rivers. There he succeeded in defeating the 

Confederates at Yorktown. Pushing northward he reached to within sight of Richmond, where the Confederate army, under General J. E. Johnston, was intrenched. Victory

Lincoln Considers Freeing Slaves. It was at this time that Lincoln decided upon the act which more than any other added to his fame. Lincoln had long believed that slavery was a curse to the South, but he had not agreed

THE CONFLICT 

465 with those who wanted to take the slaves from their masters by force.

The Constitution recognized slaves as property. If the slaves were to be freed, he had hoped that it would be in the same manner in which England had set them free in the West Indies. The English government had bought them from their owners and had given them their liberty. 

In the case of the border states, Lincoln had proposed, since the beginning of the war, that the Union purchase slaves and set them free. He had considered plans for establishing the freed slaves in a separate colony. He had agreed with Great Britain to assist her in putting an end to the slave traffic on the African coast. move.

Now after two years of war, Lincoln considered a new He felt that the effort of slave owners to carry slaves into the new territories had been the cause of the break between the North and the South. Slaves were helping the South to prolong the war. They were working in the fields to help feed and clothe the Southern armies. 

Accordingly, Lincoln decided that if Lee's army was defeated and driven back, he would celebrate the Union victory by taking a step which he hoped would lead to the freeing of the Confederate slaves.

Battle of Antietam. Emancipation Proclamation. — On 

September 17, McClellan met Lee at Antietam. Twentythree thousand men fell in the battle, and when the day was over Lee was in retreat.

Five days later Lincoln kept his vow. He issued the proclamation in which he warned the Confederates that if they did not lay down their arms and agree to remain within the Union, he would declare all of their slaves free forever.

On New Year's Day, 1863, as the South was still in arms, Lincoln issued the final Proclamation of Emancipa-

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

tion, setting the slaves in the Confederate States free, except in those regions of the Confederacy which had been taken over by Union forces - all of Tennessee, and parts of Virginia and Louisiana.

In freeing the slaves within the Confederate lines, Lincoln explained that he did so as the commander-in-chief of the United States armies, and declared his act justified by military necessity.

Declaring the slaves free was one thing. Freeing them was another. Their freedom still depended upon the victory of the Northern armies. From the first of January, men who had been slaves fought on the side of the North, and wherever the Union armies won fresh victories, new freedmen joined the Union ranks. 

After the first day of January, 1863, the Union troops were fighting not only to save the Union but also to help free Southern slaves. For a while there was enthusiasm throughout the North. But before long the Union entered upon its darkest days. There were defeats on the battlefield. There were heavy losses at sea where the Confederate raiders were capturing and sinking Union ships. 

Lincoln the Man. - Lincoln kept on at his task, but it was becoming difficult to keep up courage. He and the cause of Union had to face enemies within the Northern lines. Many of the enemies were anti-war Democrats "Copperheads," they were called. These men tried to persuade the North to give in. They tried to hurt Lincoln in the eyes of the people. Because he was a plain selftaught man they ridiculed him. They called the war a wicked slaughter.

When Lincoln stood for the stern measures by which people are held together during war, censoring the press and imprisoning without due trial those who sought to destroy the Union cause, men called him a tyrant.

THE CONFLICT 

467 In the face of all criticism Lincoln held to his course. 

He listened to the complaints of the committees of people who came to find fault - those who believed that he did not go far enough in putting down slavery, and those who believed that he went too far in putting down seditious talk and writing. He explained his stand to them so that they would see as he saw the reasons for his steps. 

Lincoln's true gentleness of spirit showed in his answers to letters of heartbroken fathers and mothers; it showed in the way in which he went into the charges against soldiers who were sentenced to be hanged. He was always on the side of lenience.

Lincoln bearded.

Whenever possible, he hastened to meet the fighting men. By his simple words of good cheer and courage he tried to give them new hope.

Lee Advances. - Lee, encouraged by these signs that the people of the North were not all supporting their President, was making a second advance. This time crossing the Potomac he was marching due north into the state of Pennsylvania. With draft riots breaking out in the

THE CONFLICT 

469 Northern cities and an antiwar spirit growing there, it seemed to many that if Lee could carry to the defenders of the Union the hardships and sufferings through which the people of the South were passing, Lincoln would be forced to yield.

On the morning of July 1, 1863, Lee's army was challenged at Gettysburg in southern Pennsylvania. Much depended on the outcome.

The federal forces under General George G. Meade outnumbered the Confederates. They were, moreover, strongly intrenched on high ground. Lee undertook to defeat these forces in order to safeguard his further advance into the 

North. For two days the battle raged without either side yielding. On the third day, July 3, Confederate troops under General Pickett made a desperate charge across the open plain in an effort to dislodge the Union forces on 

Cemetery Ridge. When this brave attempt, sometimes called "the high tide of the Confederacy," failed, Lee abandoned his plan for an invasion of the North and turned his army back toward Virginia. On July 4, 1863, Vicksburg surrendered to General Grant in the West.

Grant Advances on Richmond. Leaving Sherman to press back one Confederate army under Johnston, and to drive a wedge eastward through the Confederacy, Grant came East to lead his army against Richmond. By May he marched his army southward. "I propose to fight it out on this line if it takes all summer," he wrote the President; but in the battles of the Wilderness, at Spottsylvania Court House and Cold Harbor, he learned that the attack from the North was after all too difficult, and after six weeks of hard fighting and great losses Grant changed his plan. He decided to strike at Richmond from the South by way of the Peninsula, as McClellan had done in 1862.

Election in North. 

had come for party conventions and presidential nominations. In the South Jefferson Davis had been elected for six years under the Confederate constitution, but Lincoln had to face the prospect of an election campaign in the middle of a war. It was not a cheerful campaign for him. 

Nor was it a help to the Union cause to have his antiwar enemies, who were eager to win back their old political power, making political capital of the war weariness of the people. 

Meanwhile in the North the time

The Republican party, combined with the war Democrats, nominated Andrew Johnson, a war Democrat and the Union governor of Tennessee for the vice presidency. 

They renominated Lincoln for the presidency. But the news from the battle-front did not favor Lincoln's reëlection. Grant, who by this time was in the Peninsula, had suffered defeat at Petersburg.

Now, those Northern Democrats, who did not favor continuing the war, and who were bound by prewar memories to Southern Democrats, met in convention and nominated General McClellan to run against Lincoln. The day after the convention adjourned, the North heard of a 

Union victory in the South; Atlanta had fallen. After four months of dogged fighting, Sherman, marching west from 

Chattanooga, had reached Atlanta, the most important military center of the Confederacy. Atlanta had many of the factories which had been turning out arms, ammunitions, and army supplies for the Southern armies. Atlanta was the meeting point of a number of Southern railroads which carried supplies to the points where they were most needed. 

In the face of Sherman's victory at Atlanta, the election result was a foregone conclusion.

but three of the Union states. With the fall of Atlanta the end of the war was in sight. Sherman burned part of Atlanta and started across Georgia to the sea. With no forces to oppose his army Sherman blazed a path of destruction sixty miles wide to Savannah, which he took shortly before Christmas, 1864. Sheridan's Raids. Shenandoah Valley. - Southern troops, this time under General Early, again tried to force the withdrawal of Union forces from the Peninsula by threatening Washington. But this time General Sheridan defeated the Confederate troops, and in order to prevent others from threatening Washington through the Shenandoah Valley, he laid the valley waste. 

Richmond Taken. Lee Surrenders. Sheridan in the 

North and Sherman in the South were both free to combine forces with Grant in surrounding Lee at Richmond. 

On April 2, 1865, Lee abandoned Richmond. Grant entered the city on the third. On April 9 Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House, seventy-five miles from Richmond.

General Grant treated Lee as a brother. He asked only that Lee's men lay down their arms and return to their fields. Those who had horses were told that they could take their horses home with them to use again in works of peace.

Richmond Falls. End of War. Summary. Soon after 

Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House, the remaining Southern armies laid down their arms. The Union had been saved.

The war was ended. The federal navy blockading the 

Southern ports had shut off the Confederate trade. The federal armies acting with the navy had captured the Confederate strongholds on the Mississippi. After Con-

THE CONFLICT 

473 federate advances into Northern territory had been blocked at Antietam and at Gettysburg, the Federal armies, strengthened by the greater wealth and numbers of the North, succeeded in invading the South where they hemmed in the Confederate troops and forced their surrender. So the Confederate States lost the independence which they had sought.

Behind the Battle Lines. 

Welfare Work. The Civil 

— - 

War, like most previous wars, was terrible in its toll of killed and wounded. It differed from all previous wars in the extent to which organized efforts were made behind the battle lines to provide for the comfort of the wounded soldiers and to care for their dependent families. הנייעס 

Clara Barton 

During the Civil War the new ideas of the worth of the common man and therefore of the common soldier led to a more thoroughly organized relief work than had been common in earlier wars. Clara Barton, a war nurse, was one of the many women who both in the North and South labored to help the sick and wounded. 

In both North and South women acted as volunteer nurses in the army hospitals, women sewed clothes and prepared bandages, dressings, and food for the sick and wounded. In the North this welfare work was looked after by a national organization known as the United States Sanitary Commission, which maintained storehouses and branches in many states. 

In the North the Young Men's Christian Association, which was at the time only a few years old, established a United States Christian Commission to carry on religious

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

work among the soldiers. This commission also provided diet kitchens for the wounded.

Among the Southerners and Northerners who devoted years to army welfare work, the name of Clara Barton stands out. Soon after the war began she resigned a clerkship in the United States Civil Service to become a volunteer nurse. The fame and spirit of her work no doubt fired the imagination of many another with zeal for such helpfulness as might lessen the frightful pain and suffering which war entails.

Cost of War. Result. -The financial cost of the Civil 

War ran into billions. The federal government spent over three billion dollars before the war ended, and the interest later paid on war loans plus the pensions paid to war veterans more than doubled this cost. The Confederate states also spent large sums to meet the cost of war. Their war costs involved them in heavy debts. 

To raise funds for the needs of warfare both North and South resorted to a high tariff on imported goods, to internal taxes, to printed paper money, and to borrowing. 

After the close of the war, the debts of the Confederate 

States were canceled.

In human suffering the cost of the Civil War, as of all wars, cannot be estimated. Although the scene of battle was mostly in the South, the losses of the battlefield were felt in tens of thousands of homes on both sides of the 

Mason and Dixon Line. However, the federal Union had been preserved. Years were to pass before the bitter wounds of strife were healed; yet the day had to come when the North and the South, reunited under their common flag, were to feel more deeply than before the bonds of brotherhood.

Before that day could come the problem of reconstructing the Union had to be solved.

The New South CHAPTER XXXVI The New South 

After the Civil War the Nation, Bereft of its Great Leader, Faces the Problem of Reconstructing the Union 

After the War. - The Civil War was ended. The Union was saved, but there was still the task of reëstablishing good will between the North and the South and of rebuilding the South upon a new foundation.

Although peace was now restored, the former Confederate States found themselves in a sorry plight. The war had destroyed many of their finest men; it had choked off the export of their crops; their plantations were run down; their live stock had been used up in the army service. 

When the Northern soldiers disbanded, they returned to busy and thriving farms and to cities alive with trade and manufacture. The Confederate soldiers on going home found virtual ruin on the old plantations with few signs of hope ahead.

Το cap the burden of the Southern planters their slaves had been freed; and as they were heavily in debt owing to the cost of war, they did not have the means to pay for the 477

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

tools, the live stock, or the labor which they would need in bringing the plantations back to a paying basis. 

Weighted down by these problems, the former Confederate States had not even reorganized state governments, nor was their position with 

Northern Soldier Returns respect to the national government clear.

Lincoln Plans Recon struction. His Assassination. - Lincoln had long since made his plan for restoring state governments and for reconstructing the Union. 

According to his view of the Constitution, the South had never truly been out of the Union. The war had been a sad and terrible quarrel.

Now that it was over it was Lincoln's plan that each of the states which, by its own act, had lost contact with the national government should reconstruct its own state government. Then Congress would arrange the terms on which the state would again secure representation in the Senate and House of Repre sentatives. By Lincoln's plan, a state government could be reorganized as soon as voters equal in number to 

Southern Soldier Returns one-tenth of the total number of votes cast within the state at the election of 1860 had each taken the oath to support the Constitution.

Lincoln's plan for reconstruction was never carried out. 

In the hour of the Union's triumph the nation lost its great leader. On the evening of April 14, five days after 

Lee's surrender, as Lincoln was sitting in a theater in Washington, a half-crazed actor named Booth, brooding over the defeat of the South, entered the President's box and, creeping up behind the President, shot him through the head. Lincoln was carried to a house near by where he died early the next morning.

In the North the joy of victory was clouded by tragedy. 

In the South the gloom of defeat was darkened by the death of the man upon whom the Southerners had counted for fair dealing in the days to come. 

Congress Passes Its Own Reconstruction Acts.-Andrew 

Johnson, vice president, now became President. He did not have the tact and ability to carry Lincoln's plan through to completion. Like Lincoln, he was willing to have the Southern states speedily reorganized and free to send representatives to Congress provided they would agree to accept fully the principle of Union and the emancipation of slaves. But the task of reconstruction fell into the hands of Congress, which was determined to put difficulties in the way of the South. 

There were leaders in Congress who felt that a successful plan of reconstruction must provide not only for the reorganization of the Southern State governments and the restoration of the South to representation in the national government, but also for the protection of the freed negroes. 

Some of these men may have acted partly in the spirit of revenge against the vanquished; others may have been primarily interested in preventing the Southern planter from regaining his old political power; still others, no doubt, sincerely felt that no plan of reconstruction would work which did not establish the status of the freed negro,

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

especially since a number of the Southern states had been passing laws which might have rapidly reduced the negroes to a state of virtual slavery. To establish definitely the position of the negro, three amendments to the Constitution were suggested by Congress and adopted: the 

Thirteenth Amendment (1865), which provided that slavery should cease throughout the United States; the 

Fourteenth Amendment, three years later, which promised the negro citizen the same civil rights as the whites; and the Fifteenth Amendment, which declared that no citizen of the United States should be deprived of the right to vote by the United States or by any state on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. 

While Congress was drawing up these amendments for the protection of the negro, it was taking away almost all political power from former slave owners in practically every Southern state. Congress denied the right to vote to many of those who had borne arms against the Union. 

Under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, many of the ablest men in the South were deprived of the right to hold public office.

Instead of permitting the Southern state governments, which reorganized under Lincoln's One-Tenth Plan, to carry on, Congress divided the South into five military districts. Tennessee, which had promptly accepted the Fourteenth Amendment, was permitted to reënter the Union and to be represented in Congress; but in the rest of the ex-Confederate States, federal army officers supported by federal soldiers were in command of each of the military districts.

Under this military rule the states were to draft new state constitutions to be submitted to Congress for its approval, and not until Congress was ready would normal state representation in the national councils be secured.

One other phase of the Congressional plan of reconstruction was the establishment of the Freedmen's Bureau. 

A federal department with branches throughout the South was organized for the purpose of helping the negro to establish himself under the new conditions which he now faced. 

President Johnson Is Impeached. President John son's stand against many of the features of the Congressional plan of reconstruction led to such bitterness of feeling that his enemies in 

Congress brought charges against him. They alleged that he had violated the Tenure of Office Act and voted that he be tried on their charge. The impeachment trial was held in the Senate, as provided for in the Constitution. A verdict of guilty would have removed President Johnson from office. 

When the vote was taken, there were thirty-five votes cast for conviction and nineteen for acquittal. As a twothirds vote was required, Andrew Johnson 

Andrew Johnson was the seventeenth president of the United States 

(1865-1869). Elected to the vice presi dency with Lincoln in 1864, he succeeded to the presidency upon Lincoln's death by assassination. The principal events of Johnson's administration were those attending the problem of reconstruction; thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth amendments; impeachment trial of Johnson; purchase of 

Alaska, 1867.

Johnson was saved by a margin of one vote and he con tinued as President of the United States. 

Carpetbaggers and Scalawags Rule the South. - Eventually all of the ex-Confederate states, having no other course, agreed to the terms laid down by Congress and were

admitted to the Union. Those Southern leaders who really had the good will of their states at heart soon found that even with state government restored, the task of reconstruction within the states was beyond them. In spite of the Freedmen's Bureau the negroes were disorganized as laborers, and economic prosperity was difficult to restore. Besides, The Carpetbagger

The Legislatures of the

States. In each of the state — - headpiece of chapter for a symbolic legislatures a few carpetbaggers and scalawags were able to control the votes of the many negro representatives. 

They committed the states to a wild orgy of spending, which gave them ample opportunity to fatten their own purses. The shameless and lawless way in which these men made capital of the misfortunes which had befallen the South not only added to the impoverishment of the 

South but also increased its bitterness.

"The Ku Klux Klan " and the Negro Vote. One form of lawlessness gave rise to another. In different parts of the South members of a secret society known as the Ku Klux Klan now pledged themselves to offset the lawless rule of the negroes and scalawags, and to reëstablish the old power of the planters.

In long flowing white robes, with headdress to cover their faces, the clansmen went about at night spreading terror among their enemies. At election time they frightened the negroes from the polls. Congress, eager to safeguard the negro in his right to vote, took measures to put an end to the activities of the Klan.

The Amnesty Act. Removal of Troops. However, as the years passed and new men came into office at Washington, a more understanding spirit began to show itself in the handling of the reconstruction problem. In 1872 

General Grant, who had been elected President in 1868 to succeed Johnson, signed the Amnesty Act, removing in nearly all cases the political disabilities which had been imposed upon those who had borne arms against the Union. Congress had already taken similar action in many individual cases.

In 1877 Rutherford B. Hayes, elected to succeed Grant, went one step farther. He recalled the United States troops from the South. The carpetbaggers and the scalawags fled and the planters were in a position to play a leading part in the affairs of the Southern states. 

The New South Industrially. -The Southern states were still poor. The planters were almost penniless. The freed negroes were facing the rather disheartening truth that even free men must work. However, they were without either land or tools.

The task of bringing back prosperity was no easy one. 

To those who had always claimed that slave labor was

SECTIONAL ISSUES AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

needed for cotton and tobacco raising, it seemed an impossible one. Those few planters who still had means now worked their large plantations with paid negro help. 

The others divided their plantations into small plots which they rented to negro families. Each year, more and more of the land came under cultivation and crops increased until finally the day came when the South produced more tobacco, cotton, and rice than in the days before the war. 

COTTON GROWING STATES 

In time, with Northern capital to help, many cotton mills were built in the South. Southern coal and iron mines were developed, Southern forests were used more than ever before for ship building and supplies, such as tar and turpentine. Railroads increased in number and a new South, which was manufacturing and industrial as well as agricultural, arose to take the place of the old South with its large plantations and its army of negro slaves. 

The New South and the Negro. As for the problem of the negro vote, Southern legislatures passed a series of 

---

acts setting up such qualifications for the right to vote as were more likely to disfranchise negroes than whites. 

Some of these acts insisting upon educational standards were not unlike acts which Northern legislatures passed primarily to keep the vote from foreigners who were ignorant of the language and institutions of America and therefore not ready for citizenship.

In the South to-day, as negroes take advantage of the increasing educational opportunities, they are hoping to secure the right to share in the problem of government. 

Although hampered by many difficulties, social and industrial as well as political, the negro has made considerable progress. There is in the New South a large body of negroes who own farms and other property to the value of many millions of dollars. A great number of negroes to-day work in manufacturing plants both in the South and North. A large migration of negroes into the 

Northern states is tending to distribute the negro population more evenly throughout the country. 

Good Will between the North and the New South. —

The long quarrel between the North and South, the years of civil war, the ill will shown by some of the Northern leaders during the period of reconstruction naturally left bitter memories. Among many Southerners the feeling of bitterness against the North lingered for years; but time has healed the old wounds, and Northerners and Southerners, more firmly united than ever, have since worked together in peace; they have since fought side by side in two wars, in one case under the lead of a President who was himself a Southerner by birth.

The Arts of Peace. - With the passing of the cause and of the spirit of strife, the people of the country turned to their daily tasks with a new will and carried the arts of peace forward to new triumphs.

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP CHAPTER XXXVII Binding the New Union: Steam, Steel, and Electricity 

After the Civil War, the New West Takes Its Place Beside the 

New South in the Growing Nation. Steam, Steel, and 

Electricity Help to Bind North, South, East, and West in Closer Brotherhood 

The West Still Calls. Ranches, Mines. At the beginning of the Civil War there were thirty-three states in the Union. Two of these, Oregon and California, lay on the Pacific coast. The others reached westward from the Atlantic across the Alleghenies to the Mississippi and even beyond. In spite of the empire builders, who had been 488

pushing onward since the days of Boone, there was a stretch of almost two thousand miles of unbroken wilderness between the Western border states and the states on the 

Pacific slope.

While the Civil War was being fought, Kansas and Nevada, which both lay in this territory, became states, and fresh bands of emigrants were setting out to carry on the work of building new states in the West. Leaving the frontier which they reached by railroad, the emigrants, in their caravans of canvas-covered wagons, set out into the West. They journeyed slowly across the broad prairies, where the waving grass rolled off to meet the horizon like the billows of a boundless sea. They crossed scorching deserts where the sun baked the earth and left it dry and almost barren. They entered the passes of the Rocky 

Mountains where cold winds blew and the snows of ancient winters gleamed crystal white in the clear blue air.

In spite of the wilderness hardships, the Far West still called to the people of the East; the untamed spaces of the New World nation still called to the people of Europe as a promising realm of boundless riches and freedom. 

The finding of gold in California in 1848 had been followed at short intervals by the discovery of gold in 

Colorado, Nevada, Montana, and in the Dakotas. Silver and gold were found in Idaho; copper, lead, iron, and coal added to the lure of buried treasure with which the West tempted the adventurous fortune-hunting miners.

Western pasture lands were proving very profitable to ranch owners who were able to raise great herds of cattle and sheep on the grassy plains of Texas and the territory to the north. These herds, branded with the mark of the owner, grazed freely on the government lands until the time came for driving them to market. Then the cowboys on their ponies went out to round up the herd and started

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP THE PROSPECTOR THE COWBOY THE SHEEPHERDER HOMESTEADERS 

66 on the long drive northward to market. The herds, which grazed their way to market, were followed by the cowboys who tried to prevent stampedes which might scatter the crop of the ranch." At Kansas City or Chicago, big meatpacking firms bought live stock, and slaughtered and packed the meat for sale to the cities of the East. A profitable business was ranching and a lively one, which attracted many an adventurous man.

Homestead Act Attracts Farmers. Terms to Soldiers. 

-While cowboys and sheep herders roamed the Western pasture lands and while fortune hunters followed the trails which pioneers had blazed to the new mining fields, others went into the West for the purpose of obtaining government land and for tilling the rich soil. 

Ever since the day when

Congress had opened up the Northwest Territory, the government had been selling

Western lands, either in large blocks to land companies who resold the land in smaller par-

cels, or directly in holdings of 640 acres, then somewhat lesser amounts, and finally in 80-acre tracts at minimum prices varying from $2.00 to $1.25 an acre. By the terms of the Homestead Act, passed by Congress in 1862, the government began to give land away. Any man or woman who was an American citizen could become the owner of one hundred and sixty acres of government land upon payment of a few dollars for the drawing up of the papers. Even newly arrived immigrants from Europe, once they had declared their intention of becoming American citizens, were offered homesteads.

In all cases the homesteader was to make good his title with ax and plow. He was to build himself a home and to work upon his ground for at least five years. In the case of Union soldiers, the term of war service was deducted from the five years' 

Kit Carson 

Of the many thousands who helped to blaze the trails and break ground for the great Western states, few captured the imagination of young America as much as did Kit Carson, the Western scout and Indian fighter.

Vainly Contest Way. - After the Homestead Act was passed, tens and hundreds of thousands of immigrants coming from Europe by steamship joined the emigrants who were taking the railroad for the frontier and with them plunged into the wild land beyond. 

The pageant of the covered wagon continued to unfold itself on the Western plains, in the deserts, and in the mountain passes; and the settlers driving their canvas wagons

still had to be on guard against the Western Indian tribes who did not welcome this invasion of their hunting grounds. 

For years government troops of trained Indian fighters had to quell Indian uprisings. In 1876 one band of two hundred sixty soldiers under General Custer was completely wiped out in a battle at Little Big Horn River, in 

Montana, by the Sioux under their chief, Sitting Bull. 

A Sod House on the Plains

In the plains country, where building timber was scarce, the pioneers built houses on a light framework of wood covered over with cakes of earth. 

Many settlers and soldiers died fighting, but the struggle between the ancient owners of the land and the newcomers ended in the West as it did in the East. The white men won against the red. One after another the Indian tribes were defeated and forced to enter the Indian Reservations where the government looked after the Indians, supporting them and establishing schools for them, setting up rules for their manner of living.

Beginning about 1887 the government divided the land on the reservations among the Indians, who thereby became citizens and were to become owners of the land. 

New States in the West. The Disappearing Frontier. -

By the year 1889 the frontier was practically gone. A steady flow of settlers into the West had brought many new states into the Union. Kansas, Nevada, and Nebraska were admitted before 1870. Colorado was admitted in 

1876; North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, and

Washington became states in 1889. 

As the last of the government lands was almost gone, Western settlers were pleased to hear that the United

How to Bind Growing Nation. -The Civil War, which had cost the nation so much of its life blood, had proved that the people of different parts of the country could become enemies. The bitter quarrels and misunderstandings of the 

North and South had almost torn the nation asunder. 

How could the people not only of the North and South, but also of the old East and new West be made to feel themselves as one brotherhood facing common tasks?

Many things helped men to win and hold those broad Western lands, but it was chiefly through the aid of steam, steel, and electricity that the continent was finally con-

quered and the growing states united into an indissoluble bond.

Steam Power in the East. Pony Express in the West. 

At the time when the Civil War broke out, steamships and railroads had long been helping in the growth of the country. Fulton's steamboat, the Clermont, which first ran on the Hudson in 1807, had been followed by many others which steamed up and down the inland rivers, across the Great Lakes, even across the Atlantic. The twelve miles of railroad which had been built from Baltimore to Ellicott's Mills about 1830 had grown to thousands of miles of track along which steamdriven locomotives puffed and snorted, belching black smoke and red-hot cinders.

But as we have read, when news came to the East that there was gold in California, the way to the Pacific Coast was still long and difficult. 

The Pony Express 

The transportation needs of the Far West were served in many ways: the covered wagon, and the pony express which provided overland service; the stagecoaches which ran between Western towns; and the clippers

The goods which came up the Pacific were far too expensive. 

Seeing how great was the need for closer touch with the East, a company was formed which organized a "Pony Express" service to carry mail over the Western plains.

In California, by the time Lincoln was elected, while gold was still being mined, wheat fields were yielding harvests as profitable as gold mines; and the grape country, the orange and lemon groves, gave promise of enriching fruit growers. Building First Transcontinental Railroad. The build ing of a transcontinental railroad was a stupendous task to undertake- the building of a steel roadway across two thousand miles of wild land. There were rivers to cross, chasms to bridge, mountains to tunnel, hostile Indians to combat; but when the plans were completed, the money had been raised and the companies proceeded with the work.

One company, the Union Pacific, had its workmen start at Omaha, Nebraska. The other company started at 

Sacramento, California. Congress offered a prize of 12,800 acres of land for each mile of road built. Working their way toward one another in spirited rivalry in the scorching heat of the desert and in the blizzards of the mountains, they laid their tracks, mile after mile, until by the year 1869 the two parties of workmen met, in the presence of a large number of interested spectators, at Promontory 

Point near Ogden, Utah. A golden spike driven with a silver hammer was used to unite the rails which came from the East and the West. The two coasts were joined. 

Soon, puffing, screeching steam engines, dragging long trains filled with passengers and loaded with freight, were startling the mountain eagles in their lofty nests and the herds of buffalo in the prairies. Goods from Europe were rolling by rail from the Atlantic or Gulf ports to San Francisco, and thence by steamer on to the lands of Asia. 

The transcontinental railroad not only united the East and West; it bridged the path from the Old World to Cathay.

Railroad Progress. - In time the first transcontinental railroad was followed by others. The Santa Fe, the Southern Pacific, the Northern Pacific, the Great Northern, and many smaller railroad lines were built to bind the North and South, the East and West. A wild wave of enthusiasm

for railroad building went through the country until to-day the land is crossed by more than 260,000 miles of track. 

Loads of freight which one hundred years ago could hardly have been moved across the continent by an army of truckmen, horses, and wagons, are now carried across the

Rivers are crossed by railroads; the dangers of collision are nearly done away with by the invention of the air brake, the block signal system, the telegraph, the telephone, and the double track. 

With passenger traffic made so easy and safe by the speed of the steam engine, the North and the South have become

like brothers who live within a few doors of one another; the East and the West are like brothers who live in the same town at the opposite ends of the main street. 

Wherever railroads were built, villages, towns, cities, and states grew up along the way as if by magic. The wilderness became a land of plenty, and the railroads helped in the exchange of the rich produce of the East, West, North, and South with one another and with the outside world.

Steam, then, was the first of the great forces which opened up the whole country to the empire builders. The puffing steam engine, acting as the pulse of the nation's industrial life, helped to carry the people, their goods, and their thoughts. 

Steel Shares with Steam as Binder of Union. In the binding of the empire, side by side with steam went steel, that finely tempered metal made from iron, which gave to the industries their muscle and sinew. 

Ever since the time, thousands of years ago, when men first learned to make tools of iron instead of stone, here and there crude furnaces might be seen where iron was smelted out of the red ore of the neighborhood. For hundreds of years men used charcoal for their furnace fires, but during the eighteenth century when the demand for iron tools was increasing, an Englishman discovered that furnaces burning coal would turn out iron at less cost. 

The discovery that coal could be used in the smelting of iron was bound to mean much to the United States, which was rich in its deposits of coal and iron ore. But the nineteenth century was half spent before the needs of iron for railroad building and for farm tools and factory machinery caused Americans to see the enormous possibilities of the iron industry. Then the smelting of iron began on a large scale.

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

Iron was precious, but it had the serious fault of being brittle. It was not easily malleable and ductile. Steel, a refined form of iron, was much harder and stronger and yet more workable. Steel, however, was very costly and since the time of the ancients it had been used mainly for finely edged tools, such as swords and daggers. 

What was needed was a way to make steel less costly.

United States Mail. Electric Tele graph. In the new age of marvels, miracle was added to miracle. Steam and steel were both magical in their strength and both played their part in building the nation.

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

But while steam and steel were helping to build and to bind the Union, a new means of communication was found by which thought could be carried more swiftly. By means of electricity, copper wires were made to carry the nation's messages, and this current was used to bind the Union still more closely. 

Samuel F. B. Morse 

Morse, art teacher and portrait painter, was the inventor of the electric telegraph. By the use of a code, dots and dashes made by a humanly controlled electric magnet carried thought through space with almost instantaneous speed. Since the Civil War the electric telegraph has helped to bind all sections of the country. 

United States mail and parcels carried by railroad throughout the land have helped to bind the American people. To-day the letter, the newspaper, the magazine, the book, the latest comfort of the city dweller, are brought by mail into the most remote homes. The United States mail brings every part of the country into close touch with every other part.

However, the mail service depends largely upon train, ships, or airplanes for its speed, and messages sent by mail are carried only as fast as steam, steel, and gasoline can carry them. It was only when inventors harnessed the electric current to carry messages that communication across the continent became almost instantaneous.

Experiments with electricity had been carried on for centuries, but it was not until after Franklin's kite-flying experiment that electricity was practically applied in a series of miraculous thought-carrying inventions - the telegraph, the cable, the telephone, the wireless, each of

which has played its part in bringing the people of the nation into closer touch with one another. 

In 1844 Samuel F. B. Morse, the inventor of the tele graph, you will remember, flashed a message along an electrically charged line which had been especially built for him 

Laying a Cable 

The task of laying a cable on an ocean bed from continent to continent is a mighty one. 

The average depth of the ocean is about 12,000 feet.

Messages are transmitted along submarine cables from the United States to Europe, Asia, South America, and to the Far East practically instantaneously.

Sending a Cable Message 

The first cable messages used a code of dots and dashes. The modern operator sits at a machine like a typewriter checking off the words. The tape on which these words appear passes through the electrical transmitter; and almost on the instant perforations are punched upon a tape in Tokio, Liverpool, or Buenos Aires; the receiver, reading the perforations, translates them into words. To-day much of the international business of the world is conducted either by cable or by wireless telegraphy. by Congress from Washington to Baltimore. To every one the power of the telegraph was little short of a miracle. 

But a long time passed before the value of this discovery was generally recognized. Then slowly it came into its own, and since the Civil War it has become one of the most essential parts of the nation's life, helping to bind all sections of the country into a close-knit unit.

Alexander Graham Bell, an 

American, found a way by which the vibrations of the human voice might be carried along electric wires. He exhibited his instrument, the telephone, at the Centennial Exposition held in Philadelphia in 1876. At that time the instrument was regarded as little more than a toy. With the steam engine as the pulse of the nation's life, and steel as the sinew of its strength, the copper wires of telegraph and telephone served as the nerves of the nation. 

Millions of miles of wire covering the highways and byways of the land, entering almost every home and office in the land, combined with steam and steel to make the nation one. The danger of disunion had passed. 

Wireless Telegraphy. Radio. The Nation One Family. 

- New inventions followed in the field of electric communication. After Marconi, an Italian inventor, had helped to develop wireless telegraphy to the point where he succeeded in sending a wireless message across the Atlantic Ocean,

American inventors joined in an effort to prove that the voice could be transmitted by electricity without the use of telegraph wires. The result was the radio, which has become a household institution throughout the United 

States. Then in 1927 came wireless telephone service.

No other nation to-day is so thoroughly served by electric communication. The telegraph, telephone, and radio transmit the news of the world. The telephone and radio combined provide educational and entertainment programs in thousands of homes throughout the land; they are bringing the cultural advantages of city life to the home of the farmer, and even to the solitary camps of miners and lumberjacks.

Not only is the danger of disunion passed. Through the aid of electric communication the nation has become one family, reading the same news at the breakfast table, listening to concerts, speeches, and reports of national events programs which are nationally broadcast. It would be in

A Modern Locomotive CHAPTER XXXVIII The Age of the Machine New Tools and Power-driven Machines Increase the Yield of Farms, Mines, and Factories and Change the Daily Life of People in City, Town, and Country Civil War Followed by Machine Age. - The Civil War marked a turning point in the industrial life of the nation. 

From the time when the war began until the present day the United States has steadily forged ahead in trade, manufacturing, and agriculture until to-day the nation leads the world in these three fields. 

This leadership America owes partly to the fact that she has benefited by the invention of many remarkable new tools which have increased men's power of producing goods. 

These new tools, most of which came into their fullest use after the Civil War, have ushered in a new age which may well be called the "Machine Age. 99 Old World Tools Transplanted to America. - In the story of the United States from the time of the discovery of America to the passing of the Western frontier, tools had 510

played their part. We have seen how the discovery and the exploration of America were made possible largely through three Renaissance inventions the compass, gunpowder, and the printing press. In the discovery as well as in the exploration of the New World shores, other tools invented during the thousands of years before the Renaissance also helped. The ships which bore the adventurers across the ocean, the capstan wheels with which the sailors turned their rudders, the written alphabet with which the captain kept his log book, the woven sails which bellied out before the wind, the ship's rope, the iron anchor, the few iron tools in the chests of the ship's carpenters, the maps which the pilots read these were all inventions which had come down from the past. 

The home builders who crossed the ocean on these ships carried with them plows, harrows, flails, looms, hammers, chisels, axes, saws, fish hooks, and nets, all of which differed little from the tools used by the ancient Egyptians. The colonial glassmakers with their blowpipes, the iron workers working with bellows, furnace, and forge, the brickmakers with their kilns, the goldsmiths, the silversmiths, the wagoners, the harness makers, the cobblers, the spinners and weavers of wool, all worked as artisans had worked before them ever since the time of the Phoenicians.

The colonial water mill, the windmill, the sail ship, and the wagon were Old World inventions. In the homes of the colonists women used Old World tools in their household tasks. 

These ancient tools were the tools of the colonists at the time of the American Revolution, and except for a few new inventions, they were the tools of the majority of the people until the time of the Civil War. Most of the farmers sowed their seed by hand; they cut their crops with a scythe; they threshed their grain with hand flails. The

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

millers ground their grain between mill stones turned by the force of swiftly flowing streams. The wagon-makers, the cabinetmakers, the shoemakers, the printers, the binders, all worked with simple hand tools. Women's work in the home was still done by hand or with hand tools.

New Tools Bring Machine Age. - About the time of the 

American Revolution the invention in England of the steam engine and of new spinning and weaving machines brought the dawn of a period called the Machine Age. 

These new tools were soon introduced into the United States where they revolutionized industry, especially in the manufacture of cloth and in the use of the steam engine for transportation. Soon Americans were inventing tools which changed other industries as well, but it was not until after the Civil War that the use of machinery began to completely transform the character of the nation's industrial life.

Slater Builds First American Cloth Mill. In weaving cloth there had hardly been any changes since the days when the Pharaohs ruled in Egypt, except for spinning wheels which had come into use in Europe in the time of Queen Elizabeth. The change in the manufacture of cloth came in England toward the end of the eighteenth century through the use of the newly invented spindles and looms which were contrived to save human labor. 

It was about the same time that James Watt invented the steam engine which was in time used to run the spinning and weaving machinery in some of the cloth mills. 

In the year 1789 Samuel Slater, an Englishman, brought the plans of the new spindles and looms to this country. 

In a short time Americans in New England had built a cloth mill according to Slater's plans. The swift New England streams furnished the power for this mill.

America Leads in Invention. From this time on the industrial revolution gained ground in America, in England, and in many other countries, but some of the greatest triumphs in the making of new tools came in the United States. In the search for swifter ways of doing things, American inventors soon took the lead.

The life which the American had lived in conquering the wilderness had prepared him to jump into the world race for new inventions. The American was a pioneer, adventurous, imaginative, practical. He had proved himself a pioneer, ready to try the new when he cut the Old World ties to come to America. As a frontiersman pushing his way onward toward the unknown spaces, he had learned to handle many tools. He was skilled with ax and rifle and he was handy with his knife and needle. In his wanderings with his family he had learned to meet new conditions, to fish, to set traps, to build a house, a canoe, a flatboat. In his log cabin separated from towns by hundreds of miles, he often had to be farmer, carpenter, painter, smith, mender of tools, clocks, and harness, even shoemaker and tailor.

Labor was costly, land was cheap. But without cheap labor the land was difficult to tame. Is it any wonder that the pioneering Americans, eager to make the most of their opportunities, proved themselves resourceful in facing mechanical problems, and that among the Americans are some of the greatest inventors of all times?

Soon after the Republic was founded, the United States Patent Office was created, and a patent law made a man's patent his own property for a given number of years. 

From that time on, the number of patents increased from tens to hundreds, from hundreds to thousands, and then swiftly moved forward to tens of thousands each year. 

Whitney's Cotton Gin, 1793. One of the earliest of

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP the patents granted by the United States Patent Office and one of the most important in the life of the nation was granted to Eli Whitney's invention of the cotton gin. 

The new cloth-making machinery lent itself to the manufacture of cotton cloth as well as of woolen cloth. The mill owners were eager to buy cotton if they could get it cheap 

Eli Whitney 

Whitney invented the cotton gin which reduced the cost of removing seed from cotton bolls, and so helped to make cotton the most important 

Southern crop. Whitney also invented the principle of manufacturing guns with interchangeable or standard parts. 

This principle, later applied to most quantity production, was largely responsible for America's rapid progress as a manufacturing nation. enough. This was difficult because the removal of seeds by hand from the cotton bolls was a slow, time-consuming, and therefore an expensive, process. Even with slave labor the raising of cotton was not profitable. 

Here it was that Eli Whitney, a young New England scholar who had gone to the 

South as a teacher, came to the rescue. When he was told of the market waiting for the cotton growers, if they could clean the bolls more swiftly, he set himself to the task of making a seed-removing tool which would save time and labor. 

He was successful. His invention, the cotton gin, made it possible to rid the cotton bolls of their seeds by drawing the bolls through revolving saws.

Now one man operating a gin could clean more cotton in a day than a slave could clean in months. Cotton immediately became a well-paying crop in the South, and the manufacture of cotton cloth became a leading industry in

New England. Cotton cloth, at one time more costly than either wool or linen, now became so inexpensive that it was used as the chief fabric in the manufacture of wearing apparel for both men and women.

The Old Way 

From the time of the pyramid builders in Egypt to the birth of the American nation there had been little progress in farm tools. The Egyptians cut their grass with sickles. Americans in Washington's day used scythes, which have longer blades and longer handles than sickles. Then an American invented the cradle which had a fork above the blade to hold the cut grain. 

Here we see one man cutting wheat, a second man binding it by hand. 

The New Way 

Here we see a combined reaper and binder drawn by a tractor. This machine cuts the grain, arranges it in bundles, and binds them. The farmer guides the tractor with one hand and with the other controls the levers which bind the cut grain. It was this new type of farm machinery which made it possible for the American farmer to utilize the great plains country as farm land.

vents Reaper. -So much for the changes which came about when new tools were used for the manufacture of clothes, but how about food? In colonial days almost all men were farmers and raised much of their food them-

selves. But as city factories, using new tools, were drawing workers from the farmhouse and the village cottage, cities grew in population and more people had to depend on the farmers for their food. 

If the old spinning wheel and the hand looms had proved too slow for the new conditions, what could be said for the old wooden plow with which the farmer broke his ground? 

What power was there in the old sickle or even in the scythe with which he cut his crop? 

How feeble were the old flails with which he had so patiently threshed his grain? slowly did his mills grind grain when the population of the land was doubling and trebling and armies of workers were living where they raised not an ounce of food?

McCormick went West to the great prairies where more wheat could be raised each year than a million men could harvest in the few short days which must see the giant task performed, and he saw the part which his reaper could play, must play, in making those prairies feed the growing nation.

He established a factory in Chicago, which was then a small town with one street. 

There he built his reapers and men learned to know their worth. He sold more each year, and the reapers which went out from that factory helped to make Chicago the world's greatest grain center. They helped to build up the whole West. The very railroads which were built across the continent were built in a large measure because of the need of moving the wheat crop.

Before the reaper came into use, the United States had famine years when it was forced to buy its wheat from abroad; but after that time it fed itself and even exported great quantities of wheat to other nations.

Grain Elevators. - 

McCormick's reaper was the forerunner of many other farming tools-steel plows which can cut many furrows in place of the single furrow cut by the old plow; machine drills for the planting of seed; harvesters which cut grain, bind it, and thresh it. Grain Elevators 

A picturesque phase of modern industry is the grain elevator, a huge storage bin containing millions of bushels of grain for the feeding of the nation and of the world. Groups of these elevators are massed along the water front in the granary cities of the nation. located at favorable points of distribution for the world market. 

The Meat Industry. Packing Houses. Refrigeration 

Canning. A few of the cities which receive the grain from the Northwest prairie states are the centers of the world's meat-packing industry.

As the nation grew it was found that local farmers could no longer supply enough meat for its needs.

The raising of animals for food began to center in the 

Southwest where grazing land was cheap.

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

To-day railroads run directly from the ranches to the stockyards in the meat-packing cities. Railroads also bring to the stockyards cattle, sheep, and hogs from the grain country. These animals are then prepared for market in huge packing houses where labor-saving machines are used at every turn.

By means of electricity, storage rooms are kept at low temperature. Canning machinery puts up and preserves some of the meat.

Refrigerator Cars 

The use of refrigerator cars by railroad companies has made possible transcontinental shipments of fresh eggs, milk, meat, fish, fruits, and vegetables. 

Fresh meat from the packing centers, along with milk, fresh fruit, and vegetables from the farms are carried in railroad refrigerator cars. The meat packers aided by modern chemistry have learned how to use the hoofs, horns, hides, fat, tendons, and bones of the animal, formerly wasted, in the making of a great variety of by-products, some of which were unknown before our day. 

Chemistry in the Machine 

Age. A phase of the Machine Age which is sometimes overlooked is the part played by chemists in production. Chemical forces have been harnessed to such tasks as cold storage and refrigeration and canning, which make possible the feeding of the large cities of the Machine Age. The chemist has helped the farmer to produce better crops, and the manufacturer to produce better steel. In fact nearly every industry has its laboratory where chemists are testing old prod-

ucts and finding better ways to produce new and better goods.

Builders built the wooden houses higher and set them closer together. 

This was dangerous because of the damage which fire could do among closely set wooden dwellings. To offset the danger, houses were built of wood and brick; then of wood, brick, and steel. To-day in the great cities where there are millions of people, steel is used in building towering apartment houses. Steel is also used in the construction of mills, factories, and office buildings. 

Concrete reënforced with steel has become a structural

material of great value. Because it can be made into almost any shape and sets with the permanency of stone, it is used in the construction of buildings, bridges, dams, tunnels, conduits, roads, and sidewalks. 

High steel buildings, as well as other great engineering projects built with riveters, shovels, drills, and derricks worked by power, are as much a part of the Machine Age as are the harvesters, the 

flour mills, the cloth mills, and the clothing factories.

Machines Increase Division of Labor. The new tools which men used to provide themselves with food, clothes, and shelter brought about a great division in labor. Long ago people learned that there is an advantage in dividing work. 

Even among wilderness peoples, while men hunted, fished, and fought, women cared for the home. When men learned farming, some men living in the cities gave their time to trade and crafts, such as pottery, carpentry, and building.

The Division of Labor 

Shoe manufacture affords an excellent example of the division of labor in the modern factory. There are more than fifty distinct operations in the making of one shoe with separate machines and workers for each.

This division of labor was as nothing compared to the division of labor which came during the Machine Age. The division of work between the farm and the city became more complete. In the old days many craftsmen did some farming, farmers did some tool-making, and the wives of farmers spun and wove and even sewed family clothes by hand. In the Machine Age, millions of workers locked away from the land in cities have to depend on farmers for
