People ride beneath the earth in city subways, and even beneath the beds of rivers in deep tunnels cut from shore to shore. They ride on land in automobiles, trolley cars, and railroad trains. In the modern shoe factory, as in all other modern factories, each part of the work is done by a special machine.

Transportation and Communication in Machine Age. 

It was largely because of the increased division of labor between city and country that there was need of improved means of transportation. The steamship, the railroad, and the automobile, once invented, were rapidly developed. 

In 1896 there were only four gasoline-burning cars in the United States; to-day there are millions. 

Now, the nation's great canals, its excellent roads, its steamboats, railroads, automobiles, and airplanes are all a part of the Ma chine Age. They serve to unify the people in their political life; they also serve to make them one great family in industrial their life.

Likewise the improved means of communication - the telegraph, the cable, the telephone, the wireless, the radio - were all necessary to the Machine Age. With the growing division of labor and with the scattering of population, there was need for swifter means of sending messages to bind all the units of the industrial and political organization of the nation.

In heating the home, new heating systems have superseded the old fireplace. Now gas and electric stoves are commonly used to prepare the nation's food.

Setting Type by Hand 

Before the linotype machine was invented, printers had to set their type by hand, taking capital letters from the upper case and small letters from the lower case. After the printing, these letters had to be carefully returned to their original places.

Setting Type by Machine 

The operator of a linotype machine strikes keys which drop letter molds into a casting frame. Liquid metal is poured on to the molds. The machine casts one line of type at a time; hence the name 66 linotype." farmer as well as to the city dweller the opportunity to enjoy music played by masters. Thomas Edison 

Thomas Edison was one of the foremost of American inventors. He contributed largely to the development of the motion picture, the phonograph, the electric light, the electric car, and to many of the electric appliances which make household tasks easier. letters as quickly as a man can operate a typewriter.

With these two aids and other improvements in printing, the presses in the land are able to supply books, newspapers, and magazines for readers seeking entertainment as well as for the great army of students seeking education and knowledge. 

Never before in history has so large a percentage of people in any one land been engaged in the study of books. 

In the public schools, high schools, and universities there are millions of students. 

Although most of these are for the time being producing nothing, they are the ones who will soon step into the busy life of the nation to take their places in the crisscross pattern of the Machine Age. 

So on and on, the story runs. The daily lives of men and women are so changed that could Washington, Jackson, or even Lincoln come to life again, he would find it difficult to believe that the world which the modern inventors have made possible is the same world in which he lived. 

Thomas Edison. - Chief among the Americans, for the

reputation which he won the world over, is Thomas Edison, whom none has surpassed in the vast field of industrialelectrical invention.

Edison, like so many other American inventors, began life as a poor boy. His career is only one of the many which show how the world in which we live is still a world of romance and adventure, where high hopes of dreams accomplished occasionally come true.

Science, invention

While working as newsboy on a train, he one day saved the life of a little child who stumbled on the railroad tracks. The child's father, to show his gratitude, taught

Edison the mysteries of telegraphy, and Edison, drifting from job to job, reached New 

York. There in an office he found that men were having trouble with the electric tickers which recorded the changing prices of stocks and bonds. He studied the apparatus and showed how the ticker could be made to work more smoothly. For this little triumph of his skill he received a sum which to him undoubtedly seemed a fortune.

Leisure in the Machine Age 

With the increase in leisure which the Machine Age has helped to make possible, thousands of people, released from the countless time-consuming chores of the past, have leisure for recreation. The Machine Age has provided new forms of recreation in the motion picture and the radio. 

Electricity was his Aladdin's lamp. Aladdin had touched his lamp and the good genius had brought him wealth. Morse had touched electricity and the world was given the telegraph. Who could tell but that at the right

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

touch electricity would serve the world far more wonderfully than Aladdin had been served by the genius of his lamp?

From that time on, all of Edison's life was given over to one task. Aided by other able workers, he studied electricity night and day in the hope that he could bring it to serve man in endless ways.

His work was well rewarded. As he and his faithful coworkers in the laboratory patiently studied electricity, they evoked new powers from its current. 

Edison played a great part in making Bell's telephone practicable. He invented the incandescent lamp by which electricity could be utilized to give off a steady light which could be used for illuminating homes, buildings, and even whole cities at the touch of a single button or the pulling of a switch. He invented the phonograph to record sound vibrations, storing up the songs of singers, the speeches of orators, the music of a whole orchestra, in such a way that millions of people the world over could later hear the records.

Edison's kinetograph, for the taking of motion pictures with film, led the way in the development of the modern motion picture and its electrical projection. 

Edison did not scorn the humbler tasks which electricity might perform. He saw that the industrial age had not left the home and the old tasks of the housewife untouched. 

Spinning, weaving, sewing, baking and preserving fruits, the smoking of meats, had all been taken over by men as part of modern business. The new science of sanitation had given the home the tiled bathroom with its provision for comfort and health. Edison and his assistants, setting about to make housework still easier, helped in the invention of the electric iron, the electric washing machine, the electric stove, the electric heater, the electric cooker, and the electric vacuum cleaner, and many other household devices.

A world laughs and plays each night by the light evoked from the electric current. A world listens, and generations yet unborn may listen to mechanical records of the music of our day. Every night in motion-picture theaters, millions look on while the world's events flash before their eyes. 

The man who helped to give the night its myriad brilliant suns, the man who helped to carry the song of the singer to the multitudes of the earth and to future generations, the man who helped to bring to every boy and girl, man and woman, a living moving picture of his brothers and sisters throughout the world in their joys and sorrows, the man who helped to give women time to share with men in the enjoyment of these marvels was 

Thomas Edison, the wizard at whose touch the genius of electricity was made to serve man in ways undreamed of before his time.

Among the many uses of electricity not the least of its services to man is its work as electric power when harnessed to electric engines. 

We have seen how the invention of the steam engine ushered in the Machine Age. The steam engine which used the stored-up heat in coal to create steam power gave to man a new weapon in his conflict with the forces of nature. 

The steam engine ran railroads, ships, and factories.

Water Power 

We have observed repeatedly that the nation is well served by a long coast line on the Atlantic, the Pacific, the Great Lakes, and the Gulf of Mexico, as well as by a network of navigable rivers. In addition, the nation is rich in water power, the force of swift rushing or falling water, which is gradually being converted into electric power to help in the nation's industrial life. in the operation of ships and trains, and electric power plants are transforming the force of falling water into electric current which is used to light and to heat cities hundreds of miles away. Electric power carried from the same plants operates the machinery in city factories.

Electric power, which can be carried by copper wire from the generating plant to its distant tasks, is in many ways a cheaper and more useful servant than steam power. This being so, the great inventors of our day are planning super-plants at central points which would utilize the force of electricity to do almost all of man's work.

The Machine Age. 

Electric Age.-Writers have divided the periods of man's life on earth into the Stone

Age, the Iron Age, the Steel 

Age. In recent years the time in which we live has been called the Electric Age, which no doubt describes the character of much of our life to-day.

However, the outstanding characteristic of the United

States since the Civil War has been the use of steam as well as electric power in the operation of the myriad machines which have taken the place of the old hand tools. 

Whatever else we may call our era, it cannot be denied that this is the age of the machine.

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP Machine Civilization. Social Changes. New Problems. 

- This account of the Machine Age gives only a slight hint of the changes which have resulted from machine civilization. Machine civilization has given women more leisure and a new status in society. It has released millions of children from the need of hard, physical labor. It has made possible the acquisition of fabulous fortunes. It has expanded old professions and opened up new ones. It has furnished peoples with new forms of entertainment, and it has made it possible to carry some of the old forms of entertainment to millions. 

The machine civilization has given a new impetus to research in chemistry, physics, and other sciences which have proved of the utmost practical value in meeting the prob lems of modern industry. 

Machine civilization has made necessary the organization of modern technical education which aims to fit boys and girls for their tasks in industrial life as well as for the duties of citizenship. 

Citizenship in the Machine Age is a much more complex thing than in the earlier days. With the several changes born of machinery there came new problems - complex problems which have occupied much of the thought of the nation from the Civil War until to-day.

Power Transmission 

Copper wires acting as transmitters carry electric current for hundreds of miles from power plants where electricity is generated to distant cities. Here the current is used for lighting, for running trolleys and factory engines.

Water Power. - Besides having vast farm lands and great ranches with the right conditions of soil and climate to provide food, having raw materials to make into manufactured goods, and having iron for the building of engines, and coal and oil to run them, the United States

has great stores of water power. For a long time this water power was used directly, but since the invention of the electric dynamo, water power is used to generate electricity, as we have noted in the previous chapter. 

Man Power. Important as all of the nation's natural resources are, we must not forget the part played by the man power of this country. When we consider what little use the Indians made of the same natural resources, it becomes the more strikingly clear that much of the progress made in America was due to the Americans themselves. 

True, they were aided by tools of which the Indians knew nothing. They had the advantages of superior training and education, but, above all, they were pioneering people who had proved the energy and daring which was in them when they left the comforts of the Old World and undertook the conquest of the American wilderness.

The Problem of Good 

Government.-As the nation grew in size, and in the complexity of its political and industrial life, it became increasingly difficult to insure honest and efficient government.

The Growth of Corpora tions. Side by side with the problem of good government went the problem of defining the proper relation between the government and the big business corporations which had developed during the Ma chine Age. 

As machines changed people's mode of work, they also changed people's way of doing business. With new tools producing things more quickly and with new means of transportation and communication, it became much easier for men to do business on a national or even on an international scale. 

In one industry after another, while smaller companies failed, large corporations secured more and more of the business of the nation and of the world.

Under the leadership of John D. Rockefeller, the Standard 

Oil Corporation gradually grew until to-day it owns oil wells in all parts of the earth and it distributes its products by sea and land to every country on the face of the globe.

PARTIES, PLATFORMS, DOMESTIC PROBLEMS 553 

Andrew Carnegie laid the foundations for the powerful 

United States Steel Corporation. 

In other industries — railroading, the telegraph, the telephone, meat, lumber, mining, woolen manufacture, sugar, rubber-powerful corporations grew up. 

In the automobile industry 

Henry Ford made a position for himself on a par with 

Rockefeller in oil and Carnegie in steel.

Many independent companies have a part in these industries; but in most cases the larger corporations have a great advantage over the small companies. The large corporations with their greater capital are able to run their business in a much more efficient way, paying for the aid of inventors and scientists to save labor costs, to improve output, and to do away with waste by the manufacture of by-products. 

Benjamin Harrison 

Harrison was the twenty-third president of the United States (1889–1893). 

The leading event of his administration was the Sherman Anti-Trust Act.

Doing business on a large scale, the corporations were in many cases able to give the public better service at less cost. 

The direction of each corporation was in the hands of a few men, but the ownership of the business was generally widely distributed. Since a growing corporation needed millions of dollars for its operations, the money had to be obtained through the sale of stocks and bonds, which were bought by thousands of people throughout the land. 

Critics felt that the growth of the corporations en-

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

dangered the welfare of the people. They argued that the corporations had the power to buy legislation through making too generous contributions to election campaign funds. They insisted that railroad corporations were favoring the growth of certain sections of the country in which they were interested by special freight rates or by rebates, a practice unfair in many ways. They claimed that large corporations were crowding out smaller companies by their greater wealth and even by foul tactics. The critics of the corporations feared that once the smaller independent companies were put out of the way, corporations would be free to charge whatever prices they pleased for their goods and services.

To prevent the control of the nation's industrial life by a few corporations, some men, especially among the immigrant population, favored socialism, or state ownership of machinery and natural resources. In the political elections the small vote for the socialists proved that a large majority of people did not favor such government ownership. 

Some who were not radically opposed to the corporations nevertheless urged that the government check corporation activities by law; but for a long time the lawmakers held to the policy of "hands off."

Later this policy of inaction was changed and Congress passed laws which gave the government a large measure of control over the corporations. 

Corporations Controlled. In Cleveland's administra tion, the Interstate Commerce Commission was appointed (1887) and certain unfair practices of the railroads were forbidden. By the Hepburn Act (1906) the Interstate 

Commerce Commission was given the power to determine the freight and passenger rates to be charged by corporations bearing goods from one state into another. The 

Mann-Elkins Act gave the Interstate Commerce Commis-

sion the same power over the telephone, telegraph, and cable corporations. The La Follette Act ordered that the value of railroads be investigated so that it would be possible to say what profits they should receive in fairness to the capital invested.

Within the states and cities Public Utility Commissions were created by law and the commissioners were given a measure of control over the rates and the conditions of service offered by the local transit, telephone, and telegraph corporations. In 1890 Congress passed the Sherman Anti-Trust Act, which aimed to protect interstate trade and commerce against unlawful restraints and monopolies.

The Clayton Anti-Trust 

Law, passed later, undertook to define more clearly the kind of trust action which would be regarded as illegal restraint of interstate trade and commerce.

To prevent corporations from trying to influence politics in their favor, a "Corrupt Practices Act" was passed setting a limit to the size of election campaign contributions and ordering that the parties and the separate candidates publish a list of the names of contributors as well as the amounts contributed.

Within recent years Congress passed the Pure Foods and Drugs Act which provided that the government should

take steps to prevent the adulteration of food and to control the interstate sale, by corporations or other concerns, of foods and of drugs which might be harmful. Congress, then, has passed many laws to control corporations and to do away with some of the dangers growing out of corporation control of industry. Nevertheless corporations have been growing in wealth and power because, after all, it seems that in order to carry on production and distribution on the enormous scale required by the Machine Age, business organization must combine in large units. 

Labor Problems. - Another problem faced by the lawmakers in Congress was the establishment of amicable relations between corporations and labor. During the Machine 

Age in shops, mills, and factories, on railroads and steamships, in telegraph and telephone companies the numbers of workers increased enormously. 

What was to be the relation between these workers who ran the machines of the new age and their employers who owned the machines?

Before the Machine Age much of the manufacturing of the nation had been done in cottages or small shops. Apprentices and helpers lived close to their employers. They could look forward to the day when they in turn might become masters of small cottage workshops. Besides the rewards of their day's work, they had little farms to help support themselves. Many workers owned the homes in which they lived. 

But now most of the workers had no farms. They lived in cities in tenement houses which they did not own. 

Employers had so many helpers that it was practically

PARTIES, PLATFORMS, DOMESTIC PROBLEMS 557 

impossible for them to keep in personal touch with the lot of each. In times of unemployment the fate of the landless laborer was hard. Even when he had employment it was difficult. In many industries the workers labored from dawn to dusk, twelve, fourteen, and even sixteen hours a day for small pay.

Labor Unions Unite. Obtain Political Measures. 

Long before the Civil War, workers in many industries eager to improve their condition began to join labor unions. 

Then the local unions united in state organizations. In some industries, workers throughout the country joined together in national unions. Finally there grew up national organizations such as the Knights of Labor and later the American Federation of Labor which combined within the one organization the workers of hundreds of different industries. The first of these nation-wide amalgamations of labor unions was known as the Noble Order of the Knights of Labor, which attained a membership of about a million. This order was superseded by the American 

Federation of Labor which, under the presidency of Samuel Gompers, grew to the point where it had a membership of over four million workers.

At election time, the American Federation of Labor often threw the weight of its support as a federation to the political party which promised favorable legislation. In this way the Federation has secured city, state, and national laws favorable to labor conditions. 

Through national legislation, labor has been able to secure many advantages. As long ago as Van Buren's administration, Congress passed a law limiting the hours of men on certain government work to ten hours a day. 

Although this act did not affect a large number of workers, it was a victory for the principle of the shorter working day which labor favored. Since then labor has been able

Labor Strikes vs. Industrial Arbitration.— Although from the beginning labor unions have attempted to secure better conditions through political action, they have also used the weapon of the strike, generally as a swift means of

PARTIES, PLATFORMS, DOMESTIC PROBLEMS 559 

getting higher wages, shorter hours, or improved working conditions.

Long before the Civil War there had been strikes. It was only after that war that these conflicts between labor and capital became a serious danger in the life of the nation. 

The strikes increased in number. Some were attended by violence on one side or the other, or both. The strikes caused the workers great loss in wages. They caused the employers great loss in profit. They reduced production, often at a time when the public needed the product most. 

In the railroad industry a strike sometimes endangered the very lives of people who depended on the continued service of trains for food and safety. 

In time it became clear that strikes were wasteful and that, if possible, a better way should be found to settle disputes between capital and labor. 

Once during a coal strike Theodore Roosevelt practically forced the two sides to stop fighting and to leave their disputes to a board of arbitration which he appointed. 

Again, during the World War, which broke out in 1914, when the railroad men of the country threatened to call a nation-wide strike, Congress passed the Adamson Law, granting a new scale of wages to certain classes of railroad workers.

To-day, the nation and states as well have permanent boards which attempt to bring about the peaceable settlement of difficulties between the corporation employers and corporation employees. Some business concerns are seeking to meet the strike problem through partnership between labor and capital; through actual joint ownership; through the sale of stocks and bonds to employees; through bonuses based on profits or in other ways.

The Problem of Panics. - One problem which affects business corporations, city workers, and farmers alike is the problem of panics. For more than a century, at intervals of about twenty years, the country has passed through financial crises, when business firms failed, factories closed, workers were left unemployed, and farmers could get little money for their products. We have read of one such panic in 1837. There was another in 1857; another in 1873, and several since then. 

There are many different theories as to the exact cause of panics, but every one is agreed as to the hardships which result from them. Even before the Civil War when most people lived on the land and had at least a roof over their heads, some produce from their gardens for food, wood from the near-by forest for heat, a panic was hard enough. 

During the Machine Age panics became much harder on the people, especially on the unemployed city workers who were unable without their earnings to be sure of a home, food, or heat.

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

Many people believe the problem of panics is related to the problem of money and banking. They claim that when business is good every one is optimistic about the opportunities for big profits, and banks become generous, in fact too generous, with their loans to business. 

The result is the production of more goods than can be sold at a profit. Then as people grow fearful that the good times have reached their limit, they rush to withdraw their money from the banks, the banks call in their loans, and business firms, left with great stocks of unsold goods on hand, cannot pay. They fail. Then banks fail. Factories close and the panic is on. 

The Federal Reserve now Lessens Panic Danger. — It occurred to some men that often this loss of confidence begins in one part of the country, because the banks there have not enough money to tide them over a few difficult months; the local business firms and banks fail; they in turn drag down other banks and industries in other parts of the country. To offset this condition and to help business in many other ways, during President Wilson's administration, Congress passed the Federal Reserve Act. This act provided that instead of the old United States Bank, such as Hamilton established, the nation should have twelve federal banks controlled by a Federal Reserve Board. These banks, distributed throughout the nation, are managed in such a way that money or credit from one part of the country can be swiftly sent to any other part of the country which needs it. In this way the business. of the whole country is helped and supported by easily shifted money power.

The Problem of Immigration at Close of World War. 

Among the many problems facing the nation was the one of

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

immigration, a problem which became critical during the World War when it was realized that the end of the war in Europe might bring an influx of millions of new immigrants. 

Until the time of the World War, immigrants had been freely welcomed to this country, although with increasing 

New Americans 

In many of the larger cities, especially in the East, immigrant groups have settled thickly. Due to poor housing conditions, the congestion which resulted is unfortunate and constitutes a problem which city planners to-day are trying to meet. Nevertheless just as leaders of a century ago rose from primitive log cabins, so leading citizens in American life to-day may rise from congested "slums." restrictions toward the end of the nineteenth century.

The news of American wealth and the call of American freedom had attracted millions. With railroads to carry them across Europe, with steamships to bring them across the ocean, immigration had increased year by year until it reached what to some observers were alarming proportions. About the time of the World War, fully onethird of the population in the country was either foreign born or the children of foreign born.

After the World War many 

Americans declared that valuable as had been the contribution of the immigrants to 

America, immigration should be restricted. Some of those who wanted to shut out altogether or restrict the immigration of aliens argued that up to 1880 immigration came largely from England, Ireland, Scotland, Germany, or the Scandinavian countries, all of which had a language, a government, ideas, and ideals like ours or nearly enough like ours to make it easy for

PARTIES, PLATFORMS, DOMESTIC PROBLEMS 571 

the immigrants soon to become good Americans. It was shown that the immigration after that date was mostly from Southern and Eastern Europe, two sections of the Old World in which the mass of people were still close to the conditions of feudalism, which Northeast Europe and America had outgrown. It was claimed that the language, the government, the ideas, and ideals of the newcomers were unlike those of America, that it would take a long time to Americanize them by teaching them the American language and American ideals of law, order, and government.

Others wanted immigration restricted on different grounds. They argued that, quite apart from the character of the immigrants and the readiness with which they can be Americanized, the stream of immigration must be checked. They claimed that with the government lands practically gone, with the soldiers returning from the World War, and with more workers in the country than the industries could absorb, there was danger that the coming of cheap European labor would damage the status of American labor. They insisted that the time had come for America to partially close its doors. 

All the advocates of immigration restriction agreed that if the nation did restrict immigration, it might as well do so along selective lines. 

The American Federation of Labor favored new immigration laws and so did many other organizations. Some employers eager for cheaper labor opposed restriction. So did others who felt that America should continue to hold open the doors to all those seeking greater opportunities. 

Earlier Laws Restricting Immigration. There had been objection to unrestricted immigration ever since the Civil War. Shortly after the war the importation of Chinese coolies, as laborers in the building of the first trans-

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

continental railroad and in other contract jobs, led labor unions to ask for restrictions of this type of immigration. 

Laws were passed forbidding the immigration of Chinese laborers and all contract laborers whatever their nationality. By agreement with Japan, laborers from that country were also debarred from immigration. 

A Legislative Body in Session 

The American people through their representatives seek such action as they believe will help to solve their economic and social problems. The debates in state and national legislatures and the laws which these bodies pass indicate the nature of the problems facing the country. 

When the frontier began to disappear about 1880, and the idea came that immigration should be more drastically restricted, bars were first raised against criminals, idiots, and paupers, then against sufferers from certain diseases, and still later against anarchists. During the World War 

Congress passed, over President Wilson's veto, a law establishing a literacy test for immigrants.

PARTIES, PLATFORMS, DOMESTIC PROBLEMS 573 

- The Immigration Quota Laws. The most recent immigration legislation, passed after the World War, was far more drastic than anything which went before. The danger that war-torn Europe might turn millions of new immigrants into America at a time when the nation was facing a general condition of unemployment, overcrowded cities, lack of housing facilities, and other domestic problems, hastened a step which many had long advised. In 

Modern Steamships and the Immigration Problem 

These mammoth ocean steamships are driven forward by giant screw propellers. From 1880 to 1914 they brought to America millions of immigrants from Southern and Eastern Europe. During the World War and since, the 

United States Congress has considerably restricted immigration. This has been done to protect American labor and its standard of living against the competition of cheaper labor which might be furnished by immigrant strangers with their lower standard of living; to protect American institutions from the danger of too large a body of foreign-born residents unaccustomed to American institutions. With the reduction of immigration the steamship companies have turned great portions of their ships into tourist cabins for Americans who seek to spend a summer in Europe. 

1921 a law was passed to limit immigration from each of the foreign countries to a certain quota or percentage. The number of any nationality admitted in one year was limited to three per cent of the foreign-born persons of that nationality present in our population in the year 1910. This law was modified in its quotas in the year 1924, when the quota for each nationality was changed to two per cent of the

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

population figures given for that nationality in the 1890 census of the United States. - Americanizing the Immigrant. Restriction did not fully meet the problem of immigration. There was still the problem of Americanizing the immigrants who formed so large a part of the population of the United States. 

These immigrants contribute a large part of America's manpower. Yet there are many who claim that unless the cities, the states, and the national government take steps to bring to the immigrants an understanding of American ideals and a zealous desire to defend them, the strength and unity of the nation are threatened. 

To offset this danger, the public schools have long been teaching the children of the immigrants the history and meaning of America. However, the leaders of the Americanization movement feel that it is necessary to carry on this work among adult immigrants, and for some years past, evening schools have been teaching immigrants English, American history, and the elements of American government. Continuation classes for workers who are 

American-born as well as for immigrants also teach American history and the duties of American citizenship. 

In this way it is planned to weld the whole American population, the older stock and the more recently arrived, into a common mood of devotion to the cherished ideals of 

America. 

Tariff, Income Tax, the Cost of Government. We have read of many problems and of the laws which have been passed in the effort to solve them. We have seen how many of these laws require the aid of government departments and bureaus to enforce them. With the increase in the tasks of government there was an increase in the cost of government which mounted into the hundreds of millions annually.

PARTIES, PLATFORMS, DOMESTIC PROBLEMS 575 

This growing cost of government in city and state as well as in the nation has become one of the problems facing the people. For a long time the nation obtained much income, with which to meet its expenses, from the sale of government land and from tariffs on imported goods. 

During the costly Civil War, Congress increased the tariff rates considerably.

The Supreme Court in Session 

The nine justices of the Supreme Court are all men of the highest standing in the legal profession, appointed by the President with the approval of the Senate to serve for life. The most important duty of the Supreme Court is to decide upon the constitutionality of laws passed by Congress. The Supreme 

Court declared an Income Tax Law unconstitutional until the Constitution was amended in such a way as to give the federal government power to pass such a law. or less against high tariff, while the Republicans continued to favor it, not only for revenue but also as a means of protection for industry. From time to time, under Republican and Democratic presidents, the tariff has been modified, upward or downward, according to the party in power. 

Among the leading tariff bills are the Wilson, the Dingley, the Payne-Aldrich, and the Underwood Tariff Acts. 

Finally, a tariff commission was appointed to advise the president and Congress upon tariff problems as they arise. During Cleveland's administration, when the tariff was

INDUSTRIAL LEADERSHIP 

comparatively low, a law was passed to substitute an income tax as a new means of securing funds for the expenses of government. This income tax law was declared unconstitutional. Congress again passed an income tax bill, and this time the law stood because of the adoption of the 

Sixteenth Amendment to the Constitution. 

To-day the Federal Income Tax is one of the chief sources of government revenue. 

So much, then, for our problems at home. Several times in the course of this chapter mention has been made of the World War, a conflict which broke out in Europe in 1914 and which America entered in 1917. 

Before turning to America's part in the World War, we must first consider the foreign problems of the nation from 1860 to 1917.

Purchase of Alaska. Arbitrating Seal Fishery and Boundary Disputes. - In 1867, shortly after the Civil War, the United States bought Alaska from Russia. The purchase price was $7,200,000, a large sum for an icy wilderness, according to the critics of the purchase. However, Alaska soon proved to be a valuable possession, rich in coal and gold. The Alaskan seal fisheries alone are worth a fortune.

As careless hunting threatened to destroy the seals, the United States attempted to keep all but American hunters

INTERNATIONAL COMPLICATIONS. TREATIES 583 

from the fisheries. Great Britain protested that in the waters outside the three-mile limit her hunters had as much right as ours. This matter, like the Alabama claim, was settled by arbitration. Great Britain's claim was upheld; but laws for the protection of the seals were agreed upon.

At later dates arbitration settled other disputes. The boundary line between Alaska and Canada, and the right Seals Rich as Alaska is in gold, coal, lumber, and other raw materials, the furbearing seals off the coast of the Berry Islands add considerably to the total value of Alaskan products. of American citizens in the Newfoundland fisheries, were each settled in this peaceful manner. 

Arbitration Settles Alabama Claims. A sharp disa greement which grew out of the Civil War was that of the Alabama claims which were settled by arbitration in 1871. During the war, England had permitted Confederate warships, such as the Alabama, to be fitted in her harbors and to sail out to the destruction of United States commerce. British ministers friendly to the Southern cause had permitted this in spite of the protests of the 

American minister to Great Britain.

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

After the war, Great Britain and the United States agreed to leave the subject of fair settlement of the damages done to American shipping by these warships to an arbitration board of five men: one chosen by Great Britain, one by the 

United States, one each by Italy, Switzerland, and Brazil.

This board decided that the American claim was a just one and awarded damages.

Arbitration vs. War. Pan-American Congress. First 

Peace Conference at The Hague. - The principle of arbitration seemed to be gaining ground steadily. In 1889, at the invitation of this country, seventeen countries of 

North, South, and Central America sent representatives to a Pan-American Congress held in Washington, and here it was generally agreed that all the republics in this American portion of the world should settle by arbitration any disputes which might arise. 

Six years later, during Cleveland's administration, the United States, still believing in the Monroe Doctrine, practically insisted that Great Britain should settle a dispute with Venezuela by arbitration.

Four years later there was a meeting of the First Peace Conference at The Hague in Holland to promote international peace. At the conference a Court of Arbitration was established. This court was to act as a court of law to which nations might bring their differences for peaceful settlement.

Machine Age Sees Growth of Nationalism in Europe. 

While these moves toward peace through arbitration were being made, the strong nations were looking ahead to increase their world power by strengthening their armies and their navies, and by adding to their possessions new markets for their manufactures, or new sources of foodstuffs and other raw materials.

We have seen how, after the Civil War, the United States

INTERNATIONAL COMPLICATIONS. TREATIES 585 

rose in industrial strength largely through the use of the inventions of the Machine Age. So, too, in Europe the powers had been making rapid strides through their use of the new machinery.

Great Britain, which had long been the leader in colony building, in world trade, and in machine production, was still the strongest of the European powers. 

France, beaten by Prussia in 1870, had come out of the defeat with a new determination to strengthen her power in Europe and to add to her colonies abroad. 

The King of Prussia, victorious over Austria and France, united many separate kingdoms in the German empire which he ruled as emperor. From 1871 on, Germany made rapid advance in machine production, and soon her rulers were seeking colonies for surplus population and surplus products.

South of Germany, Austria and Hungary were united as a dual monarchy. Italy, the land where the Venetians and 

Genoese once led in the world trade of the older days, became a modern nation. By force of arms, the whole land was united and a king rules the nation which, like its rivals to the north, sought industrial progress at home and power abroad.

Russia, most backward of the large European nations, was in many ways still living in the feudal age. Yet even here the machine entered. The railroad, the steamship, the printed book, and the factory engine gradually began to make themselves felt in the life of the nation. Russia had less need than the others for seeking new lands. Her need seemed rather to obtain more seaports through which to ship her great wheat crops.

European Nations Seek Territorial Expansion. 

Except for Russia, since about 1871, each of these leading powers in Europe has been feverishly engaged in acquiring such new

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

lands as were not yet claimed by others. Between Great 

Britain, France, Italy, Germany, Belgium, and others, the greater part of Africa was taken over as colonial lands; almost half of Asia was taken over by European powers either as colonies or as "spheres of influence," in which each 

William McKinley 

McKinley was the twenty-fifth president of the United States (18971901). His second term was cut short at the hands of an assassin. Leading events of his administration were: annexation of Hawaii; war with Spain; country claimed especial trading and industrial rights and privileges. 

United States Expands. 

It happened that during this same period which saw the European countries expanding, the United States also acquired colonies partly through war, partly through annexation, partly through purchase from Spain. 

Cuban Revolt against

Spain Involves the United 

States. Of all Spain's former empire in America, that country had been able to hold only Cuba and Porto 

Rico; not, however, without difficulty, for the Cubans had frequently attempted to gain their freedom. In 1895 the 

Cubans were again in revolt.

General Weyler, acting for Spain, attempted to put down the revolution by a concentration plan which resulted in virtually starving great numbers of men, women, and children. The trouble in Cuba also brought much loss to 

American property on the island and reduced American export trade. Spain's victory might have put an end to new territory acquired in Caribbean and in Pacific; Boxer Rebellion in China

INTERNATIONAL COMPLICATIONS. TREATIES 587 

these losses, but the American newspapers, siding with the revolutionists, printed pictures of the deliberately starved Cubans, in order to arouse popular sympathy for their cause. The government was neutral, but many Americans went to Cuba to help in the struggle. 

The United States finally sent a warship, the Maine, to Cuba to protect American interests in Cuba. While in the harbor of Havana, the Maine was blown up, and two hundred sixty of her crew were killed.

The American people were angered, and their anger grew when a commission appointed by President McKinley reported that the Maine was destroyed by a submarine mine. To-day there is doubt whether such a mine was deliberately exploded by Spanish officials; but at the time there seemed no doubt. The newspapers demanded war. 

Congress declared Cuba free and empowered President 

McKinley to end Spanish rule.

The Spanish-American War. Before the end of April, 1898, war was on.

The war was swiftly won. 

By the end of April, Commodore George Dewey and his fleet, notified by cable, arrived in the Philippines from 

Hongkong, China. On May 1, 1898, he destroyed the Spanish fleet of ten warships in the harbor of Manila without the loss of a single American ship or sailor. In August, fifteen thousand American soldiers arrived to help. Manila was taken.

Meanwhile a fleet of four Spanish warships succeeded in entering Santiago Harbor in Cuba, where it was practically bottled up by a fleet which took a position outside the town. 

Soon after the outbreak of the war the American regular army was increased from 28,000 to 61,000. The President called for more volunteers. Of these American troops, some went to the Philippines and some were landed in

Peace Treaty Gives United States Island Possessions. - 

In December a treaty of peace was signed at Paris. By the terms of this treaty Spain gave up Cuba. The United 

States received Porto Rico and other smaller Spanish islands in the West Indies, as well as the smaller island of Guam in the Pacific; the United States was also to take

over the Philippine Islands on the payment of twenty million dollars.

Congress hesitated about ratifying the treaty. Many felt that for the United States to take the Philippines would mean that we, too, were embarking in the paths of European diplomacy, with a new policy of imperialistic expansion. Others argued that this was foolish talk. They said that Spain was too weak to keep the peace in the Philippines; that the Filipinos were mostly a Malay people, unaccustomed to self-government and not ready for freedom. Their claim was that if we did not take the 

Philippines, some other nation would, and that for the protection of our trade in China it would be better that we should hold the Philippines.

This view won out. Congress approved the treaty in 1899. 

United States Policy in Island Possessions. — In Cuba the United States established a temporary rule during which the island was given better health conditions and better schools. Then, when Congress felt that the Cubans were ready, it kept its war promise and declared Cuba a free republic. Once since, in a time of trouble, the United 

States again set up its government in Cuba, but as soon as the trouble was over, the officers were removed. 

Porto Rico to-day is United States territory, with a governor appointed by the President and a legislature elected by the Porto Ricans. In 1917 its inhabitants were given citizenship and a commissioner without power to vote represents them in Washington.

In the Philippines American soldiers had to fight for several years to put down an uprising led by Aguinaldo, who fought for Philippine freedom. In the end United 

States troops won. From the first days of American rule, the government attempted to introduce among the Fili-

Many other small islands were acquired to strengthen the United States' foothold in the Pacific. In 1917 the United States purchased from Denmark the Virgin Islands, known as the Danish West Indies, for $25,000,000. The islands are well situated for a naval base to defend the Panama Canal. 

Before the sale was made Denmark gave the people of the islands an opportunity to express their wishes which favored their annexation to the United States. 

Pacific Ocean New Highroad to Wealth. It will be easier to understand the interest which the United States was taking in the Pacific when we note that the trade with the East was rapidly becoming more and more important and that the Pacific Ocean, leading to the vast populations and the almost untouched natural resources of Asia, seemed likely to outrival the Atlantic as an important highroad to wealth.

Only a few years before we obtained the Philippines, several European powers had taken over great portions of China by practically forced treaties if not by actual war. 

These treaties established each of these portions as a "sphere of influence" in which the European nation in control could find opportunities for the expansion of its investments and its trade.

United States Seeks "Open Door" in East. The 

United States with its harbors on the Pacific coast is in a position to benefit naturally by the growth of Eastern trade and the development of Asia along machine lines. Naturally all the United States desired was an "Open Door" policy in which we might deal with the East on the same terms as any other nation. Now, in 1899, supported by the strength of our island possessions in the Pacific and our large navy, the United States secretary of state, John

INTERNATIONAL COMPLICATIONS. TREATIES 593 

Hay, wrote to the foreign powers asking that they grant our demand for the "Open Door." They acceded to our request. 

Boxer Rebellion. United States Troops in China. 

Meanwhile, in China, the leaders of the people, aroused by the signs that foreign nations were planning to develop Chinese industry and trade for foreign profit, took the stand, "China for the 

Chinese." In repressing a rebellion, called the "Boxer 

Rebellion," many foreigners lost their lives. Much foreign property was destroyed.

United States troops, Japa nese troops, and European soldiers combined to put down the rebellion. China was forced to sign a treaty promising to pay the foreign powers large indemnities in settlement of the damages and costs. The United States' 

share was twenty-four million dollars.

Binding Atlantic and Pacific. The Panama Canal. 

---

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

The interest of the United States in the Pacific rapidly increased and almost every year saw some new step to strengthen its position on the Western ocean. 

The next move by this country was the building of a canal to bind the Atlantic and the Pacific oceans. 

The idea of such a canal had occurred to the Spaniards when they first saw the narrow stretch of land across Central America, but nothing was done until about the year 1880, when a French company, under an engineer named De Lesseps, tried to build a canal, without success. 

Thirty years before this time the United States and Great Britain had agreed some day to jointly undertake through a private corporation the building of a canal between the two oceans. In the year 1901 Great Britain and the United 

States signed a new treaty, the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, by which it was agreed that the United States might act alone and exclusively in building a canal. 

At the insistence of President Roosevelt, Congress passed the Isthmian Canal Act in 1902, arranging for the purchase of the rights of the French Company to build a canal across the Isthmus of Panama. This isthmus was part of Colombia, a South American Republic. When Colombia refused to agree, the people of Panama revolted, set up a separate republic, and granted to the United States a lease in perpetuity to the desired territory. 

The building of the Panama Canal by Colonel Goethals, the engineer, and his workers was one of the most gigantic tasks of the Machine Age. It was aided not only by the new machinery run by steam and electric power; it was also aided by the new science of bacteriology. As experiments had proved that malaria is carried by a species of mosquito, Colonel Gorgas, sanitary engineer, waged a scientific and successful war against these pests. 

By 1914 the huge canal was completed and ships passed

INTERNATIONAL COMPLICATIONS. TREATIES 595 

through. That same year Congress withdrew a law providing that American coastwise vessels would not have to pay toll. Tolls were to be paid by our ships on equal terms with the ships of other nations which benefit by this great help in world trade. But the canal is especially important to America, serving as it does to bind our own states and colonies, West and East, by ocean. It brings our Atlantic and Gulf ports closer to Western ports, to the 

Spanish-American republics on the Pacific coast, and to the Far East. It brings our 

Pacific ports closer to our own East, closer to the Spanish-American republics on the Atlantic coast, and closer also to Europe and Africa.

World Figure. - Important as was the work of Goethals and his men, a leading figure in the building of the Panama 

Canal was Theodore Roosevelt.

Red Sea, a ship can circumnavigate the world without passing south of 

Africa and South America, as Magellan and Drake had to do. 

This New Yorker, the son of a Southern mother and a Northern father, was from first to last a champion of the thing which is now called "Americanism." He felt that America stood for something valuable in the progress of man; that it was the duty of every good American to fight the forces of evil which were at work in the land.

Roosevelt was the twenty-sixth president of the United States (19011909). Leading events of his administration were: extension of presidential power through Roosevelt's forceful policy; conservation program launched; arbitration of coal strike;

In every office Roosevelt fought not only for clean politics but also for governmental efficiency and social justice as he saw these things. 

As president, he was a champion of conservation, of laws to protect laborers against overgreedy and callous employers, of arbitration in strikes which affected public utilities. To check the wrongs done by certain corporations, he wielded what people called the "Big Stick," threatening to pass laws against the corporations unless they would of their own accord put their own house in order. 

He had no quarrel against Big Business as long as it was honest and fair. He believed in the business system of the country, but saw that there was danger in permitting the large corporations to go too far in exercising the power

INTERNATIONAL COMPLICATIONS. TREATIES 597 

which independent control gave them. And he insisted that to save law, order, and government, even Big Business itself, it was necessary to face the industrial problems of the day and to obtain a "square deal" for all. 

Roosevelt, however, was a powerful force not only in domestic affairs but also in foreign relations, in which his habit of firm action did much to bring recognition for 

America as a world power. 

Roosevelt Secures Russo-Japanese Peace. — In the year 1905, when Russia and Japan were at war, Roosevelt suggested that they cease their fighting and attempt to come to terms. The suggestion was accepted. Peace delegates met at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, but the Japanese and Russians seemed unable to agree. Then Roosevelt used his personal influence, writing directly to the home governments who wrote back to their representatives at Portsmouth suggesting that they compromise. The war was ended.

The success of this bold move on Roosevelt's part increased the growing regard of the European nations for America's position as a world power. 

Relations with Spanish-American Republics. - Not only did the Panama Canal bring all parts of America closer to the East in which the European powers were now so much interested; it also brought the United States closer to all of the twenty Spanish-American republics from 

Mexico southward.

The United States had the trade advantage of being closer to these republics. On the other hand, it had the disadvantage of being regarded with suspicion, because in the attempt to protect American interests against revolutionary disturbances, and to protect some of the almost bankrupt republics from foreign armies, the United States had occasionally taken a strong hand, using its power to

For several years the Mexican situation was our most serious foreign problem. With many American corporations and private citizens holding valuable property in Mexico, with European corporations and citizens also interested in Mexican property, the United States had the double task of defending its own citizens against losses due to revolutionary disorders and also of holding Mexico, if possible, to a policy which would prevent any European nation from sending its armies into Mexico and so breaking down the Monroe Doctrine. But America soon had a more serious problem to face.

AMERICAN NEUTRALIT CHAPTER XLII The European Maelstrom: Keeping Out of the World War When the Rivalries of European Powers Seeking World Colonies and World Trade Lead to the World War, the United 

States, in Spite of a Declaration of Neutrality, Feels Itself Being Drawn into the Conflict 

The World War Begins in Europe. Central Powers vs. Allies. On August 1, 1914, the World War broke out in Europe. 

In spite of all the talk and even the practice of arbitration, in spite of the Peace Court at The Hague, in spite of the careful balancing of European powers, the event which many had long feared took place. 

For years Europe had been an armed camp. Again and again some move by one power or another had caused a clanking of swords, but just as often the danger had passed for the moment. The underlying causes for an explosion of violence remained. Germany and Austria, 

602

the Central Powers of Europe, were interested in gaining their way through Constantinople to Persia, so reaching Asiatic trade by land, while the other powers reached it by The Slavic Balkan States stood in the way of this plan of the Central Powers. Slavic Russia had more reasons than one for supporting the Balkan peoples against the Central Powers. France, which had suffered at the hands of Germany in 1870, opposed Germany's ambition because of her fear of a powerful Germany. Great Britain, not at all pleased by Germany's success in manufacturing, had joined with her old enemies, France and Russia, for the purpose of making clear to Germany and Austria-Hungary that their every move was being watched. 

So the stage was set for war. The spark which caused the hatred, fears, and jealousies of the rival powers to flame up into war was a relatively trivial incident. An Austrian archduke and his wife, while visiting in Bosnia, one of Austria's Balkan province states, were assassinated by a Bosnian who was attempting to displace Austrian and set up Serbian rule. Austria declared that the Serbian government had favored the assassination. 

Austria made drastic demands on Serbia. Serbia yielded on all but two points and agreed to submit these to arbitration. Secret conferences were held between diplomats of the different nations. 

Just why this time the clanking swords remained unsheathed no one can yet say for a certainty. The fact is that Germany and Austria, France and Russia, all mobilized their troops. War was on, with German armies rushing through neutral Belgium in the effort to swiftly strike southward at Paris and northward toward the English Channel ports; with French troops rushing to recapture the lost provinces of Alsace and Lorraine; with Russia planning to capture German and Austrian Poland.

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

Great Britain, aroused by the violation of Belgium's neutrality, which moreover threatened her own safety, threw in her lot with France, Belgium, Russia, and Serbia. As the struggle continued, Turkey and Bulgaria entered on the side of Germany and Austria, known as the Central Powers; Japan, Italy, and a long array of other nations joined the opposing side. The nations fighting the Central 

Powers became known as the Allies. 

Wilson Declares Neutrality. The War a Maelstrom. 

The battle ground was Europe, but the troops and ships came from the four corners of the earth. Immediately after the outbreak of the war, President Wilson declared that the policy of this country would be neutrality. While many people in the United States, because of blood ties, were strongly pro-German or pro-Ally, he advised a policy of "hands off.” To a few men, however, it was clear from the beginning that with the growing interdependence of nations the war could not leave the United States untouched. The American people might try to remain neutral but their lives as well as their sympathies were bound to be drawn into the European maelstrom. 

Military Strategy of the War-Land and Sea. There is no need to concern ourselves with the detailed strategy of the European War. On land, Germany and Austria fought off the combined armies of the Allies, carrying the battle for the most part into the lands of their enemies, with ghastly loss of life on both sides. 

At sea the British navy was able to maintain supremacy, keeping the German fleet bottled up in Kiel Harbor in the 

North Sea and stopping all direct trade between Germany and the rest of the world.

Freedom of Sea Checked: British Confiscations and 

German Submarines. — The deadlock between the Central

Powers and the Allies resembled the one between Great

Britain and France during the Napoleonic Wars. As in the case of the Napoleonic Wars, each side attempted to break the deadlock by using its warships to deprive the United States and other neutrals of the freedom of the seas.

Soon after the beginning of the World War American trade with both sides increased greatly as each ordered from the United States great quantities of foodstuffs and ammunition. 

American ammunition could not reach Germany directly because, according to international law, British warships had the right to seize cargoes of war supplies destined for the enemy, and Great Britain's navy was strong enough to enforce this right. Great Britain, however, was not content with seizing war supplies. She denied the neutral nations the right to ship even foodstuffs to the Central Powers on the ground that foodstuffs, like ammunition, helped to prolong war and were therefore contraband and subject to seizure. 

Germany used her newly invented submarines to sink enemy merchant vessels without making sure that the lives of neutrals on board would not be endangered. German submarines even sank neutral merchant vessels. The 

Germans claimed that the submarine could be used only in swift and surprise attacks and that as the submarine was her only weapon against the English navy, Germany had to use it in the only way it could be used. 

Sinking of the Lusitania. Divided Feeling in America.

Wilson's Notes. - The United States protested against 

England's confiscations of American cargoes and against Germany's submarine warfare as violations of international law.

Of the two evils, the one which aroused the more bitter controversy was the German use of the submarine. When

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

the Lusitania, a British Cunard liner, was sunk off the Irish coast with a loss of more than a thousand lives including one hundred fourteen Americans, there were many in the United States who favored an immediate declaration On the other hand there was in this country a large number of citizens of Teutonic stock who, although they were shocked by the sinking of the Lusitania, sympathized with the Central Powers. Many other Americans felt that under no circumstances should the United States enter into the European conflict, on one side or the other.

President Wilson, acting as the leader of those who sought to keep the country out of the European struggle, preferred to regard the sinking of the Lusitania as something never intended by the German government. Accordingly Wilson sent a note demanding that Germany disavow the act, make reparations, and give orders which would end this sort of warfare. The note also contained a warning.

As the German reply did not satisfy Wilson, he sent a second note.

While the notes were passing back and forth, the submarines were continuing their attacks and neutral vessels were being sunk. Still Wilson sought to maintain peace. 

And when Germany in a new note, on May 4, 1916, promised not to sink merchant vessels without warning, agreeing to provide for the safety of passengers on such ships as submarines would attack unless the ships would try to escape or offer resistance, Wilson's course seemed fully justified. 

Election Campaign, 1916. "He Kept Us Out of War." - In the election campaign of 1916 the Republican candidate for President was Charles Evans Hughes. The 

Democratic candidate was Woodrow Wilson. When the

campaigning was over and the votes were counted, Wilson was reëlected. His popular vote had increased by almost three million over his 1912 vote.

Since the chief slogan of the Wilson champions was "He kept us out of War," the vote was interpreted by many to mean that a majority of the people approved of Wilson's policy of forbearance. 

Foreign Spies and Agents in United States. How ever, those who were for peace soon learned that Wilson's forbearance was not destined to prevent war. While they were still congratulating themselves on Wilson's reëlection there came proof upon proof that Germany and Austria, unable to prevent United States supplies from reaching the Allies by sea, were determined to block these exports by other means.

In the trial of criminals in open court it was shown that the German and Austrian embassies in Washington were the headquarters from which agitators, spies, and desperadoes were hired to stir up strikes, to destroy bridges, to blow up factories, to set bombs in ships. German money was being used to buy and control newspapers for the purpose of creating hatred and misunderstanding between the 

United States and the Allies. 

In the face of these proofs, President Wilson sent the Austrian ambassador home and ordered that certain of the subordinates of the German embassy must leave Washington.

Germany Renews Submarine Warfare. - About one month before President Wilson's second inauguration, Count Von Bernstorff, the German ambassador, informed the President that Germany had decided to renew her submarine warfare. The President regarded this as a direct challenge, and accordingly decided to take such swift action as would prove to Germany that the patience

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

of the American people had been strained to the breaking point. 

Without delay President Wilson sent Von Bernstorff home and while still hoping for peace, the President wrote a note warning Germany that a renewal of submarine attacks must lead to war.

Tense days followed. The people saw that the country was hanging over the dark abyss of war. Everything depended on Germany's next move. Would she force the

United States into the field against her? Soon there was news of defenseless ships torpedoed at sea; and still the war declaration was withheld.

Germany Seeks Mexico as Ally. Then United States secret service officials unearthed the fact that the German foreign secretary had written to Mexico to urge her to be ready to join with Germany in the event of war with the United States. That letter made public seems to have been the last straw. 

1 

A Declaration of War. On April 2, 1917, President 

Wilson went before a joint session of Congress and read a message in which he summed up the nation's grievances and called for action. He pointed out that it was necessary for the United States to take steps against the autocratic 

German rulers; against the German people themselves we had no ill will.

Four days later Congress solemnly declared that a state of war existed between Germany and the United States.
