CHAPTER XLIII America in the World War 

After the United States Enters the War the Nation, Through a Council of 

National Defense and Other Agencies, Organizes Its Every Resource for the Struggle.

More than a Million American Troops 

Fighting on French Soil Help to Win the Victory 

The War to End All Wars. With the action of Con gress in April, 1917, the die was cast. American troops were soon to be fighting beside the Allied forces. American men and women behind the lines, in fields and mines, in mills, shops, and factories, in business offices, scientific laboratories, schools, and homes were soon to be exerting all their energies to help win the war. 

That the American people, irrespective of the land of their birth, responded almost as one to the call of war was due first to the spirit of patriotism which had been implanted in them, and second to the fact that President Wilson had placed before them the larger issue of the war as "A War to end War."

He pointed out that if autocracy could triumph in Europe, no democracy anywhere would be safe. He urged 610

that the war should be fought not merely to defeat the power of the German Kaiser; it should have as its goal a peace which would so insure world justice that another world war would be impossible. 

His plea awakened a responsive chord in the American people, the more recently naturalized Americans as well as the older Americans, the Americans of Germanic descent as well as the Americans of British descent. It was echoed in the war-torn lands of Europe, even in the hearts of the 

Science in 

Modern Warfare 

Airplane observers directed the artillery fire and reported movements of the enemy by signals, radio, telephone, and wireless. war-weary Germans eager for the happier day of world justice and world peace which Wilson promised as the American goal in entering the war. 

Industry, Invention, and Science in Modern Warfare. - 

The World War into which America was entering surpassed in scale any other war in history; in the number of men involved, in cost, in loss of life, in destruction of property, and possibly in the social and political changes which it brought about.

Because of the need of producing supplies and equipment for the enormous numbers of men engaged, the war required a most careful organization of every phase of industry; the victory depended almost as much upon

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

sustained production and transportation of foodstuffs, clothes, and ammunition as upon actual fighting. 

New inventions such as the automobile, wireless communication, the airplane, and long-range photography played a large part in the war. Automobiles carried troops from front to front. Automobile trucks carried supplies. Ambulance cars carried the wounded back to base-hospitals. 

Armored cars clearing barbed-wire fences rooted out enemy machine-guns. Airplanes were useful in taking observations of enemy movements, and long-range photographs taken from the planes gave the position of enemy forces and guns. Combat airplanes dropping explosives were used to attack the enemy lines. Wireless communication kept all sections of the armies in touch. The Germans used submarines for under-sea attack and zeppelins for bombing enemy towns.

The part played by science in the war was twofold, partly to help in saving life and partly to destroy life. 

Army doctors, profiting by recent discoveries in preventive medicine and sanitary engineering, helped to keep down sickness and the death rate even among the wounded. On the other hand the science of chemistry, so valuable to man in peace times, furnished the opposing forces with two of their most deadly weapons, explosive bombs and poison gases.

Trench Warfare. — Because of the high-power guns and the large forces of men engaged in this war, forts played a small part in military strategy. In order to hold their relative positions after the initial German drive, the opposing forces dug themselves into trenches where they enjoyed a measure of safety from the bursting bombs fired by longrange guns or dropped by airplanes. For years before the entrance of the American troops the intrenched Allied soldiers in Belgium and in France faced the intrenched

German soldiers. There were many battles and terrific loss of life, but few gains were made on either side. 

The Council for National Defense. Industrial Resources. 

Morale. Now that America was entering the struggle the first task facing the lead- 

ers was the organization of the nation's industrial life and the support of its morale or fighting spirit.

When war was declared, the country was far from prepared, and according to the opinion of many experts, a long time would elapse before it could be ready to play an important part in the actual fighting.

The immediate question therefore was: Could the 

United States organize its industrial forces and its morale so as to bring swift and efficient aid to the Allies?

Trench Warfare 

Owing to the use of machine guns, direct attacks in mass formation were paid for with a terrific loss of life. For this reason much of the war was fought from a series of trenches, tens of miles long.

This question had been foreseen some months before

America entered the war and Congress had set out to answer it by appointing a Council for National Defense to consider some of the problems of preparedness.

Immediately after the United States entered the war this council acted through separate boards to organize the nation so that it would be able to make fullest use of its natural resources and maintain at its highest level the national morale.

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER The Shipping Board created the Emergency Fleet Cor poration which built ships for the transportation of men and goods. 

The War Labor Board undertook to obtain the maximum service from labor by arbitrating labor disputes. 

The War Industries Board watched over the industrial plants to speed up the production of war goods; and the Feeding the Allied Armies War Finance Corporation provided these industries with necessary loans.

The Food Administration, with Herbert C. Hoover at its head, took steps to increase the crops of the country and to prevent the waste of foodstuffs through the organization of a conservation program, which would save plenty of food for the American army and for the Allied armies and peoples. To this end aid was extended to farmers; school gardens and gardens in city lots added to production; the people of the country voluntarily submitted to meatless days and wheatless days. 

The Fuel Administration regulated the use of coal and

of gasoline so as to save fuel for the war industries and the army.

The Commissioner of Public Information supplied the newspapers with information to help keep public opinion aroused. His bureau sent out pamphlets by millions, and organized a body of thousands of public speakers, the Four-Minute Men, who acted as direct spokesmen for the nation in explaining its aims and plans to the people. 

To still further help in pulling all forces of the country together, the United States took over the railroads and the telephones, the telegraphs, and the ocean cables. 

Financing the War. In so far as the cost of war was concerned, it was clear from the start that if the war was to last, the nation would need billions of dollars. For one thing, as the Allies no longer had funds with which to buy supplies and ammunition, the United States government would have to make loans to them to cover their purchases. 

Before the war was over about ten billion dollars were loaned to the Allies. The actual war cost to the United 

States came to another twenty-two billions. 

About one-third of the war funds was raised on a pay-as-you-go policy. In order that the war should not impose too great a burden on future generations, the government taxed personal and corporation incomes, excess profits, the luxuries and many of the necessities which the people bought. The remainder of the war cost was secured by borrowing money from the people through the means of Liberty Bonds. 

Liberty Bonds, paying interest, were offered to the people in denominations of fifty to one thousand dollars; and with the aid of an organization of committees which reached practically every man and woman in the country, four Liberty Loan offers (and one Victory Loan after the Armistice) were subscribed. War-saving certificates and thrift

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

stamps in smaller denominations were sold through the United States post offices throughout the country. 

Welfare Work. In no other war were there so many agencies seeking to alleviate something of the horror and suffering of warfare.

Organizations such as the Red Cross, the Young Men's 

Christian Association, the Young Women's Christian 

Welfare Work in World War 

In addition to aiding the sick and wounded, welfare workers aimed to keep up the spirits of the well soldiers through extras in food and through entertainment.

Association, the Knights of Columbus, the American Library Association, the Salvation Army, the Jewish Welfare Board, all devoted themselves to the task of welfare work. 

The government also took a hand in welfare work by making monthly allotments of money to the wives of soldiers, by insuring soldiers against disability or death, by providing for the reeducation of maimed soldiers in vocations which would enable them to earn a livelihood. 

Women's Share in the War. - Not all the fighting spirit was shown by the men. Women also did their share.

The women of the Young Women's Christian Association and the Salvation Army engaged in relief work at the front. 

Women nurses under the American Red Cross worked in the base-hospitals and even on the fighting lines. Many army ambulances were driven by women. Within the 

United States, women took the place of men on farms, in factories, in business offices, and in ammunition plants. 

Women members of the various women's organizations sewed, knitted, and prepared bandages for the supply of the army. Women helped the government in raising war funds. Women in their homes carried out the government program of food conservation. 

Young People Aid the Cause. — Through the schools, women teachers as well as men teachers explained the causes and the objects of the war and enlisted the coöperation of school boys and girls in the planting of war gardens and the sale of war bonds. Children invested in thrift stamps which the government sold at the small price of only twenty-five cents as an additional means of raising funds and interesting all classes of the country in the active support of the war. Through the Junior Red Cross many useful articles were made and sent to the soldiers in the trenches and in the camps. 

The American Navy. For some time before the 

Spanish-American War the United States had been improving its navy both in the size and quality of the ships and in the training of the crews. The Philippine war proved the efficiency of the new navy. With the entrance of 

America into the World War steps were taken to further strengthen the navy by the building of additional ships. 

But there was no delay about getting the available fleet into action.

Since the German navy was not at large, the principal work that the United States warships had to do was

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

to fight the submarine peril. Almost immediately after war was declared Admiral Sims arrived in England and reported ready for action. With British coöperation the 

American ships commenced laying a line of depth-bombs, an American invention, in the path which German submarines, seeking the broad ocean, must cross. This move served to check the submarine activity considerably. 

Other United States warships were detailed to act as a coast guard to prevent submarine attacks on American 

United States Warships, 1917 

Although the United States navy had no occasion to fight a single pitched battle during the war, it played a great part in winning the final victory. shipping in American waters. When American troops began to leave for France, American warships acted as convoys for the transports to protect them against submarine attacks. So well was this work done that two millions of troops reached France with not a single transport lost. - - 

The American Army: Regulars; National Guard;

Selective Service Draft. At the outbreak of the war the Regular Army of the United States numbered less than three hundred thousand. This number was increased by act of Congress and volunteer enlistments. The National 

Guard, consisting of the state militia which had been mustered into the federal service during the recent trouble

with Mexico, numbered a few hundred thousand more. 

Not content with these numbers, Congress, upon the advice of President Wilson, passed the Selective Service Act, which provided that all American citizens between twentyone and thirty-one should be registered and that soldiers should be drafted from among them according to their classification. Those with dependents or those who were engaged in some essential industry were not to be enlisted. The age limits were later changed to eighteen and forty-five. The draftees selected in this way were enrolled in the National Army.

Through these various means the American army grew to the point where it numbered almost four million men. Before the war was over about two million of these reached France and practically two-thirds of these two million, fighting on the fighting on the battle lines, helped in winning the final victory. 

John J. Pershing 

General Pershing commanded the American army during the 

World War. A British military ex pert has written, "Without that army the war could hardly have been saved and could not have been won." 

The commander of the United 

States forces was General John 

J. Pershing, who, along with Foch, the French commander, and Haig, the British commander, formed the Supreme War Council. Toward the end of the war Ferdinand Foch was given supreme command of the combined Allied forces on the western front.

Germans' Drive. The Bat tle of Chateau-Thierry.

When the German leaders heard that Americans were arriving in France at the rate of ten thousand and more a week, they determined to break the long deadlock by again driving through Belgium to the English Channel and through France to Paris.

In Russia, the strongest of the European Allied nations in manpower, there had been a revolution, after which a group of Bolshevists, or Communists, came into power. 

The new leaders made peace with Germany at Brest- Litovsk early in 1918; and soon after Rumania, another of the Allies on the eastern front, laid down her arms. 

This left Germany free to concentrate her whole fighting strength for her new drive on the western front.

Both in Belgium and in France the Germans won new

ground and things looked desperate for the Allies. That the Germans did not break through was due in part at least to the presence of the American troops who by this time were considerable in number and fresh in spirit.

France where the German advance reached the Marne River, American troops in a hard-fought battle helped to hold the line at Chateau-Thierry. American soldiers went into the near-by Belleau Wood and after days of hard

Offensive. Meuse-Argonne 

Campaign. Foch now ordered a counter-drive against the Germans. To the Americans now organized as a distinct command under General Pershing fell a considerable and important section of the fighting front. 

American and French forces under American command captured St. Mihiel. The

Americans then fought their way through the Argonne 

Forest. After almost seven weeks of hard fighting the Allied forces, engaged in the Meuse-Argonne operation, reached their objective, Sedan, the railway center, upon which the Germans depended for supplies and reënforcements. The Germans were forced to withdraw from Sedan, and with this lost to them the position of the German armies was considerably weakened. 

These victories which Americans shared with the French were only a few of the victories won by the French, British, and Americans during the summer and autumn of 1918.

The Allied offensive in France and Belgium was successful all along the line. To the south, the Austrian army suffered defeat at the hands of Italy. 

The Armistice. - Back of the German lines, the people, despairing of a victorious end, were ready to rise in revolt. 

The Kaiser, sensing the danger, fled; the German people, establishing a republic, appealed to President Wilson to negotiate an armistice.

On November 11, 1918, the Armistice was signed. 

The German armies laid down their arms and withdrew behind the Rhine River. The Allied Forces occupied 

Germany as far east as the Rhine. The details of the peace were to be decided in a conference at Versailles. 

Anti-Aircraft Guns at Night 

During the World War the airplane was used not only for the observation of enemy movements, but also for the bombing of enemy positions. To offset the danger of airplane attacks, military engineers devised anti-aircraft guns which can be swung so as to shoot almost directly overhead. Highpower electric searchlights are used for the detection of airplanes at night.

CHAPTER XLIV Planning World Relationships 

After Wilson Secures a Treaty Which Incorporates Many of the "Fourteen Points" Including the League of Nations, Congress

Refuses to Ratify the Treaty-A Separate Peace Is Made, Yet the Problems of German Disarmament and Rep aration, Growing Partly Out of the Versailles Treaty, Remain to be Faced and Solved- Another Difficult Post-War Problem Is the Matter of Allied Debts 

The Peace Conference. Wilson's Fourteen Points. 

Setting aside all precedent, President Wilson decided to attend the Peace Conference at Versailles as the head of the American delegation. He did this, no doubt, primarily because he was eager to see the Peace Treaty realize the promise which he had made to the American people that victory in the World War would end all wars forever. 

To accomplish this purpose it would be necessary for the Peace Treaty to be just, to settle old disputes fairly, to arouse no new rancors, to put an end to the oppression or exploitation of weaker nations, to find a means for com- 626

pelling the peaceful adjustment of such quarrels as might arise between any nations large or small. 

Months before the Armistice was signed, Wilson had voiced these ideas for a just and lasting peace under fourteen points, the most important of which was the fourteenth point, providing for a league of nations which would guarantee to unite the member nations as one in the enforcement of all the other points. 

Wilson at Conference.

Seeks League of Nations. - 

When Wilson arrived at Paris he found that his task would be difficult. Some of the members of the Allied delegations were not wholly in favor of Wilson's plan. 

Because of old fears, old jealousies and rivalries, old ambitions for extended territory, these men stood out against some of the fourteen points. A few of the Allied countries were even committed, by secret treaties of ano mail 199 

Woodrow Wilson

Wilson was the twenty-eighth president of the United States (19131921). Leading events of his administration were: Underwood Tariff;

The President was extremely discouraged. His enthusiastic reception in Europe seemed to prove that the common people pinned their faith to him as a deliverer

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

who would forever abolish war. Yet it now appeared that, try as he would, the peace treaty might only serve to sow the seeds of new wars. 

Once he was on the point of an open diplomatic break with an Allied country. At another time he made preparations to return home as a protest against steps which he regarded as unjust. Finally, although he had to yield on a few of the fourteen points, he won out on the others. Above all, he had gained an agreement on the point nearest to his heart a League of Nations Covenant in the peace treaty. 

Treaty of Versailles. Major Terms. By the terms of the Versailles Treaty, the map of Europe was remade in the main along the line which Wilson had championed -the recognition of the rights of the subject peoples of Europe to the enjoyment of independence. Austria and 

Hungary became separate nations. Poland, which had been dismembered in earlier wars and had been ruled as 

Russian Poland, German Poland, and Austrian Poland, was reunited and reëstablished as a nation. Alsace and 

Lorraine, which Germany had taken from France in 1871, were restored to France.

Under the terms of the treaty Germany was stripped of much of her former power. The German colonies in Africa and her spheres of influence in China were taken from her. 

The treaty further provided that Germany must make reparations to the Allies for the cost of the war and the losses inflicted by her armies, her airplanes, zeppelins, and submarines.

A section of the treaty contained a plan for a League of Nations, its organization and its objects. All nations subscribing to the conditions set forth were eligible to membership in this league, with the exception of Germany and of Russia, which under Bolshevik rule was not recognized as a nation by the treaty-making powers.

Congress Rejects League of Nations Plan. - When the peace treaty was brought before the United States Senate for its approval, as provided for in the Constitution, there was active opposition to the League of Nations plan. This opposition centered largely around a clause which the League opponents claimed would make the United States a party to the enforced settlement of any disputes arising among nations. Now that the war was over many Americans favored a policy of aloofness, withdrawal from anything resembling an entangling alliance with European powers whose rivalries might lead to fresh wars. 

Wilson Touring for League Breaks Down. President 

Wilson, deeply hurt by the opposition in the Senate, determined to carry his case to the people. He hoped by a series of addresses all through the country to get the people to agree with him that in the new international situation which had grown out of the Machine Age, no nation could stand aloof; that world peace depended upon world coöperation in an international alliance for the preservation of peace.

In the course of his tour Wilson's health gave way. He returned to the White House, a broken man, and died not long after the end of his term of office. 

Election of Harding. Versailles Treaty not Signed. 

Separate Peace. — In the election campaign of 1920 the problem of America's entrance into the League was one of the important issues, with the Democratic candidate strongly for it, and the Republican candidate, Warren G. 

Harding, opposed, although favoring steps by the United States toward some form of international coöperation. 

Harding was overwhelmingly elected.

A separate peace, with the League of Nations plan omitted, was made with Germany.

One by one the other nations joined the League of Na-

tions which concerned itself with many world problems. 

Americans selected by the League have served in the "World Court" established by the League for the purpose of promoting international peace and justice, but these Americans had no official relation with the United States government.

Harding Dies. Coolidge President. Reparations. The 

Dawes Plan. Shortly after the conclusion of the Disarmament Conference, President Harding left Washington for a speaking tour and a trip to Alaska. On his way back to the capital he fell ill and died. Vice President Coolidge became President in 1923 and completed Harding's term of office.

During this time there was in Europe another possible cause for trouble in the settlement of the reparation claims which, according to the treaty, Germany was to pay to the Allies. France, who had suffered most heavily during the war, was to receive about half of this sum, and when Germany failed to make payment either as large or as punctually as the treaty provided, French soldiers occupied the Ruhr, a valuable coal section in Germany. 

To effect a less dangerous way of bringing about payment of reparations, an international Reparations Commission was appointed, which adopted the plan urged by Charles G. Dawes, who had been chosen as president of the commission. After fixing the sum which it seemed likely that Germany could afford, the "Dawes Plan" provided the amount to be paid off annually as well as the means of raising and handling this sum in Germany.

CHAPTER XLV The Dawn of a New Era 

After the Armistice Congress Faces the Task of Restoring the Country to a Peace Basis During This Period New Developments Open Up a New Era in World Trade and Present New Problems for Living Americans to Meet- The Depression and the New Deal 

- - Domestic Post-War Problems. Difficult as were the foreign problems which grew out of the World War, the nation had to face many other difficult problems right at home. 

With the close of war the drafted military forces had to be brought home, demobilized, and, in the case of the more or less incapacitated, aided to a new start in life. The railroads, the telephones, the telegraph, and cables, operated by the government during the war, had to be restored to their owners by the government. The fleet, owned and operated by the United States Shipping Board as a war 635

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

measure, had to be disposed of since the government found continued ownership unprofitable. Agriculture, manufacture, and trade, all of which had been organized on a war basis, also had to be readjusted to peace conditions, a difficult problem which brought in its wake the old problem of strikes. 

Shortly after the war, the farmer, the manufacturer, and the merchant found Europe no longer a heavy buyer and the American consumers far less extravagant because fearful of coming changes. For a short while, business speculation which had been going on during the war continued feverishly. Then the financial break came. There was general business depression and the nation was saved from a serious panic only through the operation of the Federal Reserve Banks which used their credit power to bring about a gradual readjustment rather than a sudden stoppage of industry.

In the face of the mounting cost of government there was the problem of planning government expenditures in a more systematic way.

To help in readjusting these various phases of the nation's life to a peace-time basis, the government, acting as the servant of the people, took a hand through special laws passed by Congress. 

The Budget Act. The problem of governmental expenditures was met during President Harding's administration by the passing of a budget act which provided that each year every department of the government must prepare a detailed statement of what it will need for the following year, and that Congress would then vote the necessary funds only after careful consideration of this budget. 

Through this improved bookkeeping, it is possible to check old-time extravagance, the government can estimate just what funds will be necessary to meet its needs

and can adjust its revenue measures accordingly. By strict economy, made possible by this plan, the government has been able to make remarkable inroads on the enormous debt which accumulated during the World War. 

The Problem of Demobilization. By the time the 

Budget Act was passed, the task of bringing the soldiers back from France had been accomplished and most of the men had been mustered out of the service. However, the restoration of millions of men to industrial life was not a simple matter. Because of decreased production in all the industries, men were being discharged rather than taken on. This situation involved considerable hardship for the ex-soldiers and soon the American Legion, a powerful organization of ex-service men, began to work for a soldier's bonus.

Congress passed a Bonus Act only to have it vetoed first by President Harding and then by President Coolidge, both of whom opposed it on the score of economy. Then 

Congress, by a two-thirds vote, passed the act over the presidential veto. In the case of incapacitated soldiers, previous wars had generally seen these left as hopeless human wreckage, symbols of the forgetfulness and ingratitude of nations. After the World War the government planned to use the modern science of medicine and its host of skillful teachers in the task of "rehabilitation," or in other words the total or partial restoration of the disabled soldier to peace-time usefulness. The government provided hospitals for cure and care of the sick and crippled, schools for the teaching of new trades or professions, better suited to the physical condition of the men. 

Readjusting Agriculture. The Farm Bloc. Farming 

Legislation.

The farmer whose crops had played so large a part in winning the war found himself hard hit by peace which reduced his world market and brought competing

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

foreign produce into his home market. In order to make more certain of helpful legislation in Congress, a number of representatives from distinctly agricultural sections of the country joined as a group, known as the Farm Bloc. 

Largely because of the firm stand of the Farm Bloc, Congress passed a series of acts designed to help the agricultural interests of the country to meet post-war conditions: acts to regulate freight rates, acts to protect the prices of the farmers' crops by imposing a tariff on certain imported farm products. The farmers, not depending wholly upon Congressional legislation, attempted to relieve the pressure of the post-war period through coöperative marketing and coöperative buying. For years before the war there had been many coöperative farmer organizations, but the movement for coöperative marketing and coöperative buying made its greatest strides after the war. 

Manufactures Return to Peace Basis. For a time it seemed that readjustment in the manufacturing industries could not be accomplished without most serious disturbances. During the war, manufactures and farming had been organized on the basis of a world market. In the case of manufacturing this meant greatly enlarged plants, increased purchase of raw materials, increased production of finished product. Shortly after the war ended it appeared that many of the manufacturing plants were far too large for ordinary peace-time needs, that they were overstocked with raw materials bought at high prices, and with unsold products for which there was a rapidly shrinking market. 

Corporations obliged to reëstimate their holdings found that in a few months their plants and stock had depreciated in value by millions of dollars. As Europe was too poor to buy American goods and as Americans began to practice thrift, the manufacturing industries seemed in a poor way. 

Although Congress swiftly raised the tariff wall against a

flood of cheap European goods, many people could see only darkness ahead.

Yet within a few years business conditions became essentially sound, and shops, mills, and factories were again prospering.

Readjusting Labor Conditions. Strikes, Injunctions, 

Government Intercession. During the period of readjustment in manufacturing, the old problem of strikes became more troublesome than at any previous period. 

While the war was going on, the cost of living had mounted steadily until at one time the purchasing value of a dollar, figured in terms of 1914 prices, had dropped to less than fifty cents.

During the war organized labor had consistently held to its patriotic course by trying to avoid strikes, and both employers and workers had been willing to settle most of their differences through arbitration, which tended to put wages at higher and higher levels. Almost immediately after the war ended when the corporations tried to reduce wages, a series of strikes broke out first in one industry, then in another. During one of these strikes the attorneygeneral obtained a court injunction against the strikers, forbidding them to use any means toward persuading men who were still at work to join them. The injunction was bitterly opposed by the labor unions. Strikes increased in number and in the bitterness of feeling on both sides. 

As these strikes were tending to completely disrupt the industrial life of the nation, the government again and again used its influence toward bringing about a settlement through compromise. 

Government Returns Railroads. Esch-Cummins Act. 

One of the early post-war acts of Congress was the return of the railroads, the telephone, the telegraph, and the cable to their owners. In the case of the railroads there was 3

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

much agitation concerning the terms under which the roads should be restored. Finally Congress passed the Esch- 

Cummins Act, which provided for the return of the railroads to the railroad companies with increased powers for the Interstate Commerce Commission; with a newly created 

Railroad Labor Board to adjust wage problems; and with a stipulation to the effect that the president shall have the right to take over the roads in the case of a national emergency. 

United States Shipping Board Sells Fleet. Congress also decided to discontinue the governmental operation of the fleet of merchant ships which it had acquired during the war, when it was hoped that the United States was on the way toward again becoming a leading ocean carrier, as in pre-Civil-War days. For some reason this hope did not materialize and many of the vessels operated by the Shipping Board were either scrapped or sold to foreign owners. 

Other Post-War Legislation. Immigration Laws. 

Amendments. It was during the process of reorganization in the post-war period that Congress passed the highly restrictive Immigration Acts, one in 1921, and a second in 1924, previously described. It was during this same period that Congress passed the Eighteenth or Prohibition Amendment, which became a part of the Constitution in January, 1919, and the Nineteenth or Woman's Suffrage Amendment, which granted women the right to vote. That this last amendment won the support of the required number of states was largely due to the great part which women played during the World War, not only in the home but also in industry, in welfare work, even in service on the fighting front.

Post-War Developments. Motion Pictures and Radio. 

-In some fields the United States has made tremendous strides since the World War, notably however in the motion-

picture industry and in the radio industry. To-day the 

United States produces about ninety per cent of the motion pictures shown in the theaters of the world. The United 

States also leads the world in the development of the radio industry with its many powerful broadcasting stations and its entertainment programs serving millions who have radio receiving apparatus.

Post-War Aviation. Ever since its military use in the 

World War, the airplane, first made practical by Curtiss and the Wright brothers, has made great progress. Interest in air travel has been helped by a series of thrilling flights, only a few of which can be listed here. In 1919 

Alcock and Brown made the first successful non-stop transatlantic flight. In 1927 Lindbergh made his famous solo flight from New York to Paris. In 1932 Mrs. Amelia 

Earhart Putnam, who as Miss Earhart flew the Atlantic with two pilots in 1928, won further fame as the first woman transatlantic solo flier. 

The first non-stop flight over the Pacific was made by 

Lieutenants Maitland and Hegenberger from California to Hawaii in 1927.

The first round-the-world flight was completed in 1924 by a fleet of United States Army service planes. In 

1931, Post and Gatty flew around the world in eight days. 

In 1933, Post bettered this record in a solo flight. 

Among the many other sensational flights, there were 

Commander Byrd's flight to the North Pole in 1926 and to the South Pole on Thanksgiving Day, 1929, and Lieutenant Commander Hawks' flight in 1933, when he flew from Los Angeles to New York in less than fourteen hours. 

That same year, Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh completed a 

29,000-mile aviation tour of the world.

There has been also an impressive development of transcontinental, high-speed, mail, express, and passenger service.

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

The Election of Herbert Hoover. In the presidential election campaign in 1928, when Alfred E. Smith, the 

Democratic candidate, made prohibition repeal a leading issue, Herbert Hoover, the Republican candidate, asked for the people's votes on the basis of the prosperity America had enjoyed under Coolidge, a Republican president. 

Hoover was elected. On 

March 4, 1929, he was inaugurated, and the American people looked forward to four more years of prosperity under a Republican president. However, there were some who claimed that party politics had little to Hoover was the thirty-first president do with prosperity, and that 

Herbert C. Hoover of the United States (1929-1933.) the prosperity the nation had enjoyed during the Coolidge years was about to collapse. 

The Depression. -In August, 1929, prosperity did collapse. There was a break in the stock market. Prices of stocks and bonds tumbled downwards. Billions of dollars worth of paper profits, the imaginary wealth created by the rising prices of the prosperity years, were wiped out within a few days.

Although few people realized it at the time, this break in the stock market marked the beginning of a period of hard times which came to be known as "The Depression."

During the depression, business corporations lost millions of dollars each year. Workers took cuts in wages or lost their jobs and joined the growing army of the unemployed. 

Farmers suffered heavily as farm prices dropped.

President Hoover hoped that the depression would pass of itself, as other periods of hard times had passed. Meanwhile he felt that Congress should do what it could to relieve the situation. To help business, Congress created the "Reconstruction Finance Corporation," which loaned money to hard-pressed banks and railroads. To help the farmer, Congress created the Federal Farm Board, which bought farm produce at prices above the market price. This produce was stored to be resold at a later date when, it was hoped, the Farm Board could get back the prices it had paid. To help relieve the unemployed, President Hoover urged that local communities contribute money to community funds for the relief of the distressed. To help create jobs for the unemployed, Congress set aside funds for federal public works, the name given to government construction work on dams, power houses, highways, or other such projects. Yet in spite of these and other forms of relief, the depression deepened, business slowed down, unemployment increased, and suffering became widespread. These conditions, it should be noted, appeared not alone in the United States, for the depression was world wide. 

Roosevelt Elected President. His Inauguration. In the summer of 1932, the Republicans renominated Hoover as their presidential candidate. The Democrats chose Franklin D. Roosevelt, then Governor of the State of New York, as their candidate. In November, Roosevelt was elected. 

On March 4, 1933, he was inaugurated as the thirty-second 

President of the United States. 

Four years earlier, when Hoover was inaugurated, the

United States seemed to have reached the height of prosperity; on the day of Roosevelt's inauguration, the nation seemed to have reached the depths of depression. 

Thousands of business firms were facing failure. Tens of thousands of farmers were facing the loss of their farms.

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

There were about twelve million unemployed workers. 

Billions of dollars of the people's money were tied up in banks that had failed. To check a wild rush of depositors to withdraw their funds, the governors of Michigan, Maryland, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts,

Illinois, and other states declared a "Bank Holiday" just before Roosevelt's inauguration.

President Roosevelt in his inaugural address had said, "We must act and act at once." The months that followed were, indeed, crowded with action. 

Republicans joined with Democrats, in Congress and out, to meet the crisis that the nation was facing. 

To understand President Roose velt's remarkable and novel program of action, let us consider his acts with respect to (1) national planning, (2) the money problem, (3) the problem of farm recovery, (4) the problem of industrial recovery, (5) the problem of unemployment relief, and (6) international problems. 

Franklin D. Roosevelt 

I. National Planning and the New Deal. During his campaign Roosevelt had promised that, if elected, he would give the American people a "New Deal." By the New 

Deal, President Roosevelt meant a national plan to fight the depression through a greater Federal control of the economic life of the nation. This national plan would be aimed toward guiding the farmer, the worker, and the business man toward economic recovery. 

II. The Problem of Money. The Banking Crisis. 

Roosevelt began immediately on the banking crisis. To restore to the people confidence in the banks, Roosevelt

took the following steps. closed all the banks in the country. On March 9th, Congress met in special session at his summons. This Congress passed the "Emergency Banking Act," which gave him complete control of the banking situation. Congress also made it illegal for any American to hoard gold; all gold was to be turned into the United States Treasury. Government officials examined the banks to decide which ones were sound. Sound banks were permitted to reopen their doors. 

The people trusted the reopened banks with their money, and the banking situation was gradually improved. 

On March 6th, he officially

To increase confidence in the reopened banks, Congress made other changes in the banking laws in 1935. It was also provided that deposits in banks connected with the Federal Reserve system should be insured against loss. 

The Federal Securities Act. To help protect the public against investment in unsound stocks, Congress passed the "Securities Act of 1933." This Act provided that the stocks or bonds of a new corporation should not be offered for sale unless these were first registered with the Federal government, along with true information concerning the soundness of the corporation, and that this information must be made known to the buyer. 

The Federal Budget. The Federal government had been spending more money than it had been receiving. Of course, that could not go on forever. The government needed to have a balanced budget; to reduce its expenses and increase its income until the amount of money received was at least equal to the money spent. However, because of the extraordinary expenses made necessary by the New 

Deal, the Federal debt mounted by billions.

Shall the Currency Be Inflated? - President Roosevelt and many other persons felt that one way to relieve the general depression of the country would be to raise prices

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

and particularly to raise prices of farm produce. With this idea in mind, a majority in Congress agreed that inflation of the currency or, in other words, the deliberate cheapening of the dollar and of its purchasing power, would help to raise the prices of farm produce and thus help the farmers to meet their debts. Consequently, in 

June, 1933, in an amendment to the "Agricultural Adjustment Act," Congress gave President Roosevelt power to inflate the currency, which it was suggested he could do by printing more paper money or by putting less gold into the gold dollar that backs the paper dollar.

President Roosevelt reduced the amount of gold in a dollar to $.5906, and tried a plan to manage the currency. 

This plan had several features: (1) the United States gave up paying its debts in gold (went off the gold standard); (2) hoarding of gold money was forbidden by law; (3) newly mined gold and silver were purchased by the Federal government at higher prices than had prevailed before, and gold was also purchased abroad. The effect of this plan has been to lower the value of the dollar and thus raise prices to some extent. 

III. The Problem of Farm Recovery. - Under the New 

Deal the President and Congress tried to help the farmer in three ways: first, by creating a Farm Credit Administration; second, by passing the Agricultural Adjustment Act; third, by giving the President power to use some measure of inflation if necessary, as agreed upon in the amendment to the Agricultural Adjustment Act. We have considered inflation above as part of the problem of currency. Let us now consider the other two measures for farm aid. 

The Farm Credit Administration. — Under Roosevelt, 

Congress abolished the Farm Board and set up in its place the "Farm Credit Administration," which made loans against farm mortgages both to farmers and banks.

The Agricultural Adjustment Act. — Making loans to the farmers would help them only if the farmers could later regain prosperity and repay the loans. To help bring back prosperity to the farmers, Congress passed the "Agricultural Adjustment Act." This Act was planned to raise the prices of farm products in these ways: (1) The Department of 

Agriculture suggested that the farmers agree to raise less live stock and to plant less wheat, corn, and cotton. It was hoped thus to avoid overproduction with the low prices that follow it. (2) The Department of Agriculture paid cash to the farmers to repay in part those who agreed to raise less live stock or less wheat, corn, and cotton. (3) To get back this money that it gave the farmers for reducing their farm products, the government taxed the companies that buy these farm products and prepare them for general use the packers that can meat, the millers that grind grain, and the textile-makers that spin cotton.

The President and Congress believed that when the farmers had money to buy more manufactured goods, industry would employ more men and women and pay them more wages, and so in time prosperity would return for all. Meantime, the government was also taking direct steps to help industry to recover.

The "Na- 

IV. The Problem of Industrial Recovery. 

tional Industrial Recovery Act" was planned and passed by Congress to help labor and industry. This N.R.A. plan set aside some of the antitrust laws and allowed competing business men to combine. Codes or sets of rules were set up for each industry, fixing minimum wages to be paid and limiting hours of labor. Child labor was virtually abolished. 

Trade unions were to be recognized. It was hoped that the 

N.R.A. would increase production and employment. 

Public Works. To carry out the plans for public works there was set up the Public Works Administration (the

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

P.W.A.), and Secretary Ickes, its administrator, was given billions of dollars to use. He divided the country into ten regional zones with a regional director for each. He then made grants of Federal money for various public works, such as highway construction, the building of a power dam on the Colorado River, a vehicular tunnel for New York City, low-cost housing, and many other undertakings. 

Under a separate act, Congress provided for another great public work by creating the "Tennessee Valley Authority" to develop the property owned by the government in the Tennessee Valley. In 1916, Congress had voted for the building of nitrate and power plants near Muscle Shoals in the Tennessee Valley. By 1920 the Wilson Dam was completed. Now the T.V.A. has power to develop this and other projects in the Tennessee Valley to aid in the production of nitrates for war and fertilizer, supply power to industry, improve navigation, and help flood control. 

V. The Problem of Unemployment and Federal Relief 

Work. The President hoped that all these measures enacted by Congress would speed up recovery. But he knew that for a time there would still be millions of unemployed. 

He was eager that Congress provide for direct Federal aid to help relieve these unemployed workers. This relief took a number of forms, especially (1) the establishment of a 

Civilian Conservation Corps, (2) home-mortgage relief, and (3) the appointment of a Federal Relief Administrator to provide direct Federal aid to the needy. (1) As one form of immediate unemployment relief, Congress enacted a law providing for the creation of the "Civilian Conservation Corps," numbering over 250,000 men. These men enlisted voluntarily for upkeep and $30 a month to live in camps and do various types of conservation work, especially in reforestation. (2) To help home-owners, who through lack of work or

money were unable to make payments of interest or principal on their mortgages, Congress passed the "Home Owners' Loan Act." This Act provided for government aid in refinancing mortgages, making it possible for the home-owner to pay off his mortgage along with his interest over a period of fifteen years. (3) Various agencies, the C.W.A., E.R.A., and later the 

W.P.A. (Works Progress Administration) were organized and furnished with millions of dollars. They gave employment on projects of benefit to the local communities. 

Social Security Act. In 1935, the Federal Social Secur ity Act was passed by Congress. This Act offered Federal money contributions toward state funds providing security for children, aid to the blind, extension of public health service, vocational rehabilitation, and social welfare in the form of help to dependent mothers and children. 

Under the terms of the Social Security Act, the Federal government also offered to share with the states in setting up a Federal plan for paying a monthly pension to workers past the legal age of retirement. The Act provided, however, that the funds for these pension payments were to be collected like insurance premiums from the workers and their employers, who were each to contribute from one to three per cent of the amount of the worker's monthly pay towards the common pension fund.

A third feature of the Social Security Act was the provision for a tax on employers having eight or more employees (with certain exceptions) for the purpose of raising funds to be used for "unemployment compensation."

By these various plans it was hoped to establish security for workers against unemployment, and against penniless old age.

Criticism of the New Deal. - Critics of the New Deal objected to it on the following grounds:
