2. They insisted that there were entirely too many “alphabetical agencies" of government, such as A.A.A., N.R.A., P.W.A., C.W.A, C.C.C., and other agencies. 

3. Critics of the New Deal objected further that the New 

Deal was leading to the “regimentation" not only of business but of the lives of the people, bringing them all under direct government control, instead of allowing them to help themselves through their own "rugged individualism." 

4. New Deal critics believed that some of the New Deal laws were unconstitutional, because they dealt with purely state matters on which the separate states should pass their own laws. 

The Supreme Court and the New Deal. In 1935-1936, the Supreme Court of the United States declared several of the New Deal laws unconstitutional. Supreme Court decisions ended the activities of the N.R.A. and the A.A.A. 

The control of industry and labor as set up by the N.R.A. was ended, but in so far as farming was concerned, Congress quickly passed an act to take the place of the Agricultural Adjustment Act. This was the Soil Erosion Act which made it possible for the government to continue to exercise some control over farm production and to pay benefits to farmers in the name of a soil conservation program. A serious drought in 1935, followed by dust storms which had blown away vast quantities of soil, had made it clear that some comprehensive national law such as the Soil Erosion Act was needed to conserve the fertility of the land. 

VI. International Problems. In Europe the political situation became more tense. In 1917, Russia set up a 

Communist state, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, under Lenin, later succeeded by Stalin. In 1922, Italy be-

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

came a Fascist state under the dictatorship of Mussolini. 

In 1933, the German Nazis (National Socialists) organized Germany as a Fascist nation with Adolf Hitler as dictator. 

Both the Communists and the Fascists set up governments to exercise complete state control of the economic life of the people under the rule of a dictator. Japan also fell under army influence. 

Under Mussolini's dictatorship, Italy waged war on Ethiopia in 1936. In spite of the League of Nations, which tried to prevent Italian victory through "economic sanctions" or the stopping of trade and credit relations with Italy, Italy won the war and claimed Ethiopia as part of the "Italian Empire." 

Under Hitler's dictatorship, Germany denounced the

Versailles Treaty and rearmed her citizens. Hitler later sent troops into the Rhineland, next to France, and fortified it. 

France remained democratic in government. However, alarmed by the growing military spirit of a rearmed Germany, in 1936 she signed a treaty of alliance with the Soviet government in Russia. 

To heighten the growing danger of a general war, in 1936 a civil war broke out in Spain, which had become a republic only a few years earlier. Although other European countries entered into an agreement not to help either side in Spain, there were charges that the Fascist Italian and German governments were helping the rebels and that communistic Russia was helping the Spanish loyalist or government forces.

The Fascists and Nazis, looking ahead towards war, claimed that they were the defenders of civilization against the spread of Communism. The Russian Communists claimed that the Fascists were seeking to provoke war because they coveted Russian territory and raw materials. 

While peace lovers the world over prayed that somehow

a general world war might be averted, President Roosevelt and Congress began seeking for practical ways to keep the United States out of any war which might break loose. 

The Nye Armament Investigation. In the United 

States, in 1935, a Senate investigation of armaments, led by Senator Nye, led to revelations concerning the huge profits in the armaments trade, as well as to certain unpatriotic and corrupt acts and deals of munitions and armament makers. The investigation aimed to prove that the sale of arms by neutral nations to warring countries tended to drag the selling nation into the war. 

These revelations led Congress to pass a "Neutrality Act," controlling the sale of arms and ammunition, as well as other acts of American citizens which might tend to draw the nation into war. 

The 

Other Moves to Promote Peace and Trade. 

eagerness of the United States for peace and neighborliness was proved by the Roosevelt administration in a series of events. Thus, in November, 1933, the United States Government officially recognized the Soviet Republic and opened diplomatic and trade relations with Russia. 

Realizing that the high tax walls set up by most nations were interfering with trade and endangering peace, Roosevelt encouraged his Secretary of State, Cordell Hull, in his program of reciprocal tariff treaties between Canada, Brazil, and other countries on the one hand and the United States on the other. Canada, for example, agreed with the 

United States to reduce tariffs on specified imports from the United States, if the United States in turn would reduce tariffs on goods which Canada was eager to export. These reciprocity treaties aided both export and import trade. 

Mr. Hull furthermore carried out what Mr. Roosevelt called the "Good Neighbor Policy" by seeking to win the confidence of the Latin-American countries in the good

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

faith of the United States. Since Latin-American diplomats had objected to the idea that the Monroe Doctrine gave the United States the right to interfere in Latin-American affairs, Mr. Hull made a special effort, not only in the reciprocal trade treaties, but in other ways as well, to prove that the United States is acting as a friend and good neighbor in her Pan-American relations. His efforts in this direction were seconded by President Roosevelt in the autumn of 1936 when, after his reëlection to the presidency, he made a trip to a conference of delegates from the Latin- American Republics in Buenos Aires, gathered together to formulate plans for a peace policy which would help the American republics to maintain their neighborly peace under all conditions.

The 1936 Presidential Election. In the 1936 election campaign, with Franklin D. Roosevelt for reëlection on the 

Democratic ticket and Alfred M. Landon on the Republican ticket, the New Deal, sometimes called the Roosevelt 

Recovery Program, became the leading issue.

The huge popular vote for Roosevelt with its eleven million plurality proved that the people favored the continued leadership of Roosevelt. The election strengthened 

Democratic control in Congress. There was also a large increase in the number of Democratic state governors.

By November, 1936, the nation had come a long way out of the depths of the economic depression but there still remained the great problems of relief, unemployment, conservation, a fuller industrial recovery, especially in world trade, and above all, the problem of world peace. 

The Twentieth Amendment. In 1933 there was ratified the Twentieth Constitutional Amendment, which fixed the ending of the terms of office of the President and the Vice President at noon of January 20 and of the Senators and Representatives at noon of January 3. The new law was

first applied in January, 1937. Previously the terms of all these officials ended at noon of March 4, and it happened often that a session of Congress held after an election would find among its members many who had failed to be reëlected. Because such defeated officials are popularly called "lame ducks," the Twentieth Amendment is often called the "lame duck amendment."

The Twenty-first Amendment. In the same year, 1933, the Twenty-first Amendment was ratified by a series of conventions in the states. It was by this amendment that the Eighteenth Amendment was repealed, national prohibition was abolished, the sale of alcoholic liquor became legal in many states, and, as we have seen, the Federal income was increased by Federal taxes on liquor. 

The Supreme Court Issue. — Shortly after Roosevelt's reëlection, he favored a bill for the reorganization of the Federal courts. Among the provisions of this bill was a plan by which the Supreme Court might be enlarged from nine justices to fifteen. For each Supreme Court justice who reached the age of seventy and failed to retire, the 

President might after six months name one additional justice, up to the total of fifteen. 

When the Supreme Court plan was proposed in Congress, it soon became clear that the Democrats were no longer united in support of the President. There were New Deal 

Democrats, anti-New Deal Democrats, and Democrats who wanted to consider each new bill on its own merits and vote as they thought right, rather than along party lines. Some anti-New Deal Democrats joined with the 

Republicans, who claimed that the President's Supreme Court plan was an attempt to tamper with the Constitution by "packing the Court." New Dealers pointed to

Roosevelt's large majority as proof that the people wanted New Deal legislation and that therefore the President had

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

the right to seek a means towards getting Supreme Court decisions favorable to the New Deal. The number of 

Supreme Court justices had been changed from time to time. They saw no harm in changing the number again. 

In the end Congress defeated the Supreme Court plan, but meanwhile the Supreme Court had apparently changed its attitude towards New Deal laws by a decision upholding the constitutionality of the Wagner Labor Relations 

Act. 

Wagner Labor Relations Act: Union Right to Col lective Bargaining. This Act had been passed by Congress during Roosevelt's first administration. The purpose of the Act was, in part, to save one of the provisions of the N.R.A. which gave labor the support of the Federal government to "collective bargaining" with employers, through the labor union's duly elected representatives. "Collective bargaining" means that labor has the right to insist that employers may not hire workers individually for as little pay as they can get the workers to accept, but must hire their workers under the conditions of a contract. 

This contract, in which the workers bargain collectively through their representative, sets the terms on which the worker is selling his services - terms as to pay, hours of work, working conditions, the right to their jobs, and other related matters.

The idea of collective bargaining was not new. Unions had been entering into such contracts for many years. 

What was new was the government's support of the position that in all industries labor had the right to sell its services collectively and that the employer must bargain with the elected representatives of their workers. 

The Wagner Labor Relations Act provided that a Na tional Labor Relations Board would try to settle any conflicts which might arise in the application of the Act.

The Problem. Which Union Has the Collective Bar gaining Right: Company Union, A.F. of L., or C.I.O.?

The chief source of conflict in the enforcement of the 

Wagner Labor Relations Act arose from this question: 

Which union has the collective bargaining right? The employers in many cases had their own company unions, to which their workers belonged. Many skilled workers were organized in the local and national unions of the American Federation of Labor. Other workers, unskilled laborers and "white-collar" workers such as office clerks, were being organized into unions by a Committee on In dustrial Organization (C.I.O.), or the Congress of Industrial 

Organizations, as it eventually came to be known. 

John L. Lewis, the head of the C.I.O., was himself a chairman of the United Mine Workers, an A.F. of L. union, but he believed that the old methods of the A.F. of L. had failed to take care of unskilled workers in such industries as steel, iron, coal, rubber, aluminum, and oil. Under his leadership, the C.I.O. planned to organize the workers in these industries.

William Green, President of the A.F. of L., opposed 

John L. Lewis and the plans of the C.I.O. Under Green's leadership the C.I.O. was read out of the A.F. of L. So there arose a three-cornered fight in the applications of the Wagner Act a fight involving company unions, the A.F. of L., and the C.I.O. for the right to represent labor in its "collective bargaining." 

The A.F. of L. and the C.I.O. both accused the employers of seeking by improper means to force their workers into company unions that would be under the control of the employers and so would have no real bargaining power. The 

C.I.O. claimed that the unions of the A.F. of L. were failing properly to protect all of the workers in the mass industries, since they were especially concerned with skilled

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

workers. The A.F. of L. claimed that the C.I.O. was too radical in its ideas and methods and that it was being controlled by members of the Communist party. 

Soon the National Labor Relations Board was busy with many cases in which it had to decide which of these three unions really had a majority of the workers, because only the unions chosen by the majority could be regarded as the bargaining agent for the workers. 

"Sit-down Strikes" in the Steel, Automobile, and Other

Key Industries. In a number of key industries, such as steel and automobile manufacturing, the C.I.O. conducted strikes to win recognition for C.I.O. unions as the bargaining agents. During these strikes these unions introduced the method of the "sit-down" strike as a means of compelling the employers to come to terms with them. In earlier strikes, strikers usually picketed the company plants to try to prevent strike-breakers from entering and taking their jobs away. In a "sit-down" strike the workers stopped working but they stayed on at their places in the shops to make sure that no others would take their jobs. 

Feeling during these sit-down strikes ran high. There was some violence, even some bloodshed. Many people felt that the sit-down strike was too dangerous and revolutionary a weapon to allow any body of men to use; and the C.I.O. itself in more recent strikes seems less inclined to order its men to "sit-down." 

Nevertheless, "sit-down" or no "sit-down," there is conflict in the camp of labor between the A.F. of L. and the C.I.O., and there is conflict between both sets of unions and the employers. The National Labor Relations Board has its hands full trying to adjust the many problems arising out of collective bargaining and out of the many strikes.

Hours and Wages Act. - While the National Labor

Relations Board was busy endeavoring to bring the labor unions and their employers to terms, Congress, after several years of consideration, passed the Labor Standards Act, otherwise known as the Hours and Wages Act. This Act went into effect on October 24, 1938. The Act provides for a minimum wage of twenty-five cents an hour, and that forty-four hours shall be the maximum number of hours in a working week. 

A New Crop Control Act to Aid the Farmer. The victories of labor, in so far as these victories brought about higher wages and shorter hours, tended towards higher prices for manufactured goods. Because higher wages had increased the purchasing power of the workers, one would think that their victories might raise farm prices; and so, theoretically, labor victories might help the farmers too. 

But actually farm prices were still not rising in proportion to the increased cost of manufactured goods. In fact, farm prices were falling. So both the President and the 

New Dealers felt that they had to continue their efforts in the interest of higher farm prices. 

In February, 1938, Congress passed a new Crop Control Act. This Act was meant to improve upon the Soil Conservation and Farm Allotment Act, which was passed after the Supreme Court had declared the A.A.A. unconstitutional.

Among the provisions of the new Crop Control Act were the following: (1) It continued a program for soil conservation. (2) It provided for a given acreage allotment for each crop, based on an estimate of the total amount of that crop which American farmers could sell at a price that would bring them a fair return. (3) It provided that if the price for a given crop of corn, for example, was too low at the time of harvesting, the farmers might borrow money with their crop as security for the loan. The crop could

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

then be stored until it would bring higher prices. (4) The most novel feature of the Act was the provision for crop insurance, which is explained in the next paragraph. 

Crop Insurance. The Farmer Insures against Drought. 

- One of the dangers of crop control is that when the government asks the farmer to limit his production so that prices will not go too low, a drought may come and lead to a shortage in the crop. A crop shortage due to drought leads in turn to high prices, but that is no help to the farmers who have insufficient crops for sale. To insure the farmer against a poor crop due to local drought, and to insure the nation against a national shortage due to widespread drought, the Crop Control Act of 1938 provided that farmers may buy crop insurance from the government. The method is as follows: The wheat grower pays his insurance premiums to the government in the form of wheat. The amount of wheat he pays depends upon the amount of insurance he is carrying, which in turn depends upon his acreage. The wheat payments go into a national granary. Crop losses in poor years can then be paid out from this granary. In good years this granary grows richer, and it is the reserve store of grain built up in this way that protects the farmer against loss and the nation against food shortage.

The Slump in American Business: Recession or De pression? During the summer of 1937 there was a considerable drop in the stock market, followed by a rapid decline in manufacture, trade, employment, and farm prices.

The Republicans now grew more bitter in their attacks on President Roosevelt and New Deal legislation. When 

New Deal Democrats called the slump a temporary recession, the anti-New Dealers insisted that it was the same old depression. As unemployment increased, the Repub-

licans asserted that the New Deal laws were only halting business recovery. They argued that business was being hurt (1) by the load of taxation, (2) by the steadily mounting national debt, which had gone above thirty billions of dollars, (3) by the mounting cost of labor and strikes due, as they claimed, to the Wagner Labor Relations Act, and (4) by the business man's fear that the New Dealers would pass more laws for Federal control of labor and busi- "Let us alone," was the anti-New Deal plea. "Cut out government regulation of farm, labor, and business and see how soon business will recover and national prosperity will be restored.”

In spite of these criticisms, Congress proceeded to pass added New Deal laws, which were planned to help towards business recovery. The Steagall Housing Act offered government loans to stimulate building, in the belief that a large increase in the building of homes would create jobs for workers in steel, iron, lumber, cement, brick, glass, paint, plumbing fixtures, and electrical equipment, and would also help the workers in the building crafts. 

The government proceeded with its Public Works projects, especially in the field of electric power, constructing dams and power plants throughout the country. Leaders in the public utilities field insisted that they could not afford to spend the billions of dollars on improvement and extension of their own power plants as long as they had the fear of government competition in electric service at lower cost. But in the autumn of 1938, some of these public utilities leaders announced that they would proceed with a large spending program. Apparently they must have felt reassured that the New Deal power plants would not be used to hurt their industries, but only as "yardsticks" of the fair cost of power to the people. 

In regard to governmental spending and the unbalanced

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

budget, President Roosevelt and his advisers announced that they were as eager as anyone for a balanced budget. 

However, the New Dealers insisted that as long as there was an army of unemployed numbering about ten million, with a million and a half needing relief, and as long as the government had to lay out money for "pump-priming" to aid recovery through its housing program and its Public Works projects, it would be difficult to keep the budget down. The government promised it would cut down its spending program just as soon as recovery in business gave employment to the unemployed, making work relief and pump-priming unnecessary. 

One thing that was playing a large part in holding back American business during 1937 and 1938 was the state of world disorder, which tended to create an atmosphere of business uncertainty in regard to world trade and world peace. Such a condition is never a help to business recovery. We shall therefore turn to view the world situation during the two years following Roosevelt's reëlection. 

America and the World Unrest. During Roosevelt's second administration, the foreign news grew increasingly startling; Americans reading their daily papers and listening to radio reports were alarmed by a series of crises in world affairs. Each crisis threatened to become the starting point of a world war, into which the United States might be drawn.

We have seen that, when Italy invaded Ethiopia and European nations declared an economic war against Italy, the United States hastened to protect its peace by means of the Neutrality Act of 1936. 

When a civil war broke out in Spain, and when Italy and Germany went to the aid of the rebels while Russians aided the loyalists, Congress extended the Neutrality Act to apply to civil wars. Congress was eager that the United

States should not become involved if a world war should grow out of the Spanish situation. 

When, in July, 1936, Japan invaded China in an undeclared war, and when in the course of the warfare Japanese airplanes bombed the Panay, a United States ship, President Roosevelt and Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, took a firm stand for the protection of American rights. However, the United States was not unduly warlike in its attitude and accepted Japan's apologies and offer of payment for damage done to life and property. 

In the spring of 1938, Germany annexed Austria. When, in the autumn of the same year, Germany demanded that the Sudeten area of Czechoslovakia, occupied by Germans, be turned over to Germany, and when it appeared that a world war might break out at any moment, with France, England, and Russia on one side and Germany, Italy, and probably Japan on the other, President Roosevelt, appealing in the name of humanity, intervened in letters to the governments involved. He pleaded that the two sides continue discussions and seek a peaceful solution. The discussions were continued and resulted in the Munich Pact for the partition of Czechoslovakia, under terms agreed to by England, France, Italy, and Germany.

However, no matter how carefully the United States tried both to prevent wars and to keep from becoming involved in the actual warfare going on in the world, American farmers, American business men, and American laborers found that their economic life was involved in this world unrest and consequent world disorder. The world disorder stood in the way of a sound revival of world trade, world peace, and world-wide recovery from the depression. 

American Diplomacy, a Five-Point Program. — In the face of a world situation that seemed to be steadily drifting towards war, the United States found itself compelled

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

to seek a policy that would protect both its economic interests and its peace.

To choose such a policy was by no means easy. In fact, America's recent diplomacy has proceeded along five separate lines, which will be discussed under five different captions. 

American Diplomacy. (1) The Program of National 

Isolation. Throughout the United States there were millions of Americans who felt that the only proper course for the nation to follow, while the rest of the world was fighting its undeclared wars and was apparently moving towards a world war, was one of isolation. 

The policy of isolation called for a complete separation of the United States as a nation from any share in European and Asiatic conflicts and disputes. "Keep the United

States an island of peace in the midst of this warring world. Under no circumstances make a move that may tend to drag us into the next world war, if and when it comes. European and Asiatic nations have old scores to settle; let them fight their own battles. Let us keep out of other people's wars," is the slogan of the isolationists. 

It was the desire for isolation that led Congress to pass the neutrality laws in February, 1936, to extend their provisions to the Spanish Civil War in January, 1937, and to reënact these laws in March, 1937.

The extreme isolationists have even offered the Ludlow 

Resolution, which would take away from the President and Congress the power to declare war unless the people through a national referendum approved such a declaration. The Ludlow plan was defeated in Congress, but it is worth mentioning to show how far the isolationists go in their desire to prevent America's entrance into foreign wars.

The critics of the neutrality laws claim that these laws

do not necessarily help to keep the United States out of war. They insist that in case of a world war, events will sooner or later force us to take a side. They further insist that our neutrality laws are not really neutral, since the shutting off of loans to and trade with both sides may hurt one side more than another. They claim that our neutrality laws may even be responsible for some of the war spirit abroad, since nations poor in the raw materials needed for war have an added argument for seeking to gain by conquest territory rich in these raw materials. 

American Diplomacy. (2) Help World Peace by Helping World Trade. We have read how Cordell Hull, Sec retary of State, has been arranging reciprocal trade agreements between the United States and foreign nations. By the summer of 1937, Secretary Hull had arranged fifteen such agreements, and in the fall of 1938 an Anglo-American trade pact was signed.

Many nations are suffering from lack of trade because they have insufficient raw materials for their manufacturing, insufficient foodstuffs to feed their workers, insufficient opportunity to sell exports, and insufficient money from exports to pay for imports of food and raw material. Such nations seek to become "autarchies," or economically selfsufficient countries. They try either to raise the crops they cannot afford to import or they use chemical substitutes for these crops. They are strongly tempted to get raw materials for their industries and markets for their manufactures by conquest of neighboring territories. To keep their money at home and to protect home industries, they create high tariff walls, which tend to choke off imports. 

To Secretary Hull and other champions of foreign-trade agreements, the world trend towards autarchy in which nations try to become economically independent of one

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

another, is one of the chief sources of the world disorder. 

It prolongs the economic depression. It is a prime cause of the drift towards a world war. 

The reciprocal-trade treaties therefore are more than they appear to be on the surface. They are planned not only to promote world trade; they are part of a diplomatic program to promote world peace by promoting world trade. The World Economic Conference, called by Presi dent Roosevelt and held in London shortly after his first election, failed to arrive at any conclusions. But the 'peace through trade" champions believe that sooner or later there must come a world conference on trade, rearranging terms for give-and-take in the trade between nations. 66 The United States has a great stake in an increased flow of world trade. Because of this fact, and because in October, 1938, Japanese victories in China threatened to shut off much of our trade with China, Secretary Hull, in a letter to Japan, restated the right of the United States to an "Open Door" in its trade with China. This claim was emphatically rejected by Japan. 66 

American Diplomacy. (3) Collective Security against Aggressor Nations. - On October 5, 1937, President 

Roosevelt, in a speech at Chicago, denounced the attempt of aggressor nations" to rule the world by force and threats, and indicated that the democracies, as peaceseeking nations, must hold firmly together in the defense of their principles. This speech by Roosevelt seemed to be aimed at the alliance between Germany, Italy, and Japan. The speech expressed the sentiment of all of those 

Americans who believe that the only way to save world peace and the peace of the United States would be a policy of collective security. Let the democracies show, if only through the outspoken utterances of their leaders, that

they will stand together and fight together if need be, and the "aggressor nations" will take heed and change their tone and behavior.

Critics of collective security as a program argued that 

Roosevelt's speech was a dangerous one to make; that unless we really mean to fight alongside other nations on one side of a world war, we should not publicly denounce the other side. These critics saw the danger of the United 

States once again getting itself into the position that it held in 1917, when it entered a war to "make the world safe for democracy." Aided by the United States, the 

Allies won the war; but were the democracies made safe? 

Since the victory in the last world war solved no old problems but only left the world to face new and more difficult problems arising out of war, by all means let the United States beware of a collective security program, which in the end would mean fighting to secure victory for foreign nations and to settle foreign issues.

So spoke the critics of the kind of collective security that would place the United States beside France and Great Britain as defenders of democracy against aggressors.

When England and France, under a threat of force, joined with Italy and Germany in the Munich Pact, the idea of a collective-security program, based on an alliance of old and new world democracies, received a setback. 

American Diplomacy. (4) Collective Security for the 

Americas. The New Monroe Doctrine. — In the light of recent old-world disasters in Europe and in Asia, there are many who feel more than ever before that North and South America have everything to gain by coöperation in a plan for the collective security of the Western Hemisphere. The old Monroe Doctrine, by which the United 

States undertook to keep old-world territorial wars out of

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

the New World, had one weakness. From the point of view of Latin-American countries, the United States was taking too much of the Big Power attitude. Some Latin- 

American countries felt that the attitude of the United States as their protector was a blow to their pride, and when the United States actually interfered in their affairs by a show of force, they began to suspect our strength as a danger to their own sovereign rights as independent nations. For some time the move towards a better understanding among the nations of North and South America had been taking shape in the Pan-American Conferences of the Pan-American Union. President Roosevelt and 

Secretary Hull, as we have seen, made much of the "Good Neighbor" policy towards the Latin-American republics. 

But within the last few years the importance of Pan- American unity has grown clearer. As European and 

Asiatic nations seek new colonies and a position of economic advantage in world markets, it becomes evident that European and Asiatic influence will be felt in the Latin- American countries, and that this influence may prove dangerous to the peace and economic welfare of all the 

American peoples.

For this reason, United States diplomacy is joining with Latin-American diplomacy towards a strengthening of Pan- American ties and towards an understanding that all of the American peoples will collectively endeavor to enforce the Monroe Doctrine as the guarantee of the collective security of the Americas. To the extent that the Monroe 

Doctrine is regarded as the doctrine not of the United States alone, but as a guiding policy for all of the American peoples, it is a new Monroe Doctrine. 

American Diplomacy. (5) Increased Armaments. — In spite of all the various paths to peace sought by United States diplomacy, the President and Congress have taken

the stand that in a world in which nations are using force or threat of force to extend their territorial, military, and economic power, the United States must be well armed. 

Military and naval appropriations for 1937 and 1938 were increased by many millions. In spite of the feeling of the pacifists that large armies and large navies lead to wars, the government claims that large armaments may help to preserve peace; that to be too weak from a military viewpoint is to invite attack, and since attack may come from either European or Asiatic sources or from both simultaneously, the United States arms program must now look to the protection of two ocean fronts by a two-ocean navy. 

The Main Strength of America, the Faith in Freedom. — 

In the face of the old-world trend towards Fascism and Communism, through which people are ruled by dictators who deny them the most elementary forms of freedom as we have learned to cherish freedom, there is need in the United States and throughout the Americas of continuing faith in the value of that freedom.

The knowledge that the American people are united in their faith in freedom is the main strength of the America that is still in the making. Other nations may try to weaken that faith through un-American propaganda. To yield to this propaganda against democracy and freedom would be to weaken the United States from within and to open its doors to the enemy. 

Republican Gains in the 1938 Elections. In the Presidential campaign of 1936, the Republican party captured the electoral vote in only two states, Maine and Vermont. 

In the mid-term election of 1938, the Republican party regained much of the ground that it had lost. New state governors were elected, majorities in state legislatures were secured, the number of Republican seats in the United States Senate was increased by eight, and in the House of

WORLD RESPONSIBILITY AND WORLD POWER 

Representatives by about eighty. On the other hand, the 

Democratic party retained a substantial majority in both the House and the Senate. 

Congress has important business facing it, both at home and abroad, and it is to be hoped that all political parties will join forces in the common search for a path to fuller economic recovery at home and to a world peace based upon good will and fair dealing among the peoples of the earth.

A Modern City School THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION CHAPTER XLVI 

Major American Accomplishments

Considered in Its Relation to the History of World Civilization, American Civilization Has Made at Least Three Major Contributions: the Conquest of a Vast Wilderness; 

the Development of Many Modern Inventions;

the Example of a Peaceful Union 

Based on Good Will

Ideals and Accomplishments. - In reviewing the accomplishments of American civilization, we are not boasting about things done, but rather attempting to see more clearly the meaning of American history in its relation to world his- 675

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

tory. There have been critics of America who have always insisted that everything which America has it owes to other civilizations, and that it has contributed nothing of its own to civilization.

The Swift Conquest of the Wilderness. — As we re-live in our imagination the story of American civilization, it becomes clear that the outstanding accomplishment of the American people was their swift conquest of the American wilderness. Never before in history did a people sweep for thousands of miles across a wild continent and in the brief space of a few centuries transform it into a civilized land. 

In the earliest civilizations of the Old World, farmers and townsmen fighting the wilderness had no such tools as the Americans of the last century possessed; yet even allowing for those tools, the swift conquest of the American wilderness must be regarded as one of man's mightiest accomplishments a distinct gift by American civilization to world civilization. 

American Inventions and World Civilization. — The tools which helped the American people to conquer the wilderness were all important in the life of America. In a larger sense, the cotton gin, the steamboat, the reaper, the sewing machine, the telegraph, the telephone, the airplane, and many other American inventions were gifts of American civilization to world civilization. 

Some of these inventions might not have been possible if it had not been for the work of many European scientists and inventors. Yet there can be no denying that most of these inventions were first made practical in America and were first applied on a large scale to American life. The success of American inventors in helping to build American prosperity is causing other countries all over the world to introduce American tools and American methods of production.

MAJOR AMERICAN ACCOMPLISHMENTS 

677 

American Industrial Lead. International Corpora tions. Another accomplishment of American civilization is the gigantic organization of American industrial life. In 

America more than one hundred million people are fed, clothed, sheltered, carried, kept in touch with one another and with the rest of the world. 

Naturally, after the opening of ocean trade to all nations, and more especially after the steam engine helped in manufacturing, many nations began to make great progress in trade and industry. For a time England held the lead in manufacture, and other countries were more productive than the United States in their agriculture and mining, but to-day, as we have seen, the United States leads the world in all of these fields. 

This is due in a large measure to the wealth of America's natural resources and to the use of the new tools invented by Americans, but much of the credit for American prosperity in the Machine Age is due to the skill of the American people in industrial organization and in machine production.

A little over one hundred years ago the United States like the rest of the world was supplying its needs with hand tools, and most business was conducted on what would seem to us a very small scale. The farmers raised wheat and grain for the near-by village; and so in many other fields of work people labored for a small market which was not far from their doors.

When new tools were invented, conditions in industry changed, and in each of the great divisions in industry the American people showed especial ability to meet the new industrial conditions through the organization of companies which have a nation-wide, even a world-wide, market. 

In feeding the nation there are giant meat companies which buy cattle, sheep, and hogs on a large scale from the

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

ranch owners of the Southwest or from the live-stock farmers of the Corn Belt. They then prepare the meat for market and distribute it to every part of this country and to many foreign lands. There are giant sugar companies which buy cane sugar from Cuba and the Philippines or beet sugar from the American farmers. These companies refine the crude sugar and sell it to a world-wide market. 

The companies which supply the farmers with their farming tools are also mightily organized. So are the flour corporations which buy the farmers' grain, grind it, and then sell the mill flour to a waiting world. 

In clothing the nation, in building its houses, in transporting goods to the people, in sending messages, the nation is served by giant industries. Textile corporations transform wool, silk, or cotton into the cloth from which our clothes are made. Lumber companies cut down forests, transport logs, saw logs in huge mills, and send the cut lumber to the builders to put up our buildings. The companies which provide steel and iron for our buildings, the companies which supply coal or oil for fuel, the railroad companies which carry the nation's goods by land, the steamship companies which carry them by water, are all giant corporations, which through their workers serve a hundred million people at home and many more abroad. 

The American Government. Union with Peace, a 

Major Accomplishment. - Possibly the most important accomplishment of the American people is the American government itself. Although the American form of government may have been borrowed from the Old World, the Constitutional plan for a union of free states under a central national government was an essentially American creation; and the success of the American government, meeting and responding to new conditions as these arose, has been one of the nation's outstanding achievements.

MAJOR AMERICAN ACCOMPLISHMENTS 

679 The American government is in a sense a creation of the whole American people and of their will to live together in peace. At no previous time in history did a free people peacefully unite under a constitution and government of their own creation and then maintain that government for so long a time and over so large an area. Except for the crisis of the Civil War, whenever new conditions have made necessary changes in the government, it has been possible, under the Constitution, for the people to secure these changes in a peaceful, lawful, and orderly way. 

To-day the President and his Cabinet, Congress, the Supreme Court, the various state departments, and an almost endless number of bureaus are employed in serving the American people in a thousand and one ways besides those which occupied the thoughts of the government officers of Washington's day. Besides engaging in the actual business of lawmaking, law-enforcing, the raising of revenues, and provision for the national defense, the government undertakes to serve the people directly through such means as the Post Office Department, the Weather Bureau, the Bureau of Fisheries, Agricultural Experimental Stations, to mention only a few forms of government service.

To raise money for these departments, the government used various methods, all of which were agreed upon by the chosen representatives of the people sitting in session in Congress. The government receives a large part of the money which it requires through a tariff on imports, an inheritance tax, and the income tax. 

So the American people willingly help to pay the expenses of the government which expresses their desire for a union for the common welfare maintained in peace and good will.

CHAPTER XLVII America's Place In Science 

Americans, although Occupied for the Greater Part of Their History with the Crude Tasks of Conquering the Wilderness and Winning Their Way to Industrial Leadership, Have Made Important Contributions to Pure Science and Many to Applied Science In the course of the story of America we have now and then read about American scientists or American workers in the fine arts. In the main, however, Americans have had to face the practical tasks of conquering the soil, building homes and barns, shops and factories, cities and industries. In the early period those who went to college usually prepared themselves for the ministry; others made a profession of soldiering. Yet, the time did come when many Americans found time for the study of science and the arts. The story of America would not be complete without a record of American progress in each of these fields. 

Science a World Contribution. Scientists a World 

Brotherhood. To appreciate the part played by Ameri- 

680

cans in the field of science, let us first review the scientific accomplishments of the Old World civilizations. The 

Egyptians, the Babylonians, the Greeks, and the Romans knew much of mathematics and of astronomy. Except in these two fields, the scientific study of nature and her laws did not begin much before the time of the crusades. Such knowledge as the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans did have of science, added to by the Mohammedan Arabs, was carried into Europe partly by the crusaders, and partly by the Moors who also were Mohammedan. Many of our chemical words, our numerals, and some of the laws of algebra, have come down to us through Arabian scholars. 

During the Renaissance, which followed the crusades, scholars in the European universities gave more time to scientific ways of study; they observed some one field of nature closely and they tried to guess why certain things happened in certain ways. They made experiments and studied further to learn whether their guesses were true. Sometimes, often in fact, one scientist's guesses were wrong, but other scientists, profiting by his observations and their own, came closer to the truth. In a few short centuries during the years which saw the building of 

America, European scientists, working in many fields, increased man's knowledge of the laws of nature, and the number of sciences increased.

Finally the day came when American colleges and universities had well-trained scientists of their own. 

In science as in invention, which has been largely helped by science, great as any one man's work may be, he generally builds on the work of many others in the same field. 

For the last century or more, the scientists of the world have been a brotherhood, working together with the one common object, the increase of human knowledge and understanding. Within each country only a few scientists

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

have attained national or world fame. In honoring those few, we must not forget the many other faithful scientific workers who helped them on their way. 

Franklin's Fame as a Scientist. The first American who achieved world fame as a scientist was Benjamin Franklin, who learned much from the scientists of Europe; but he fully repaid the debt by his own contributions to science, especially by his discovery that lightning and electricity are one. 

Joseph Henry. - Almost every American has heard of

Benjamin Franklin and his kite-flying experiment. Not so many have heard of Joseph Henry, who was the first secretary of the Smithsonian Institution established at Washington, D.C., for scientific study and research. 

Henry invented a method for producing more powerful electromagnets than had ever been known before. It was his proof that a magnet could be acted upon by an electric current which gave Samuel F. B. Morse the idea for the electric telegraph.

So frequently the scientist, interested first and foremost in understanding the forces of nature, learns things which others use to help mankind in practical ways. Joseph

Henry, studying electricity in his laboratory, was unknowingly helping to bind the American people into one. 

John James Audubon Studies American Birds. - A 

scientific study which may seem to have little practical use is the study of birds. Yet to-day, the scientists in this field have learned that certain birds help the nation. Birds feeding on those weeds, bugs, or worms which infest farmers' crops save millions of dollars' worth of food. 

The first and greatest student of bird life in America was John James Audubon. After many years of hardship spent in studying and drawing birds in every part of the country, he published, in four large volumes, Birds of America. The

books contain hundreds of colored plates with over a thousand life-size studies of birds native to every section of the country. Birds of America remains to this day the most ambitious study of its kind ever made. Audubon also made a series of studies of American animals, called Quad rupeds of America. 

Louis Agassiz Inspires American Students. Asa Gray. 

- Shortly after Audubon completed his Birds of America there came to this country Louis Agassiz, a noted Swiss scientist. Agassiz accepted a professorship in an American university and did much to inspire and train a large group of young Americans for scientific research. 

Agassiz himself traveled all over this country and contributed to science a study of American fish and American rock forms. His studies of the geology of this country tended to prove that in North America, as in Europe and in Asia, there had once been a cold glacial age. 

What Audubon did for the study of American birds, what Agassiz did for the study of American rocks and fish, Asa Gray did for the study of American plant life. Gray was not a pupil of Agassiz or Audubon, but his work like theirs reveals a deep devotion to science. 

American Astronomers. Scientists in Other Fields. 

The study of the stars may have begun among the first nomad shepherd tribes, guiding their flocks at night. 

During the rise of the early civilization scholars studied the heavenly bodies. Then during the Renaissance in 

Europe, lenses were invented, and astronomers, using these lenses in their telescopes, were able to observe the heavens more closely. From this time on, the science of astronomy made rapid strides.

In the nineteenth century a number of American astronomers, including John William Draper, Henry Draper, and Louis Morris Rutherford, used the new art of photog-

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

raphy in their study of the sun, moon, and stars. They developed ways of using the lenses and reflectors in their telescopes in such a way as to record pictures of the moon and stars upon sensitive camera plates. 

One of the youngest of the sciences is psychology, or the study of the human mind. In America William James and 

John Dewey became leaders in this field and they influenced many others to devote their lives to the study of psychology as well as to the study of pedagogy, or the science of training the mind through education. 

In history, which aims to be the scientific study of the story of peoples and their civilization, America has produced a group of brilliant students. Among those who have made a special study of American history, Bancroft, Parkman, Fiske, Wilson, and Channing are the most famous. 

Of late years, scientists the world over have been studying the habits of uncivilized tribes in various parts of the world who still live somewhat like the early hunters or herdsmen. American scientists working in this field have made a special study of the American Indians to record as much as they can of the ancient ways of the red man. 

In other sciences, such as physics, chemistry, biology, and bacteriology, American scholars to-day hold an important place, and the work of the men and women in these fields has been much more valuable than most people realize; for they have helped to shape the destinies of 

America to-day. These sciences have had their practical application in the everyday life of the people and in the development of America's industrial life. 

Professions Based on Science. Medical Practice. - 

Among the professions which are based upon the studies of one or more sciences are the various branches of the medical and dental professions as well as the profession of engineering. In colonial times, these professions had not been

developed to any great degree either in Europe or America. 

In the case of medicine, little was known about the human body, people believed certain diseases to be caused by witchcraft, and they used charms to ward off sickness. 

The fact that the heart propels the blood and keeps it circulating through a system of arteries and veins was first discovered by Harvey, an English scientist, in 1628. The fact that germs which are invisible bacteria can carry disease was first learned by Pasteur, a French scientist, during the years 1854-1857.

In the time of President Washington so little was known about medicine that blood letting was the principal remedy for many forms of illness. All through colonial times the doctor, here as elsewhere, was frequently the village barber as well. But during the last hundred years or so doctors in America have profited by the work of scientists who have studied anatomy, physiology, hygiene, chemistry, biology, and psychology. Medical colleges and universities give courses in these subjects, and the modern doctor applies these sciences in his practice.

The outstanding gift of American medical practice to civilization is the discovery of the use of ether as an anæsthetic. Among those who shared in the discovery of this anaesthetic and who helped to demonstrate its great value in the field of surgery were Dr. Crawford W. Long, Dr. Horace 

Wells, Dr. William Morton, and Dr. Charles Jackson.

The American medical profession has done valuable work in preventive medicine, or the application of medical science to the prevention of disease. The building of the Panama Canal might have proved impossible had doctors not learned how to control malaria. Dr. Walter 

Reed, an American army officer, while working in Cuba proved that the cause of yellow fever is a germ carried and spread by a species of the mosquito. Using this

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

knowledge he fought these mosquitoes and freed Cuba from yellow fever. Later Dr. Gorgas, the sanitary engineer in the 

Building a Skyscraper

There is romance and adventure in the building of the modern skyscraper with its mighty towers rising almost over night. At every level in these structures, as well as in the building of the new bridges, tunnels, trestles, and other engineering works, the triumphs of modern science and invention serve the builders. Hour after hour structural workers face dangers to life and limb with a calm faith in themselves and in their mastery of the tools they use.

Canal Zone, waged a similar fight against the malariacarrying mosquito; malaria was checked and the canal was built.

Within the states and cities boards of health served by doctors are fighting for better health conditions, and in many places they have reduced the death rate considerably. Through their influence children in school are being taught the care of their bodies and the laws of good health.

In the work of preventive medicine the American dental profession has also helped. 

The first dental college in the world was established at Baltimore less than a century ago, and since then American dentistry has led the world.

Such organizations as the 

American Red Cross carry on a continuous health program and send their trained workers to scenes of flood and disaster to care for the injured and to fight against pestilence which usually follows in the wake of such calamities.

Civil Engineering. The profession of civil engineering has to do with the planning of large public works, especially dams, canals, bridges, roads, and water supply systems. 

Even in the early civilizations man built public works of great magnitude. In ancient Egypt engineers planned and constructed the pyramids. The Romans were able engineers, skillful builders of roads and bridges, and of aqueducts which brought water from the mountains to the cities as well as of sewage systems for the disposal of city waste.

The American civil engineer has more than vied with the great engineers of the past. He has built huge and handsome bridges across broad rivers, he has tunneled mountains for the passing of railroads, he has built tunnels under the rivers, he has planned the modern waterworks which carry waters from distant mountains into the cities, subways which help in transportation, enormous dams and irrigation projects, by means of which the Western desert lands are being turned into good farm land.

Serving the Modern City 

Beneath the streets of the modern city there is a vast network of pipe lines which serve the city, aiding the city workers in almost countless ways. 

This underground service has been made possible by modern science and engineering.

Electrical Engineering. -In the field of electrical engineering, which has been developed only within the last fifty years, American engineers took a leading place from the start. Their work helped to make possible the development of our telephone, telegraph, cable, and wireless systems. They planned the giant power houses which convert the force of rushing water, the heat in coal or oil, into electric power for the heating and lighting of American cities and for the operation of the giant machinery in American industrial plants. 

Mechanical Engineering. — Mechanical engineers de signed the machinery which helps in the nation's work. In 

America, the mechanical engineers have carried beyond any other country the idea of making tools and machines in replaceable or standard parts. In an automobile, for example, if any part wears out, the owner can buy a new part which will fit his machine as well as the original one did. This idea was first applied in the manufacture of 

American guns and watches. It has since been applied to the manufacture of many other American products. Today European mechanical engineers also use this idea of standard parts; but America's start along this line has helped to win for her the position of leadership among the manufacturing nations.

Working in his laboratory 

Chemical Engineering. over his small flame and test tubes, the chemical engineer has added much to the wealth and strength of the nation.

Only six or seven hundred years ago, many of the men who were studying the chemical action of metals and other substances were interested either in obtaining gold from more common metals or in mixing a drug which would

prove to be an "elixir of life," a beverage imparting eternal youth to those who drank it.

During the Renaissance, chemists broadened their studies, and ever since they have made great strides in learning the nature and action of solids, acids, and gases. Their knowledge has been used in many ways helpful to mankind. 

The modern chemist has helped to make steel cheap. 

The chemical engineer discovered the way to obtain crude oil, gasoline, and kerosene from petroleum, as well as many valuable by-products commonly known to every person. He has shown the world how to obtain many useful by-products from coal and other raw materials. 

The chemist has taught people how to preserve food, through pasteurization, through canning, and through refrigeration. 

The chemist has added to the knowledge of drugs which can check or cure disease.

The chemical engineer has learned many things about the nature of the soil and plant growth-things which are a great help to the farmer of to-day. In fact there is hardly an industry which does not depend on the expert chemical engineer for more economical and improved ways of manufacturing products.

Modern chemistry is almost a new science, and for that reason, in chemical engineering as in mechanical engineering, Americans were able to play an important part almost from the start. 

Museums of Science. Making Science Popular. 

To aid in the teaching of science some cities have scientific museums housing collections of plant life, animal life, rock formations, and other material interesting to students of science. Many cities have botanical gardens or zoölogical gardens, which are in a sense scientific museums. A few magazines especially devoted to the popular side of

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

science have a large circulation among American boys and girls and help to stimulate scientific interest, especially on the side of invention. 

Research: Universities, Industrial Laboratories, Scien tific Foundations. A large portion of the scientific research in this country is being conducted in universities which either through public support or private endowment have been enabled to equip themselves with the apparatus for scientific study. Much valuable research has been done by industrial corporations which have set aside sums for laboratory equipment and for the uninterrupted labor of able scientific workers. Besides these two agencies for scientific research there are a number of foundations established by private bequests. The most famous of these are the Rockefeller, the Carnegie, and the Sage foundations, each endowed to extend the boundaries of human knowledge. 

Popular Scientific Education.- At no previous time in history and probably in no other land to-day has the study of science become such an important part of the school work of boys and girls. 31 113

CHAPTER XLVIII The Arts In America With Prosperity and Leisure, America Has Produced Native 

Painters, Sculptors, Architects, Musicians, Writers, and Workers in Other Arts Who Have Ex pressed Something of the American 

Spirit in Their Work 

American Painting. In the field of painting, America could hardly boast a native painter of note before about the middle of the eighteenth century. Beginning about that time there grew up in the colonies a group of portrait painters, many of whom continued to paint into the years of the early republic. Most famous among these painters were John Singleton Copley, Gilbert Stuart, Charles Wilson 

Peale, John Trumbull, Thomas Sully, and Benjamin West.

It was Stuart who painted the most cherished portrait of Washington. Benjamin West, who studied in London and who set up a studio there, became famous as a painter of historical pictures. It was he who painted the "Death of 691

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

Wolfe on the Heights of Abraham," clothing his figures in the style of the period, instead of in Greek or Roman costume, which was the usual practice in historical painting of the time.

The next group of American painters to achieve reputation became known as the Hudson River School. The members of this group devoted themselves to painting mountain views in northern New York. This interest in 

American landscape painting led Bierstadt to paint panoramic views of the Rocky Mountains, and Thomas Moran to paint the marvels of the Yellowstone and Yosemite valleys.

An American painter who painted nature not for her grandeur but for her intimate charm and beauty was 

George Inness. 

As the years passed, the number of American painters increased, and art schools were established in America, but in almost all cases artists also went abroad to complete their studies.

Toward the end of the nineteenth century American painting began to take on a character of its own; and a few American painters won world-wide fame and recognition. Among these were John La Farge, a mural painter, who also designed beautiful stained glass windows for churches; Winslow Homer, a painter of the sea; John

Singer Sargent, noted principally as a portrait painter; 

James Abbott McNeill Whistler, painter of portraits and of landscapes and a master in the art of etching.

An outstanding figure in recent American art was George Bellows, who painted with great vigor scenes from life in the modern American city. Especially interesting are his lithographs, drawings made on stone and printed from the stone.

Bellows was also a very able illustrator, excelling in a

field in which America can point to many capable workers. 

Perhaps the most famous of America's illustrators was Howard Pyle, who did especially interesting work in his illustrations of American history. 

Art Museums and Associations. - One development in the progress of the arts in America was the formation of clubs and associations for the advancement of the fine arts. 

Another development was the establishment of art museums in many of the larger cities. These museums were in some cases the gift of one or more citizens. Some museums received additional support from the cities, and now work with the public schools to help train boys and girls in art appreciation. In order to bring greater beauty into the designing of the things which people use in their daily lives, art museums coöperate with American manufacturers in such crafts as the making of textiles, pottery, jewelry, and furniture.

The American Federation of Fine Arts is the leading national association for the promotion of art in America. 

It is interested in painting, architecture, sculpture, and in the application of art to industry. 

American Sculpture. Shortly after the founding of the nation, American sculptors began to attract attention by their work. Most of these sculptors studied abroad, especially in Italy, where they could see the classic work of the old Roman sculptors.

One of these sculptors, Horatio Greenough, carved in Italy the heroic seated statue of George Washington which has been set up in front of the Capitol building. 

Hiram Powers, another of the sculptors trained in Italy, was noted for his portrait busts of famous Americans of his period. The figure of Freedom, on the dome of the Capitol building at Washington, was modeled by Thomas Crawford who also studied in Italy.

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

Later American sculptors have abandoned the Italian classical style and have worked in a freer and more natural manner.

Augustus Saint-Gaudens studied sculpture both in Paris and Italy; he returned to this country at the age of twentysix and devoted the rest of his life to art. Among his great works are the statue of Admiral Farragut, which stands in Madison Square, New York; and his "Lincoln" in Lincoln Park, Chicago.

Daniel Chester French, who was practically self-taught, first achieved fame with his "Minute-Man," unveiled 

April 17, 1875.

Frederick MacMonnies, who studied under Saint- Gaudens, carved the well-known statue of "Nathan Hale." 

At the present moment there are in America many other sculptors, both men and women, who are finding inspiration for their work in American themes. 

American Architecture. The story of American architecture is closely related to the rest of American history. 

We have seen how, when the colonies were first planted, the early settlers built their homes with roughhewn logs; and how, as soon as they were better settled, the more prosperous colonists built frame and even brick houses. 

During the colonial period, the style of many of these houses was influenced by the style of home building in Europe.

About the time of the American Revolution, Europe began to take fresh interest in Greek and Roman art, and European architects imitated the classical models of ancient times. The imitation of classical models in European architecture led to the use of columns in the building of some of the more stately private homes in the New Republic, and especially in the designing of public buildings. The vogue for colonnaded private homes has long since passed,

but to this day many of our public buildings are designed after the model of Greek temples.

Other signs of the influence of ancient architecture are to be found in the stadiums, which have been built in the Greek style on the grounds of some American universities. 

In a few of the larger cities there are cathedrals built in the style of the Middle Ages, and churches built in a modified Roman style. 

Yet not all American architecture is borrowed. On the contrary America has made an interesting contribution to the art of building in the design and construction of its skyscrapers.

When new processes made cheap steel possible, American builders learned to use the material with increasing skill until they evolved the steel skyscraper. Zoning laws recently passed in the larger cities have forced architects to plan these skyscrapers with the upper stories set back from the front elevation. The result has been the development of a new and interesting variation of the skyscraper. 

The high-terraced or pyramidal structures which are being built in many of the larger cities are among the most distinctively American contributions to architectural form. 

Using steel and concrete and other new building material, Americans have done beautiful work in the designing of mighty bridges.

American Music. — During the centuries of American growth, Europe was the home of many great musicians who enriched the world with their compositions for the voice and for the various musical instruments. 

In colonial days, none of the leading musicians of Europe came to America. As they depended for their livelihood on the support of their wealthy patrons at home, they naturally saw little reason for crossing the ocean to the struggling colonies.

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

The colonists, however, brought with them memories of the songs they had known and sung. Some of the early colonists brought with them violins, flutes, and other instruments which they may have played in their new homes when time allowed. In later colonial days, music teachers arrived, and the daughters of the rich learned to play the harpsichord or the spinet, two instruments resembling the more modern piano.

In colonial days, too, many of the churches encouraged music through the singing of psalms and hymns by the congregation or by small choirs of selected voices. To this day churches have continued to play a part in keeping alive in the people the spirit of song.

After the founding of the republic, with growing peace and prosperity, the interest in European music increased; foreign musicians visited America. Opera companies and orchestral societies, organized in America, played European compositions. Then, before very long, American musicians were offering their own compositions to the American music-loving public, which has grown steadily with the years.

Of the many American composers, John Philip Sousa and Victor Herbert achieved national fame. At least one, Edward MacDowell, has achieved world fame.

Sousa, who was the conductor of a military band, wrote a number of stirring marches. Victor Herbert, who had a gift for melody, wrote light operas. One of these, “Natoma," was based on an Indian theme. Edward MacDowell wrote more serious compositions for voice and instruments. 

His "Indian Suite" was based largely on the music of the 

American Indians. 

Strangely enough, the American music which is best known abroad is the popular jazz which many music critics say is not music at all. The composers of jazz melodies use

the syncopated rhythm of negro music. The negroes have also given to America music of a more serious nature in their "spirituals" or religious songs.

An American composer who has come very close to the hearts of the people is Stephen C. Foster, the composer of "Swanee River" and "Ole Black Joe." 

To-day America has excellent musical conservatories in which teachers are training the musicians of to-morrow.

In the large cities the people patronize orchestral and operatic music, and with the radio to help, this music is being brought into the homes of millions.

The most famous literary character of the colonial period was Benjamin Franklin, who for years published a calendar, Poor Richard's Almanac, for which he wrote many practical maxims.

Irving is best known as a writer of fine prose stories and essays, in which he treats American themes with a light, fanciful humor. His "Legend of 

Sleepy Hollow" and "Rip Van Winkle" have long been studied as school classics. Unlike Poe, Irving's talent was recognized during his life, which was, on the whole, easy and care free. 

Franklin also wrote an autobiography, a simple record of his career.

American Drama. In this field practically no work was produced in America during the colonial period. After the colonial period, an occasional company of English players performed in some of the larger cities of the East. Then, gradually, theatrical companies were formed and a few American actors, such as Edwin 

Booth and Joseph Jefferson, and American actresses like

Charlotte Cushman, helped to create a larger interest in the American stage. About a generation after the Civil 

War, Americans began to devote themselves to writing plays about American themes. Bronson Howard's Shenandoah, a drama of the Old South, and William Vaughan 

Moody's The Great Divide, a drama of the West, belong to this period.

At the present moment, the Americans are a theater-

loving people. If they actively support good plays, they may help to further a truly great American school of drama. 

Vaudeville and Motion Pictures.- Alongside of the more serious forms of art, such as painting, sculpture, architecture, music, and literature, there has grown up American vaudeville, with its program of music, acrobatic acts, monologues, and one-act sketches. 

Almost entirely taking the place of vaudeville as a form of popular entertainment today are the motion-pictures. 

In the United States there are tens of thousands of moving-picture theaters with a daily attendance of millions of people. Naturally, the average motion-picture play, like the average novel, stage play, or musical comedy, is hardly a work of art, but occasionally the screen presents a picture in which a good story is directed and acted with fine imagination. 

The Art of Journalism. Newspapers and Magazines. 

Although journalism is not, strictly speaking, one of the fine arts, no story of America would be complete without some reference to the remarkable development of American newspapers and magazines and to their hold upon the imagination of the American people. 

The entire story of American journalism would take too long to tell. In place of the few periodicals of colonial times, there are now hundreds of daily newspapers and scores of weekly magazines. Almost every adult who can read, reads a newspaper daily, scanning local, national, and international news gathered by reporters and by means of the telephone, the telegraph, the cable, and the wireless. 

The papers contain cartoons, pen-and-ink illustrations, comics, and photographs, some of which are now electrically transmitted across oceans and continents. The 

Sunday issues of many newspapers seem like a whole library and picture gallery neatly wrapped up in a small parcel.

THE MEANING OF AMERICAN CIVILIZATION 

So it is with the magazines. Although a few date back to the period before the Civil War, most of the magazines have appeared within the last fifty years and new ones crop up almost from month to month. Many of these magazines, like many of the newspapers, make their appeal to the millions. Others are published for a smaller audience interested in one field of activity or some particular point of view. 

Considered together, the newspapers and the magazines published in America to-day may be reckoned among the most important forces in forming the taste of the people and in expressing their ideals. 

The Newspapers and National Sports. One function of American newspapers is the detailed reporting of events in the field of national sports. In the course of this story very little has been said about the subject of games since colonial times. The reason is simple. Games have hardly changed in character until recent years, when the Americans as a people have interested themselves in such sports as tennis, golf, football, basketball, and baseball, the latter regarded by many as the great American game. 

Joaquin Miller 

Miller's poem "Columbus" is a school classic.

Newspapers and Advertising. The cheap price at which newspapers and magazines are sold to the public is, in many cases, made possible by the advertisements which they display. Although the art of advertising like the art of journalism is not a fine art, the American advertiser of

to-day frequently combines in his work honest writing, excellent illustration, well-chosen type or lettering, and tasteful arrangement. There has been in the past considerable dishonest advertising, but for years the manufacturers and the advertising agencies have stood together in a campaign against this evil. American advertisers to-day give employment to thousands of illustrators, painters, designers, letterers, writers, and printers. Advertising is a powerful agent in American industrial life, helping to maintain the American's standard of living and even to increase the American's desire for luxuries. Marco Polo and the crusaders, who came back from the East with stories of Eastern luxury, were in a sense advertisers of Eastern wares. Modern American advertising is helping to sell American wares in the Eastern as well as in the 

Western world.

America a Trial Ground for Democratic Ideals. 

the beginning America has been a trial ground for the ideals of democracy. It was here in America that a nation carried farther than ever before in the history of civilized peoples
